Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.

papers.title: What Malware Actually Does: An Empirical Analysis of Post-Infection Behavior Across Malware Families
papers.abstract: Most malware detection research focuses on identifying whether a file is malicious before it executes. Far less attention goes to what happens after infection. This paper presents an empirical analysis of post-infection malware behavior across 37 families, grounded in dynamic sandbox execution using CAPEv2. Behavioral traces are modeled as heterogeneous graphs with five node types and seven typed edge relationships, preserving relational structure that flat feature vectors discard. A voting ensemble trained on graph-derived structural features achieves 94.44% accuracy and MCC of 0.863, outperforming a flat behavioral baseline by 7.4 percentage points in MCC. A multiclass classifier distinguishes 24 malware families, and a per-family behavioral fingerprint analysis characterizes post-infection activity across registry, network, process, and API dimensions. An LLM explanation layer generates analyst-readable reports with MITRE ATT&CK mappings grounded in observed behavioral evidence. The full pipeline is deployed as HeteroScan at https://ama-andam.github.io/heteroscan.

papers.title: 3D dark matter map of the JWST COSMOS-Web field using diffusion-based generative priors
papers.abstract: Mapping the three-dimensional distribution of dark matter is key to tracing the growth of cosmic structure. Two-dimensional weak lensing mass maps recover its projected distribution, but they blend structures at different distances along the line of sight. We reconstruct the three-dimensional matter distribution in the 0.54 deg$^2$ COSMOS-Web field using deep James Webb Space Telescope imaging, with an effective source density of 121 galaxies arcmin$^{-2}$ We combine a physical weak lensing forward model with a diffusion-based Bayesian generative prior learned from cosmological simulations, yielding a posterior distribution of the matter field across 20 lens planes to $z \simeq 2$, doubling the redshift reach of previous Hubble Space Telescope-based 3D reconstructions and approaching cosmic noon, an epoch of rapid galaxy growth. The reconstruction separates structures that overlap in projection and recovers non-Gaussian matter structure across a range of spatial scales, including over-densities associated with independently identified galaxy clusters that were not detected in earlier weak lensing maps. Posterior sampling quantifies the range of three-dimensional matter distributions allowed by the data, enabling a probabilistic visualization of the cosmic web while propagating uncertainties in its inferred structure. Null and simulation-based tests show that the recovered structures are supported by the lensing signal and are consistent with expectations from the fiducial $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. These results extend three-dimensional weak lensing mapping into the high-redshift, non-Gaussian regime and establish a route towards probabilistic mapping of the evolving cosmic web with current wide-field lensing surveys.
papers.summary: Two-dimensional weak lensing mass maps mix together structures at different distances along the line of sight, so they cannot show how dark matter is arranged in depth. The authors rebuild the three-dimensional matter distribution in the 0.54 square-degree `COSMOS-Web` field from deep James Webb Space Telescope imaging. They combine a physical weak lensing forward model with a diffusion-based generative prior trained on cosmological simulations, which gives a posterior over 20 lens planes out to redshift about 2. That is **double the redshift reach of earlier Hubble-based 3D reconstructions**, and the maps separate overlapping structures and recover galaxy clusters that earlier lensing maps missed, with null and simulation tests supporting the results.

papers.title: BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA
papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. At the same time, strong prediction of average effects can conceal weaker prediction of context-specific effects, and accurate prediction of combined mutation effects does not imply accurate prediction of their interactions. In design tasks, model predictions can reduce the number of candidates needed to find a desired response, but still leave substantial room for better design choices, particularly for context-specific and multi-cell objectives. Our benchmark reveals that genomic models now display signs of general utility but have yet to saturate on performance in even simple tasks.
papers.summary: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits, but existing benchmarks do not test the capabilities that design actually needs. `BEND 2.0` (BENchmark for DNA language models) covers eight tasks built on five experimental datasets and tests both how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether those predictions can guide sequence design. **Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or beat models' native outputs** and transfer well across assays and genes, and functional post-training substantially improves results. However, strong prediction of average effects can hide weak prediction of context-specific effects and mutation interactions, and design tasks still leave a lot of room for improvement.

papers.title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data
papers.abstract: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.
papers.summary: `AIRoA-0` is a bimanual manipulation system trained on 16,151 hours of demonstrations recorded with `YUBI`, an open-source handheld gripper, without collecting any robot data, teleoperation, or reinforcement learning. Using only a camera on each wrist, it learns which parts of each view matter, predicts which stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. It carries out long-horizon tasks such as sorting small parts and swapping a robot vacuum's mop pads, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across ten tasks it averages **78% success, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models** post-trained on the same demonstrations. It runs on several robot types that mount the gripper, and the dataset, weights, and post-training recipe are being released.

papers.title: PianoBench: Evaluating Musical Perception and Reasoning in Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: https://gclef-cmu.org/pianobench.
papers.summary: `PianoBench` tests which musical features language models can perceive and reason about, using matched audio and symbolic versions of piano performances. It is built from a new dataset of more than 20,000 hours of music transcripts interleaved with spoken commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models reach at most 52.8% accuracy, barely above a no-audio control, while **frontier models using chain of thought reach up to 93.2% when given the music as text transcripts**, which points to a gap between hearing musical features and reasoning about them once they are written out. Mid-training on the interleaved instructional data raised `Qwen 3.5 9B Base`'s zero-shot accuracy from 42.8% to 56.0%.

papers.title: Probabilistic Steering of Generative Priors for Lab-in-the-Loop Antibody Optimization
papers.abstract: Therapeutic antibody development is often framed as comprising two discrete stages: initial discovery of novel binders followed by iterative optimization to refine these hits into therapeutic-grade molecules. Models and methods often reflect these stages, with generative structure models applied to discovery and probabilistic black-box optimization methods applied to refinement. Here we propose to unify these stages by smoothly transitioning a generative discovery model into iterative optimization, allowing the handoff between the structure-based prior and supervision from wet lab data to be guided by the posterior uncertainty of a probabilistic surrogate. We show that this yields improvements in optimization efficiency in the low-N regime, as well as improved diversity amongst the optimized molecules.
papers.summary: Therapeutic antibody development usually treats discovering binders and optimizing them as separate stages, with generative structure models used for the first and probabilistic black-box optimization for the second. The authors merge the two by gradually turning a generative discovery model into an iterative optimizer. The balance between the structure-based prior and wet-lab feedback is set by the posterior uncertainty of a probabilistic surrogate model. The approach **improves optimization efficiency when only a few lab measurements are available** and yields more diverse optimized molecules.

papers.title: LaplaceDiag: Fault Diagnosis through Changes in Learned Actuator Effects
papers.abstract: Identifying faulty components from sensor anomalies is difficult because fault effects can propagate through a plant and different faults can produce similar observations. Detailed component models and labeled fault examples may also be unavailable. We introduce LaplaceDiag, a data-driven method that uses changes in actuator effects to narrow the search for faulty equipment. Actuators act on specific devices and mechanisms, so their changed effects can provide clues to root causes. LaplaceDiag learns a healthy plant model with LaplaceNet, a neural network that operates in Laplace space. It separates nonlinear prediction based on measured history from an explicit matrix that describes how actuator values affect sensor values. Keeping the history predictor fixed allows current actuator effects to be estimated by linear regression without retraining the neural network. Comparison with a healthy reference accounts for estimation uncertainty and normal variation to detect changes and generate actuator-related diagnostic hypotheses. The method supports online and offline diagnosis, providing an intermediate step between anomaly detection and identifying faulty components. We successfully evaluate LaplaceDiag on two datasets.
papers.summary: Finding which component has failed from sensor anomalies is hard because fault effects spread through a plant and different faults can look alike, often with no detailed component models or labeled fault examples to work from. `LaplaceDiag` learns a model of the healthy plant with `LaplaceNet`, a neural network that operates in Laplace space and keeps a nonlinear predictor based on past measurements separate from an explicit matrix of how actuators affect sensors. Because the history predictor stays fixed, **current actuator effects can be re-estimated by linear regression without retraining**. Comparing these effects with a healthy reference produces actuator-related hypotheses about the root cause, and the method was evaluated successfully on two datasets.

papers.title: Predictive gains, causal losses: why interventional competence cannot be learned from data alone
papers.abstract: Retaining predictive gains can require persistent errors in a model's response to interventions. For deterministic predictors with finite second moments under squared-error loss, any observational advantage over the best predictor using only an outcome's direct causes requires dependence on other inputs, regardless of the learning rule. When admissible interventions vary inputs while preserving the worldly outcome, this dependence yields a positive lower bound on root-mean-square intervention-response error. We identify conditions under which population gradient updates introduce this dependence from a parent-only baseline or damage a previously correct mechanism through shared parameters while improving other predictions. These dependencies can also make model behavior vary with how the same intervention is realized. We characterize interventional alignment through a common output mapping across internal states and physical processes realizing the same intervention target and relevant context. Correction is limited by the causal hypotheses currently admitted within inquiry. The relevant hypothesis class comprises these causal alternatives, rather than the function class the computational system could in principle represent. For predictions restricted to these alternatives, interventional mean error cannot fall below the best approximation they permit, whether evidence is observational or interventional. Reducing error below a positive limit requires admitting better hypotheses, which may entail revising the causal variables, mechanism structure, or intervention interpretation. Interventional criticism constrains replacements without determining them. We conjecture that reliably acquiring and maintaining interventional competence when causal commitments fail requires autonomous participation in proposing alternatives, testing their consequences, and revising them in response to error.
papers.summary: The paper argues that a model can keep gains in predicting observational data only by making persistent errors in how it responds to interventions. For deterministic predictors under squared-error loss, any advantage over the best predictor that uses only an outcome's direct causes requires depending on other inputs, and when interventions change those inputs without changing the outcome, this **gives a positive lower bound on intervention-response error, whatever the learning rule**. The author identifies conditions under which gradient updates introduce such dependence or damage a mechanism that was previously correct through shared parameters. They also show that correction is limited by which causal hypotheses are currently being considered, and conjecture that reliable interventional competence requires an agent to propose, test, and revise causal alternatives itself.

papers.title: Dr. No: Feature Steering for Abstention in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract:
Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model.
  Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.
papers.summary: Foundation models often answer even when the visual or textual evidence is not enough to support a reliable conclusion. `Dr. No` finds sparse autoencoder (SAE) features linked to abstaining or committing to an answer, then adjusts a small set of them during the prefill pass at inference time, without retraining the model. Tested on `LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B` with `UNK-VQA` and `MM-UPD`, and on `Qwen3.5-2B` with `AbstentionBench` subsets, **feature steering balances correct answering against appropriate abstention better than post-hoc rejection baselines based on uncertainty**. Gains are weaker on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA such as `MuSiQue`, which suggests that the signals controlling abstention depend on the type of task rather than forming one universal signal.

papers.title: ExaTune: Exhaustive Hyperparameter Landscape Exploration at Scale
papers.abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) returns a single optimal configuration, systematically discarding the explored performance landscape that encodes how results depend on configuration choices. Fitness landscape analysis comprises a robust collection of methods from evolutionary computation offering ruggedness indices, autocorrelation functions, and fitness-distance correlation that have never been applied to machine learning hyperparameter spaces at scale, given that fine-grained ground-truth enumeration data has not existed. We present ExaTune, an open-source HPC system to produce a new artifact class: the hyperparameter landscape map. ExaTune exhaustively evaluates every point on a discretized hyperparameter grid via $K$-fold cross-validation, aggregates results into reproducible parquet benchmarks, and applies a suite of five formalized landscape metrics: spatial autocorrelation (Moran's $I$), ruggedness, local optima density, fitness-distance correlation (FDC), and variance-based parameter importance. We release a benchmark collection of 8 complete landscape maps (totalling 285,080 exhaustively evaluated configurations) spanning five model families (SVMs, random forests, XGBoost, ridge regression, and $k$-nearest neighbors) across six classification and two regression benchmarks, hosted on HuggingFace. Empirical analysis demonstrates that Bayesian optimization, Optuna, Hyperband, and Random Search at standard trial budgets systematically miss instability regions, secondary optima, and parameter interaction effects that are visible in complete landscapes; information that is structurally unavailable to any optimizer by design.
papers.summary: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) returns one best configuration and throws away information about how performance changes across the rest of the search space. `ExaTune` is an open-source high-performance computing system that evaluates every point on a discretized hyperparameter grid with K-fold cross-validation, then measures the resulting landscape with five metrics from evolutionary computation, including ruggedness, local-optima density, and fitness-distance correlation. The authors release eight complete landscape maps totaling 285,080 configurations across five model families, including SVMs, random forests, and `XGBoost`. They show that **`Bayesian optimization`, `Optuna`, `Hyperband`, and random search at standard budgets systematically miss instability regions, secondary optima, and parameter interactions** that the complete landscapes reveal.

papers.title: Learning Almost Complex and Complex Structures
papers.abstract: We study the numerical constructions of almost complex and complex structures on spheres and products of spheres up to real dimension six. Our general set-up parametrises almost complex structures via a global matrix field in an ambient Euclidean space, compressed by the tangent projector. The projector's algebraic residual measures the almost complex condition, while its Nijenhuis tensor is evaluated in the intrinsic norm of the round product metric. Polynomial features and neural networks are trained without prescribed targets to perform general searches for these structures. The almost complex search passes numerical admissibility checks on all nine examples that admit such structures and rejects $S^4$, where a topological obstruction is known. A matrix correction then enforces the almost complex identity, subject to a novel uniform admissibility condition. For integrability, a free polynomial representation with Levenberg-Marquardt optimisation learns the complex structures on $S^2\times S^2$, $S^3\times S^1$, $S^3\times S^3$ and $S^5\times S^1$, with the largest Nijenhuis norms found by adversarial search all below $10^{-9}$. These general searches were unsuccessful on $S^6$, $S^4\times S^2$ and $S^4\times T^2$. Therefore, for these three cases direct numerical reconstructions were built in torus-fibred coordinates. They are integrable by construction, satisfy their compatibility conditions to better than $10^{-11}$, and corroborate the recent constructions on $S^6$ and $S^4\times S^2$.
papers.summary: The authors use machine learning to search numerically for almost complex and complex structures on spheres and products of spheres up to real dimension six. They parametrize candidate structures as a matrix field in an ambient Euclidean space and train polynomial features and neural networks, with no target structures given, to minimize the algebraic residual and the Nijenhuis tensor. The search finds almost complex structures on all nine spaces that admit them and correctly rejects S^4, where a topological obstruction is known. It also **learns integrable complex structures on four product spaces with Nijenhuis norms below 10^-9**. For S^6, S^4×S^2, and S^4×T^2, where the general search failed, direct numerical reconstructions in torus-fibred coordinates support recently published constructions.

papers.title: INSIGHT-HPC: An Interpretable System Intelligence for Global HPC Telemetry
papers.abstract: Modern high-performance computing (HPC) clusters integrate multi-generation CPUs and GPUs, which generate rich, high-dimensional telemetry streams from out-of-band baseboard management controllers (BMC), job schedulers, and facility power distribution units. Detecting anomalies within this telemetry is critical to prevent energy waste and costly node failures. Existing approaches often rely primarily on statistical deviations and require stronger labels than actual production environments can provide. In addition, these detectors have a limited operational context for interpreting alerts. We present INSIGHT-HPC, a multi-plane anomaly-detection architecture that combines statistical, workload-aware, and physics-guided evidence into operator-interpretable episodes. INSIGHT-HPC integrates heterogeneous, large-scale telemetry streams and transforms noisy minute-resolution observations into de-duplicated fault episodes with operator-facing explanations. This design allows the system to distinguish workload-explained behavior from genuine infrastructure anomalies while producing interpretable alert summaries for operators. On production HPC telemetry with weak operational labels and controlled HPC-relevant fault injections, INSIGHT-HPC achieves a stronger precision-recall balance than all evaluated baselines. The system achieves a precision of 0.913, a recall of 0.817, an F1 score of 0.862, and an AUROC of 0.896. These results demonstrate the value of combining workload context, physical consistency, and explainable episode-level fusion.
papers.summary: High-performance computing (HPC) clusters produce large, heterogeneous telemetry streams from baseboard management controllers (BMC), job schedulers, and power units, and existing anomaly detectors depend on statistical deviations, need labels that production systems rarely have, and give operators little context. `INSIGHT-HPC` combines statistical, workload-aware, and physics-guided evidence to turn noisy minute-level readings into de-duplicated fault episodes with explanations for operators. This lets it tell workload-driven behavior apart from genuine infrastructure faults. On production telemetry with weak labels and controlled fault injections, it reaches **an F1 score of 0.862** (precision 0.913, recall 0.817), better than all evaluated baselines.

papers.title: Embedding Semantic Entropy: NLI-Free Semantic Uncertainty Estimation with Geometry-Aware Clustering
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate fluent yet incorrect responses, making un- certainty estimation important for reliable deployment. Semantic Entropy (SE) estimates uncertainty by clustering responses based on semantic equivalence, but it relies on hard entailment-based clustering. We propose Embedding Semantic Entropy, which replaces entailment-based clustering with K-Medoids in semantic embedding space and uses dynamic cluster selection to account for intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation. We evaluate the method on TriviaQA, SQuAD, NQ-Open, SVAMP, and BioASQ using Falcon- 7B-Instruct, LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, and Gemma-7B. Results show competitive AUROC and AUARC performance, suggesting that NLI-based entailment clustering can be replaced with embedding-space clustering with limited degradation while improving the inspectability of semantic grouping. This matters because semantic uncertainty scores depend on underlying semantic groups; by making these groups explicit, compact, and separable in embedding space, Emb-SE turns uncertainty estimation from a black-box en- tailment decision into an inspectable clustering problem.
papers.summary: Semantic Entropy (SE) estimates the uncertainty of a large language model (LLM) by grouping sampled responses by meaning, but it relies on hard clustering based on natural language inference (NLI) entailment. `Embedding Semantic Entropy` instead clusters responses with `K-Medoids` in a semantic embedding space and chooses the number of clusters dynamically based on how compact and well separated they are. Tested on `TriviaQA`, `SQuAD`, `NQ-Open`, `SVAMP`, and `BioASQ` with four 7B-scale models, it achieves **competitive AUROC and AUARC with only limited loss compared with entailment-based clustering**, while making the semantic groups explicit and easier to inspect.

papers.title: The Information Limits of Neural Controlled Differential Equations Under Sparse Observations
papers.abstract: Neural controlled differential equations (Neural CDEs) evolve hidden states along continuous paths constructed by interpolating discrete observations. Sparse measurements leave the input between observation times undetermined, and admissible continuous paths consistent with the same data can produce different terminal states. We characterize this ambiguity for planar drivers with bounded speed. The set of compatible terminal states admits a leading-order zonotopic approximation determined by feasible signed areas and transported Lie brackets. Its projection onto a scalar prediction yields a computable, target-specific ambiguity certificate. We also study the number of measurements needed to reduce the remaining uncertainty. For nondegenerate planar CDEs, the optimal worst-case radius over deterministic adaptive sampling policies scales as $N^{-1}$ when speed is bounded and $N^{-2}$ when both speed and acceleration are bounded, where $N$ is the number of observation intervals. Synthetic experiments assess the certificate using admissible continuous completions and examine the role of path regularity.
papers.summary: Neural controlled differential equations (Neural CDEs) evolve hidden states along continuous paths interpolated between observations, but when measurements are sparse, many different paths fit the same data and can lead to different predictions. For planar input paths with bounded speed, the authors show that the set of possible terminal states is approximated to leading order by a zonotope determined by feasible signed areas and Lie brackets. Projecting this set onto a scalar output gives a computable certificate of how ambiguous a specific prediction is. They also prove that **the best worst-case uncertainty shrinks as N^-1 with bounded speed and N^-2 when acceleration is also bounded**, where N is the number of observation intervals.

papers.title: Hardware-Aware Design and Layout Selection in Quantum Reservoir Computing for Insurance Claims Forecasting
papers.abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) processes temporal information through quantum dynamics, but it remains unclear whether small QRC models can forecast real data competitively with classical models and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. We address both questions for a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. Five reservoir candidates were selected and frozen using hardware-native interaction graphs, Trotterized Ising dynamics, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. On 232 held-out test days, the ideal candidates reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66-6.12 claims/day, compared with 5.36 for ridge regression. For four of the five, the difference from ridge was not significant under a 95% block bootstrap, and their accuracy was comparable with classical recurrent and reservoir baselines. On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor, we ran 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds, comparing hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization level 1 layouts. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with a maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), and avoided the severe transfer failures seen for some random layouts. Most of the hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short hardware probe on training inputs detected before the test runs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without a consistent gain in forecasting accuracy or hardware transfer. Small QRC models can thus reach competitive accuracy on this task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent.
papers.summary: The authors test whether a small six-qubit quantum reservoir computing (QRC) model can forecast next-day motor-insurance claim counts and whether its accuracy survives the move from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. In ideal simulation, five frozen reservoir designs reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66 to 6.12 claims per day against 5.36 for ridge regression, and for four of the five the difference was not statistically significant. On IBM's 156-qubit `Kingston` processor, **hardware-aware qubit placement gave lower error than `Qiskit`'s default layout in every one of 21 paired rounds** and avoided the severe failures seen with some random layouts. Most hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short probe on training inputs could detect before the test runs.

papers.title: EpiLoRA: Fusing Many LoRA Adapters into Low-Precision GEMMs for Serving and RL
papers.abstract: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) let one base model serve many fine-tuned variants: multi-tenant engines keep a single copy of the base and batch the requests of many tenants, each with its own adapter. As base models move to 8-bit (FP8) and 4-bit formats, their general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) become cheaper, but the adapters do not: engines run them as separate small GPU kernels beside the GEMM, whose latency takes a growing share of every decoding step. An adapter projects its input down to a low rank and back up, and our key observation is that the GEMM needs the down-projection only in its epilogue, the final stage in which it writes its output. EpiLoRA, a plugin for the vLLM engine, therefore launches the down-projection first and the low-precision GEMM as a dependent kernel that streams its weights meanwhile and adds every tenant's up-projection in its epilogue. On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, EpiLoRA decodes for a single adapter with up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration, and faster than SGLang and TensorRT-LLM; with many tenants, its adapter kernels deliver more throughput than vLLM's on most GPU-model pairs we tested. The same low-precision base also trains: a LoRA reinforcement-learning trainer that computes on the engine's FP8 weights needs no 16-bit copy, so a 27B model trains on one 48 GB GPU, and an engine that then keeps activations in 16 bits removes most of the remaining mismatch between the model generating training data and the one trained.
papers.summary: As base models move to 8-bit (FP8) and 4-bit formats, their matrix multiplications get cheaper, but Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters still run as separate small GPU kernels and take up a growing share of each decoding step. `EpiLoRA`, a plugin for `vLLM`, runs each adapter's down-projection first and then adds every tenant's up-projection in the final output stage (the epilogue) of the low-precision base matrix multiplication. On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs it **decodes with up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration** and beats `SGLang` and `TensorRT-LLM`. The same FP8 base can also be used for LoRA reinforcement learning without a 16-bit copy of the weights, so a 27B model trains on a single 48 GB GPU.

papers.title: When Latent Dynamics Meet Data Assimilation: A Benchmark of Koopman-Type Representations
papers.abstract: Koopman representations describe nonlinear dynamics through linear evolution in a transformed space, offering an attractive framework for their linear simplicity and generality. Yet these advantages do not necessarily translate into improved performance in deep latent data assimilation (LDA). We systematically compare seven representative methods and structural baselines across five systems spanning approximately periodic to strongly chaotic dynamics and a broad range of state dimensions. We evaluate forecast and assimilation accuracy, physical state recovery, latent-trajectory behavior, and dynamical consistency, and assess Gaussian error assumptions, objective convexity, and uniqueness of analysis solutions. Our results reveal a trade-off between representational flexibility and optimization tractability. Linear evolution of the latent state can stabilize short-term forecasts but restrict expressiveness in strongly chaotic and high-dimensional systems, without consistently improving assimilation accuracy. Parameterized linear operators offer greater flexibility, yet their joint optimization with the encoder--decoder remains nonconvex. Methods with closed-form analysis updates generally perform better and exhibit greater robustness in our experiments, although matrix inversion remains a computational bottleneck. These findings show that the practical benefits of Koopman structure depend on both sufficient observational information and the choice of assimilation procedure.
papers.summary: Koopman representations model nonlinear dynamics as linear evolution in a transformed space, but it is unclear whether this helps deep latent data assimilation (LDA). The authors benchmark seven methods and structural baselines on five systems ranging from nearly periodic to strongly chaotic, measuring forecast and assimilation accuracy, physical state recovery, and dynamical consistency. They find **a trade-off between how flexible the representation is and how tractable it is to optimize**: linear latent evolution stabilizes short-term forecasts but limits expressiveness on chaotic, high-dimensional systems. Methods with closed-form analysis updates were generally more accurate and robust, although matrix inversion remains a computational bottleneck.

papers.title: Sequential auditing of connected forecast errors under partial observations
papers.abstract: Graph forecasting systems often rely on prediction intervals to quantify uncertainty across connected locations, but the true outcomes needed for evaluation may be only partially observed. We study how an auditor can selectively retrieve missing outcomes to determine whether there exists a connected group whose outcomes violate the same side of their respective forecast intervals. The audit stops when the observed labels determine the event or the query budget is exhausted. On three public graph time series, MOMS reduces mean queries by 19.6% to 38.5% relative to screened random acquisition when 30% of labels are hidden. Under localized masking on METR-LA, shortest witness finds more positive cases within ten queries, although the difference depends on node ordering. Direct component traversal reproduces all 9,696 screened random traces without enumerating connected subsets. The experiments show that reducing queries to a decision does not necessarily improve early event discovery or reduce local computation.
papers.summary: Graph forecasting systems report prediction intervals at connected locations, but the true outcomes needed to check those intervals may be only partly observed. The authors study how an auditor can choose which missing outcomes to retrieve in order to decide whether some connected group of locations all fall outside their intervals on the same side, stopping once the answer is determined or the query budget runs out. On three public graph time series with 30% of labels hidden, their `MOMS` strategy **cuts mean queries by 19.6% to 38.5%** compared with screened random acquisition. However, needing fewer queries to reach a decision did not always mean finding positive cases earlier or doing less local computation.

papers.title: Accelerating FastDEC Clustering Algorithm with GPUs
papers.abstract: Fast Dominance Estimation Clustering (FastDEC) is an efficient variant of Density Peak Clustering (DPC) that achieves high clustering quality through dominance-based density estimation, but remains constrained by the computational cost of exact k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) construction and dominance component (DC) processing. We present SymWarp-FastDEC, a GPU-accelerated implementation of FastDEC. At its core is SymTrikNN, an exact self-k-NN kernel that exploits search symmetry using upper-triangular traversal and warp-cooperative top-k selection. We also introduce WP-DC, a warp-parallel DC reduction algorithm designed for modern GPUs. Combined with memory-adaptive execution planning and stream scheduling, WP-DC eliminates DC reduction as a runtime bottleneck. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that SymWarp-FastDEC produces clustering outputs identical to the original FastDEC on all evaluated equivalence benchmarks. Compared with a FastDEC variant using FAISS GpuIndexFlatL2 for exact k-NN search, our approach achieves approximately 1.7x to 4.9x higher end-to-end performance, with the advantage generally increasing with dimensionality. Compared with the original single-threaded Python FastDEC implementation, speedups reach approximately 2.5 x 10^4 in a very high-dimensional case where its k-d-tree-based search degrades; this extreme result is not representative of typical acceleration.
papers.summary: Fast Dominance Estimation Clustering (`FastDEC`), a variant of Density Peak Clustering, is slowed down by exact k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) search and dominance component (DC) processing. `SymWarp-FastDEC` moves the algorithm to GPUs with `SymTrikNN`, an exact k-NN kernel that exploits search symmetry and selects top-k neighbors cooperatively within GPU warps, plus `WP-DC`, a warp-parallel DC reduction. It produces clustering output identical to the original and runs **about 1.7x to 4.9x faster end to end than a `FAISS`-based GPU variant**, with the advantage generally growing with dimensionality. The authors note that a 25,000x speedup over the original single-threaded Python code in one very high-dimensional case is not typical.

papers.title: Camera Radar LiDAR Fusion via Point-Cloud Projection for Multi-Task Learning
papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles require robust perception systems to operate safely under diverse environmental conditions. While cameras provide high-resolution visual data, their performance significantly degrades in low-light and adverse weather. High Definition (HD) radar offers superior reliability and angular resolution under such conditions but lacks rich visual feature recognition. LiDAR, though expensive, delivers highly precise distance measurements and dense point clouds. Each sensor exhibits unique trade-offs, necessitating the development of advanced sensor fusion algorithms to harness complementary strengths while minimizing computational complexity and maintaining accuracy. In this study, the proposed fusion architecture performs early fusion by combining camera images with perspective-view point cloud data from HD radar and LiDAR sensors. The proposed model is trained to detect vehicles and segment free drivable space simultaneously. Experiments are performed on the RADIal dataset where we demonstrate that fusing point cloud data with camera images in front-view surpasses the performances of the most recent standalone and fusion models.
papers.summary: Autonomous vehicles need perception that holds up across conditions, but cameras degrade in low light and bad weather, high-definition radar lacks visual detail, and LiDAR is precise but expensive. The proposed architecture performs early fusion by projecting radar and LiDAR point clouds into the camera's front view and combining them with the images. A single model then both detects vehicles and segments drivable free space. On the `RADIal` dataset, **this front-view fusion outperforms recent single-sensor and fusion models**.

papers.title: We Ran a Research Sprint With AI. The AI Worked. The Research Didn't
papers.abstract: Generative AI tools for research are widely deployed, yet individual productivity gains do not guarantee better team research. We argue that how AI use is structured matters alongside access. Personal AI tools may amplify two failures under deadline pressure: a consumption bottleneck, in which generation outpaces team-visible evaluation, and AI-induced research silos, in which private human-AI loops displace shared decision-making. We motivate this position with a mechanism-generating pilot: a 100-minute research sprint with twelve researchers in three independently operating teams, within a seventeen-person session. Both patterns recurred across teams and evidence sources. Of 33 logged AI interactions, one was accepted outright and 27 lacked a recorded disposition; missing records alone do not establish absent evaluation. A parallel autonomous pipeline produced a complete draft without in-session human evaluation, illustrating production capacity rather than comparative quality. We propose Human-AI-Human collaboration: an interaction topology in which AI connects researchers' contexts and supports inspectable collective evaluation and decision-making. The pilot does not isolate AI-specific effects from time pressure or workflow practices. We close with seven modular, falsifiable design hypotheses, prioritizing shared context and team-visible evaluation checkpoints for controlled follow-up.
papers.summary: Using a 100-minute research sprint with twelve researchers in three teams as a pilot, the authors argue that how AI use is organized matters as much as whether researchers have access to it. They describe two recurring failures: a consumption bottleneck, where AI generates material faster than the team can visibly evaluate it, and AI-induced silos, where private human-AI loops replace shared decision-making. **Of 33 logged AI interactions, one was accepted outright and 27 had no recorded decision**, and a parallel autonomous pipeline produced a full draft without any in-session human evaluation. The authors propose a Human-AI-Human collaboration pattern in which AI links researchers' contexts and supports shared evaluation, and they offer seven falsifiable design hypotheses while acknowledging the pilot cannot separate AI effects from time pressure.

papers.title: Do We Still Need Rotation-Invariant Architectures? A Statistical Robustness Benchmark for Point Cloud Classification
papers.abstract: A substantial line of work builds rotation invariance directly into point cloud architectures. We benchmark 10 architectures (PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, RIConv, RIConv++, RISurConv, PointMLP, PointTransformer, and the equivariant VN-PointNet and VN-DGCNN) across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion, and analyze the results with confirmatory hypothesis tests rather than point estimates. The three rotation-invariant (RI) architectures achieve the best pose robustness but rank among the lowest on noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains. We ask whether this cost is intrinsic to invariance or specific to how invariance is obtained. We retrain all 10 architectures unchanged, with a simple invariance loss on the embedding and three training seeds each, and evaluate all models on the independently designed ModelNet40-C. Invariance training transfers narrowly but reliably. It improves exactly the corruption families its perturbations target wherever the baseline has headroom (mean occlusion +10.5, lidar +13.4 percentage points of accuracy). At matched training budget the best standard backbone and the best RI architecture end on par on unseen corruptions (within 2.5 percentage points in every seed), and invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model. Once rotation augmentation is widened, standard backbones concede only a flat, angle-independent accuracy offset under full-sphere rotation. We release the benchmark along with a package for analyzing point cloud robustness and reproducing our results.
papers.summary: Point cloud classifiers often build rotation invariance directly into the architecture. The authors benchmark 10 architectures, including `PointNet++`, `DGCNN`, `RIConv++`, `PointTransformer` and `VN-DGCNN`, across 5 domains under pose, noise and occlusion, and evaluate them with confirmatory hypothesis tests instead of point estimates. Rotation-invariant (RI) models are the most robust to pose but among the least robust to noise. When every architecture is retrained with a simple invariance loss and tested on `ModelNet40-C`, the gains are narrow but reliable (for example, +10.5 points on occlusion and +13.4 on lidar), and **the best standard backbone and the best RI architecture finish within 2.5 percentage points of each other on unseen corruptions**.

papers.title: P$^2$-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors
papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P$^2$-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P$^2$-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P$^2$-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.
papers.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation merges several expert models into one student by supervising the student's own generated outputs, while task arithmetic merges them without training by linearly combining their weights. `P²-MOPD` treats the linear combination of student and expert parameters as one differentiable model and trains both the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the distillation objective. Because the student stays trainable, the experts act as parameter priors rather than limits on where the merged weights can go. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scale, it surpasses the final recovery of standard `MOPD` in half the training steps, and **the 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery versus 80.9%**.

papers.title: Forget What Comes Next: LLM Unlearning via Statistical Independence
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce fragments of their training data, raising privacy and legal concerns that motivate machine unlearning. Yet poisoned training examples can remain statistically detectable after unlearning, which raises the question of whether current unlearning objectives remove what the model has memorized at all. In this work, we introduce PINT, a novel algorithm for machine unlearning that uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to reduce the statistical dependence between tokens to be forgotten and the internal representations used to predict them. We formally relate our HSIC-based objective to Exact Memorization through a computable upper bound, connecting the training objective directly to the model's ability to reproduce the forgotten tokens. In extensive experiments, we compare forgetting-utility trade-offs across eight settings with models up to 7B parameters and demonstrate scalability to 70B parameter models. Our evaluations cover unlearning Gaussian poisons, personal information, hazardous knowledge in biology and cybersecurity, and copyrighted books and news articles. PINT achieves the strongest forgetting-utility trade-off on average and is the only method to make Gaussian poisons undetectable while maintaining near-original model utility. Code is available at: https://github.com/shkabrii/PINT
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize training data, and current unlearning methods may leave forgotten data statistically detectable, so it is unclear whether they actually remove memorized content. `PINT` uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (`HSIC`) to reduce the statistical dependence between the tokens to be forgotten and the internal representations used to predict them, and proves an upper bound linking this objective to exact memorization. Experiments cover Gaussian poisons, personal information, hazardous biology and cybersecurity knowledge, and copyrighted text, on models up to 7B parameters, with scaling demonstrated up to 70B. `PINT` gives the best average trade-off between forgetting and utility and is **the only method that makes Gaussian poisons undetectable while keeping near-original utility**.

papers.title: Sampling Interventional Distributions with Orthogonal MMD Flow
papers.abstract: Many causal inference problems require sampling from interventional outcome distributions rather than estimating low-dimensional summaries. Existing approaches often rely on fitting generative models of the target distribution together with additional nuisance components, which can be computationally demanding for high-dimensional outcomes. We propose Interventional Maximum Mean Discrepancy Flow (IMMD-Flow), a particle-based method that instead represents the target interventional distribution through its kernel mean embedding. This kernel embedding admits a doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal estimator with finite-sample guarantees and can be efficiently reused to sample from the interventional distribution via MMD gradient flow. IMMD-Flow accommodates both hard and soft interventions, admits theoretical guarantees for estimation and particle approximation, and extends to high-dimensional image outcomes through frozen encoders. Across image-based benchmarks, IMMD-Flow matches or improves upon state-of-the-art generative approaches while showing significant speed advantages.
papers.summary: Many causal inference problems require samples from interventional outcome distributions, but fitting generative models plus additional nuisance models is expensive for high-dimensional outcomes such as images. `IMMD-Flow` instead represents the target distribution through its kernel mean embedding, estimates that embedding with a doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal estimator, and draws samples via a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) gradient flow over particles. The method handles both hard and soft interventions, comes with guarantees for estimation and particle approximation, and works on images through frozen encoders. On image-based benchmarks it **matches or beats state-of-the-art generative approaches while running significantly faster**.

papers.title: Ermakov--Based embeddings as a parameter-free layer for physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Evolution equations with time-dependent coefficients force a neural solver to spend capacity on a scale that the equation already determines. We show that a single classical object, the Ermakov-Pinney scale function $\rho$, can be written into the input layer of a physics-informed neural network as a parameter-free embedding. One construction covers three problem families through the two signs of the Pinney constant $c$: linear diffusion ($c=-1$, $\omega\equiv0$), diffusion in a time-dependent confining trap ($c=-1$, $\omega\neq0$), and the quantum oscillator with time-dependent frequency ($c=+1$). An exact moment identity gives $\rho$ in closed form from the initial data alone, so no auxiliary network or knowledge of the solution is needed. Our central finding is comparative: each family requires a different component of the construction and has a different honest control. In family I, the diffusive-time reparametrisation alone reproduces most of the gain, so that family is a poor test of the idea and shows why an ablation is mandatory. In family II no time reparametrisation exists, the control degrades accuracy, and the amplitude prefactor becomes essential (40.8x). In family III the adiabatic approximation also fails, and the quadratic phase factor is what matters (5.7x). The method does not help when the reduced solution does not converge to a fixed point: its extrapolation advantage then disappears. The reduction itself is the classical scaling-variable change of the self-similar-asymptotics literature; what is new is the moment identity that makes it architectural for time-dependent coefficients, and the comparative anatomy above.
papers.summary: Neural solvers for evolution equations with time-dependent coefficients spend capacity learning a scale that the equation already determines. The authors place the classical Ermakov-Pinney scale function into the input layer of a physics-informed neural network as a parameter-free embedding, computed in closed form from the initial data through a moment identity. Ablations show that each of the three problem families needs a different part of the construction: time reparametrization alone explains most of the gain for linear diffusion, while the amplitude prefactor gives **a 40.8x improvement for diffusion in a time-dependent trap** and the quadratic phase factor gives 5.7x for the quantum oscillator. The method stops helping when the reduced solution does not converge to a fixed point.

papers.title: Stacking-Based Weighting for Large Language Bayes in M-Open Settings
papers.abstract: Large Language Bayes (LLB) transforms a natural language problem description into a collection of candidate probabilistic programs and performs inference within each model, combining their predictions using Bayesian model averaging. While this provides a flexible framework for probabilistic inference without manual model specification, the resulting candidate model set is often misspecified in practice, and likelihood-based aggregation can concentrate on a single model, under-representing uncertainty across the sampled models. We propose a stacking-based aggregation method for LLB that selects model weights by optimizing predictive performance rather than marginal likelihood, while preserving the original language-model-driven model generation and within-model inference pipeline. Because leave-one-out predictive quantities are intractable in latent-variable models, we derive a variational lower bound that yields a tractable ELBO-based stacking objective. Across real-world probabilistic inference tasks, our method achieves comparable predictive performance to Bayesian model averaging while yielding more dispersed model weights, reducing concentration on a single candidate model under misspecification.
papers.summary: Large Language Bayes (`LLB`) turns a natural-language problem description into several candidate probabilistic programs and combines their predictions with Bayesian model averaging, which tends to concentrate on a single model when every candidate is misspecified. The authors replace that averaging with stacking, which chooses model weights to optimize predictive performance, and derive a tractable stacking objective based on the evidence lower bound (ELBO) because leave-one-out quantities are intractable in latent-variable models. On real-world inference tasks, the method **matches the predictive performance of Bayesian model averaging while spreading weight more evenly across candidate models**.

papers.title: One Mistake, Three Layers: Persistence Rules Under Depth Correlation
papers.abstract:
Probing frozen representations layer by layer is now standard practice, but reporting when a signal first becomes decodable requires a rule for reading a depth curve, and the obvious rule is wrong. On synthetic curves with known ground truth, requiring a probe score to exceed a null-calibrated threshold for three consecutive stages reports an onset nineteen stages early under transformer-like depth correlation, with every resample returning an onset. The failure follows from correlation between neighboring layers, a hazard known in neuroimaging but not, to our knowledge, checked for depth curves.
  We give an estimator whose error rate is calibrated rather than assumed. Null trajectories are built by permuting labels within each evaluation unit and holding each permutation fixed across depth, preserving the correlation structure the rule must survive; thresholds are per-layer order statistics; and the persistence requirement is calibrated rather than chosen.
  Applied to pocket information in a frozen co-folding trunk, stratifying 1,820 post-cutoff targets by protein-family and pocket familiarity, the five-stage rule fires on 4 to 7 per cent of null trajectories against a nominal 5 per cent and the three-stage rule on 12 to 17: the synthetic failure reproduces on real data. Pocket membership is decodable above threshold at all 48 blocks in all four regimes, so the onset cannot discriminate them; the pre-declared accumulation depth does, and is latest for familiar families with structurally novel pockets in every feature set. That regime is also the weakest, by a margin surviving controls for length, pocket measure and alignment depth.
  Separately, a widely used public co-folding checkpoint loads against its own code with 128 trunk parameters missing; those would be randomly initialized, and every representation extracted would be partly noise while appearing normal.
papers.summary: Layer-by-layer probing of frozen representations commonly reports the first layer where a signal becomes decodable, often by requiring a score to stay above a threshold for three consecutive layers. On synthetic curves, correlation between neighboring layers makes this rule **report the onset nineteen stages too early**, so the authors propose an estimator that calibrates its error rate using label permutations held fixed across depth, per-layer thresholds and a calibrated persistence requirement. Applied to pocket information in a frozen protein co-folding model across 1,820 targets, the three-stage rule fires on 12 to 17% of null trajectories against a nominal 5%, which reproduces the failure on real data. Separately, a widely used public co-folding checkpoint silently loads with 128 trunk parameters missing, so representations extracted from it are partly random noise.

papers.title: Rapid Mean-Field Formation Transport with a Shared-Representation Neural Fokker-Planck Controller
papers.abstract: This paper develops a mean-field formation transport method with low online computational cost for large-scale multi-agent systems. Classical mean-field planners often require repeated solutions of coupled forward and backward partial differential equations, making online replanning computationally demanding. Density and control are therefore approximated by a common parameterized nonlinear map with separate scalar density and vector control outputs. Parameters are optimized using Fokker--Planck and initial-condition residuals, formation-matching costs on numerically simulated closed-loop particle trajectories, and control effort. Numerical computations are restricted to a bounded region of the state space, with an additional penalty on probability flux across its boundary. For the periodic-domain model, we establish well-posedness of the induced density evolution and bound the density-approximation error in terms of the dynamics and initial-condition residuals. Parameter optimization precedes online operation, during which controller coefficients remain fixed. Experiments quantify the accuracy--runtime trade-off relative to a mean-field planner, show lower transport error than classical feedback baselines, and demonstrate the benefits of the common parameterization.
papers.summary: Mean-field planners for steering large swarms of agents into formations usually solve coupled forward and backward partial differential equations repeatedly, which makes online replanning slow. The method trains one shared neural network offline, with separate outputs for density and control, using Fokker-Planck residuals, formation-matching costs on simulated particle trajectories, control effort, and a penalty on probability flux leaving a bounded region. The authors prove well-posedness and an error bound for the periodic-domain case. Experiments show **lower transport error than classical feedback baselines** and quantify the accuracy-versus-runtime trade-off against a mean-field planner, with the controller kept fixed during online operation.

papers.title: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection. We propose OLIVIA, a protocol for such tests: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once through a logged lock. We apply it to AI decision models, non-generative language models that return probabilities for typed questions, reading news about S&P 500 stocks: an open-weights model we fine-tuned on 2024-2025 data, three commercial models and standard baselines. The fine-tuned model's signal replicated on two validation quarters (daily information coefficients 0.055 and 0.065) but fell to 0.020 (t = 1.7) on the blinded January-July 2026 test. The commercial models' readings line up with the overnight move to the open (information coefficient 0.074 to 0.077) but not with the move after it, so the news is priced by the time a trader can act on it at the open. No model can tell over- from under-reaction, and no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio. Commercial models identify masked companies in 62% to 74% of cases against a 28% baseline: masking hides names, not companies. The market reads the news first.
papers.summary: Backtests suggest that large language model (LLM) readings of company news predict stock returns, and the authors test how much of that survives once look-ahead bias, memorization and selection effects are ruled out. Their protocol, `OLIVIA`, uses point-in-time inputs with company names masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once. A fine-tuned open-weights model's signal held up on validation but fell to an insignificant level on the blinded 2026 test. Commercial models' readings predict only the overnight move to the open, so the news is already priced in by the time a trader can act, and **no pre-registered strategy survives trading costs**. Commercial models also identify the masked companies in 62 to 74% of cases.

papers.title: FlagRot: Selective Rotation for Low-Bit KV Caches
papers.abstract: Long-context inference is bound by the KV cache, which 2-bit codes could shrink about sixfold if their error stays in check. The usual remedy rotates keys before quantizing, assuming rotation always helps. However, we observe that it does not: rotation flattens a spiky piece of a key but can give a flat one a new peak, and both coexist within one key. We therefore propose FlagRot, which stores each 32-channel piece rotated or as is, whichever has the smaller calibrated attention error, and rotates the query instead when reading. We further show that how often to decide follows the quantization axis: per-channel caches such as KIVI need one decision per head, at no write cost, while per-token caches decide per key, with the choice stored in existing sign bits. At 2.5 bits per value, FlagRot lowers the twelve-model KL divergence of KIVI from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3, below RotateKV on 9 of 12 models. Served as a vLLM plugin, it raises RULER at 128k tokens by +2.9 points and the LongBench v1 mean by +0.4 to +1.9 points on the three of four models where 2-bit KIVI loses accuracy. It also lowers the error of 4-bit integer and FP4 caches.
papers.summary: 2-bit KV cache quantization could shrink long-context memory about sixfold, and the usual fix for its error is to rotate keys before quantizing. The authors observe that rotation flattens spiky parts of a key but can create new peaks in flat parts, so `FlagRot` decides for each 32-channel piece whether to store it rotated or unrotated based on calibrated attention error, and rotates the query instead at read time. Per-channel caches such as `KIVI` need only one decision per head, while per-token caches store the choice in existing sign bits. At 2.5 bits per value, **FlagRot cuts KIVI's twelve-model KL divergence from 18.7 to 12.4 ×10⁻³**, and as a `vLLM` plugin it improves `RULER` at 128k tokens by 2.9 points.

papers.title: WASP-Mem: Let Agent Organize Procedural Memory. Human Spend Effort on Diagnosis
papers.abstract: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.
papers.summary: LLM agents struggle with enterprise procedures because fixed, pre-built tooling cannot capture proprietary policies or recovery paths that only appear during execution. `WASP-Mem` (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory) distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages that the agent maintains, which lets it keep learning without training. On `TheAgentCompany`, it raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6 to 6.1% over the strongest baseline while using 57 to 61% less storage. A controlled study finds that human-imposed schemas and deduplication rules hurt performance, while **a single round of human diagnosis of failures beats four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0 to 10.9%**.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Identification of Tensegrity Prestress across Taut-Slack Transitions
papers.abstract: Prestress governs the stability, stiffness, and dynamic behavior of tensegrity structures, but it is not directly observable from sparse structural measurements, and it may decrease during service life. Under strong excitation, the cables may slacken and the dynamics become nonsmooth. Existing identification methods are limited to the taut regime, and physics-informed networks for tensegrities solve only the forward problem of predicting the response from known member parameters. This study formulates the inverse problem. Neural networks are trained on the equation-of-motion residual in constrained Cartesian coordinates, where the mass matrix is constant and the force densities enter linearly. The force densities, damping, and axial stiffness are trainable parameters, and the tension-only cable law is kept. A Fisher-information analysis shows, before inversion, which member parameters a record can determine. The method is tested on simulated planar tensegrity frames with up to five modules and a three-dimensional prism, and on measured records of a biomimetic leg and a full-scale tensegrity simplex. On the one-module frame, the identifiable force densities are recovered within 1.5% from noisy accelerations at half the free coordinates, on records with and without taut-slack transitions. Records with transitions determine members that taut records leave undetermined. On the five-module frame, a 16-cable two-span bridge, the median force-density error rises moderately, to 4.2%. On measured records, an identified spring stiffness is within 0.1% of its independently measured value on average, and the identified simplex prestress at 13 levels agrees with its cable force transducers to 2.9% root-mean-square.
papers.summary: Prestress, the built-in tension that governs the stability of tensegrity structures, cannot be measured directly from sparse sensors, and existing identification methods only work while all cables stay taut. The authors frame identification as an inverse problem for a physics-informed neural network trained on the equation-of-motion residual, with force densities, damping and stiffness as trainable parameters and the tension-only cable law kept. A Fisher-information analysis shows in advance which parameters a recording can determine. On simulated frames, identifiable force densities are recovered **within 1.5% from noisy data**, and recordings in which cables go slack pin down members that taut recordings cannot. On a full-scale physical structure, identified prestress matches the cable force sensors to 2.9% RMS.

papers.title: Decision Transformer with Task-Aware Representations for Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: To enable effective generalization in offline meta-RL, it is essential to accurately infer the underlying task through latent task representations, which provide a compact and transferable summary of task-specific characteristics for guiding policy generation. In this paper, we propose Contrastive Task-Aware Decision Transformer (CoTA-DT), a DT-based offline meta-RL framework that learns task representations by jointly integrating four complementary components: (i) contrastive learning from offline trajectories, (ii) alignment with natural-language task descriptions, (iii) one-step supervision via a task-conditioned world model, and (iv) long-term supervision via a task-conditioned Q function. The learned task representations are used as conditioning signals for a DT-based policy, enabling task-aware meta-policy learning. To further support generalization in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, we design a language-grounded, self-adaptive strategy that enables effective and reliable adaptation to unseen tasks. Notably, in CoTA-DT, the pretrained LLM serves as a shared backbone for language encoding, world modeling, Q-function estimation, and policy learning. This unified design facilitates parameter sharing, improving both efficiency and generalization. Extensive experiments across diverse offline meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate that CoTA-DT consistently outperforms prior methods, particularly in challenging zero-shot generalization scenarios.
papers.summary: Offline meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) must infer which task the agent faces from a compact task representation in order to generalize to new tasks. `CoTA-DT` learns these representations by combining contrastive learning on trajectories, alignment with natural-language task descriptions, one-step supervision from a task-conditioned world model, and long-term supervision from a task-conditioned Q function, then uses them to condition a `Decision Transformer` policy. A single pretrained LLM serves as the shared backbone for language encoding, world modeling, Q estimation and the policy, and a language-grounded adaptation strategy supports zero-shot and few-shot settings. It **outperforms prior methods across offline meta-RL benchmarks, especially in zero-shot generalization**.

papers.title: Language Model Augmented Decision Transformer for Multi-Task Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) aims to learn a unified policy from heterogeneous offline datasets that generalizes across tasks. However, existing offline MTRL methods often struggle with two fundamental issues: severe per-task data scarcity and limited cross-task generalization. In this paper, we propose Language-Model Augmented Decision Transformer (LaMA-DT), a unified sequence-modeling framework that leverages a single large language model (LLM) for both trajectory augmentation and multi-task policy learning. LaMA-DT uses natural-language task descriptions to guide task-aligned trajectory augmentation through a set of supervised generation and alignment objectives, and incorporates a scoring-and-filtering mechanism to retain high-quality augmented trajectories. The same LLM is then repurposed as a language-conditioned Decision Transformer and fine-tuned on a mixture of real and augmented data.
