As a stopping rule, it matched established rules only at low noise and detected corrupted samples less well than simple label-free scores. An exploratory extension of 280 runs covering Fashion-MNIST, pair-flip noise, and four training variants yielded similar results under uniform noise, but not pair-flip noise, where complexity peaked within two epochs. Conclusions are limited to this architecture, two small datasets, and synthetic noise.
papers.summary: The authors ask how much label noise a multilayer perceptron memorizes and when, decomposing predictive information into signal, memorization, and heterogeneity terms with a Fano-type bound. Across 89 pre-registered `MNIST` runs, normalized memorization information rose with the memorized fraction on training samples, stayed near zero on held-out samples, and sat close to its Fano bound. Statistical complexity **peaked before memorization at corruption rates up to 40%**, but as a stopping rule it matched established methods only at low noise and found corrupted samples less well than simple label-free scores. An extension of 280 runs on `Fashion-MNIST` replicated the results for uniform noise but not for pair-flip noise.

papers.title: Impact of Input Resolution in Mammographic Mass Detection: A Controlled Multi-Architecture Study
papers.abstract: Deep-learning-based mass detectors usually downsample mammograms, trading fine image detail for lower computational cost. However, published studies cannot reveal how much accuracy this trade-off sacrifices, since they also differ in architecture, preprocessing, and evaluation protocol. In this work, we isolated the effect of input resolution in a controlled study on the VinDr-Mammo dataset, training 18 detectors at six input resolutions ranging from 512 x 416 to 1600 x 1280 pixels, for 108 model-resolution combinations. Whole mammograms were resized without cropping or tiling. For each model, preprocessing, model initialization, augmentation, and evaluation procedures were kept fixed across resolutions. Detection accuracy was evaluated by mAP50 on the 219 mass-positive images of the official test split, and 57 combinations with test mAP50 of at least 0.60 were analyzed. From the lowest to the highest resolution, median mAP50 rose from 0.626 to 0.660 and the best mAP50 from 0.670 to 0.709. The best result, achieved by DINO with a ConvNeXt-S backbone, is the highest mAP50 reported to date on mass-positive VinDr-Mammo images. Gains were concentrated in small masses: for the smallest third of lesions, median mAP50 rose by 0.074 (from 0.367 to 0.441), compared with 0.007 and 0.032 for medium and large masses. Median training time increased from 0.45 to 1.40 h, and median inference time from 23.6 to 113.7 ms per image. Therefore, higher input resolution mainly benefits the small masses that are hardest to detect, at a computational cost that remains practical.
papers.summary: Published mammography mass detectors differ in architecture, preprocessing, and evaluation at the same time, so the cost of downsampling images is unclear. The authors train 18 detectors at six resolutions from 512×416 to 1600×1280 on `VinDr-Mammo`, keeping everything else fixed across resolutions. From lowest to highest resolution, median mAP50 rose from 0.626 to 0.660, and `DINO` with a `ConvNeXt-S` backbone reached **0.709, the best reported result on mass-positive VinDr-Mammo images**. Most of the gain came from the smallest masses, while inference time grew from about 24 to 114 ms per image.

papers.title: Point interpolation and distributional universality in flow-based generative models
papers.abstract: Motivated by the expressive power of neural ordinary differential equations in flow-based generative modeling, we study the approximation of probability measures by pushforwards generated by parameterized families of Lipschitz vector fields. For Wasserstein distances, we establish a quantitative relationship between finite-sample point interpolation and distributional approximation, and derive universality criteria based on $L^p$-approximation of transport maps. In particular, affine-invariant families containing a non-affine vector field are universal from compactly supported absolutely continuous base measures. For total variation, we show that coordinate-wise dynamics are insufficient in dimensions $d\geq 2$ and establish sufficient conditions based on one-dimensional Sobolev approximation and shear-type mixing. We further examine the role of point interpolation, establishing when different regimes relate to one another and when approximate interpolation can be made exact.
papers.summary: Motivated by neural ordinary differential equations in flow-based generative models, the authors study how well pushforwards of parameterized Lipschitz vector fields can approximate probability distributions. For Wasserstein distances, they link finite-sample point interpolation quantitatively to distributional approximation and show that **affine-invariant families containing a single non-affine vector field are universal** from compactly supported absolutely continuous base measures. For total variation, coordinate-wise dynamics are insufficient in two or more dimensions, and sufficient conditions are given based on one-dimensional Sobolev approximation and shear-type mixing.

papers.title: Two-Layer Random ReLU Networks Can Separate Disjoint Classes
papers.abstract:
Set separation by continuous linear functionals is fundamental in functional analysis and convex optimization and underlies binary classification in machine learning. Support vector machines provide maximum-margin affine separators for linearly separable data, while kernel methods represent nonlinear decision rules through linear separation in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space. We study when two classes, not necessarily convex or linearly separable in the input space, can be separated with positive margin by finite ReLU networks and by random ReLU features.
  At the deterministic level, we prove that positive-margin separation by a finite ReLU network is equivalent to the existence of finite closed convex covers whose opposite-label members have positive pairwise distances, and exactly two hidden layers suffice. For random separation, suppose each class is represented as a finite union of nonempty closed convex cells, possibly unbounded. If every opposite-label cell pair has positive distance and its closed difference cone is pointed, then two independent random ReLU layers yield a common positive-margin affine separator with high probability.
  The first layer separates the feature image of each negative cell from the feature image of the positive class by a hyperplane through the origin. It also controls all cross-class distances uniformly. The second layer combines cellwise scores through Chebyshev polynomials and realizes the resulting polynomial using Gaussian Hermite features, followed by a uniform finite-width approximation. With the remaining geometric, bias, and confidence parameters fixed, each sufficient width is quadratic in the largest Gaussian width of a spherical difference-cone section, hence at most linear in its span dimension. An example shows that this squared Gaussian-width dependence is sharp for both layers.
papers.summary: The authors ask when two classes that are neither convex nor linearly separable can be separated with a positive margin by finite ReLU networks or by random ReLU features. Deterministically, such separation is equivalent to the existence of finite closed convex covers whose opposite-label members are at positive distance, and **exactly two hidden layers suffice**. For random features, if each class is a finite union of convex cells with positive pairwise distances and pointed difference cones, two independent random ReLU layers give a positive-margin separator with high probability. The required width grows quadratically in a Gaussian-width measure of the geometry, and an example shows this dependence is sharp.

papers.title: Tokenizer Myths and Where To Find Them
papers.abstract: Tokenization is a fundamental component of modern language models: before a model sees data, its tokenizer has already determined how the data appears. We identify and challenge three myths in the tokenization research literature. Myth #1: Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) is agnostic to the tokenizer and/or the vocabulary size: BPB is tokens per byte times bits per token, and the two factors do not cancel; using untrained models, we show that BPB prefers some tokenizers over others: the model has learned nothing, but the tokenizer--model pair has. Myth #2: lower BPB means a better model: On untrained models, BPB strongly prefers some vocabulary sizes, even though accuracy remains at chance, and on real models trained on the same data, BPB correlates weakly with downstream performance. Myth #3: different "tokenizer-agnostic" metrics yield consistent results: The "unigram-normalized loss" is not tokenizer-agnostic; its reported correlation of 0.989 with BPB comes from a confounder and falls to 0.057 once fixed; from the same data the two metrics select different vocabularies at each model size. We present a tokenizer trilemma: no metric can score only the true distribution best, give the same predictions the same score, and tie all untrained models, so choosing a metric is choosing a research question. We conclude with a caution for reading the tokenization literature and a conjecture for future work.
papers.summary: The authors challenge three common beliefs in tokenization research. Using untrained models, they show that Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) is not tokenizer-agnostic: it prefers some tokenizers and vocabulary sizes even when the model has learned nothing, and on trained models it correlates only weakly with downstream accuracy. The reported 0.989 correlation between `unigram-normalized loss` and BPB comes from a confounder and **falls to 0.057 once fixed**. They also prove a trilemma: no metric can rank only the true distribution best, give identical predictions the same score, and tie all untrained models, so choosing a metric amounts to choosing a research question.

papers.title: LENS: Reliability-Aware Stock Prediction via LLM-Extracted Priors and News-Driven Semantic Graphs
papers.abstract: Predicting stock returns requires modeling persistent company relations and time-varying market signals. Graph Neural Network (GNN) approaches combine static priors with dynamic relational graphs, but treat every extracted edge as a trustworthy binary fact, ignoring heterogeneous reliability across relational sources. We propose LENS (LLM-Extracted priors and News-driven Semantics), a static--dynamic graph framework for stock return prediction and ranking that models relational reliability as a first-class signal across the pipeline. On the static side, we extract a multi-relational company graph from a Large Language Model and aggregate it over multiple runs with confidence weighting to downweight low-consistency edges. On the dynamic side, we build a news-driven semantic graph with exponential-decay temporal aggregation to capture changing market context under uneven coverage. A context-dependent gated fusion module rebalances the two graphs at the per-stock, per-day level. On S&P 500, LENS improves AR@5 by 16.4% and SR@5 by 22.6% over the strongest baseline, and on NASDAQ 100 it achieves comparable improvements (15.5% and 20.9% respectively). Ablations isolate each component's contribution, and a human-validation study of sampled relations supports that the aggregation is grounded, providing evidence that reliability-aware LLM relations and news-based semantic graphs carry complementary information for graph-based financial prediction.
papers.summary: Graph-based stock prediction models usually treat every extracted company relation as a reliable binary fact. `LENS` builds a static multi-relational company graph by querying a large language model several times and weighting edges by their consistency, and adds a dynamic news-driven semantic graph with exponential time decay. A gated fusion module balances the two graphs per stock and per day. On the S&P 500, `LENS` **improves AR@5 by 16.4% and SR@5 by 22.6%** over the strongest baseline, with similar gains on the NASDAQ 100.

papers.title: GC-MoE: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with FP8/FP4 Grouped GEMM via CUDA Green Contexts
papers.abstract: Under expert parallelism, mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers pay all-to-all token dispatch, grouped GEMMs, and a combine step in every layer. In decode each rank holds only 1-256 tokens: dispatch latency and weight traffic dominate while tensor-core utilization is inherently low. In fused operators such as DeepGEMM's Mega MoE, dispatch and computation overlap only by sharing every SM: dispatch warps compete with TMA/MMA and epilogue warps for registers, shared memory, and issue slots; every phase shares one CTA resource budget, synchronization spans the whole SM array, and every replay ends with a workspace-clean pass and a cross-rank barrier. We present GC-MoE, an open-source FP8/FP4 MoE inference operator for NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that uses CUDA Green Contexts to split the device into a small communication partition and a large compute partition. Each role gets its own kernel, resource budget, and synchronization domain, so dispatch and GEMM tune independently. A three-node CUDA Graph (four on Hopper with fused shared experts) launches the dispatch and grouped-GEMM kernels as concurrent roots; a token-ring handshake starts computation on the first filled ring blocks, and double-buffered receive counters remove the trailing cross-rank barrier between replays. The compute partition runs operand-swapped tcgen05 block-scaled MMA on Blackwell and register-A WGMMA with in-register FP4 decoding on Hopper, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts. On 8 H20 GPUs GC-MoE accelerates DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode by 1.188x on average on both the routed and shared-expert suites (peaks 1.296x and 1.353x); on 8 B300 GPUs it accelerates GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.106x (1.123x with fused shared experts, peak 1.209x), beating Mega MoE at all 54 measured points at matched accuracy. GC-MoE reserves only 20 of 148 SMs on B300 for dispatch.
papers.summary: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) decoding with expert parallelism, token dispatch latency and weight traffic dominate. Fused operators such as `Mega MoE` force dispatch and compute to share every streaming multiprocessor (SM), so they compete for the same resources. `GC-MoE` is an open-source FP8/FP4 MoE inference operator that uses CUDA Green Contexts to split the GPU into a small communication partition and a large compute partition, each with its own kernel and synchronization. A ring handshake starts computation as soon as tokens arrive, and double-buffered counters remove the barrier between graph replays. It speeds up `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` decode by 1.188x on 8 H20 GPUs and **beats `Mega MoE` at all 54 measured points** on B300 while reserving only 20 of 148 SMs for dispatch.

papers.title: LIRA: A More Interpretable Dynamic Loss-Informed Rank Allocation for Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large pretrained models. However, standard LoRA typically assigns a fixed rank profile despite layer- and stage-dependent adaptation needs, while recent adaptive-rank variants often rely on heuristic or first-order signals that provide only an indirect link between rank reallocation and local loss behavior. This leaves the rationale behind each rank reallocation insufficiently interpretable. Motivated by this gap, we propose LIRA (Loss-Informed Rank Allocation), a dynamic-rank LoRA method designed to make online rank reallocation more interpretable. LIRA scores each layer by the estimated magnitude of the local loss perturbation associated with its recent LoRA-factor movements under a second-order approximation, making the basis for each rank change interpretable term by term. By periodically applying DELTA (Displacement-Evaluated Loss-Trajectory Allocation), a displacement-based algorithm for LoRA rank reallocation, LIRA produces discrete effective ranks under matched budgets while remaining compatible with standard (A,B) adapters. On RoBERTa-base GLUE under the La-LoRA/LoRA protocol, LIRA outperforms the uniform-LoRA and adaptive-rank baselines reported under this protocol; Trajectory EMA attains performance competitive with Fixed-point Fisher at lower estimation cost.
papers.summary: Standard low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`) gives every layer a fixed rank, and adaptive-rank variants reallocate rank using heuristic signals that are hard to interpret. `LIRA` scores each layer by a second-order estimate of how much its recent LoRA-factor movements perturbed the loss, so each rank change can be explained term by term. It periodically reallocates rank with an algorithm called `DELTA` under a matched budget and remains compatible with standard adapters. On `RoBERTa-base` with `GLUE`, **`LIRA` outperforms uniform LoRA and the reported adaptive-rank baselines**.

papers.title: OmniST: Topology-Invariant Spatiotemporal Forecasting with Guaranteed-Coverage Uncertainty at Unseen Sensor Locations
papers.abstract: Standard spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks need a fixed-size adjacency matrix, coupling model weights to a specific sensor count N; they cannot produce any output at a sensor absent from training. We present OmniST, a topology-invariant forecaster whose computation has zero structural dependency on the number of nodes, and which, composed with inductive split-conformal calibration, gives distribution-free, coverage-guaranteed prediction intervals at arbitrary (including never-seen) sensor locations, preserving that guarantee as sensors are added or removed. Topology invariance follows from coordinate-based tokenization, k-nearest-neighbor attention from geographic coordinates at each forward pass, and per-node temporal processing via a bidirectional GRU. On real Delhi air-quality data (37 stations, 2019-2023), OmniST attains a 30-day PM2.5 MAE of 31.0 ug/m3 and degrades at most 1.1 percent when 40 percent of stations are removed. Its inductive forecasts at unseen stations beat nearest-neighbor interpolation (about 12 percent) and a learned kriging GNN (IGNNK, about 21 percent), and, unlike either, carry a finite-sample coverage guarantee. The guarantee holds at 90 percent or above under 30-50 percent node dropout across four real datasets over three domains (Delhi and Beijing air quality, NOAA GHCN weather, Caltrans PeMSD7-M traffic), and still holds at 325 real sensors (full PeMS-BAY). We also fix a temporal-drift failure: static conformal under-covers over time (about 0.50 late), but a rolling adaptive-conformal estimator restores target coverage (0.89 overall, 0.96 late) at the cost of wider intervals.
papers.summary: Standard spatiotemporal graph networks are tied to a fixed sensor count and cannot forecast at sensors absent from training. `OmniST` tokenizes nodes by their coordinates, attends over k-nearest neighbors computed from geography, and processes each node's time series with a bidirectional GRU, so its weights do not depend on the network topology. Combined with split-conformal calibration, it gives **distribution-free, coverage-guaranteed prediction intervals at never-seen sensor locations**. On Delhi air-quality data it degrades at most 1.1% when 40% of stations are removed and beats `IGNNK` kriging by about 21% at unseen stations. A rolling adaptive conformal estimator fixes the under-coverage that static calibration suffers as data drifts over time.

papers.title: Integrating Machine Learning and Uncertainty Quantification for Real-Time Decision-Making in Digital Twins: A System-Centric Review and Perspective
papers.abstract: Digital Twins are evolving from passive virtual representations into closed-loop systems that continuously synchronize with physical assets and drive real-time decisions. Yet predictive modeling, machine learning (ML), uncertainty quantification (UQ), and decision-making have been studied as separate capabilities, leaving limited understanding of their integration and maintenance during online operation. This narrative review, scoped by the functional requirements of real-time decision-making rather than by Digital Twin terminology alone, examines how such decisions are generated and sustained in engineering Digital Twins. We first examine foundational decision-making architectures and representative engineering applications, followed by methods that address their limitations across the decision loop. We identify optimization-based, policy-based, and knowledge-based approaches as the major pathways from virtual representation to action. Across them, ML plays three roles in decision-making: enabling efficient surrogate modeling, transforming heterogeneous physical feedback into decision-relevant information, and accelerating or directly generating decisions. UQ supports uncertainty-aware decisions and model adaptation, while continual validation, drift detection, and adaptation help maintain reliable operation as the physical system evolves. Together, these findings underscore the need for a shift from a model-centric to a system-centric perspective on Digital Twins, where its performance depends on the interactions with sensing, state estimation, computation, decision-making, and adaptation rather than on their standalone performance. Therefore, future research should shift from isolated algorithm development toward system-level co-design, scalable decision-making, and approaches to design, and data-efficient continual adaptation and validation for AI-enabled autonomous systems.
papers.summary: Digital twins are moving from passive virtual models to closed-loop systems that drive real-time decisions, but prediction, machine learning (ML), uncertainty quantification (UQ), and decision-making have mostly been studied separately. This narrative review groups decision pathways into optimization-based, policy-based, and knowledge-based approaches. It identifies three roles for ML: surrogate modeling, turning physical feedback into decision-relevant information, and generating decisions directly. The authors argue for **a shift from a model-centric to a system-centric view**, with system-level co-design and continual validation and adaptation.

papers.title: Deep Learning Compilers: Architecture, Optimization, and Empirical Characterization
papers.abstract: As deep learning (DL) models become increasingly complex and hardware architectures grow more heterogeneous, DL compilers play a critical role in optimizing computational efficiency and enabling scalable deployment. This paper presents a systematic analysis of DL compilers, covering their architectural evolution, compilation workflows, optimization techniques, and emerging research directions. We organize DL compiler architectures into frontend, middle-end, and backend stages, emphasizing the role of the middle-end in connecting high-level model representations with hardware-specific optimizations. We further examine representative DL compilers and recent optimization techniques across different compilation stages. Beyond architectural and technical analysis, we conduct an empirical evaluation of compiler behaviors to investigate the effectiveness of graph optimization, compilation overhead, and dynamic-shape handling. Experiments using PyTorch/TorchInductor on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 demonstrate that compiler benefits depend strongly on workload characteristics, with speedups of up to 8.21\times for fusion-friendly computation graphs, while other workloads exhibit limited improvements. Our results further reveal that compilation overhead can require thousands of executions to amortize, and dynamic-shape compilation reduces cumulative shape-transition costs by approximately 70\% at the expense of modest steady-state performance degradation. By combining systematic architectural analysis with quantitative experimental evidence, this work provides insights into the design, optimization, and practical deployment of modern DL compilers.
papers.summary: The authors survey deep learning compilers, organizing them into frontend, middle-end, and backend stages and reviewing representative systems and optimization techniques. They also measure `TorchInductor` in `PyTorch` on an RTX A6000. Speedups depend heavily on the workload, **reaching 8.21x for fusion-friendly graphs** and staying small for others. Compilation overhead can take thousands of runs to pay back, and dynamic-shape compilation cuts shape-transition costs by about 70% at a modest cost in steady-state speed.

papers.title: How Risky Is Your Data-Driven Policy?
papers.abstract:
Data-driven algorithms are ubiquitous across industries, and there is an extensive literature on analyzing their \emph{average} performance. The risk profile of such algorithms, while critical, is much less understood. This paper quantifies the risk of data-driven policies and isolates its sources. We evaluate a policy through the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of its loss over the training sample, any policy randomization, and the future outcome, at a fixed unknown distribution. Regret against an oracle that knows the distribution decomposes into expected post-sample regret (PS), the average outcome-only CVaR gap of the selected action, and a sample-risk premium (SR), the additional tail risk omitted by averaging those evaluations. The analogous premium vanishes under expected loss.
  We characterize when the premium vanishes and how large it is relative to post-sample regret. For losses with a continuous density near the tail cutoff, we identify conditions under which both components decay at the same rate, yet the limiting ratio of the premium to post-sample regret can reach the thousands. When a probability mass at the cutoff moves with the action, the premium can decay more slowly and dominate post-sample regret. We establish conditions under which sample average approximation learns the oracle action at rate $n^{-1/2}$ in both settings, but its combined-risk regret is of order $n^{-1}$ in the first and $n^{-1/2}$ in the second. In finite-sample numerical examples of SAA in both settings, the premium accounts for approximately $74\%$--$97\%$ of regret.
papers.summary: Data-driven decision policies are usually analyzed by their average performance, while their tail risk is less understood. The authors evaluate policies by the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of their loss over the training sample, the policy's randomness, and the future outcome. Regret then splits into expected post-sample regret plus a sample-risk premium, a term that disappears under expected loss. The premium can be thousands of times larger than post-sample regret in the limit, and in finite-sample examples of sample average approximation it accounts for **about 74–97% of regret**.

papers.title: Reciprocity Can Erase Direction:tructural Boundaries and Controlled Utility of Magnetic Graph Networks
papers.abstract: Magnetic graph networks encode direction through phase, but a learned graph can erase the intended directional mechanism before prediction. We characterize this failure for support-based magnetic Laplacians. Exact identities relate imaginary energy and distance from zero phase to amplitude-weighted reciprocity. Top-$k$ selection forces complete collapse when the observed-node count satisfies $m\leq k+1$, and dense support imposes a lower bound on reciprocal-arc fraction. We then construct paired propagation examples with identical node features and symmetric amplitudes but opposite labels, giving a provable chance-level limit for direction-erasing representations. In 72 fixed neural fits, support phase achieved test AUROC 1.0000 on a unilateral ring but 0.5000 on reciprocal ring and complete supports; continuous score phase and a real directed comparator achieved 1.0000 throughout. All models solved the direction-free control. These are oracle-direction mechanism tests, not evidence of learned clinical direction. In the preserved public DeepDRiD development study, continuous phase was active but its robustness difference from zero phase was only $+0.0036$ (descriptive 95\% interval $-0.0014$ to $+0.0095$) on validation patients used for checkpoint selection. The contribution is a structural and experimental framework for distinguishing erased direction from unestablished task utility. It provides a precise circumstance in which magnetic phase preserves useful information, without asserting universal or clinical superiority.
papers.summary: Magnetic graph networks encode edge direction as a complex phase, but when the graph itself is learned, reciprocal edges can erase that directional signal before prediction. The authors derive exact identities linking phase energy to reciprocity and show that top-k neighbor selection forces complete collapse when few nodes are observed. On constructed examples that differ only in direction, support-based phase **drops to chance-level AUROC on reciprocal graphs** while continuous score phase and a real directed baseline stay perfect. On the `DeepDRiD` diabetic retinopathy dataset, continuous phase gave only a negligible robustness gain, so the authors present the work as a framework for diagnosing erased direction rather than evidence of clinical benefit.

papers.title: Nearly Linear-Time Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader for Weakly Observable Graph Bandits
papers.abstract: We study online learning with directed weakly observable feedback graphs and propose a Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) policy that achieves best-of-both-worlds guarantee with nearly linear expected time complexity. To preserve the simple structure of FTPL, we develop a novel graph-based loss estimator that combines forced exploration, conditional geometric resampling and adaptive learning rates with surrogate probabilities. Our policy achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\delta_*^{1/3} T^{2/3})$ regret for adversarial regimes as well as $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\delta_* \log T / \Delta_{\min}^2)$ regret for stochastic regimes, where $\delta_*$ and $\Delta$, respectively, denote the fractional weak domination number and the suboptimality gap. These results show that refined guarantees for problems with minimax regret of $\Theta(T^{2/3})$ can be obtained through appropriately designed adaptive learning rates and loss estimators without sacrificing the simplicity of FTPL.
papers.summary: The authors study online learning with directed, weakly observable feedback graphs and propose a Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (`FTPL`) policy that runs in nearly linear expected time. A new loss estimator combines forced exploration, conditional geometric resampling, and adaptive learning rates with surrogate probabilities. The policy achieves **best-of-both-worlds guarantees**: Õ(δ*^{1/3}T^{2/3}) regret against adversaries and Õ(δ* log T / Δ_min²) in stochastic settings, where δ* is the fractional weak domination number. This shows refined guarantees are reachable without giving up the simplicity of FTPL.

papers.title: What Is the Influence of Task Order in Continual Learning? An Empirical Study and Order-Aware Evaluation for Motion Forecasting
papers.abstract: Aggregate scores for continual learning algorithms rest on a distribution over task orders that is rarely stated. We formulate algorithm comparison as an expectation over a declared order distribution, which separates training variation from order variation, and apply it to motion forecasting with four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset, all 24 task orders, four algorithms, and three training replicates (288 runs). Task order accounts for 65\% to 91\% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and 90\% to 99\% of this order effect comes from the identity of the starting task: the smallest task cannot be learned from a cold start. Beyond the first stage, the order effect is comparable to training variability. In most orders, the leading algorithm in current-task error and backward transfer is within one replicate standard deviation of the runner-up. Backward transfer depends on the order mainly through its reference term, which weights the first task most heavily, so relative improvement and final error identify different leading algorithms for displacement error. A transition-direction descriptor computed from task statistics tracks the position of the smallest task, and weighting orders by it leaves the algorithm ranking unchanged. These results call for benchmarks that declare their order distribution and report order-resolved, starting-task-resolved, warm-start, and final errors alongside aggregate scores. The code and data are available \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/task-order-cl-4f7b/}{here}.
papers.summary: Continual learning benchmarks report aggregate scores that implicitly average over a task-order distribution that is rarely stated. The authors frame algorithm comparison as an expectation over a declared order distribution and test it on motion forecasting with four road-layout tasks from the `INTERACTION` dataset, covering all 24 orders, four algorithms and three replicates (288 runs). Task order explains **65% to 91% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer**, almost all of it from which task comes first, because the smallest task cannot be learned from a cold start. After the first stage, the order effect is about as large as ordinary training variability, and the leading algorithms usually differ by less than one replicate standard deviation. The authors recommend that benchmarks declare their order distribution and report order-resolved and starting-task-resolved errors.

papers.title: Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: We introduce a training-free sparse attention method that builds a prompt-specific key index to accelerate both prefill and decoding. The method clusters the keys into large semantic blocks that group tokens from noncontiguous positions. Each query position selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them. Queries that select the same block are processed together, so prefill stays fast even though each query chooses its own blocks. Large blocks make centroid scoring and this grouped processing cheap, so each query can attend to more tokens in the same time. Larger blocks with a larger token budget can thus be both faster and more accurate on long-context tasks than smaller blocks with a smaller budget. We evaluate two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, on one NVIDIA H200. Including the cost of building and using the index, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention are 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval, yet outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B, whose latency is similar at 512K, on all three benchmarks.
papers.summary: The authors present a training-free sparse attention method that speeds up both prefill and decoding by clustering keys into large semantic blocks that can span noncontiguous positions. Each query scores block centroids and attends to the original keys and values in the blocks it selects, and queries that select the same block are processed together, so large blocks keep selection cheap and allow a larger token budget. On one NVIDIA H200, `Qwen3.5-4B` and `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` reach whole-model speedups over dense attention of **2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens**, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M tokens. The 35B model stays close to dense accuracy on `RULER`, `LongBench-v2` and `MRCR`, while the 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval but still beats a dense `Qwen3.5-2B` of similar latency.

papers.title: Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.
papers.summary: Linearization converts a pretrained Transformer into a cheaper hybrid of sliding-window attention (SWA) and a constant-size recurrent memory. Studying an SWA plus Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, the authors find that long-context retrieval is concentrated in a few anchor layers and that the other layers' recurrent states hold similar information under layer-specific transformations. `Anchor` places TTT memory only at those anchor layers and shares one cross-layer recurrent state that each layer reads through its own learned map. On `Llama-3.1-8B` and `Mistral-7B` it achieves **2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher `MMLU` accuracy than `LoLCATs` with a 10x smaller recurrent state**, and it cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x compared with softmax attention.

papers.title: CORA: Teacher-Guided Causal O-RAN Adaptation for Jamming Detection
papers.abstract: In mission-critical networks, a missed jamming event is costlier than a false alarm, so detectors should favor recall, operate causally, and work without labeled attack data. Retrospective Key Performance Indicator (KPI) detectors meet the label-free requirement but rely on future context and cannot run in streaming operation. We present CORA, a teacher-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework that transfers the hindsight of a retrospective detector to a causal one without labels during training or deployment. Offline, a retrospective KPI detector evaluated on unlabeled historical logs defines a recall-weighted reward for a masked controller that adapts the sensitivity, persistence, and grace of a causal KPI detector. At deployment, the teacher is removed and the frozen controller acts causally, with no ground-truth labels and no target-specific calibration. The design maps onto offline training in the Non-Real-Time RIC and causal control in the Near-Real-Time RIC of an Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). Under leave-one-out transfer across ten 5G O-RAN testbed configurations, CORA reaches recall-oriented operating points on the deployable frontier that none of the evaluated baselines covers. A Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) controller raises mean recall from 0.687 to 0.771 over a fixed default detector on all ten configurations, while a Deep Q-Network (DQN) achieves a comparable F2-score to the best teacher-selected static configuration, with 61% fewer false alarms. Removing the teacher lowers recall on every configuration.
papers.summary: Jamming detectors in mission-critical 5G networks need high recall, must run causally on streaming data and cannot rely on labeled attacks. Retrospective Key Performance Indicator (KPI) detectors work without labels but depend on future context. `CORA` uses a retrospective detector, run on unlabeled historical logs, as a teacher that defines a recall-weighted reward for a reinforcement learning controller, which tunes the sensitivity, persistence and grace of a causal detector. The controller is then frozen and deployed in the Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) controller without the teacher. Across ten testbed configurations with leave-one-out transfer, a `PPO` controller **raises mean recall from 0.687 to 0.771** over a fixed default detector, and a `DQN` controller matches the best static configuration's F2-score with 61% fewer false alarms.

papers.title: Proper Agnostic Learning of Affine Halfspaces under Log-Concave Marginals
papers.abstract: We give a proper constant-factor agnostic learner for affine halfspaces under full-dimensional log-concave marginals. For arbitrary binary labels, the algorithm uses independent labeled samples and returns a single affine halfspace with error at most $C\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$. Its sample and real-arithmetic complexity are polynomial in dimension, inverse accuracy, and the logarithm of the reciprocal failure probability. The mean and covariance of the marginal need not be known, and the sample complexity can be made linear in this logarithmic confidence factor. The main geometric result compares global disagreement with disagreement on a balanced restriction: for a minority halfspace of mass $p$, global disagreement is within universal constant factors of $p$ times conditional disagreement, provided the latter is sufficiently small. To construct the restriction from noisy labels, we estimate the minority cap's mean and covariance robustly, approximately minimize the classical zonoid-depth dual objective, and expand a superlevel set to a marginal quantile. The disagreement comparison cancels the noise amplification caused by conditioning and allows the learned halfspace to be used on the entire space. The analysis combines degree-four sum-of-squares moment bounds for log-concave laws with a translation-based reduction from balanced affine learning to homogeneous halfspace learning.
papers.summary: The authors give a proper agnostic learner for affine halfspaces under full-dimensional log-concave marginals: for arbitrary binary labels it returns a single affine halfspace with **error at most C·OPT + ε**, using polynomial sample and arithmetic complexity and without knowing the marginal's mean or covariance. The key geometric result shows that, for a minority halfspace of mass p, global disagreement is within constant factors of p times the disagreement on a balanced restriction, which cancels the noise amplification caused by conditioning. The algorithm builds this restriction from noisy labels through robust moment estimation and zonoid-depth optimization, and the analysis relies on degree-four sum-of-squares moment bounds together with a reduction from affine to homogeneous halfspace learning.

papers.title: Sparse Internal Control of Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly used in text generation, decision support, and automated interaction, creating a need for localized, reversible, and selective control of their behavior. Activation steering demonstrates that internal interventions can alter the behavior of frozen models, but how to select and evaluate compact, multi-site control interfaces remains an open question. I introduce sparse internal control, a framework for steering target behavior by applying inference-time interventions to a small set of internal model nodes. A local target-controllability formulation characterizes candidate site--direction pairs by their behavioral effects and specifies constraints on target recovery, off-target preservation, and intervention energy. Two complementary selectors instantiate this formulation: Driver-OMP selects nodes for sparse reconstruction of a desired behavioral displacement, while Coverage-Driver favors stable coverage across prompts. I propose a six-axis control-evaluation protocol measuring reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse. Exploratory experiments on indirect object identification, MMLU multiple-choice question answering, sentiment steering, and refusal steering provide evidence for the feasibility of steering task-defined behavior through sparse internal interventions. The six-axis evaluation characterizes these interventions beyond target movement, revealing distinct control properties that depend on the task and available direction information. Together, the formulation, reference algorithms, and evaluation protocol provide a foundation for the systematic study and development of internal control methods for language models.
papers.summary: Activation steering can change the behavior of a frozen language model, but there is no systematic way to choose and evaluate small sets of intervention sites. The author introduces `sparse internal control`, a formulation that scores candidate site and direction pairs under constraints on target recovery, off-target preservation and intervention energy, with two selectors, `Driver-OMP` and `Coverage-Driver`. The paper also proposes a **six-axis evaluation protocol covering reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation and held-out reuse**. Exploratory experiments on indirect object identification, `MMLU`, sentiment steering and refusal steering suggest that sparse interventions can steer these behaviors, and that their control properties depend on the task.

papers.title: Benchmarking Unsupervised Jamming Detection in 5G Open RAN
papers.abstract: Radio Frequency (RF) jamming threatens fifth-generation (5G) networks. Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN) telemetry enables jamming detection without dedicated spectrum monitoring equipment, but labeled attack data are rarely available across deployments, motivating unsupervised detectors. Comparing such detectors across algorithmic families, however, remains difficult without ground-truth labels. This paper benchmarks statistical and reconstruction-based unsupervised jamming detectors using a symmetric evaluation interface that combines detection confidence and temporal interval coherence into a detector-independent composite score. We compare a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) detector against Vanilla, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Variational Autoencoder (VAE) baselines on Key Performance Indicator (KPI) telemetry from ten heterogeneous 5G environments with fixed and variable jamming bursts and dynamic jammer gains. Under leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation, SEM achieves a mean composite score of 0.906, compared with 0.688 for the best autoencoder (AE) per fold. Ground-truth validation yields a mean F1-score of 0.918 for SEM, compared with 0.521 for the best AE variant. The composite ranks SEM first in all environments, consistent with F1 rankings. However, in both within-trace and cross-trace evaluation, it fails for detectors that flag far fewer samples than the jamming prevalence, indicating that rankings are reliable only when detection rate matches the expected prevalence.
papers.summary: Unsupervised jamming detectors for 5G Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN) telemetry are hard to compare without ground-truth labels. The authors benchmark a Statistical Ensemble Method (`SEM`) detector against vanilla, Long Short-Term Memory (`LSTM`) and Variational Autoencoder (`VAE`) baselines on KPI telemetry from ten 5G environments, using a label-free composite score that combines detection confidence with temporal coherence. Under leave-one-out evaluation, `SEM` reaches **a mean ground-truth F1 of 0.918 compared with 0.521 for the best autoencoder**, and the composite score ranks it first in every environment. However, the composite score fails for detectors that flag far fewer samples than the true jamming prevalence, so its rankings are reliable only when detection rates match the expected prevalence.

papers.title: Aligning Training and Rollout Policies for End-to-End FP4 RL on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.abstract: In this work, we study end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models. Recent work on FP4 RL has introduced effective recovery recipes that restore accuracy under aggressive low-precision quantization for dense models, but we find that the same approach yields no improvement over the naive FP4 baseline in the MoE setting. We conduct an in-depth study to understand why. Our analysis identifies the root cause in the routing mechanism unique to MoE: because the router makes discrete expert-selection decisions, training-inference policy alignment becomes acutely sensitive to whether the same recovery technique is applied symmetrically on the training and inference sides. When an asymmetric recipe is used-including the dense-model approach, which corrects only the rollout-training-inference alignment deteriorates sharply, as measured by the Pearson correlation coefficient between training and inference probabilities, and router selection matching rates. Building on this finding, we propose MoEResQ, a quantization-recovery recipe for MoE RL post-training that enforces symmetry between the training- and inference-side corrections. MoEResQ restores training-inference alignment and substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision, establishing symmetric recovery as the key principle in FP4 RL for MoE models.
papers.summary: The authors study end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning post-training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models and find that recovery recipes that work for dense models give no gain over naive FP4 here. The cause is the router's discrete expert choices: when quantization corrections are applied only on the rollout side, the probabilities and expert selections during training and inference drift apart sharply. Their recipe, `MoEResQ`, applies the corrections symmetrically on both sides, restores training-inference alignment and **substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Low-bit (FP4) quantization makes RL post-training cheaper. However, the residual-correction method that recovers accuracy for dense LLMs (`RolloutResQ`) fails on Mixture-of-Experts models. The router's discrete top-k expert choice turns small numerical differences between training and rollout into different expert selections. The proposed `MoEResQ` fixes this by applying the same residual correction on both the training side and the rollout side, so the two policies stay aligned.

- `MoEResQ` splits each FP4 linear layer's computation in two: one product with the quantized activation and a second with its quantized leftover error, using the same correction in rollout and in the training forward pass. It also applies the correction to the output gradients and inputs in the backward pass, while keeping the routers (under 0.5% of parameters) in `BF16`.
- On `Qwen3-30B-A3B` trained with `GRPO` on `DAPO-Math-17K` in `HiF4`, asymmetric `RolloutResQ` scores *below* the naive FP4 baseline on three of four benchmarks; for example, `AMC23` drops to 62.34 against 65.23 for plain FP4 and 85.10 for BF16.
- Alignment metrics explain the failure: correcting only one side leaves the correlation between training and inference probabilities near FP4's 0.94. Correcting both sides restores it to **0.994** (BF16 is 0.995) and brings middle-layer exact top-k expert matches back from about 0.62 to about 0.87.
- Quantizing both attention and expert layers, `MoEResQ` narrows the gap to BF16 from 19.87 to **0.65 points** on `AMC23` and from 24.27 to 3.75 points on `AIME24`. Quantizing only the expert layers (up to 94.66% of parameters) brings every benchmark within **1.5 points** of BF16.
- All experiments use simulated quantization on one model and on math benchmarks only, with no measured speed or memory gains, so the efficiency benefit is assumed rather than shown.

papers.title: Spin Spherical Fourier Neural Operators: Efficient Equivariant Learning for Vector and Spin Fields on the Sphere
papers.abstract: Many fields of physical interest on the sphere, such as wind, the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background and the shear of weak gravitational lensing, are spin fields, whose values change phase when the local frame rotates. We extend spherical Fourier neural operators (SFNOs) to fields of any spin, through lifted spherical convolutions that are exactly rotationally equivariant. Lifting spin fields to Mackey functions on the rotation group provides the conceptual framework, while computation is performed exactly and efficiently through their harmonic representation and by appealing to sampling theorems on the sphere and rotation group. We construct spin SFNOs (S$^2$FNOs) from these building blocks. We demonstrate empirically that rotational equivariance holds to machine precision for these layers. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on existing benchmarks, and introduce new benchmarks on which spin-aware models outperform their scalar counterparts.
papers.summary: Many physical fields on the sphere, such as wind, cosmic microwave background polarization and weak-lensing shear, are spin fields whose values change phase when the local frame rotates. The authors extend spherical Fourier neural operators to fields of any spin, building spin SFNOs (`S2FNO`) from lifted spherical convolutions that are exactly rotationally equivariant and are computed efficiently in harmonic space using sampling theorems on the sphere and the rotation group. Equivariance holds **to machine precision**, the models reach state-of-the-art results on existing benchmarks, and on new spin-field benchmarks they outperform scalar counterparts.

papers.title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
papers.summary: `Aero-VPA` is a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for quadrotor navigation on edge hardware. It avoids the many sequential decoding passes of autoregressive Vision-Language-Action models by combining a compact RGB-D Vision Transformer, an ensemble latent predictor trained without pixel reconstruction, and a two-step Conditional Flow Matching action head. In PX4 software-in-the-loop forest missions, behaviour cloning failed on every mission because the policy copied its last command, and `DAgger` plateaued at 11-21% success. A map-free runtime safety shield **raised success from 21.1% to 52.2% and cut crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%** on 180 paired missions, though timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%.

papers.title: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly act on information retrieved from public sources they treat as credible, which turns a manipulated recommendation into a transaction, a dependency, or a decision with physical consequences. The security literature models this threat as instruction injection, in which an adversary writes a command into retrieved content and deployed defenses learn to recognize command syntax. We show that an attacker can instead steer an agent through the agent's own harm-avoidance. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to disqualify the legitimate options and select the attacker's target by its own reasoning, with no command for a detector to recognize. We call this voluntary servitude. These payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), and deployed injection detectors score them as benign, so behind a filter they are 1.7-4.4x more effective. We measure this at the generation stage across six models and ten consumer-service domains, for three attack families, and show that it transfers to production browser agents, outperforming instruction injection, and to a retrieval pipeline (1.0-57.0% end-to-end success, depending on the retriever). We then show that a corroboration requirement added to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. With the requirement in place, the agent still reads the planted hazard and no longer acts on it.
papers.summary: Security work on LLM agents usually models manipulation as instruction injection, and deployed defenses learn to recognize command syntax. The authors show that an attacker can instead exploit the agent's own harm-avoidance: a single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to rule out legitimate options and pick the attacker's target by its own reasoning, which they call `voluntary servitude`. Across six models and ten consumer-service domains these payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), but injection detectors score them as benign, so they are **1.7-4.4x more effective behind a filter**, and the attack transfers to production browser agents and to retrieval pipelines. Adding a corroboration requirement to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining.

papers.title: SWAP-INR: Implicit Neural Representation with Switchable Attention Paths for Time-varying Multivariate Scientific Data Compression
papers.abstract: Visualizing multivariate scientific simulation data is essential for understanding complex physical phenomena, yet the massive scale of such data imposes a severe storage bottleneck in high-performance computing environments. Implicit neural representations (INRs) have emerged as a promising continuous alternative to traditional lossy compressors, but existing methods struggle to explicitly capture cross-variable interactions and to adapt to the diverse spectral characteristics of physical variables. To address these limitations, we propose SWAP-INR, an architecture for high-fidelity compression of multivariate, time-varying simulation data. SWAP-INR introduces two key components: (1) The switchable attention path (SWAP) module explicitly models cross-variable interactions through a cross-variable attention layer, then routes each variable to an attention or non-attention path by a deterministic, loss-driven criterion, and prunes the inactive layers for structural compression. (2) The adaptability amplification SIREN (A2-SIREN) replaces rigid frequency scaling with channel-wise learnable modulation, adapting to heterogeneous physical features with negligible overhead. Combined with post-training 16-bit quantization, SWAP-INR achieves state-of-the-art performance on small modular reactor (SMR) datasets and remains competitive on public physics simulation datasets, while maintaining a constrained memory footprint. Our code is https://github.com/hvcl/SWAP-INR.
papers.summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) can compress large scientific simulation outputs, but existing methods struggle to capture interactions between variables and the different frequency content of each variable. `SWAP-INR` adds a cross-variable attention layer, routes each variable through an attention or non-attention path according to a loss-based criterion and prunes the inactive layers, and replaces fixed SIREN frequency scaling with learnable per-channel modulation (`A2-SIREN`). With 16-bit post-training quantization it achieves **state-of-the-art compression quality on small modular reactor datasets** and remains competitive on public physics simulation datasets.

papers.title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
papers.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.
papers.summary: Language models are usually accurate at long arithmetic, but that accuracy is estimated from samples and gives no guarantee on unseen inputs. In `Sketchpad`, `Qwen3.5-0.8B` with a low-rank adapter carries out arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet: each forward pass sees a three-cell view and emits one step, while a fixed runtime moves the view without writing any result digits. The authors prove in `Lean` that the model is **exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on a finite set of views**, and all 2,446 views pass on a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model handles arbitrary-length addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, square roots and GCDs, solving 220 of 220 large-number problems versus 217 for the strongest of ten other models compared, and it powers a symbolic polynomial solver.

papers.title: Near-Zero Token Embeddings Silently Stall Training in Gated Sequence Models
papers.abstract: Among 291 surveyed open-weight language model repositories (280 distinct embedding tables), 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints (20/38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below $10^{-6}$, compared with 0% of weight-tied models. Such near-zero rows can arise during pretraining when unseen rare or template tokens receive zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings. In tested Transformer configurations, non-initial positions or a BOS token prevent this failure mode. In gated sequence models (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, xLSTM), a near-zero token can amplify input-embedding gradients by more than 30 orders of magnitude (up to 35). At zero input, current-token readout factors (SiLU gates or linear queries) vanish, suppressing historical-state readout. Residual RMS values can then fall below the square root of the RMSNorm floor across consecutive layers, causing Pre-RMSNorm to amplify backward gradients by up to $10^3$ per layer. When a gradient entry exceeds $1.84 \times 10^{19}$, FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer, and FSDP2 can overflow to infinity and zero the current batch's gradients. In Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, this discards updates on approximately 20% of steps and leaves triggered rows frozen. We propose two remedies. For released checkpoints, GroupClip decouples input-embedding clipping using a 64-bit or rescaled norm; its rescaled implementation eliminates update loss and heals triggered rows in one step with negligible measured end-to-end overhead. For pretraining, GateFloor ($\mathrm{SiLU}(z) + \delta$, $\delta \in [0.01, 0.1]$) keeps the gate positive at zero input, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude in experiments up to 370M parameters, with perplexity comparable to the baseline.
papers.summary: In a survey of open-weight checkpoints, 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid models contain reachable input embeddings with norms below 1e-6, a side effect of weight decay shrinking embeddings for tokens that never receive gradients. In gated sequence models such as `Mamba`, `Gated DeltaNet` and `xLSTM`, such a near-zero token can amplify gradients by up to 35 orders of magnitude through vanishing gates and Pre-RMSNorm, until FP32 global-norm clipping in `PyTorch`, `Hugging Face Trainer` and `FSDP2` overflows to infinity and silently zeroes the batch's gradients. In continual pretraining of `Nemotron-3-Nano-4B` on Telugu, this **discarded updates on roughly 20% of steps**. The authors propose `GroupClip`, which clips input embeddings separately with a 64-bit or rescaled norm, for released checkpoints, and `GateFloor`, which adds a small offset to the SiLU gate, for pretraining.

papers.title: SaMA: Morpho Adaptation via Asymmetric Expansion of Kronecker Product
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has attracted significant attention in the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) landscape. However, its design suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, its invariance manifold induces flat directions in the loss landscape, creating an optimization bottleneck for adaptive optimizers. Second, its effective rank scales only linearly with the parameter budget. In this paper, we propose Scalable Morpho Adaptation (SaMA), a PEFT method grounded in a principled generalization of the Kronecker product. By relaxing the shared-block constraint in the perfect-shuffle factorization, SaMA spans from low to full rank and achieves a practical rank that scales quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full-rank. Furthermore, we show that its invariance manifold collapses to a diagonal group, making it structurally more optimizer-friendly. Empirically, SaMA consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks while being more parameter-efficient.
papers.summary: Low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`) has flat directions in its loss landscape that slow adaptive optimizers, and its effective rank grows only linearly with the parameter budget. `SaMA` (Scalable Morpho Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that generalizes the Kronecker product by relaxing the shared-block constraint in its perfect-shuffle factorization. Its **practical rank grows quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full rank**, and its invariance set reduces to a diagonal group, which makes it easier to optimize. It outperforms strong parameter-efficient baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks while using fewer parameters.

papers.title: Theoretical Analysis of Muon on Transformers for Next-Token Prediction
papers.abstract: Muon has recently shown strong empirical performance in training Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), yet its optimization dynamics remain poorly understood from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we analyze the training dynamics of Muon for next-token prediction (NTP) in Transformers. The training procedure consists of two phases: the preprocessing phase learns the output-value component, while the main phase learns the key-query component. For the preprocessing phase, we characterize the optimization trajectory exactly and show that the normalized spectral margin is optimal after each update. For the main phase, we establish nonasymptotic convergence rates for the training loss and the normalized margin gap under softmax attention. These results suggest that Muon's update rule can help models efficiently learn which tokens matter for prediction, offering a possible explanation for its strong performance in large language model training. The learned weight structure also yields a generalization guarantee for unseen contexts. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical insights with experiments on next-token prediction tasks.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer performs well when training Transformer language models, but its dynamics are poorly understood. The authors analyze `Muon` on next-token prediction in two phases: a preprocessing phase that learns the output-value weights, where they characterize the trajectory exactly and show that the normalized spectral margin is optimal after every update, and a main phase that learns the key-query weights, where they prove **nonasymptotic convergence rates under softmax attention**. The results suggest that `Muon` helps models learn efficiently which tokens matter for prediction, and the learned weight structure yields a generalization guarantee for unseen contexts, which experiments support.

papers.title: Hierarchical Intelligent Evolutionary Optimization for UAV-Assisted NOMA-MEC Systems
papers.abstract: The integration of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), mobile edge computing (MEC) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) provides an effective solution for computation-intensive and latency-sensitive services in infrastructure-deficient environments. However, the joint optimization of UAV trajectories, task offloading, communication and computing resources under heterogeneous task priorities results in a highly coupled mixed-integer non-convex problem. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Hierarchical Intelligent Evolutionary Algorithm (HIEA) for priority-aware multi-UAV cooperative NOMA-MEC networks, which integrates multi-head deep Q-network (MH-DQN)-based intelligent decision generation, communication-aware initialization, adaptive evolutionary exploration and successive convex approximation (SCA)-based precision refinement. Specifically, a novel communication-aware initialization mechanism, termed Channel Quality Indicator (CQI)-guided Load-Aware Trajectory Initialization (CQI-LATI), is designed to incorporate CQI and task workload characteristics into evolutionary population construction, generating high-quality and diversity-preserving initial populations. Theoretical analysis characterizes HIEA's search-space reduction, the quality-diversity trade-off of CQI-guided initialization, and the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of SCA refinement, and extensive simulations demonstrate that HIEA outperforms benchmark schemes, with gains of up to 6.5% in throughput, 13.6% in task completion rate and 15.3% in energy efficiency.
papers.summary: Jointly optimizing drone trajectories, task offloading and radio and computing resources in UAV-assisted mobile edge computing networks with non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA-MEC) is a coupled mixed-integer non-convex problem. The proposed Hierarchical Intelligent Evolutionary Algorithm (`HIEA`) combines decisions from a multi-head deep Q-network, a population initialization guided by channel quality and workload (`CQI-LATI`), adaptive evolutionary search, and refinement by successive convex approximation. In simulations it improves on benchmark schemes by **up to 6.5% in throughput, 13.6% in task completion rate and 15.3% in energy efficiency**.

papers.title: KeyWise: Efficient Video-Only Piano Transcription with a Lightweight Per-Key Architecture
papers.abstract: Audio-based piano transcription is hampered by the sustain pedal and by noisy or missing soundtracks, problems that video-only transcription avoids, since a top-view video shows directly when each key is pressed and released. Most visual transcription networks, however, describe the whole keyboard with one global feature vector and must learn where each key is. In this paper, we propose KeyWise, a lightweight per-key architecture that exploits the known geometry of the keyboard instead of learning it. The rectified keyboard is divided into 88 equal tiles that serve as regions of interest (ROIs), and one small recurrent network, shared by all keys, follows each key over time. On PianoVAM, KeyWise reaches the onset accuracy of the state-of-the-art V2N (95.0% vs. 94.7% onset F1 at 50 ms and 97.8% vs. 97.0% at 100 ms) with 1.3 M instead of 28.2 M parameters, and it runs 4.7 times faster on the same GPU. At 100 ms, it is also significantly more accurate when the key releases (97.0% vs. 95.5% F1) or the velocities (89.4% vs. 84.5% F1) must be correct as well. On PianoYT, KeyWise pre-trained on PianoVAM reaches 69.4% onset F1 at 100 ms, comparable to the best published result, although it needs fine-tuning for new recording conditions.
papers.summary: Video-only piano transcription avoids the sustain-pedal and missing-audio problems of audio-based methods, but most visual models describe the whole keyboard with one global feature vector and must learn where each key is. `KeyWise` uses the known keyboard geometry instead, splitting the rectified keyboard into 88 tiles and tracking each key over time with one small recurrent network shared by all keys. On `PianoVAM` it matches the state-of-the-art `V2N` onset accuracy **with 1.3M instead of 28.2M parameters, running 4.7x faster**, and it is more accurate when releases or velocities must also be correct. On `PianoYT` it reaches results comparable to the best published ones but needs fine-tuning for new recording conditions.

papers.title: Bridging CLIP with DINO: Cross-Modal Information Maximization for Online Test-Time Adaptation
papers.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP enable zero-shot classification from arbitrary class names, but under test-time corruptions, their visual encoder projects distorted features onto incorrect textual anchors with high confidence: a phenomenon we term modality bias. Standard entropy minimization reinforces these overconfident errors, which creates a confirmation-bias loop and collapses the predicted label distribution. We propose an online test-time adaptation (TTA) method that breaks this loop at three levels. At the representation level, a frozen self-supervised backbone (e.g., DINO v2) is combined with CLIP through a cross-covariance logit ensemble. CLIP text prototypes are projected into the feature space of this text-free backbone, so the self-supervised branch classifies native image features and is less affected by the text bias of CLIP. At the optimization level, a gated test-time information-maximization objective pairs per-sample sharpening with batch-level diversity, while an adaptive gate excludes unreliable samples from the gradient. At the prediction level, an online logit adjustment corrects the residual class-distribution skew. CDIM outperforms the compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on ImageNet-C, CIFAR10-C, and CIFAR100-C, and remains competitive in continual and mixed-domain TTA. Extensive analyses and ablation studies verify the contribution of each of its components. Our code is available at https://github.com/B1ueC1oud/CDIM
papers.summary: Under image corruptions, `CLIP`'s visual encoder confidently maps distorted features to the wrong text anchors, and entropy minimization during test-time adaptation (TTA) reinforces these errors until the predicted label distribution collapses. `CDIM` addresses this at three levels: it ensembles `CLIP` with a frozen self-supervised backbone such as `DINOv2` by projecting text prototypes into that backbone's feature space, it uses a gated information-maximization objective that leaves unreliable samples out of the gradient, and it applies an online logit adjustment to correct class skew. It **outperforms the compared CLIP-based online TTA methods on `ImageNet-C`, `CIFAR10-C` and `CIFAR100-C`** and remains competitive in continual and mixed-domain settings.

papers.title: Hybrid Particle-Voxel Dynamics for Multimodal 3D World Simulation
papers.abstract: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.
papers.summary: Many action-conditioned world models for robotics predict future frames in 2D image space, which makes it hard to stay consistent across viewpoints and over long interactions. `3D World Simulator` compresses point clouds into compact voxel latents with a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder and predicts how those latents evolve under robot actions, jointly producing appearance, geometry and tactile signals from one 3D representation.
