We consider $n$ components with joint mean-squared smoothness $L$ and condition number $\kappa$, started from a point with primal gap at most $\Delta$ and joint gradient norm at most $\sqrt{2L\Delta}$. For $\varepsilon^2/(L\Delta)$ below a universal constant, every randomized adaptive algorithm with exact component values, gradients, and proximal responses needs $\Omega(n+\min\{\sqrt n\,\kappa,n^{3/4}\sqrt\kappa\}L\Delta/\varepsilon^2)$ component queries in the worst case to find an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of the value function. A method using only component gradients attains this rate up to a factor $\log^2(2+\kappa)$, including initialization. Zhou (arXiv:2610.04944) concurrently proves the same rate for zero-respecting first-order methods. In our hard instances, every component admits proximal steps with the same step sizes, and a response for a component reveals hidden directions only up to the first one assigned to another component.
papers.summary: Finite-sum nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problems, which arise in adversarial training and distributionally robust learning, previously had complexity lower bounds only for restricted algorithm classes. Those bounds left open whether exact proximal steps on individual components could help, since a proximal step can reveal directions that gradients do not. The authors prove that **neither unrestricted adaptivity nor exact proximal access improves the polynomial query complexity**, establishing an Ω(n + min{√n·κ, n^{3/4}√κ}·LΔ/ε²) lower bound for any randomized adaptive algorithm. A method using only component gradients matches this rate up to a log² factor in the condition number κ.

papers.title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This work investigates the application of Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks to the binary classification of sleep-disordered breathing events in time-series data, aiming to distinguish between apneic and normal breathing episodes. A variational classical--quantum architecture is proposed and evaluated against classical Recurrent Neural Network models. Experiments were conducted on multiple real-world datasets with varying levels of complexity to assess the strengths and limitations of the quantum approach. In the comparative analysis, both classical and quantum models showed comparable performance. The quantum model achieved superior performance on the smallest dataset, while yielding slightly weaker results in the most complex setting. However, the quantum approach exhibited notable strengths, such as competitive performance despite a drastically reduced parameter count and low-qubit regime, as well as good generalization capabilities. These results suggest that, despite current hardware and algorithmic limitations, variational quantum recurrent models represent a promising alternative for time-series classification as Quantum Computing technologies continue to mature.
papers.summary: A hybrid classical-quantum recurrent neural network built on variational quantum circuits is applied to classifying breathing episodes as apneic or normal, and compared against classical recurrent networks on several real-world datasets of varying complexity. **Overall, the quantum and classical models performed comparably.** The quantum model did better on the smallest dataset and slightly worse on the most complex one, while using far fewer parameters and only a few qubits.

papers.title: Feeling of Knowing in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Post-training updates change what large language models (LLMs) can answer, but may leave their answerability judgments misaligned. We study this knowledge-judgment desynchronization through functional feeling of knowing (FoK), which supports selective generation, retrieval triggering, and model routing without implying subjective experience. We propose two trainable channels: a knowledge channel that changes answerability and a FoK channel that judges the current knowledge state. Three stages train them: on-policy supervised fine-tuning (OP-SFT) updates knowledge from corrected on-policy answers; knowledge-delta FoK training (K$\Delta$-FT) adapts judgments across intermediate knowledge states; and FoK-guided policy optimization (FGPO) trains the subsequent answer or explanation. Factual-QA experiments, cross-dataset evaluation, and three sequential updates show that explicit FoK alignment improves judgment quality on updated knowledge. MMLU and ARC-Easy separately assess capability preservation.
papers.summary: Post-training updates change which questions a large language model (LLM) can answer, but its own judgments about what it can answer may not update with them. The authors frame this as a mismatch between knowledge and a functional feeling of knowing (FoK), which supports selective generation, deciding when to retrieve, and model routing, without implying subjective experience. They train two channels in three stages: on-policy supervised fine-tuning (`OP-SFT`) updates knowledge, knowledge-delta FoK training (`KΔ-FT`) adapts answerability judgments across intermediate knowledge states, and FoK-guided policy optimization (`FGPO`) trains the answer or explanation that follows. On factual question answering, across datasets and over three sequential updates, **explicitly aligning FoK improves judgment quality on updated knowledge**, and `MMLU` and `ARC-Easy` are used to check that general capability is preserved.

papers.title: Anomaly Detection on Resource-Constrained Devices with Reservoir Computing
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection at the edge requires the deployment of models that achieve competitive performance, while minimizing computational cost and memory footprint. In this article, we investigate the suitability of the Mahalanobis Distance of Reservoir States (MDRS), an unsupervised time-series anomaly detection method, for resource-constrained devices and propose two optimizations to reduce its computational requirements. Specifically, we replace random reservoir connectivity (MDRS-Rand) with a circular shift (MDRS-Circ) and show that the anomaly score for an entire time series can be computed from the final reservoir state alone. Furthermore, we show that exploiting the reservoir's temporal memory enables more efficient input preprocessing, further reducing computational cost. We evaluate the MDRS variants on the MLPerf Tiny anomaly detection benchmark against the reference autoencoder and other anomaly detection methods, and deploy their inference kernels on a NUCLEO-F401RE microcontroller to assess latency, estimate energy consumption, and measure memory footprint. Among the evaluated methods, only MDRS and the autoencoder meet the benchmark's performance target, with MDRS requiring fewer operations and smaller models. With optimized preprocessing, MDRS achieves an ROC AUC of 0.869, a model size of 24 KB, an estimated energy consumption of 24 uJ per inference, and a latency of 0.32 ms, corresponding to a 75.9x speedup over the autoencoder with standard preprocessing.
papers.summary: The authors adapt `MDRS` (Mahalanobis Distance of Reservoir States), an unsupervised time-series anomaly detector based on reservoir computing, for microcontroller-class devices. They replace random reservoir connectivity with a circular shift (`MDRS-Circ`), show that the anomaly score for a whole series can be computed from the final reservoir state alone, and use the reservoir's temporal memory to make input preprocessing cheaper. On the `MLPerf Tiny` anomaly detection benchmark, only `MDRS` and the reference autoencoder meet the performance target, and `MDRS` needs fewer operations and a smaller model. Deployed on a `NUCLEO-F401RE` board, it reaches an ROC AUC of 0.869 with a 24 KB model, about 24 µJ per inference and 0.32 ms latency, **a 75.9x speedup over the autoencoder with standard preprocessing**.

papers.title: Found by Search, Broken by a Shortcut: Transfer and Tampering of Searched Intrinsic Rewards
papers.abstract: Can a search over innate drives find intrinsic rewards that help a reinforcement-learning agent learn, transfer to a task it never saw, and resist an exploit that was absent during the search? Each candidate reward combines four generic events (a new view, a pickup, a drop and a toggle), each with a weight, a relief and a refill rate. We ran three pre-registered stages; the search protocol was locked in a public, timestamped commit before any search result existed. CMA-ES and an equal-budget random search used 1,560 PPO training runs, and the final evaluation and tamper test used 340. On the held-out task, KeyCorridorS3R2, the CMA-ES-selected reward (E) beat task-only PPO, episodic novelty and the random-search-selected reward (R) in all 3 registered comparisons, all of them meaningful by the registered size rule. Among these generic rewards E transferred best; the earlier paper's satiation reward, which on this task is given hand-wired key and locked-door events, did better (20 of 20 seeds solved against 4 of 20; descriptive). On UnlockPickup, where that reward uses generic events, E's mean area exceeded it by 0.276 (descriptive). On the training tasks there was no registered difference between E and R: both E-over-R tests missed. A free reset action, absent during the search, collapsed E's learning on DoorKey-8x8 (mean area 0.829 without it, 0.136 with it; registered) to below task-only PPO (descriptive). The searched drives helped on every task tested, but a reward given task-specific events did better on the held-out task, and selection gave E no protection against an exploit absent from the search.
papers.summary: A pre-registered study asks whether intrinsic rewards found by search can help a reinforcement-learning agent learn, transfer to an unseen task, and resist an exploit that was absent during the search. Each candidate reward weights four generic events (a new view, a pickup, a drop and a toggle), and `CMA-ES` is compared with an equal-budget random search over 1,560 `PPO` training runs. On the held-out `KeyCorridorS3R2` task, the `CMA-ES`-selected reward beat task-only `PPO`, episodic novelty and the randomly selected reward, though a prior hand-wired satiation reward that receives task-specific events did better. **Adding a free reset action that was absent during the search collapsed the searched reward's learning on `DoorKey-8x8` (mean area 0.829 down to 0.136)**, so selection offered no protection against the unseen exploit.

papers.title: DLER: Dual-Logit Experience Replay for Online Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Online continual learning aims to continuously train neural networks on a non-stationary data stream in a single pass. Rehearsal-based methods alleviate catastrophic forgetting by replaying stored samples, but the imbalance between current and previous data often leads to predictions biased toward current classes. Many approaches have been proposed to overcome the forgetting problem by correcting the bias; however, they still need to be improved in an online fashion. By decomposing the dot-product logits into an angle factor and a norm factor, our analysis reveals that the angle factor efficiently captures novel knowledge but is particularly susceptible to prediction bias, whereas the norm factor helps preserve historical knowledge. Based on these observations, we propose Dual-Logit Experience Replay (DLER), which exploits dual-logits for both model optimization and memory management. Specifically, DLER learns current samples using cosine logits and incorporates additional dot-product logits when replaying previous samples to mitigate prediction bias. To strengthen dual-logit learning under limited replay memory, an auxiliary supervised contrastive objective promotes angular compactness within each class, extending corrections learned from limited replay samples to other samples of the same class. Meanwhile, we introduce a memory update strategy that preferentially retains samples for which dot-product prediction assigns a higher probability to the correct class than cosine prediction, aligning sample selection with dual-logit training. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DLER, particularly under limited memory budgets.
papers.summary: Online continual learning trains a network in a single pass over a shifting data stream, and replay-based methods tend to bias predictions toward the newest classes. Splitting dot-product logits into an angle factor and a norm factor, the authors find that the angle captures new knowledge but is prone to this bias, while the norm helps preserve old knowledge. Their method, `DLER` (Dual-Logit Experience Replay), learns current samples with cosine logits and adds dot-product logits on replayed samples. It also uses a supervised contrastive objective that keeps each class angularly compact, and a memory update rule that keeps samples where the dot-product prediction outperforms the cosine one. Experiments on three datasets show gains, **particularly under limited memory budgets**.

papers.title: FourSight: Stable FP4 RL Post-Training via Sequence Filtering and Sparse Channel Compensation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training increasingly targets low-bit deployment, with NVFP4 weight-and activation quantization (W4A4) becoming the state-of-the-practice format. However, integrating NVFP4 into RL degrades rollout quality and amplifies cross-engine training-inference mismatch (TIM), destabilizing training. We show that these failures are concentrated rather than uniform - severely mismatched tail tokens concentrate in a few outlier sequences, while policy weights remain largely intact and quantization error concentrates in a few high-variance activation channels. Guided by this, we present FourSight, an algorithm-system co-design with two targeted solutions: TIM-aware sequence filtering that excludes drifted trajectories from policy updates, and sparse precision compensation that keeps only top-variance channels in BF16 while retaining native NVFP4 elsewhere. We further design a fused SpliceGEMM kernel with specialized prefill and decode datapaths to minimize overhead. FourSight sustains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality across models and engines, while improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76-2.60x and staying within 2.3% of FP4 step time up to 120B-scale models.
papers.summary: Using the `NVFP4` 4-bit weight-and-activation format during reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training degrades rollout quality and widens the training-inference mismatch (TIM) between engines, which destabilizes training. The authors find that these failures are concentrated: badly mismatched tokens cluster in a few outlier sequences, and quantization error clusters in a few high-variance activation channels. `FourSight` filters out drifted trajectories from policy updates, keeps only the top-variance channels in BF16, and adds a fused `SpliceGEMM` kernel with separate prefill and decode paths. It **sustains near-BF16 accuracy while improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76-2.60x**, and its step time stays within 2.3% of pure FP4 on models up to 120B parameters.

papers.title: Fault-tolerant shallow recurrent decoders for sparse sensing with missing sensor measurements
papers.abstract: Real-world sensing systems are inherently imperfect: sensors may fail, intermittently disconnect, operate with asynchronous sampling rates, and be subject to noise, leading to measurement streams that are irregular, incomplete, and heterogeneous. Nevertheless, sensing strategies for real-time state reconstruction typically assume synchronous and continuously active sensors, a constraint that substantially limits their applicability in operational environments. In this work, we introduce fault-tolerant sparse sensing strategies in the context of shallow recurrent decoders (SHRED) to enable high-dimensional state estimation from sparse, asynchronous, and missing sensor measurements. Specifically, we consider naive imputation strategies, fault-tolerant recurrent temporal encoders, and we introduce four different transformer-based masking mechanisms to make SHRED explicitly aware of sensor availability through the binary data-availability mask. Moreover, we further introduce a multi-step decoding training objective for SHRED, resulting in smoother latent trajectories and more robust predictions. Throughout a synthetic benchmark and three real-world problems in hydrodynamic and ocean modeling, we show that (i) transformer-based masking mechanisms outperform standard imputation techniques and fault-tolerant recurrent architectures, (ii) the multi-step decoding training objective enhances reconstruction fidelity and robustness in the presence of heterogeneous missing-data patterns, while (iii) the computational efficiency of SHRED is preserved, with no additional inference-time overhead.
papers.summary: Real sensor networks suffer failures, dropouts, asynchronous sampling and noise, yet methods for reconstructing a full system state from a few sensors usually assume clean, synchronous inputs. The authors make shallow recurrent decoders (`SHRED`) fault-tolerant by comparing naive imputation, fault-tolerant recurrent encoders, and four new transformer-based masking mechanisms that take a binary sensor-availability mask as input. They also add a multi-step decoding training objective that smooths latent trajectories. On a synthetic benchmark and three real hydrodynamic and ocean-modeling problems, **transformer-based masking outperforms imputation and fault-tolerant recurrent architectures** without adding inference-time cost.

papers.title: Attending to Memory Writes Reduces Seed Variability in Recurrent Length Generalization
papers.abstract: Recurrent memory requires learning useful updates, but attention added to assist learning can also compromise length generalization. We study bounded delta attention: causal attention over uncorrected update proposals whose bounded correction enters the recurrent update. Its implementation in TraceRelay combines additive phase recurrence with attention computed before a parallel scan. On prefix-supervised modulo-5, trained at lengths 1--40, three findings characterize its behavior at length 80. First, upper delta attention attains $70.81\pm8.26$% accuracy across seven seeds, versus $69.21\pm22.42$% for the local-attention recurrent baseline (mean $\pm$ sample SD): a 63.2% reduction in SD with a similar mean. Upper state attention also reduces variation, reaching $74.75\pm6.24$%, so this benefit is not unique to update-level attention. Disabling the upper delta correction retains $70.62\pm8.60$%. Second, blocking gradients at the delta-attention inputs changes accuracy to $65.25\pm12.40$% in the matched seven-seed comparison, increasing SD by 50.2%. It also delays a 99% validation threshold on average among the same six seeds that reach it; the 95% threshold is reached earlier on average with input-gradient blocking across all seven seeds. Third, lower delta attention exhibits substantially less extrapolation degradation than lower state attention: 62.60% versus 19.40%, against a 71.06% baseline. Removing its correction reduces accuracy to 22.56%; its advantage over lower state attention also persists under input-gradient blocking. These observations motivate bounded update-level attention as a recurrent learning scaffold, combining reduced seed variation with less severe degradation in a placement where state attention fails.
papers.summary: Adding attention to a recurrent memory can help it learn useful updates but can also hurt its ability to generalize to longer sequences. The authors propose bounded delta attention, implemented in `TraceRelay`, in which causal attention operates over proposed memory updates and a bounded correction feeds into the recurrent update. Trained on a modulo-5 task at lengths 1-40 and tested at length 80, upper-layer delta attention matches the baseline's mean accuracy (about 71%) while **cutting the standard deviation across seeds by 63.2%**, although state attention reduces variance similarly. Placed in the lower layer, delta attention degrades much less than state attention (62.6% versus 19.4% accuracy).

papers.title: Cool Graphs: Active Property Search Towards Quantum Nano-Refrigerators
papers.abstract: Nanodevices that absorb energy from their thermal environment can act as quantum refrigerators. Finding suitable configurations, however, is a needle-in-a-haystack problem: the many-body state space scales exponentially with the size of the device, where each candidate configuration requires an expensive quantum-chemical computation. We introduce a search framework that couples a Graph Variational Autoencoder (GVAE) with an uncertainty-driven Active Learning (AL) loop to efficiently identify energy-absorbing configurations in electronic junctions with a 2D "working material" to be optimized. The GVAE maps physical parameters - site energies, coupling matrices, temperature - into a smooth latent space that distinguishes cooling from dissipative parameter regimes, achieving a classification discriminability of $0.920 \pm 0.004$ on held-out configurations and $0.895 \pm 0.010$ on unseen extrapolation topologies. An AL pipeline based on Monte Carlo dropout then targets the decision boundary, iteratively selecting the candidates where the model is least certain for simulation. Over 32 AL cycles, the uncertainty-driven strategy discovers energy absorbing systems at rates consistently exceeding the random baseline across all tested topologies (where only 1.9-8.4% of configurations exhibit the desired property), providing a data-efficient pathway for navigating a combinatorically large design space. The learned latent space organizes configurations along physically interpretable axes, that correlate with underlying microscopic model parameters. This hints at the existence of "cooling coordinates" - low-dimensional, physically interpretable quantities separating cooling from non-cooling regimes. Our framework, thus, paves a new way towards effective cooling of nanoscale electronic information processing devices, to reduce the environmental footprint of high performance computing.
papers.summary: Finding nanodevice configurations that absorb heat from their environment and act as quantum refrigerators is a needle-in-a-haystack search, because every candidate needs an expensive quantum-chemical calculation. The authors pair a Graph Variational Autoencoder (`GVAE`), which embeds site energies, couplings and temperature into a latent space, with an active-learning loop that uses Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty to choose which configurations to simulate next. The `GVAE` separates cooling from dissipative regimes with a discriminability of 0.920 on held-out configurations, and **uncertainty-driven search finds cooling configurations faster than random sampling across all tested topologies**, even though only 1.9-8.4% of configurations have the property. The latent space also organizes along physically interpretable axes.

papers.title: MiCaDe: Online LiDAR-Camera Miscalibration Change Detection for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Reliable multi-sensor perception in autonomous vehicles requires accurate calibration between cameras and LiDAR. However, calibration drift is often unavoidable in long-term deployments: vibrations, thermal effects, and minor mechanical shocks may alter the relative pose between sensors, leading to systematic errors in downstream fusion tasks. We propose MiCaDe (Miscalibration Change Detection), an online solution detecting when the extrinsic LiDAR-camera calibration parameters are no longer accurate by means of sequential change detection. MiCaDe requires no calibration targets, or modification of the perception stack, providing low false-alarm rates with negligible computational overhead. Our key insight is that 3D and 2D bounding boxes produced by standard object detectors should remain geometrically consistent under correct calibration. By matching cross-modal detections, we derive geometric consistency metrics that serve as sensitive indicators of extrinsic drift. These metrics are aggregated into fixed-size batches and scored against a reference distribution, producing a likelihood stream that is monitored by a Change Point Model (CPM). Crucially, the CPM accumulates statistical evidence over time, enabling detection of subtle drifts that would otherwise go unnoticed. Experiments on multiple long-sequence datasets and on a real-world dataset with physically induced miscalibration confirm reliable detection under diverse conditions. Code available at: https://github.com/CarloSgaravatti/MiCaDe.
papers.summary: Over long deployments, vibration, heat and small shocks can shift the alignment between an autonomous vehicle's LiDAR and its cameras, which corrupts downstream sensor fusion. `MiCaDe` (Miscalibration Change Detection) detects this drift online, without calibration targets or changes to the perception stack, by checking whether 3D and 2D bounding boxes from standard object detectors stay geometrically consistent. Consistency metrics are batched, scored against a reference distribution, and monitored by a Change Point Model that accumulates evidence over time, so that **subtle drifts are caught with low false-alarm rates and negligible compute**. Experiments on several long-sequence datasets and a real-world dataset with physically induced miscalibration confirm reliable detection.

papers.title: Modulating Merging Strengths via Joint Loss Estimation for LoRA-based Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to adapt models to new tasks while preserving previously learned knowledge. Recently, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a representative Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method, has gained increasing attention in CL due to its efficiency and scalability. Several LoRA-based merging methods maintain a single inference model by scaling the newly learned LoRA update with one coefficient and merging it into the previous weights after each task. However, they usually control the whole update with a shared scalar factor, although different update elements may affect previous and current tasks in different ways. To address this issue, we propose Merging Strength Modulation via Joint Loss Estimation (M2LE). It consists of Hessian Information-guided Adaptive Merging (HIM) and Task Simulation Perturbation for Merging (TSP). Instead of searching for a global merge coefficient, HIM directly solves for the target merged update under a joint objective over previous and current tasks. Solving this objective gives an analytic solution that naturally takes the form of element-wise modulation over the current task LoRA update. To improve the stability of the learned update under subsequent merging, we introduce TSP which simulates different tasks interference. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that M2LE consistently outperforms existing PEFT-based continual learning methods. Code is available at https://github.com/bbdeeer/M2LE_NeurIPS2026.
papers.summary: Continual-learning methods based on Low-Rank Adaptation (`LoRA`) often merge each new task's update into the model using a single scaling coefficient, even though different elements of the update affect old and new tasks differently. `M2LE` (Merging Strength Modulation via Joint Loss Estimation) instead uses Hessian information to solve analytically for the merged update under a joint objective over previous and current tasks, which yields **element-wise modulation of the LoRA update instead of one global scalar**. A task-simulation perturbation step makes the update more robust to interference from later merges. Across multiple benchmarks, `M2LE` consistently outperforms existing parameter-efficient continual-learning methods.

papers.title: Deep Neural Operator Learning for stochastic heat equations and applications
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish a universal approximation theorem for solution operators of semilinear stochastic heat equations in spatial dimension \(d\ge2\), extending deep neural operator approximation results to SPDEs with distribution-valued Gaussian forcing. A smooth Fourier cutoff reduces the forcing to finitely many measurements, while Besov and Schauder estimates control the resulting solution error. The finite-dimensional solution map is then approximated by ReLU branch networks together with grid-based trunk functions, yielding explicit bounds on the numbers of forcing measurements and trunk functions and approximation in every finite stochastic moment. For linear equations, the reduction coincides with truncation of the first Wiener chaos. Lastly, as an application, we prove a high-probability local-in-time approximation theorem for stochastic Navier--Stokes equations, with finite measurements of both the initial condition and forcing and an explicit sensing rate.
papers.summary: The authors prove a universal approximation theorem for the solution operators of semilinear stochastic heat equations in two or more spatial dimensions, extending deep neural operator results to stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) driven by distribution-valued Gaussian forcing. A smooth Fourier cutoff reduces the forcing to finitely many measurements, and the resulting finite-dimensional solution map is approximated by `ReLU` branch networks with grid-based trunk functions, giving **explicit bounds on the number of measurements and trunk functions** and approximation in every finite stochastic moment. As an application, they prove a high-probability local-in-time approximation result for stochastic Navier-Stokes equations.

papers.title: ZEMA: confidence-calibrated signed descent with only one state
papers.abstract: Recent work characterizes the Adam optimizer as sign descent modulated by gradient uncertainty: the update is the sign of the batch gradient, scaled by how strongly the batch supports that sign. We apply this view directly and introduce ZEMA (Z-score Evidence Momentum Adaptation), which measures that support with a per-coordinate $z$-score computed from the per-example gradients in the current batch, converts it into a sign probability, and smooths the resulting update with a single exponential moving average. Because the probability is formed before smoothing rather than after, ZEMA keeps one state per parameter instead of Adam's two, at a $4.6$ increase in per-step time; the per-example variance it requires can also be estimated from a small fraction of the batch. In fine-tuning and pretraining experiments, ZEMA is competitive with Adam, reduces the variability of the validation loss, and in some settings recovers the sign of the full-dataset gradient more consistently. We close with two directions this opens: extending confidence adaptation beyond the sign geometry, to methods such as Muon, and to differentially private training.
papers.summary: Building on the view of `Adam` as sign descent scaled by gradient uncertainty, `ZEMA` (Z-score Evidence Momentum Adaptation) computes a per-coordinate z-score from per-example gradients in each batch, converts it into the probability that the gradient's sign is correct, and smooths the result with a single exponential moving average. Because the probability is computed before smoothing, **`ZEMA` needs only one state per parameter instead of Adam's two**, at a 4.6x increase in per-step time, and the per-example variance can be estimated from a small fraction of the batch. In fine-tuning and pretraining experiments it is competitive with `Adam`, reduces the variability of validation loss, and in some settings tracks the sign of the full-dataset gradient more consistently.

papers.title: Exact Selective Inference for Spectral Clustering via Piecewise-Constant Graph Perturbation
papers.abstract:
Cluster labels are often used twice: first to discover groups, and then to test whether the discovered groups differ. This double use of the data makes ordinary two-sample $p$-values anti-conservative. Selective inference fixes this by conditioning on the clustering event, but for spectral clustering the event appears difficult because the algorithm combines an affinity map, an eigendecomposition, and a rounding step.
  We show that, for spectral clustering based on unweighted $\varepsilon$- or $k$-nearest-neighbor graphs, the obstruction is the affinity construction rather than the eigendecomposition. Along the one-dimensional perturbation used by the truncated-$\chi$ selective test, graph changes occur only at finitely many real roots of data-dependent quadratic distance comparisons. Between these breakpoints, the graph, Laplacian spectrum, embedding, rounding, and reported cluster pair are deterministic functions of a finite graph state. Consequently, in real arithmetic and under a known-scale spherical Gaussian model, the selection set is an exact finite union of intervals, yielding finite-sample selective $p$-values for selected spectral-cluster pairs. The same argument gives feature-wise truncated-normal tests. We also record direct extensions to known feature covariance, eigengap-selected $K$, and auxiliary-coordinate graphs. We validate null and partial-null calibration, operational power, numerical sensitivity, and model-scope diagnostics, and give a working-model PBMC algorithmic illustration. Smooth kernels such as RBF affinities fall outside the finite-state guarantee.
papers.summary: Testing whether clusters differ, using the same data that discovered them, produces anti-conservative p-values, and selective inference corrects for this by conditioning on the clustering outcome, which has seemed intractable for spectral clustering. For spectral clustering on unweighted ε- or k-nearest-neighbor graphs, the authors show that along the test's one-dimensional perturbation the graph changes only at finitely many roots of quadratic distance comparisons, so everything downstream is piecewise constant. This makes the selection set **an exact finite union of intervals, yielding finite-sample selective p-values**, with extensions to known feature covariance, eigengap-selected cluster counts and feature-wise tests. The guarantee does not cover smooth kernels such as RBF affinities.

papers.title: Auditing Multi-Proxy Explanations of Web User Preferences: Identification Boundaries and Abstention
papers.abstract: Web systems infer user preferences from behavior, ratings, text, and LLM-generated profiles, yet explaining a proxy may reveal its measurement process rather than the preference of interest. We develop an audit framework distinguishing point identification, partial identification, and abstention relative to an explicit reference distribution. Under feature-dependent, arbitrarily signed proxy bias, a strict majority of uncontaminated proxy attributions lets the coordinatewise median recover latent-attribution support and direction and, with externally justified positive scales, magnitude. We prove this threshold sharp using response-valid indistinguishable worlds, characterize sharp minimax error and exact compatible-target sets under approximate cleanliness and scale uncertainty, and propagate clean-proxy attribution error. A frozen known-truth benchmark spans two response families, four proxy counts, all contamination counts, three bias strengths, and eleven methods, with a focal comparison confirmed on twenty unseen seeds. Under correct budgets, a direct attribution-tensor audit achieved 100% coverage, 95.40%-97.05% active-driver sign decisions, and no false signs. In a temporally separated Amazon study, median aggregation reduced comparator-relative conditional sign error for all four targets; six of eight prespecified target-metric contrasts had Bonferroni intervals excluding zero. A controlled real-covariate perturbation favored the median on the prespecified focal metric for all four targets. Compatible sets showed that the current proxy configuration rarely licensed strict-sign conclusions. Weak comparator calibration limits the Amazon evidence to fitted-surface alignment rather than latent-preference recovery.
papers.summary: Web systems infer user preferences from proxies such as behavior, ratings, text and LLM-generated profiles, but explaining a proxy may reveal how it was measured rather than the underlying preference. The authors build an audit framework that separates point identification, partial identification and abstention, and prove that **when a strict majority of proxy attributions is uncontaminated, the coordinatewise median recovers the sign and support of the latent attribution**, with this threshold shown to be sharp. On a known-truth benchmark the audit achieved full coverage and no false signs under correct budgets, and in an Amazon study median aggregation reduced sign error for all four targets. The authors note that weak calibration limits the Amazon evidence to fitted-surface alignment rather than true preference recovery.

papers.title: Unifying and Beyond the Theory of Pervasive Capability Degradation in LLM Post-training SFT from Feature Interference
papers.abstract: Pervasive Capability Degradation (PCD) refers to the phenomenon in which supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while adapting a large language model (LLM) to a target task, often erodes the general capabilities acquired during pre-training. Prevailing explanations attribute PCD to macroscopic distribution shift and therefore lack microscopic manipulability, leaving existing mitigation methods without a complete theoretical foundation. In this paper, we first develop a bottom-up geometric theory of PCD grounded in feature interference under superposition: narrow-domain SFT data disrupt the almost-orthogonal feature structure formed during pre-training, and the resulting interference drives activations across decision hyperplanes in the output Laguerre-Voronoi geometry, flipping predictions on general tasks. This theory unifies existing methods into six paradigms and reveals both the source of their efficacy and their theoretical limits. We then prove that cross-entropy under one-hot supervision cannot resolve PCD on its own, and accordingly propose the AEGIS loss, which directly constrains the drift of activation margins along all competing token directions, thereby decoupling interference suppression from task adaptation. Across 3 model families and 14 SFT tasks, AEGIS outperforms representative methods of every paradigm on target tasks and pervasive capabilities simultaneously, at only about 1.3 times the computational cost of standard SFT. Its generality, scalability, and mechanistic interpretability offer a new perspective on fully resolving PCD.
papers.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of a large language model on a narrow task often erodes its general capabilities, a phenomenon the authors call pervasive capability degradation. They explain it through feature interference under superposition: narrow SFT data disrupt the nearly orthogonal features learned in pre-training and push activations across decision boundaries, flipping predictions on general tasks. The theory groups existing mitigations into six paradigms and shows that one-hot cross-entropy alone cannot fix the problem. Their proposed `AEGIS` loss directly limits drift in activation margins along competing token directions, and across 3 model families and 14 SFT tasks it **beats representative methods on both target-task and general capability at about 1.3x the cost of standard SFT**.

papers.title: Can saliency maps flag chest radiograph classifier errors at a new hospital? An external validation study
papers.abstract: Saliency maps are offered as a safeguard for medical image classifiers, but whether they reveal individual errors at a new hospital remains largely untested. We trained a convolutional network and a vision transformer on NIH ChestX-ray14 and evaluated 303,768 decisions per model at the training hospital and at two external sites, in the USA and Vietnam, with radiologist-consensus labels. We scored each explanation by its anatomical enrichment, the area-normalized concentration of attribution in a segmented thoracic region, and tested whether it detects errors beyond the model's confidence. Grad-CAM localized findings less often than radiologists (hit rate at most 0.575 versus 0.888). Adding enrichment to a confidence-based error detector calibrated at the training hospital never raised its area under the curve by more than 0.011, and for the convolutional network the relation between enrichment and correctness reversed between hospitals, degrading the transferred detector. Model confidence, not saliency, should anchor deployment monitoring.
papers.summary: Saliency maps are often presented as a safeguard for medical image classifiers, so the authors test whether they flag individual errors when a model is used at a new hospital. They trained a convolutional network and a vision transformer on `NIH ChestX-ray14` and evaluated 303,768 decisions per model at the training hospital and two external sites in the USA and Vietnam, scoring explanations by how concentrated their attribution was in segmented thoracic regions. `Grad-CAM` localized findings less often than radiologists (hit rate at most 0.575 versus 0.888), and **adding saliency to a confidence-based error detector never improved its AUC by more than 0.011**, with the relationship reversing across hospitals for the convolutional network. The authors conclude that model confidence, not saliency, should anchor deployment monitoring.

papers.title: Rethinking GA2Ms: performance and out-of-distribution generalisation
papers.abstract: Generalised Additive Models (GAMs) are a cornerstone of interpretable machine learning, offering transparent predictions through structured additive decompositions. Despite advances from classical GAMs to modern neural and spline-based variants, two notable gaps remain. First, comprehensive benchmarking of spline-based GAMs on large-scale tabular learning tasks, the dominant modality in applied settings, is lacking. Second, their robustness under distribution shift, a setting where structured inductive biases should confer advantages, remains unexplored. We propose a multi-resolution, higher-order Composite Generalised Additive Model (CoGA2M) and evaluate it on the TALENT benchmark suite. CoGA2M ranks in the top third across all baselines (29 for regression, 32 for classification), establishing competitive performance with state-of-the-art tabular methods. We further extend TALENT with out-of-distribution (OOD) splits exhibiting train-test distributional shift and benchmark CoGA2M against LightGBM, a consistently top-performing model on TALENT. Under distribution shift, CoGA2M outperforms LightGBM, demonstrating a clear structural advantage. Our results position spline-based GAMs as strong contenders for tabular prediction and reveal a previously unrecognised benefit of additive structure in the OOD regime.
papers.summary: Generalised Additive Models (GAMs) are a staple of interpretable machine learning, but spline-based GAMs have not been benchmarked thoroughly on large tabular tasks or under distribution shift. The authors propose `CoGA2M`, a multi-resolution, higher-order composite GAM, and evaluate it on the `TALENT` benchmark suite, where it ranks in the top third among roughly 30 baselines for both regression and classification. On new out-of-distribution splits of `TALENT`, **`CoGA2M` outperforms `LightGBM`**, suggesting that additive structure gives a real advantage under distribution shift.

papers.title: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
papers.abstract: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton-Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four.
papers.summary: Using matrix factorization as a model of neural-network training, the authors study continuous-time dynamics of the `Muon` optimizer, which applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized gradient. They show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change which rank is selected early in training and **can let the trajectory bypass the first saddle point that gradient flow approaches**. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, they prove that the bypass happens for all sufficiently large finite depths and give an explicit threshold, and they construct an example in which that threshold is four.

papers.title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
papers.abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.
papers.summary: In continual learning for physical AI, small per-step policy errors can compound over a trajectory and cause closed-loop failure. `DRAP` (Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity) is a replay-free method that fits a local linear model to expert transitions and uses the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix to estimate how much a one-step perturbation will be amplified. It weights squared action gradients by this risk to build a per-tensor importance memory, then scales down each tensor's `AdamW` learning rate on later tasks according to its accumulated importance. Applied to a `KappaTune`-selected subnetwork of `OpenVLA` across the `LIBERO` Spatial, Object and Goal suites, **`DRAP` retains previously learned behaviors substantially better than standard fine-tuning and `EWC`** while still learning new suites well.

papers.title: Comparing model representations and fitting methods for port-Hamiltonian system identification
papers.abstract: Port-Hamiltonian models describe physical systems by separating stored energy, dissipation and external inputs. Learning such models from data requires a choice of representation and fitting method. We compare using neural networks, analytic expressions and combinations of the two for representing the different components of the port-Hamiltonian system, and compare fitting the models with gradient-based optimisation or sparse regression. Testing on simulations of mechanical and electrical systems, with and without added noise, we present prediction accuracy and computational cost of the different approaches.
papers.summary: Port-Hamiltonian models describe physical systems by separating stored energy, dissipation and external inputs, and learning them from data requires choosing both how to represent each component and how to fit it. The authors compare neural networks, analytic expressions and hybrids of the two as representations, and gradient-based optimization against sparse regression as fitting methods. On simulated mechanical and electrical systems, with and without noise, they report **the prediction accuracy and computational cost of each combination**.

papers.title: Federated Transfer Learning for Medical Image Classification under Mixed Skew
papers.abstract: Deep learning in medical imaging is constrained by data scarcity and by privacy regulations that make centralizing patient data across institutions impractical. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these constraints by keeping data local, but its distributed nature exposes training to strong statistical heterogeneity. Multicentric medical data is particularly affected, exhibiting a mixed skew that combines feature, label, concept, and quantity shifts across centers. Personalized FL mitigates heterogeneity by tailoring a model to each client, yet most methods assume training from scratch, which is unrealistic given the high dimensionality of medical features relative to the limited data available. We propose the Personalized Aligner Federated Pretrained (PAFP) framework, a personalized FL approach built on a pre-trained backbone. PAFP inserts client-specific Feature Alignment modules before the fine-tuned blocks to realign hidden feature distributions toward a server-aggregated target. On the FedISIC benchmark, PAFP attains the highest unweighted balanced accuracy while reducing inter-client performance variance roughly six-fold relative to the strongest baseline, yielding accuracy and cross-client equity jointly. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Alexandre-Leclercq/PAFP.
papers.summary: Medical images held at different hospitals vary in features, labels, concepts and data volume all at once, a 'mixed skew' that makes Federated Learning (FL) hard. Personalized FL methods, which tailor a model to each client, also usually assume training from scratch, which is unrealistic with so little medical data. The proposed `Personalized Aligner Federated Pretrained` (`PAFP`) framework starts from a pre-trained backbone and inserts client-specific Feature Alignment modules before the fine-tuned blocks. These modules pull each client's hidden feature distributions toward a target aggregated on the server. On the `FedISIC` benchmark, `PAFP` reaches the highest unweighted balanced accuracy and **cuts the variance in performance across clients roughly six-fold** compared with the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Positional Encoding is All You Need for Scalable Equivariance Constraint Relaxation
papers.abstract: Equivariant neural networks incorporate known symmetries of the data, such as permutations, rotations, or translations, directly into their architecture, often improving sample efficiency and generalization. However, strict equivariance can make optimization difficult, for example, when the data only approximately satisfy the assumed symmetry, or when the equivariance constraints induce a challenging loss landscape. Recent studies have shown that relaxing equivariance during training by introducing non-equivariant dense linear layers can ease optimization in such cases and improve the performance of the resulting strictly equivariant model, after removing the relaxation layers at test time. While effective, this approach incurs a significant computational overhead, limiting its applicability in scalable architectures. In this work, we propose a more efficient constraint-relaxation method based on positional encoding (PE). Our framework injects a positional encoding with learnable scale that breaks the model's original symmetry. This positional signal is gradually annealed to zero, recovering the original equivariant model by the end of training. Empirically, we demonstrate significant improvements for translational and rotational equivariant models with only marginal compute and memory overhead.
papers.summary: Equivariant networks build symmetries such as rotations or translations into their architecture, but strict equivariance can make optimization hard. Earlier work relaxed the constraint during training by adding non-equivariant dense linear layers, which works but adds a lot of compute. This work instead breaks the symmetry by injecting a positional encoding (PE) with a learnable scale, then anneals it to zero so that training ends with the original, strictly equivariant model. Experiments on translation- and rotation-equivariant models show **significant performance gains with only marginal compute and memory overhead**.

papers.title: Effects of Parton Pair Correlations on Direct-Photon Yields and Elliptic Flow in Heavy-Ion Collisions
papers.abstract: Direct photons escape heavy-ion collisions with little rescattering, carrying information from the full emission history. Yet describing the measured direct-photon yield and the sizable elliptic flow $v_2$ together remains a long-standing challenge. Here we explore how correlations between emitting partons may affect both observables. The local $2\to2$ photon rate depends on the joint distribution of incoming partons, so a connected correlation between them can change photon emission without changing the one-particle distribution of medium particles. Once folded over the evolving medium in Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions, the correlation raises the photon yield toward the fitted PHENIX and ALICE data and increases $v_2$ mainly at intermediate $p_T$. The fitted temperature dependence accounts for most of the net flow increase in this region, suggesting that the correlation changes the relative contributions between hotter and cooler regions.
papers.summary: Models of heavy-ion collisions have long struggled to reproduce both the measured yield of direct photons and their sizable elliptic flow, written $v_2$. The authors note that the local 2-to-2 photon emission rate depends on the joint distribution of the incoming partons. A correlation between partons can therefore change photon emission without changing the distribution of single particles in the medium. Applied across the evolving medium in Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions, the correlation **raises the photon yield toward the fitted `PHENIX` and `ALICE` data and increases $v_2$ mainly at intermediate transverse momentum**. The fitted temperature dependence explains most of the increase, which suggests the correlation shifts the relative contributions of hotter and cooler regions.

papers.title: Ablating Design Choices for Protein Ensemble Generators Across Structural Regimes
papers.abstract: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles inherit much of their design from structure prediction for folded proteins. Ordered and disordered proteins, however, occupy distinct structural regimes, and we investigate how design choices hold up across them. Using a minimal C$\alpha$ flow-matching model, we ablate choices of architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training source, and evaluate each variant against experimental SAXS and NMR chemical-shift data partitioned into ordered, disordered, multi-domain and transitional proteins. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, a smaller protein language model performs worse on ordered proteins but not on disordered ones, and alignment in the loss degrades agreement with SAXS. Replacing coarse-grained simulations of disordered proteins with fragment-assembled ensembles improves agreement with chemical shifts at a cost to SAXS, while an equal mixture of the two keeps most of the gain at a smaller cost. This points to the training data, rather than the architecture, as the main constraint.
papers.summary: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles borrow many design choices from structure prediction for folded proteins, even though ordered and disordered proteins behave very differently. Using a minimal C-alpha flow-matching model, the authors ablate architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training data. Each variant is scored against experimental small-angle X-ray scattering (`SAXS`) and `NMR` chemical-shift data, split into ordered, disordered, multi-domain and transitional proteins. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, and alignment in the loss hurts agreement with `SAXS`. Changing the training ensembles for disordered proteins moves results the most, which leads the authors to conclude that **the training data, not the architecture, is the main constraint**.

papers.title: Data informed Ansatz Selection for Variational Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Choosing a variational quantum circuit (VQC) usually means searching over ansatze and depths, and training each candidate. We give three rules that fix these choices from the data and the gate set alone, before any training. First, a circuit without entangling gates has a rank-one Fourier coefficient tensor on every subset of qubits. A singular value decomposition of a dataset's Fourier coefficients therefore indicates whether entanglement is needed, which qubits it connects, and a lower bound on the error of omitting it. Second, the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix grows by $p_0$ per layer, after a first-layer deficit $d_0$, until it reaches a ceiling set by the dynamical Lie algebra. This law fixes the depth. Third, reading out all $2^N - 1$ Pauli-Z products from one batch of shots resolves half of the state's directions, the most any single-basis readout can. A single-qubit readout resolves an exponentially small fraction. For the Madelon dataset, the rules prescribe 7 blocks of 3 qubits at depth 3: a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy, found without a grid search. Ablations confirm three predicted effects: shallower circuits, smaller blocks and dropping reuploading all lower accuracy.
papers.summary: Choosing a variational quantum circuit (VQC) usually means training many candidate ansatze at different depths. The authors give three rules that fix these choices from the data and the gate set before any training. A singular value decomposition of the dataset's Fourier coefficients shows whether entanglement is needed and between which qubits. A growth law for the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix sets the depth, and reading out all Pauli-Z products resolves the most state directions possible from a single measurement basis. On `Madelon`, the rules prescribe **a 239-parameter classifier reaching 78.5% test accuracy without any grid search**, and ablations confirm that shallower circuits, smaller blocks, or removing data reuploading all lower accuracy.

papers.title: CRONOS: Benchmarking Non-Episodic Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce CRONOS, a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. CRONOS leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using CRONOS, we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cronos/
papers.summary: Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) for robots is held back by the need for frequent human scene resets, and non-episodic RL has mostly been studied with small policies trained from scratch. `CRONOS` is a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models without episodic resets, using high-fidelity physics and multiple tasks that share one scene. Naive fine-tuning fails because object configurations and end-effector poses drift, but targeted reset allocation and correcting biases in the pre-trained models mitigate this. The authors also find that **non-episodic training improves long-horizon manipulation and generalization to unseen object configurations and task sequences**.

papers.title: Dual-VaDE: Efficient and Robust Prototype Learning via Variational Dual-Domain Mixture Priors
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose Dual-VaDE, an unsupervised generative framework for learning interpretable anatomical prototypes from unlabeled medical images. In contrast to previous variational methods that rely on a single spatial latent code, which often entangles global geometry with local textures and fails to capture their cross-domain dependencies, Dual-VaDE introduces a dual-domain Gaussian mixture prior that explicitly couples spatial anatomy with phase-preserving Fourier spectral representations. We derive an exact, closed-form variational lower bound that fuses this joint prior into the decoder and optimizes the entire network end-to-end via an alternating EM formulation, avoiding heuristic two-stage clustering while ensuring superior training stability and robustness. Evaluated on OASIS-3 brain MRI, Dual-VaDE delivers substantially sharper and more plausible prototypes, achieves superior cluster separation with improvements of up to 94% over spatial-only baselines, exhibits markedly reduced variance across random seeds, and incurs negligible inference overhead (0.28 ms per image).
papers.summary: `Dual-VaDE` is an unsupervised generative framework for learning interpretable anatomical prototypes from unlabeled medical images. Earlier variational methods use a single spatial latent code, which mixes global geometry with local texture. `Dual-VaDE` instead uses a Gaussian mixture prior that couples spatial anatomy with a phase-preserving Fourier spectral representation. It is trained end-to-end through a closed-form variational lower bound and an alternating expectation-maximization (EM) scheme, with no separate clustering stage. On `OASIS-3` brain MRI it produces sharper prototypes, **improves cluster separation by up to 94% over spatial-only baselines**, varies less across random seeds, and adds only 0.28 ms of inference time per image.

papers.title: Molecular Prior Networks
papers.abstract: Predicting affinity between small molecules and their protein targets remains one of the central problems in drug discovery. Due to the substantial cost of wet-lab experiments, machine learning models of drug-target affinity are usually trained on relatively small datasets, ranging from tens to hundreds of molecules. Given the inherent difficulty of generalization between different targets and chemical series, existing datasets of protein-ligand affinities are typically not used for new projects. At the same time, tabular foundation models, including Prior-data Fitted Networks, have recently shown how transformers can be used to solve machine learning problems in a single forward pass of the network, after being trained over a large corpus of, typically, synthetic datasets. Inspired by that line of work, we propose a novel affinity modelling approach, in which the labels of the query molecules are predicted from the labelled support molecules in a single forward pass of a transformer model. The model is trained on thousands of existing affinity datasets, enabling it to capture the general patterns of molecular activity across different targets, chemical series and dataset sizes. For the smallest support sets, our model matches the state of the art on the regression variant of the FS-Mol benchmark, while being faster than existing methods, thanks to the lack of task-specific training. A comparison against a reduced variant of our architecture, which amounts to kernel regression in a meta-learned feature space, shows that the predictive performance of the transformer model is only partially explained by simple molecular similarity.
papers.summary: Drug-target affinity models are usually trained on small per-project datasets of tens to hundreds of molecules, and existing affinity data is rarely reused for new targets. Inspired by Prior-data Fitted Networks, the authors train a transformer on thousands of existing affinity datasets so that it predicts labels for query molecules from a labelled support set in a single forward pass, with no task-specific training. For the smallest support sets it **matches the state of the art on the regression variant of `FS-Mol`** while running faster than existing methods. A comparison with a reduced variant, equivalent to kernel regression in a meta-learned feature space, shows that the transformer's accuracy is only partly explained by simple molecular similarity.

papers.title: Beyond Multi-Index Models: Learning Intersections of Degree-2 PTFs
papers.abstract:
We give an algorithm for PAC learning intersections of $k$ degree-2 polynomial threshold functions over $R^d$ under a Gaussian distribution. Our algorithm achieves classification error $\epsilon$ using $d^{O(k)}2^{O_k(\log^3(1/\epsilon))}$ time and samples, improving over the $d^{O(k^2/\epsilon^2)}$ running time of the polynomial regression approach. To our knowledge, our result is the first to obtain a dimension exponent independent of the accuracy parameter, even for $k=2$. We complement our algorithmic result with an SQ lower bound showing that the complexity dependence of $d^{\Omega(k)}$ is unavoidable.
  Lifting the input to polynomial features turns the target into an intersection of $k$ halfspaces. This suggests using the first two labeled moments for subspace recovery. In the lifted space, however, these moments can reveal nothing. Our starting point is a Gaussian comparison theorem showing that, for sufficiently regular defining quadratics, the labeled moments needed for subspace recovery are approximately preserved. To handle arbitrary defining quadratics, we establish a new structural result showing that every direction with significant resampling influence can be detected through degree-$O(k)$ moments. These results yield an initial $d^{O(k)}2^{\mathrm{poly}_k(1/\epsilon)}$-time learner using adaptive restrictions.
  To improve the exponential dependence on $1/\epsilon$, we develop a two-stage dimension-reduction approach that avoids the costly adaptive partitioning. After identifying a subspace containing all directions with large influence, we use generalized regularity and Gaussian comparison to recover the remaining relevant quadratic features through a new derivative-based moment operator. The recovered features support an intersection close to the target. Combining them with robust hinge-loss minimization gives our quasipolynomial-time learner.
papers.summary: The authors give an algorithm for PAC-learning intersections of $k$ degree-2 polynomial threshold functions (PTFs) under a Gaussian distribution. It runs in $d^{O(k)}2^{O_k(\log^3(1/\epsilon))}$ time and samples, improving on the $d^{O(k^2/\epsilon^2)}$ cost of polynomial regression. It is **the first result whose exponent on the dimension does not depend on the accuracy parameter**, even for $k=2$. The method combines a Gaussian comparison theorem, a structural result showing that influential directions can be detected through low-degree moments, and a two-stage dimension reduction followed by robust hinge-loss minimization. A statistical query (SQ) lower bound shows that a $d^{\Omega(k)}$ dependence is unavoidable.

papers.title: Distributed Linear Bandits for Freshness-Aware Preprocessing in MEC-Enabled Digital Twin Networks
papers.abstract: Digital twins (DTs) require timely updates from Internet of Things (IoT) devices to accurately represent the state of the corresponding physical systems, but transmitting large data volumes can compromise freshness. Moreover, different task classes have distinct computational demands and freshness requirements, while stochastic task generation and sizes complicate resource allocation. In this paper, we propose a freshness-aware framework in which multi-access edge computing (MEC) servers preprocess IoT data, reducing transmission volume and DT-server processing load. The framework establishes mutual support between DT and MEC servers. The DTs determine feasible CPU-allocation strategies guaranteeing class-specific age-of-information (AoI) requirements under specified workload, delay, and update-generation bounds. MEC servers collaboratively identify the feasible strategy minimizing expected freshness-normalized preprocessing delay. We formulate CPU-strategy selection as a fixed-confidence distributed best-arm identification problem in linear bandits, with MEC servers as agents and CPU allocations across task classes as arms. We employ DistLinGapE, a distributed collaborative learning method, to coordinate exploration and share observations. Numerical results show that the method identifies the optimal feasible strategy and reduces preprocessing delay when deployed under stationary task-class assignments and workload statistics. Collaboration yields an identification speedup nearly proportional to the number of participating MEC servers in the evaluated settings.
papers.summary: Digital twins (DTs) need timely updates from Internet of Things (IoT) devices, but sending large volumes of raw data hurts the freshness of those updates. In the proposed framework, multi-access edge computing (MEC) servers preprocess IoT data. The DTs work out which CPU allocations satisfy class-specific age-of-information (AoI) requirements, and the MEC servers jointly search for the feasible allocation with the lowest freshness-normalized delay. That search is cast as distributed best-arm identification in linear bandits and solved with `DistLinGapE`. In simulations with stationary task statistics, the method finds the optimal feasible strategy, and **collaboration speeds up identification nearly in proportion to the number of participating MEC servers**.

papers.title: Towards an Optimal Control Foundation of Early Exits - Turnpikes and ResNets
papers.abstract: The feed-forward propagation through neural networks is crucial for training and inference. To trade off efficiency and accuracy, it has been proposed to consider intermediate outputs of hidden states as data-dependent regularization during training and, ultimately, as early-exits during inference. In this work, we analyze the joint optimization of loss functions computed for the output layer and intermediate layers using optimal control theory. We prove that ResNets trained in this joint fashion exhibit the so-called turnpike phenomenon, this implies that the number of layers required to reach a prescribed loss level is bounded from above independently of the overall network depth. This induces a similarity property across the internal representations of early-exiting networks of varying depths. We connect the turnpike to the overthinking phenomenon, and provide theoretical insights into the success of early-exit criteria derived from softmax probabilities, specifically entropy and max-probability. In a range of experiments, we demonstrate the existence and effect of turnpikes and the resulting similarity in the early-exit performance for ResNets of varying depths.
papers.summary: Early-exit networks take predictions from intermediate layers to trade accuracy for speed, and training them jointly optimizes losses at the output and at intermediate layers. Analyzing this joint training with optimal control theory, the authors prove that such ResNets show a turnpike phenomenon: **the number of layers needed to reach a given loss level is bounded independently of total network depth**. This implies that early-exit networks of different depths learn similar internal representations. The analysis also connects the turnpike to the 'overthinking' phenomenon and explains why exit criteria based on softmax entropy and max-probability work well. Experiments on ResNets of varying depths confirm the turnpikes and the predicted similarity in early-exit performance.

papers.title: Do Ray-Traced Cities Make a Better Channel Prior for an Unseen Site? A Pre-Registered Study in Simulation, and a Test on Measured Channels that Reverses It
papers.abstract: Channel estimators at a newly deployed base station usually start from 3GPP stochastic channel models, which describe no particular street. We ask whether a channel prior pooled from many ray-traced cities serves an unseen site better than the 3GPP CDL models, and whether learned estimators make the difference. With Sionna RT on 14 city scenes, LMMSE estimation from covariance priors, leave-one-city-out evaluation, and pass/fail bars written down before each main experiment, we find in simulation that the pooled prior sits about 0.6 dB from a site-trained estimator with no site measurements, about what CDL reaches after 50 measurements. Learned models added little: at most 0.65 dB in estimation, and in channel prediction a simple classical method beat CNN predictors by 1.8-12 dB from 2 ms ahead. On measured channels from the DICHASUS outdoor dataset (1.272 GHz, three 2x8 arrays on one building) the result reversed: the pooled ray-traced prior was 3.2-4.1 dB worse than CDL. The simulated channels were too clean; with users at the real distances, even a scattering level tuned from 50 site measurements left the prior about 2 dB behind CDL. A pre-registered follow-on on two more measured environments found the generic CDL prior 2.1-4.7 dB from a site-trained one: no further in a factory hall than on the street, furthest in a small lab room. Finally, a hallway model calibrated to measurements by differentiable ray tracing reproduced delay spread, but as a prior in an unmeasured part of the hallway it was 4.5 dB worse than CDL on the full array. All measured results come from one sounder.
papers.summary: A newly deployed base station usually estimates the wireless channel starting from the generic 3GPP CDL stochastic channel models. This pre-registered study asks whether a prior pooled from ray-traced simulations of many cities works better. In simulation with `Sionna RT` across 14 city scenes, the pooled prior comes within about 0.6 dB of a site-trained estimator with no site measurements, and learned estimators add little, with a simple classical predictor beating CNN predictors. On measured channels from the `DICHASUS` dataset, however, **the result reverses: the ray-traced prior is 3.2 to 4.1 dB worse than CDL** because the simulated channels are too clean. Follow-on tests in other measured environments and with a calibrated differentiable ray-tracing model support the same conclusion, though all measurements come from a single channel sounder.

papers.title: Solving the Nonlinear Westervelt Equation in Ultrasound Propagation Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Modeling the nonlinear acoustic wave propagation in biological tissues needs accuracy, especially in ultrasound imaging and therapeutic applications. The 1D Westervelt equation, \( p_{xx} - p_{tt} + \gamma\, p_{ttt} + \eta\,(p^{2})_{tt}=0, \) could be used to describe a finite-amplitude ultrasound propagation in these tissues. This equation accounts for nonlinearity, \(\eta\), and attenuation, \(\gamma\). To solve this equation, we observe that traditional solvers may struggle to do so correctly. This is due to the difficulties arising from the nonlinear nature of the equation. We solve the equation by defining three synthetic cases - linear (\(\eta=0.001\), \(\gamma=10^{-6}\)), shock-dominated (\(\eta=0.02\), \(\gamma=10^{-6}\)), and dissipation-dominated (\(\eta=0.01\), \(\gamma=5\times10^{-4}\)) - and using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to showcase the solution. A sinusoidal activation function is used to capture the oscillatory behavior of the problem. The results of our study, with PDE residual converging to at least \(10^{-6}\), boundary condition loss to \(10^{-5}\), and the PINN loss converging to \(10^{-5}\) for each case at \(30,000\) epochs, show that \(\gamma\) scales the rate of amplitude decay, while \(\eta\) governs frequency-dependent phase speeds.
papers.summary: The 1D Westervelt equation models finite-amplitude ultrasound propagation in tissue with nonlinearity and attenuation terms, which makes it hard for traditional solvers. The authors solve it with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) that use a sinusoidal activation function to capture oscillatory behavior. They test three synthetic regimes: nearly linear, shock-dominated and dissipation-dominated. In each case the PDE residual converges to at least $10^{-6}$ within 30,000 epochs, and the solutions show that **attenuation sets the rate of amplitude decay while nonlinearity governs frequency-dependent phase speeds**.

papers.title: PAC Learning with Multiple Correct Answers
papers.abstract: We study PAC learning when each example comes with a set of at most $\ell$ correct labels and a prediction is correct if it belongs to this set. Training may reveal the full set, only whether a proposed label is correct (bandit feedback), or one correct label chosen by a demonstrator (demonstrations). Our main finding is that demonstrations can be much harder than full sets, and even than bandit feedback, both in which classes can be learned and in how many examples are needed. For finite label spaces, a generalized Natarajan dimension characterizes learnability from full sets and from bandit feedback, in both the realizable and the agnostic setting. From demonstrations, however, a class is realizably learnable if and only if the intersections of at most $\ell+1$ of its hypotheses are learnable from full sets. Already with three labels, this condition can fail for a class learnable from a single full-set example or even a single bandit answer. When the condition holds, we show that $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-\ell})$ demonstrations suffice, and the exponent $\ell$ cannot be improved in general, even for classes learnable from $\widetilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ full sets or bandit answers. For countable label spaces and $\ell \geq 2$, our packed dimension, which asks for many disjoint groups of at most $\ell+1$ hypotheses with no common label, characterizes full-set learnability, and demonstrations still reduce to intersections.
