Agnostic learning from demonstrations, already for finite label spaces, is not determined by the dimensions of the intersection class that characterize realizable learning. Finally, we show that the uniform bound $\ell$ on the number of correct labels is essential. Without this bound, it is impossible to characterize learnability by any dimension determined by finite subclasses.
papers.summary: The authors study PAC learning when each example has a set of up to $\ell$ correct labels. During training, the learner may see the full set, only whether a proposed label is correct (bandit feedback), or a single correct label chosen by a demonstrator. The main finding is that **learning from demonstrations can be much harder than learning from full sets or even from bandit feedback**, both in which classes are learnable and in how many examples are needed. A generalized Natarajan dimension characterizes learning from full sets and from bandit feedback. Demonstration learnability reduces to whether intersections of $\ell+1$ hypotheses are learnable, with a $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-\ell})$ sample complexity that cannot be improved in general. The authors also show that the uniform bound on the number of correct labels is essential for any dimension-based characterization.

papers.title: A Random Matrix Analysis of Symmetric Tensor Unfolding
papers.abstract: We study a fundamental problem in machine learning: partial recovery of a planted signal $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ from a spiked tensor $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{X}} = \lambda \, \boldsymbol{v}^{\otimes p} + \boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$, where $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ has symmetric Gaussian entries of variance $\asymp n^{-1}$. While previous works replace $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ by an i.i.d. standard Gaussian tensor to circumvent technical difficulties caused by dependencies, this paper directly analyzes the symmetric model via random matrix theory. We show that the square unfolding algorithm is subject to a sharp phase transition for partial recovery at $\lambda \asymp n^{(p-2) / 4}$, validating an open conjecture from Montanari and Richard (2014). We get precise expressions for the limiting spectral distribution, deterministic equivalent, phase transition threshold and overlap. The main message is that unfolded symmetric tensors spectrally behave like standard Wigner matrices, up to simple transformations accounting for high-order symmetries. We consider extensions to multiple orthogonal spikes, recursive unfolding and non-square unfolding via disproportionate random matrix theory, leading to an interesting conjectured statistical-computational tradeoff regarding the choice of unfolding: square versus long.
papers.summary: The authors study recovering a planted signal from a spiked symmetric tensor by unfolding it into a matrix. Unlike earlier work, they analyze the symmetric Gaussian noise directly with random matrix theory instead of replacing it with an i.i.d. tensor. They prove that square unfolding has **a sharp phase transition for partial recovery at $\lambda \asymp n^{(p-2)/4}$, confirming a conjecture of Montanari and Richard (2014)**. They also derive precise limiting spectra, thresholds and overlaps, showing that unfolded symmetric tensors behave spectrally like Wigner matrices after simple corrections. Extensions to multiple spikes, recursive unfolding and non-square unfolding lead to a conjectured statistical-computational tradeoff between square and long unfoldings.

papers.title: Beyond Foundation Models: PFN Priors Improve Tabular Hyperparameter Optimization
papers.abstract: Synthetic priors have so far served one purpose: pretraining tabular foundation models. We ask whether the same priors can improve conventional tabular models, which are trained from scratch on each dataset. We propose PriorTune, a method that meta-tunes hyperparameter configurations on synthetic tasks alone. Offline, for a given model, we fit a pool of configurations on datasets sampled from a published PFN prior and greedily select the subset with the highest winrate over the random baseline. Online, a new dataset fits only the selected configurations, so the gain comes at no extra cost. Empirically, we observe that scaling both the number of configurations and synthetic datasets has an equal scaling effect on the performance of the final subset of configurations, which we also explain theoretically. On the full BeyondArena benchmark, LightGBM with TabPrep features with our configurations ranks above TabPFN-3 and RealMLP, while being much more efficient at inference. Overall, our results establish existing PFN priors as a scalable source of meta-training data for hyperparameter selection for non-foundational tabular models.
papers.summary: Synthetic priors from Prior-data Fitted Networks (PFNs) have so far been used only to pretrain tabular foundation models. `PriorTune` uses them instead to meta-tune hyperparameters for conventional models that are trained from scratch on each dataset. Offline, it fits a pool of configurations on datasets sampled from a published PFN prior and greedily selects the subset with the highest winrate. Online, a new dataset is fitted only with the selected configurations, at no extra cost. On the full `BeyondArena` benchmark, **`LightGBM` with `TabPrep` features and `PriorTune` configurations ranks above `TabPFN-3` and `RealMLP`** while being much cheaper at inference. The authors also observe, and explain theoretically, that scaling the number of configurations and the number of synthetic datasets improves results by equal amounts.

papers.title: Macrocanonical Generator Networks: Data-Efficient Neural Surrogates for Amortized Physics Simulation
papers.abstract: Many scientific simulations are computationally expensive, limiting their use in simulation-based inference, uncertainty quantification, and decision making. We introduce macrocanonical generator networks, a framework for learning fast, data-efficient neural surrogates for amortized simulation of stationary physical processes by matching multiscale statistics of a target process. Inspired by microcanonical maximum-entropy synthesis, which matches feature statistics per sample by inner-loop optimization, our approach instead trains a neural generator to satisfy the same constraints in expectation, preserving physically realistic sample-to-sample fluctuations. We prove that gradient-descent training induces preconditioned gradient-descent dynamics in sample space that inherit the symmetry-preservation properties of the microcanonical gradient descent of Bruna and Mallat, amortizing its per-sample inner-loop optimization into a single training run after which every sample is generated in one forward pass. We further show that residual generator parameterizations initialized near the identity, trained with a small learning rate, preserve entropy locally during early optimization and mitigate mode collapse. Experiments on cosmology and fluid simulations show that macrocanonical generators recover realistic samples from extremely small training sets, in some cases a single training example, while generating new realizations more than $10^6$ times faster per sample than the reference simulator and more than $10^3$ times faster than microcanonical gradient descent. The trained generators can be reused for downstream pretraining, including simulation-based inference, providing a data-efficient route to multi-fidelity scientific machine learning workflows.
papers.summary: Expensive scientific simulations limit inference, uncertainty quantification and decision making, so fast neural surrogates are valuable. Macrocanonical generator networks train a neural generator to match multiscale statistics of a target stationary process in expectation, rather than optimizing each sample separately as microcanonical maximum-entropy synthesis does. The authors prove that training inherits the symmetry-preservation properties of microcanonical gradient descent, and that near-identity residual generators help avoid mode collapse. On cosmology and fluid simulations, the generators learn from very small training sets, sometimes a single example, and **generate samples more than $10^6$ times faster than the reference simulator**. The trained generators can also be reused to pretrain models for simulation-based inference.

papers.title: Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding
papers.abstract: Vision-language verifiers judge whether an image faithfully matches a textual description, yet existing training pipelines typically rely on static supervision from stronger external judges or curated hard-negative data. Such supervision requires external generation or annotation, is teacher-bounded, and is difficult to adapt as model failures evolve. We introduce PROVE (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for Vision-Language Evaluation), a self-play framework that trains verifiers through a closed perturb-verify-repair-verify loop. Starting from a known-correct image-caption pair, a Mutator introduces a typed perturbation over objects, attributes, counts, or relations. The verifier then judges the perturbed caption and provides textual feedback, which a Repairer uses to recover a faithful caption for re-verification. These two verification rounds produce structured rewards for informative mismatches and visually grounded repairs. Since perturbation, verification, and repair are role-conditioned behaviors of the same evolving multimodal backbone, updating the shared parameters also improves the verifier itself. Experiments show that PROVE improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families and strengthens visual-detail robustness on the reference backbone, with limited, benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks.
papers.summary: Vision-language verifiers judge whether an image matches a text description, but they are usually trained on static supervision from stronger judges or curated hard negatives. `PROVE` (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for Vision-Language Evaluation) trains a verifier through self-play. Starting from a correct image-caption pair, a Mutator perturbs objects, attributes, counts or relations in the caption, the verifier judges it and gives feedback, and a Repairer uses that feedback to restore a faithful caption for re-verification. All three roles share one multimodal backbone, so the structured rewards from the two verification rounds also improve the verifier itself. Experiments show that **`PROVE` improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families**, with limited, benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks.

papers.title: Basin2Vec: Learning Basin-Centric Embeddings for Scalable Hydrological Modeling
papers.abstract: Reliable streamflow prediction across time and in ungauged basins requires representations that capture hydrologically relevant basin characteristics. Existing methods rely on either fixed handcrafted attributes or general-purpose Earth observation embeddings not tailored to basin structure. We introduce \textbf{Basin2Vec}, a self-supervised framework that learns compact basin representations from hydroclimatic and physiographic data without observed streamflow. Basin2Vec organizes representation learning around basin scale and relationships across space and time. Across multiple forecasting architectures, it consistently outperforms predefined attributes and general-purpose geospatial embeddings in temporal generalization and zero-shot spatial transfer. Basin2Vec provides average relative gains of up to 8.3% temporally and achieves 3.5x the median predictive performance of the strongest baselines on unseen basins. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of basin-centric pretraining for transferable hydrologic prediction. Code is available at https://github.com/Muhammad-Talha-MT/basin2vec
papers.summary: Predicting streamflow over time and in basins without gauges requires representations that capture what matters about each basin, yet current methods rely on handcrafted attributes or general-purpose Earth observation embeddings. `Basin2Vec` learns compact basin embeddings through self-supervision on hydroclimatic and physiographic data, without using observed streamflow. Training is organized around basin scale and relationships across space and time. Across several forecasting architectures, it gives average relative gains of up to 8.3% for temporal generalization and **3.5 times the median predictive performance of the strongest baselines on unseen basins**.

papers.title: Learning Behaviorally Relevant Dynamics in Multimodal Neural Recordings
papers.abstract: Multimodal neural data can enable a more complete understanding of brain dynamics underlying behavior. Modalities such as spiking activity, local field potentials (LFPs), and behavior capture diverse spatiotemporal aspects of brain processes, yet prior neural-behavioral models that separate sources of variability rely on a single neural modality. By leveraging these complementary strengths, multimodal neural fusion can provide a unified, rich representation of brain-behavior processes and address the limitations of single-modality analyses. Here we develop BREM-NET, a nonlinear multimodal dynamical model that integrates behavior with multiple neural modalities having distinct statistical characteristics and temporal resolutions. BREM-NET performs multimodal neural fusion during inference while separating behaviorally relevant and residual neural dynamics via a structured learning framework. In a public multimodal non-human primate dataset with simultaneous spiking and local field potential recordings during a 2D reaching task, BREM-NET separates these two types of dynamics and learns them more accurately, as reflected in better behavior decoding, better neural prediction, and stronger latent alignment with behavior, and it retains these capabilities when neural modalities are asynchronous or suffer dropouts, which are major challenges in real-world recordings. This framework provides a new tool for studying behaviorally relevant neural computations across spatiotemporal scales of brain activity.
papers.summary: Earlier neural-behavioral models that separate behaviorally relevant brain dynamics from other neural variability use only one neural modality. `BREM-NET` is a nonlinear dynamical model that combines behavior with several neural modalities, such as spiking activity and local field potentials (LFPs), even though they differ in statistics and time resolution. A structured learning framework separates behaviorally relevant dynamics from residual ones. On a public non-human primate reaching dataset, it gives better behavior decoding, better neural prediction and stronger latent alignment with behavior, and **it keeps these advantages when modalities are asynchronous or have dropouts**.

papers.title: Provably Learning Mixtures of Linear Experts
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely deployed in modern machine learning. However, few convergence guarantees exist for gradient-based training of MoEs: the objective is nonconvex, and even simple mixtures trap first-order methods in spurious local optima. We analyze a canonical gated mixture featuring linear experts and a gate induced by Gaussian clusters in the input space, and give, to our knowledge, the first global convergence guarantee for jointly training the gate and the experts of such a model by gradient EM on its likelihood. Given a logarithmic overparameterization relative to the true number of experts $m$, gradient EM converges from randomly initialized gates and least-squares-initialized experts to any prescribed accuracy in polynomially many iterations, under a separation condition on the gate centers. Our analysis establishes a gradient-dominance inequality for the coupled dynamics by decoupling the loss into per-cluster subproblems. Empirical results validate the predicted $m\log m$ phase transition and suggest that the least-squares warm start required by our analysis is not needed in practice: randomly initialized experts perform nearly as well. We also find that leaving the mixing weights unconstrained concentrates routing onto the true number of experts, whereas load-balancing penalties spread it, so that the fitted model can be pruned to a fraction of its width without loss of accuracy.
papers.summary: Gradient-based training of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models has few convergence guarantees, because the objective is nonconvex and even simple mixtures trap first-order methods in spurious local optima. The authors analyze a gated mixture of linear experts whose gate comes from Gaussian clusters in the input space. They prove that `gradient EM` on its likelihood jointly trains the gate and the experts with **the first global convergence guarantee for this setting**. Accuracy is reached in polynomially many iterations, given logarithmic overparameterization and well-separated gate centers. Experiments confirm the predicted m log m phase transition and suggest that randomly initialized experts work about as well as the least-squares warm start the proof needs. Unconstrained mixing weights concentrate routing on the true experts, so the fitted model can be pruned, whereas load-balancing penalties spread routing out.

papers.title: Stepsize modulation for cross entropy from local quadratic optimization
papers.abstract:
Two methods are presented that perturb a given learning rate schedule in stochastic gradient descent with cross entropy loss.
  Both methods use an extra forward pass to estimate various derivatives of the minibatch loss.
  The first method selects a value $\eta$ by linearising the softmax values and minimizing the squared error $\tfrac 1 2 ||y - q - \eta q'||_F^2$, where $q$ is the matrix representing the softmax values of the minibatch and $y$ is the matrix with one-hot encodings of the labels. The second method considers a quadratic Taylor approximation of the minibatch loss under the outer approximation of the Hessian. Thus, it minimizes $L(0) + \eta L'(0) + \tfrac 1 2 \eta^2 L''(0)$. Here, the derivatives $L'$ and $L''$ are computed from the derivatives of the logits (using the outer approximation of the Hessian of the loss).
  We observe that both methods give very similar values of $\eta$.
  Finally, these estimated $\eta$ are used to slightly increase or decrease the learning rate of an existing schedule. The method is evaluated on Cifar10 and Cifar100 datasets for training Resnets, where they decrease the loss faster than the schedule that is perturbed and increase monotonicity. For Cifar10 it also leads to a small improvement of test accuracy, but in Cifar100 test accuracy remains the same.
papers.summary: Two methods nudge an existing stochastic gradient descent learning-rate schedule up or down when training with cross-entropy loss, each using one extra forward pass. The first linearizes the softmax outputs and picks the step size that minimizes a squared error against the one-hot labels. The second minimizes a quadratic Taylor approximation of the minibatch loss, using the outer-product approximation of the Hessian. The two estimates turn out very similar. On `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100` with `ResNet` models, the modulated schedules **lower the training loss faster and more monotonically**. Test accuracy improves slightly on `CIFAR-10` and is unchanged on `CIFAR-100`.

papers.title: Ensembles of Random Partition-Based Models under Covariate Shift
papers.abstract: Distribution shifts, including covariate shifts, are ubiquitous in real-world applications of machine learning. Empirical evidence suggests that, across a variety of models with and without downstream adaptation, ensembles tend to be more robust to covariate shift than single models. We extend the theory of covariate shift severity from single models to ensembles, providing theoretical justification for the empirical trends. We introduce new discrepancy measures of covariate shift severity to control the risk of partition-based kernel estimators. We then show that with sufficient ensemble size, these models can achieve minimax-optimal risk convergence rates under covariate shift. Our results suggest that modelers can expect to need larger ensemble sizes for more severe covariate shifts.
papers.summary: Ensembles are empirically more robust to covariate shift than single models, and this work gives a theoretical explanation by extending covariate-shift severity theory from single models to ensembles. The authors introduce new discrepancy measures that control the risk of partition-based kernel estimators under shift. They show that **sufficiently large ensembles of random partition-based models reach minimax-optimal risk convergence rates under covariate shift**. The results imply that more severe shifts call for larger ensembles.

papers.title: Empirical Bayes Flow Matching for Continuous Cryo-EM Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: We address the problem of learning generative priors over high-dimensional latent variables from indirect, noisy observations, with a focus on continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In this setting, 3D atomic structures $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N_a}$ are never directly observed and must be inferred from 2D projection images $y$ generated by a complex, non-linear forward operator. We propose Empirical Bayes Flow Matching (EB-FM), a method that learns a flow matching prior $p_\theta(x)$ directly from observations using a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. EB-FM alternates between an E-step that performs approximate posterior sampling from $p_\theta(x \mid y)$ via guided flow-based generation while maintaining persistent latent estimates through stochastic approximation, and an M-step that updates the flow model using these stabilized latent variables as training targets. This approach eliminates the need for pretraining on clean data and naturally accommodates non-linear forward models. We validate our method on controlled inverse problems using two-moons and MNIST data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses, showing that EB-FM can recover continuous distributions of protein conformations directly in atomic-coordinate space.
papers.summary: In cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), 3D atomic structures are never observed directly, only through noisy 2D projections produced by a nonlinear forward operator, so learning a prior over protein conformations is hard. `Empirical Bayes Flow Matching` (`EB-FM`) learns a flow-matching prior directly from these observations within a Monte Carlo stochastic-approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. The E-step draws approximate posterior samples via guided flow generation while keeping persistent latent estimates, and the M-step retrains the flow on those estimates. The method was validated on `two-moons` and `MNIST` inverse problems and on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses. It **recovers continuous distributions of protein conformations in atomic-coordinate space without pretraining on clean data**.

papers.title: Multi-Objective Generative Optimization via Expected Hypervolume Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires plausible designs spanning useful trade-offs among competing properties: a molecule with strong binding affinity, for example, may be difficult to synthesize. Pretrained generative models, e.g., flow and diffusion generators, provide a foundation for proposing such designs, but steering them toward high-quality, complementary trade-offs remains challenging. Inference-time search incurs high per-sample costs, while fine-tuning typically relies on fixed per-candidate rewards that do not capture how designs complement one another. We introduce Hypervolume Fine-Tuning (HVFT), which adapts a single pretrained generator to maximize the expected hypervolume of its samples while controlling departure from the pretrained distribution. Expected hypervolume jointly rewards candidate quality and collective trade-off coverage. Nonetheless, we show that it cannot be expressed as the expectation of a fixed per-candidate reward and therefore cannot be optimized directly with standard techniques. A key observation of this work is that its first variation corresponds to the expected marginal hypervolume contribution of a candidate, which yields a tractable adaptive reward via an unbiased estimator based on model samples. HVFT uses this reward to decompose the objective into a sequence of KL-proximal scalar-reward subproblems. We establish concavity, relative smoothness, and convergence guarantees for the resulting distributional procedure. Across therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks spanning discrete diffusion and continuous flow-matching models, HVFT achieves state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage.
papers.summary: Scientific design problems need sets of candidates that cover trade-offs among competing properties. Steering pretrained diffusion or flow generators toward such sets is hard: inference-time search is costly, and standard fine-tuning uses fixed per-candidate rewards that ignore how designs complement one another. `Hypervolume Fine-Tuning` (`HVFT`) fine-tunes a generator to maximize the expected hypervolume of its samples while limiting drift from the pretrained model. The authors show this objective cannot be written as a fixed per-candidate reward. Its first variation, however, equals a candidate's expected marginal hypervolume contribution, which yields an adaptive reward with an unbiased sample-based estimator and a sequence of KL-regularized scalar-reward subproblems with convergence guarantees. Across therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks using both discrete diffusion and flow-matching models, `HVFT` achieves **state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage**.

papers.title: Privacy for Free in Efficient Agnostic Halfspace Learning
papers.abstract: We provide the first computationally efficient, differentially private algorithms for agnostically learning halfspaces. In particular, we study three different settings of agnostic learning: improper learning under Gaussian and log-concave marginals; proper learning under Gaussian marginals; and semi-agnostic learning under Gaussian marginals. In all three aforementioned settings, the added cost in the sample complexity due to privacy matches the respective non-private sample complexity, implying that we get privacy for free.
papers.summary: The authors give the first computationally efficient differentially private algorithms for agnostically learning halfspaces, which means fitting the best linear classifier when the labels may be arbitrarily noisy. They cover three settings: improper learning under Gaussian and log-concave marginals, proper learning under Gaussian marginals, and semi-agnostic learning under Gaussian marginals. In all three, **the extra sample cost of privacy matches the non-private sample complexity**, so privacy comes essentially for free.

papers.title: Physics-informed traditional and generative Mori-Zwanzig-reduced models for multiscale systems
papers.abstract: Model reduction via the Mori-Zwanzig (MZ) formalism is well understood for coarse-grained representations constructed from standard basis functions such as Fourier functions. We show that the same formalism can be used to build reduced-order models in bases discovered by physics-informed machine learning. The fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT) is used to close the resulting non-Markovian evolution equations for the expansion coefficients of the learned basis. We further introduce a complementary, generative closure model. Relative to the Markovian dynamics alone, both the MZ and generative closures substantially improve predictions of the filtered states.
papers.summary: The Mori-Zwanzig (MZ) formalism for building reduced models of multiscale systems is well understood for standard bases such as Fourier functions. This work extends it to bases discovered by physics-informed machine learning. The fluctuation-dissipation theorem closes the resulting non-Markovian equations for the coefficients of the learned basis, and the authors also propose a complementary generative closure model. **Both the MZ closure and the generative closure substantially improve predictions of the filtered states** compared with the Markovian dynamics alone.

papers.title: Fusing Earth observation embeddings and spaceborne terrain with meteorological forcing for flood peak depth prediction from high-water marks
papers.abstract: Flood peak depth on normally dry land governs damage and risk to life, but is observed only sparsely, by post-event high-water mark (HWM) surveys, and depth derived from satellite flood extent is produced after the event and inherits the vertical error of the digital elevation model (DEM) it is computed from. Deep-learning flood models have in turn been trained on hydrodynamic simulations rather than on observed depths. We ask whether flood peak depth can be learned from field observations and predicted before the peak from spaceborne terrain, geospatial foundation-model embeddings and antecedent meteorological forcing. We assembled 5689 USGS HWM surveys from 39 events (2011-2025) in 24 U.S. states and Puerto Rico, assigned each a peak time from nearby sensors, paired each with a rain-free window at the same site, and linked them to Copernicus GLO-30 terrain, AlphaEarth embeddings and 144 h of hourly forcing masked to the lead time. A cross-modal fusion network trained on these observations predicts depth at the surveyed marks with a mean absolute error of 0.39 m 6 h ahead of the peak. Supervision by surveyed depth corrects the DEM error implicitly: differencing the measured peak water level with the same DEM gives 0.93 m at the same marks, 2.4 times larger, although it uses the measured water level and the model does not. Forcing accounts for 77% of the attributed reduction in depth error; terrain and the embeddings are statistically equivalent to each other and contribute the remaining 23%. On eleven held-out events the model still separates flooded from rain-free conditions but no longer resolves depth at the marks (R2 = 0.03), so the skill reported here is confined to the events and regions sampled. Field-surveyed depths can thus supervise flood depth prediction and correct terrain error that extent-based estimation cannot, while transfer to unseen storms remains the open problem.
papers.summary: Peak flood depth is observed only sparsely, through post-event high-water mark surveys, and deep-learning flood models are usually trained on simulations rather than on measured depths. The authors assembled 5,689 `USGS` high-water marks from 39 U.S. events. They trained a cross-modal fusion network on `Copernicus GLO-30` terrain, `AlphaEarth` embeddings and up to 144 hours of meteorological forcing, which predicts depth with **a mean absolute error of 0.39 m six hours before the peak**. That is 2.4 times lower than differencing the measured water level against the elevation model. Meteorological forcing accounts for 77% of the error reduction. On eleven held-out events the model no longer resolves depth (R2 = 0.03), so transfer to unseen storms remains unsolved.

papers.title: Fairness Metrics based on the AUC in Clinical Predictive AI
papers.abstract: Fairness evaluation of clinical prediction models for binary outcomes often involves fairness metrics that compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC, or c-statistic) across subgroups. However, the AUC has been shown to be a non-collapsible metric, meaning that its subgroup specific and overall values are not directly comparable as often implicitly assumed. This raises important questions about how existing AUC-based fairness metrics should be used and interpreted. We examine eight AUC-based fairness metrics proposed in the literature, including: within-group AUC parity; cross-group AUC (xAUC) parity; gap-to-overall AUC; equity-scaled AUC; minimum-based metrics; $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$; $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$; and $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ or $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ parity. We characterise their estimands, relate them to the decomposition of overall AUC (into within- and cross-group components), and critically appraise them. We then illustrate their behaviour using simulations based on the EuroSCORE II, a clinical prediction model for in-hospital mortality. We recommend reporting an AUC matrix, containing the overall AUC and all within- and cross-group AUC components, alongside population characteristics. When fairness metrics are needed, we recommend reporting the within-group AUC parity, with cross-group AUC parity providing supplementary information but requiring caution due to its potential conflict with calibration. Metrics involving $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ and $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ have merit, summarising within- and cross-group AUCs into single values, but their interpretation is non-trivial, and they should be used with caution. Gap-to-overall AUC, equity-scaled AUC, and minimum-based metrics compare quantities that should not be compared and it is unclear how to operationalise them, making them not fit for purpose and generally not recommended.
papers.summary: Clinical prediction models are often checked for fairness by comparing the area under the ROC curve (AUC) across subgroups, but the AUC is non-collapsible, so subgroup and overall values are not directly comparable. The authors examine eight published AUC-based fairness metrics, characterize what each one estimates, and relate them to a decomposition of overall AUC into within-group and cross-group components. They illustrate the metrics with simulations based on the `EuroSCORE II` mortality model. They recommend reporting a full AUC matrix and using within-group AUC parity as the primary fairness metric. They find that **gap-to-overall AUC, equity-scaled AUC and minimum-based metrics are not fit for purpose**.

papers.title: PLANTEUR: A Crop-Type Segmentation Benchmark for Tropical Regions
papers.abstract: We introduce PLANTEUR, a benchmark for crop-type mapping from satellite images in the French overseas territories. Building on the PASTIS design, PLANTEUR provides georeferenced and aligned Sentinel-2, Sentinel-1, and Landsat-8 sequences with parcel-derived labels spanning six tropical regions and an 8-class label space. We define both a standard test split and a leave-one-island-out protocol to measure cross-territory generalization, and evaluate fully supervised models, linear probes, and fine-tuned foundation models. The benchmark code and data are open source and available on GitHub and Hugging Face.
papers.summary: `PLANTEUR` is a benchmark for mapping crop types from satellite imagery in tropical French overseas territories, modeled on the `PASTIS` design. It provides aligned `Sentinel-2`, `Sentinel-1` and `Landsat-8` time series with parcel-level labels across six regions and eight classes. It defines a standard test split and a **leave-one-island-out protocol to measure cross-territory generalization**, and evaluates supervised models, linear probes and fine-tuned foundation models. The code and data are openly released.

papers.title: Learning curves in natural and artificial systems
papers.abstract: A general mathematical model of experience formation is considered, in which the learning level is defined as the probability that the next value of the uncertainty factor has already been mastered and not forgotten. Within this model the shape of the learning curve is derived, and it turns out to be determined primarily by the distribution of situation occurrence: a uniform distribution yields an exponential curve, whereas a power-law distribution yields a power-law curve whose exponent equals the ratio of the distribution exponent to that same exponent increased by one. Both mechanisms generating power-law curves, established earlier in the analysis of debugging, assembly and repair activities, are shown to have been independently rediscovered in deep learning theory as the "frequency" and "spectral" mechanisms of scaling laws for artificial neural networks, while the exponential curves of machine learning (contraction operators, strongly convex optimization, stationary reinforcement) are generated by the same constancy of the contraction coefficient that was revealed half a century earlier in models of radioactive decay, the first-order lag element, and others. A solution is given for the problem of choosing a training distribution that differs from the deployment distribution. A methodological consequence is discussed: three distinct mechanisms generate curves indistinguishable in shape, so an observed learning curve does not allow one to judge the "internal" structure of the learning system.
papers.summary: This work develops a general mathematical model of experience formation in which the learning level is the probability that the next situation has already been mastered and not forgotten. It derives the shape of the learning curve from this model. A uniform distribution of situations gives an exponential curve, while **a power-law distribution gives a power-law curve whose exponent is set by the distribution's exponent**. The author argues that the 'frequency' and 'spectral' mechanisms behind neural scaling laws rediscover mechanisms found decades earlier in studies of debugging and repair work. Because different mechanisms produce curves of the same shape, an observed learning curve cannot reveal the internal structure of the learning system.

papers.title: Post-Inference Model Chaining: A Problem Statement and a Model-based Bootstrap for Training End-to-End Digital Twins
papers.abstract: End-to-end digital twins can be constructed by fitting separate stage models and connecting them after inference. We investigate the Frequentist prediction properties of a commonly used Monte Carlo simulation scheme that forwards complete predictive draws through such a chain when measured stage outputs contain independent normal errors, but the latent stage means are deterministic. Analytical two-stage examples show persistent asymptotic interval and coverage inflation and, with quadratic propagation, mean bias dependent on the parameters to be estimated. Simulations of four- and eight-stage linear-quadratic univariate chains with 7, 15 or 30 training runs demonstrate pronounced input-dependent distortions. A diagnostic using error-free latent training predictors shows that the effect is mainly not attributable to errors in variables, but to the MCSim approach even showing underestimation of coverage. We propose a model-based bootstrap: an initial chain forwards fitted means, bootstrap chains are refitted on fixed-center bootstrap data while forwarding their mean prediction, and a target-stage future error enters a studentized prediction root. Across the investigated scenarios, relative mean bias is substantially reduced, and coverage is closer to the nominal 90%. At sample size 30, the eight-stage bootstrap has mean width ratios of 1.16-1.42 relative to the known-parameter normal reference, compared with 4.11-4.97 for observed-to-observed MCSim. These results support improved endpoint prediction in the tested setting. Further investigations of the bootstrap scheme in the supplement for a bivariate 6-stage process show similar satisfactory results.
papers.summary: End-to-end digital twins are often built by fitting separate models for each stage and chaining them after inference, forwarding complete predictive draws through Monte Carlo simulation. The authors show analytically and in simulations of four- and eight-stage chains that this scheme inflates prediction intervals and can bias the mean. They propose a model-based bootstrap that forwards fitted means, refits bootstrap chains, and builds a studentized prediction interval. At 30 training runs, the eight-stage bootstrap's interval widths are **1.16 to 1.42 times the known-parameter reference, versus 4.11 to 4.97 for the Monte Carlo approach**, with coverage closer to the nominal 90%.

papers.title: Regret-based Characterization, Information Limits, and the Sample Complexity of Auditing Adaptive Policies
papers.abstract:
A policy can earn its performance by where it locates on average or by reacting to information. For any Markov policy $\pi$ in a finite-horizon MDP, let $
u$ be its open-loop marginal, which plays $\pi$'s average action distribution at each step. We show that $J(\pi)-J(
u)$ equals $\sum_t tr Cov(Q^
u_t,\pi_t)$ under endogenous dynamics. Audits based on immediate costs alone can have the wrong sign. Writing the covariance as a joint-versus-product gap gives the bound $|J(\pi)-J(
u)|\le\sum_t span_t\sqrt{I(s_t;a_t)/2}$, with a sharp constant. Hence, an MDP's adaptivity gap is bounded by the information that its optimal policy uses. Estimating $J(\pi)-J(
u)$ from $\pi$'s own bandit-feedback logs takes $\Theta( ar\chi^2 \log(1/\eta)/\delta^2)$ rounds, where $ ar\chi^2$ is an average $\chi^2$-divergence. At the same time, deterministic non-constant policies cannot be audited at all. We also provide an importance-sampling auditor for episodic MDPs.
papers.summary: The question here is how much of a policy's performance in a finite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP) comes from reacting to information rather than from its average behavior. The authors compare a policy with its open-loop marginal and show the performance gap equals a sum of covariances between Q-values and actions. They show that audits based on immediate costs alone can get the sign wrong. An information-theoretic bound follows: **an MDP's adaptivity gap is bounded by the mutual information between states and actions that the optimal policy uses**. Estimating the gap from bandit-feedback logs takes a number of rounds governed by an average chi-squared divergence, and deterministic non-constant policies cannot be audited at all.

papers.title: Post-stratified importance sampling
papers.abstract: Importance sampling is a building block of modern statistical computing, but the weighted estimate is prone to high or infinite variance. Moreover, its empirical standard error is often unreliable, leaving importance sampling without practical uncertainty quantification. Motivated by multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) in survey sampling, we propose post-stratified importance sampling (PIS) for estimating target expectations from proposal draws. PIS reformulates arbitrarily high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional probabilistic modeling problems: regression for the conditional mean given the importance ratio and marginal density estimation for the importance ratio. Different modeling choices yield a family of PIS estimators, encompassing ordinary importance sampling as a special case. We develop a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression for the conditional mean and score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation for the marginal law, using both the observed weights and the available density evaluations. We study the oracle gains of PIS and establish consistency under general and model-specific conditions. Simulations and applications to cross-validation demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.
papers.summary: Importance sampling is widely used but can have very high variance, and its empirical standard errors are often unreliable. Borrowing from multilevel regression and poststratification in survey sampling, `post-stratified importance sampling` (`PIS`) turns high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional problems. One is regressing the target on the importance ratio, and the other is estimating the ratio's marginal density. The implementation combines `Gaussian process` regression with a heavy-tailed density estimate that uses score information, and it contains ordinary importance sampling as a special case. Simulations and cross-validation applications show **improved estimation accuracy and more reliable uncertainty quantification**.

papers.title: Shrinkage prior for implicit generative models
papers.abstract: Implicit generative models based on deep neural networks have revolutionized many scientific fields, from weather research to language generation. They successfully model complex random objects arising in real-world problems. In this work, we propose a sample-efficient training mechanism for these models. Our approach leverages regularized inference with shrinkage priors and generalized Bayes. In the large $p$ (parameter dimension) and small $n$ (sample size) setting, sparsity-inducing priors have been successfully used for linear regression when $p \gg n$. However, their application to implicit generative models remains challenging due to the intractability of the likelihood function. To address this, we adapt a scoring rule posterior based on a strictly proper scoring rule, following the generalized Bayes framework. We then propose a block SGMCMC within Gibbs sampling mechanism. This enables efficient exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces by identifying a sparse representation of neural implicit generative models. We demonstrate the performance of our proposed method through experiments on $p \gg n$ linear regression and an application of neural generative models.
papers.summary: Neural implicit generative models need a lot of data, and the sparsity-inducing priors that work for linear regression with many more parameters than samples are hard to apply because these models have no tractable likelihood. The authors use a generalized-Bayes posterior built on a strictly proper scoring rule. They sample it with a block `SGMCMC`-within-Gibbs scheme that **finds sparse representations of neural implicit generative models** in high-dimensional parameter spaces. They demonstrate the approach on high-dimensional linear regression and a neural generative modeling application.

papers.title: Logarithmic Regret for Alternating Mirror Descent
papers.abstract: Alternating online mirror descent (AltOMD) is a simple learning rule for zero-sum games, which improves upon simultaneous OMD numerically and theoretically. Previous work obtained $O(T^{1/3})$ and $O(T^{1/5})$ regret bounds for AltOMD, by leveraging modified-energy-function-based analyses. However, settling whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret has remained an open question. In this paper we resolve the question of whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret in the affirmative. In particular, we show an $O(log(T))$ regret bound on the sum of the players' external regrets for any two-player zero-sum bilinear game with compact convex strategy sets, under mild regularity assumptions on the regularizers. We verify that our assumptions hold for the negative entropy regularizer, thereby obtaining logarithmic regret for the alternating multiplicative weights updates algorithm. The regret bound also yields an $O(log(T)/T)$ duality gap bound for the averaged strategies.
papers.summary: Alternating online mirror descent (`AltOMD`) is a learning rule for two-player zero-sum games that outperforms the simultaneous version, but its best known regret bounds were O(T^{1/3}) and O(T^{1/5}). The authors settle the open question of whether it achieves near-constant regret. They prove **an O(log T) bound on the sum of external regrets** for any bilinear zero-sum game with compact convex strategy sets, under mild assumptions on the regularizers. The assumptions hold for negative entropy, which gives logarithmic regret for alternating multiplicative weights and an O(log T / T) duality gap for the averaged strategies.

papers.title: Going Deeper With Memories
papers.abstract: Byte level language models avoid tokenizer dependence and provide universal coverage, but processing every byte at full resolution is expensive. We introduce DeepMem, a causal multiscale architecture that separates semantic compression from exact byte preservation. A learned invertible subband transform constructs a hierarchy of shorter sequences, while a lossless carrier and explicit detail sidebands preserve byte identity. Fast weight memory blocks operate along the encoder, with iterative shared state computation at the compressed bottleneck, while an attention based super resolution decoder restores byte resolution representations. DeepMem achieves stronger language modeling performance than a matched byte level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19, and obtains the best macro average performance across the evaluated FLORES languages. It also improves PIQA accuracy while remaining competitive on code modeling, multiple choice reasoning, and byte level corruption robustness. Bottleneck refinement requires approximately $7{,}600\times$ fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full resolution reasoning, while maintaining competitive evaluation throughput.
papers.summary: Byte-level language models avoid tokenizers but are expensive because they process every byte at full resolution. `DeepMem` is a causal multiscale architecture that uses a learned invertible subband transform to compress sequences, while a lossless carrier and detail sidebands preserve exact byte identity. Fast-weight memory blocks and iterative computation run at the compressed bottleneck, and an attention-based decoder restores byte resolution. It beats a matched byte-level `Transformer` on `FineWeb-Edu` and `PG19`, has the best macro average across `FLORES` languages, and improves `PIQA`. Its **bottleneck refinement uses about 7,600 times fewer FLOPs than equivalent full-resolution reasoning**.

papers.title: NovoCRF: Globally Normalized De Novo Peptide Sequencing on a Prefix-Mass Lattice
papers.abstract: De novo peptide sequencing has moved from dynamic programming over hand-designed or generative scores to large transformers that learn the task end to end. We present NovoCRF, a conditional random field (CRF) whose states are prefix masses, so that its paths are exactly the peptides within +/-0.06 Da of the precursor mass. A small network scores each edge from physics-derived ion-match features and is trained with its scores globally normalized over all mass-feasible peptides. To our knowledge, NovoCRF is the first de novo method trained with exact normalization over all mass-feasible peptides. Our software has three modules, each with exactly one job: a precursor mass finder recovers the accurate precursor mass from MS1, the CRF finds the peptides that fit the precursor mass by exact k-best decoding, and two BiGRU rerankers add sequence context and internal-fragment evidence. The model has 310k parameters and trains in about 17 GPU-hours. On seven held-out data-dependent acquisition datasets published in 2026 (126,262 labeled spectra), NovoCRF's mean peptide recall is 42.4%, against 39.1% for Casanovo v5 with five beams, and its amino-acid recall 64.0% against 53.1%, at 1,746 spectra/s on 18 CPU threads, 55x Casanovo's throughput on a GPU. Split by fragment evidence, NovoCRF leads on labels with up to three peptide bonds without a b or y ion, and Casanovo only beyond. NovoCRF can also search modifications it was never trained on at their exact mass: it finds 32.1% of the hydroxyproline peptides of a lion bone sample.
papers.summary: De novo peptide sequencing reads peptide sequences directly from mass spectra, and recent methods use large transformers trained end to end. `NovoCRF` instead uses a conditional random field (CRF) whose states are prefix masses, so every path is a peptide matching the precursor mass. It is the first de novo method trained with exact normalization over all mass-feasible peptides. A small network scores edges from physics-derived ion-match features, and `BiGRU` rerankers refine the results. With only 310k parameters, it reaches **42.4% mean peptide recall versus 39.1% for `Casanovo` v5** on seven held-out datasets. It runs on CPUs at 55 times Casanovo's GPU throughput and can find modifications it was never trained on.

papers.title: Gaussian Partitioning for Reliable Learning of Multi-Index Models
papers.abstract:
We introduce Gaussian partitioning, an algorithmic primitive for distributions smooth with respect to a Gaussian. It partitions space into polyhedral regions so that almost all mass lies in thin strips restricting a few orthogonal directions. Within each strip, the conditional distribution approximately matches low-degree Gaussian moments in the unrestricted directions. Our construction builds on logconcave partitioning of Diakonikolas, Kane, and Ma (FOCS 2026).
  Under input marginals smooth with respect to the standard Gaussian, we obtain agnostic learners with error $(1+c)\mathrm{opt}+\epsilon$ for broad classes of Boolean multi-index models, including functions of halfspaces, low-dimensional convex concepts, and low-dimensional polynomial threshold functions. For functions of $k$ halfspaces, both agnostic and testable agnostic learners achieve this error with dimension dependence $d^{\mathrm{poly}(k/c)}$, improving the previous exponential dependence on $k/c$ in the agnostic exponent.
  For learning from positive examples with imperfect unlabeled data (PUI), we give algorithms and Statistical Query (SQ) lower bounds that qualitatively characterize complexity through Gaussian moment matching. For fixed smoothness and positive-mass parameters, we learn intersections of $k$ halfspaces with dimension dependence $d^{O(\log(k/\epsilon))}$ and matching SQ lower bounds, improving the previous $d^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon)}$ upper bound even for one halfspace. A general reduction from agnostic reliable learning to PUI yields negative reliable learners for these intersections with the same dimension dependence, for fixed smoothness.
  Finally, for PQ learning and testable learning with distribution shift, we prove qualitatively optimal SQ lower bounds of $d^{\Omega(1/\epsilon^2)}$, even for intersections of two halfspaces with Gaussian training data and arbitrary test distributions.
papers.summary: `Gaussian partitioning` is a new algorithmic primitive for distributions that are smooth relative to a Gaussian. It splits space into polyhedral regions where most mass lies in thin strips, and within each strip the conditional distribution approximately matches low-degree Gaussian moments. Using it, the authors obtain agnostic learners for Boolean multi-index models such as functions of halfspaces, low-dimensional convex concepts and polynomial threshold functions. For functions of k halfspaces, **dimension dependence improves from exponential in k/c to d^{poly(k/c)}**. They also give new algorithms with matching Statistical Query (SQ) lower bounds for learning from positive and imperfect unlabeled examples, and nearly optimal SQ lower bounds for learning under distribution shift.

papers.title: Stabilizing On-Policy Targeted Guidance in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Naive on-policy RL is often bottlenecked by the capabilities of the base model --- insufficient coverage can result in an inability to learn from certain rewards. At the same time, rewards in modern post-training systems often come from rich textual sources, e.g. judge models with a rubric of criteria. Can we utilize such structures to provide a rich directional signal that enables improving on otherwise difficult to optimize rewards? In this work, we examine a framework we refer to as targeted guidance that learns from per-turn textual feedback via an on-policy self-distillation objective. Our focus is not only on directly improving hard-to-optimize behaviors, but on how to do so throughout the training process without degrading baseline RL performance. Over a range of settings across an agentic multi-turn software engineering environment, we find success by combining targeted self-distillation with a per-criteria RL reward, and by limiting feedback to turns where the policy specifically fails. We further examine the design choices that lead to stable entropy and reduce oscillatory behavior throughout training.
papers.summary: On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) for LLM agents is limited by what the base model can already do, even when rewards come with rich textual feedback such as rubric-based judge critiques. The authors study 'targeted guidance', which learns from per-turn textual feedback through an on-policy self-distillation objective. They focus on improving hard-to-optimize behaviors without degrading baseline RL performance. In a multi-turn agentic software engineering environment, the approach works best when **targeted self-distillation is combined with a per-criterion RL reward and feedback is limited to turns where the policy actually fails**. The authors also identify design choices that keep entropy stable and reduce oscillation during training.

papers.title: iGC: Antibody Optimization via Reinforcement Learning over a Learned Somatic Hypermutation Prior
papers.abstract:
Antibody affinity maturation is a natural optimization process in which B cells acquire mutations through somatic hypermutation (SHM), undergo selection for improved antigen binding, and iteratively evolve toward higher affinity. Computationally modeling this process requires capturing both biologically plausible mutations and antigen-specific selection. However, existing mutation models do not directly optimize binding, while affinity optimization often neglects realistic mutation trajectories.
  We introduce iGC (in silico Germinal Centers), a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework for antigen-specific antibody optimization. Stage 1 learns an SHM mutation prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees and adapts it to a target affinity-maturation dataset. Stage 2 initializes an RL policy from this prior and optimizes antigen binding with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization toward the frozen prior. To prevent reward exploitation, including repetitive high-reward substitutions and structurally tolerated framework mutations, we introduce a Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective. RewardNet smooths the affinity landscape, while TaxNet penalizes reward overexploitation, jointly defining a learned meta-reward for policy optimization.
  We evaluate iGC on mutation prediction, SHM consistency, affinity optimization, and mutation diversity. The mutation prior more than doubles the strongest baseline in mutation-site prediction. Following RL optimization, iGC maintains SHM sequence structure. It also achieves a strong exploration-exploitation balance, yielding competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs. These results demonstrate that iGC integrates biologically plausible mutation generation with antigen-specific affinity selection, providing an in silico framework for iterative antibody affinity maturation.
papers.summary: Computationally imitating antibody affinity maturation requires mutations that are both biologically plausible and selected for antigen binding, but existing mutation models never optimize binding while affinity optimizers produce unrealistic mutation trajectories. `iGC` (in silico Germinal Centers) splits this into two stages: learn a somatic hypermutation (SHM) prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees, then initialize a reinforcement learning policy from that prior and optimize binding with Kullback-Leibler regularization back toward the frozen prior. A Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective guards against reward exploitation, with `RewardNet` smoothing the affinity landscape and `TaxNet` penalizing overexploitation of repetitive high-reward substitutions. The prior **more than doubles the strongest baseline at mutation-site prediction**, and after reinforcement learning the policy keeps SHM-like sequence structure while reaching competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs.

papers.title: De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes
papers.abstract: We attempt to alleviate failure modes of classical physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in scenarios of topological pathologies corresponding to punctures, holes, poles, and voids by introducing de Rham cohomological augmentations, or Hodge-de Rham PINNs. Vanilla PINNs often encounter pitfalls in hole-based settings due to discontinuous interfaces, nonzero closed path integration, path dependence, correspondence to exact forms via the exterior derivative, etc., therefore we absolve traditional failures via parameterizing a 1-form by the Hodge-Morrey-Friedrichs (HMF) decomposition for manifolds with boundary, drawing a connection to de Rham cohomology such as through the HMF isomorphism theorem. 1-forms can act as representations of scalar-valued PDE solutions through integral operator mappings. We propose performing a PINN-based loss on the parameterized 1-form through an associated PDE, which subsequently solves the potential-based PINN problem and moreover remedies the failures of vanilla PINNs via the Sobolev-regular operator under a Fr\'echet differentiation interconnection. The operator relationship often has a nontrivial closed-form and often requires integration or a case-by-case analysis, which we address thoroughly in our experiments. When an integrability condition is not met on our losses, we can equip exhaustion functions to train the networks. We demonstrate our methods on the Aharonov-Bohm effect, which, to our understanding, is largely nonexistent in PINN literature. We develop theoretical guarantees of our methods and demonstrate our pathological safeguards on a broad selection of topologically-adverse problems, including scenarios of inexact forms, and those of nontrivial harmonics and coexact terms.
papers.summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) break down on domains containing punctures, holes, poles, or voids, where closed-path integrals are nonzero and solutions become path-dependent rather than derivable from a single potential. The proposed Hodge-de Rham PINNs instead parameterize a 1-form via the Hodge-Morrey-Friedrichs decomposition for manifolds with boundary, train a PINN loss on that form through an associated partial differential equation, and recover scalar solutions through integral operator mappings, falling back on exhaustion functions when an integrability condition fails. Alongside theoretical guarantees, the method is demonstrated on a range of topologically adverse problems including inexact forms and nontrivial harmonic and coexact terms, and notably on **the Aharonov-Bohm effect, which the authors report is largely absent from the PINN literature**.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction at Performative Equilibrium: The Price of Performativity
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample coverage when calibration and test points are exchangeable, but exchangeability can fail when deployment changes the data distribution. We study conformal prediction in performative settings, where the deployed predictor affects the data distribution, and seek prediction sets valid at performative equilibrium: coverage must hold under $D(f^\star)$ for a performatively stable predictor $f^\star$. Under total-variation $L$-sensitivity of the distribution map, we prove a phase transition at $L=1$. If $L \ge 1$, no finite-sample procedure can uniformly guarantee both equilibrium-valid coverage and nontrivial prediction sets. If $L<1$, the minimax excess miscoverage over informative procedures is $\widetilde{\Omega}(1/((1-L)\sqrt{n}))$, implying a sample-complexity inflation of order $1/(1-L)^2$ for fixed excess miscoverage. Our main technical tool is a transfer theorem: any procedure returning a predictor within $\varepsilon$ of equilibrium yields equilibrium-valid coverage up to an additive $L\varepsilon$ term after split-conformal calibration. We instantiate the theorem with two retraining algorithms: a model-free method for discretizable classes and a parametric tail-averaged method that matches the $n$- and $L$-dependence of this rate up to logarithmic factors. Experiments, including semi-synthetic credit scoring, demonstrate the predicted threshold behavior and scaling laws.
papers.summary: Conformal prediction's finite-sample coverage guarantee assumes calibration and test points are exchangeable, which fails when deploying a predictor changes the distribution it will be judged on. Framing this as performative prediction, the authors require coverage at performative equilibrium and prove a phase transition in the total-variation sensitivity L of the distribution map: **when L is at least 1 no finite-sample procedure can deliver both equilibrium-valid coverage and non-trivial prediction sets, while below 1 the minimax excess miscoverage scales as 1/((1-L) times the square root of n)**, inflating sample complexity by a factor of 1/(1-L)^2. The main tool is a transfer theorem showing any procedure that returns a predictor within epsilon of equilibrium yields equilibrium-valid coverage up to an additive L-times-epsilon term after split-conformal calibration, instantiated with a model-free and a parametric tail-averaged retraining algorithm and checked on semi-synthetic credit scoring.

papers.title: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment. Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency. We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell these two framings apart, even though they lead to different levels of misalignment. These results suggest a risk for model updates, where training a model that does not adopt the new fact as true can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on narrowly harmful data can make it broadly misaligned, but models are rarely trained on explicitly harmful content in practice. The experiments here use data with no harmful content at all, only answers the model believes to be false, and find that across mathematics, trivia, cooking, and sports the more strongly the model disbelieves what it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes: **on mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers get more wrong**, with little loss of general capability. Multiple-choice probabilities still favor the true answers after fine-tuning, suggesting the misalignment stems from that internal inconsistency; the same pattern holds when a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing. Framing the false fact inside a coherent story makes the model adopt it more deeply and stay more aligned than instructing it to assert the fact, yet content filters and persona vectors cannot distinguish the two framings.

papers.title: GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL
papers.abstract: Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies -- typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets -- capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal. Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy's support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy's support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Project website and open-source code at https://charlesxu0124.github.io/gsbr/ .
papers.summary: Regularizing online reinforcement learning toward a pretrained base policy improves sample efficiency but usually constrains improvement too tightly: behavioral-cloning regularizers penalize dropping the base policy's suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid any action just outside its support. `GSBR` (Geometric Support Behavior Regularization) instead penalizes an action by its distance from the base policy's support, estimated from a finite set of base-policy samples, so in-support actions are free and out-of-support actions are penalized smoothly enough that a large enough value gain still justifies them. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks it **raises average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%**, the best among compared methods, with roughly 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best reinforcement learning method.

papers.title: Universal Hardness From Masking Channels
papers.abstract: We prove a broad learning-theoretic generalization of the celebrated hardcore lemma concerning the average-case complexity of computing a Boolean function (Impagliazzo, 1995). Our starting point is the observation that the classic notion of a hardcore measure, which reweights a function's input distribution, is equivalent to an input-dependent masking channel that injects randomness into the function's output distribution until it appears fully pseudorandom. The analogue of density of the measure is the fidelity of the channel. From this viewpoint, we develop a general framework for certifying hardness that allows for non-Boolean functions $f$ and a wide range of notions of hardness besides the classic 0-1 loss, by choosing the right notion of fidelity via convex duality. We show the difficulty of learning $f$ using a class $\mathcal{C}$ to minimize a convex loss is tightly characterized by the maximum fidelity possible for a masking channel, which measures the least amount of noise the channel must add to hide the structure of $f$ and make it $\mathcal{C}$-indistinguishable from random noise. Using our framework, we derive a number of multiclass generalizations of the hardcore lemma, and reveal some unexpected subtleties in going to larger alphabets. We construct a universal masking channel that applies to many natural notions of hardness simultaneously. Such channels are dual to omnipredictors, which optimize multiple losses at once (Gopalan, Kalai, Reingold, Sharan, and Wieder, 2022). We observe a symmetry between masking channels and generalizations of the hardcore lemma using pseudoentropy. We present a tight characterization of pseudoentropy using the MaxEnt algorithm from machine learning. A long line of research has shown that learning and hardness are two sides of the same coin; our framework gives a crisp and general formulation of this principle via convex duality.
papers.summary: Impagliazzo's hardcore lemma is recast by observing that a hardcore measure reweighting a function's input distribution is equivalent to an input-dependent masking channel that injects randomness into the output until it looks fully pseudorandom, with the channel's fidelity playing the role of the measure's density. Choosing the right notion of fidelity through convex duality yields a general hardness-certification framework covering non-Boolean functions and losses beyond 0-1, in which **the difficulty of learning a function with a given class under a convex loss is tightly characterized by the maximum fidelity achievable by a masking channel that hides it**. The authors derive multiclass generalizations of the hardcore lemma, surface unexpected subtleties at larger alphabets, construct a universal masking channel dual to omnipredictors, and give a tight characterization of pseudoentropy via the `MaxEnt` algorithm.

papers.title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.
papers.summary: Looped transformers reuse the same layers across multiple loop steps to match much larger models with fewer parameters, but each loop step stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with loop count and becomes the memory bottleneck. `LoopVQ` exploits the observation that this cache is highly redundant along the loop axis while loop steps differ in quantization sensitivity, jointly vector-quantizing channels from several loop steps and fine-tuning the codebooks to match full-precision outputs. At 0.5 bits per element it beats KV-cache vector quantization methods built for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought, and long-context retrieval tasks with `Ouro` and `Huginn`, and composed with `TaSQ` it retains much of `BF16` accuracy at 0.25 bits. Implemented in `SGLang`, it nearly halves decode latency at a 32K-token context and **raises peak serving throughput by up to 4.3x and 6.1x on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Looped transformers reuse their weights across loop steps, but every loop step still writes its own keys and values, so the KV cache grows with loop count and becomes the main memory cost. `LoopVQ` exploits the strong correlation of the cache across loop steps by vector-quantizing channels from several loop steps jointly under one shared index, which pushes KV storage to **0.5–0.25 bits per element**.

- In `Ouro-1.4B`, a key channel correlates with the same channel at the adjacent loop step at about **|r| = 0.85**, but with the other channels in its sub-vector at only about 0.16, so each 8-bit code spans G/4 channels across 4 consecutive loop steps instead of G channels of one step, which roughly halves k-means reconstruction error at no extra bit cost.
- Because quantizing the first loop step degrades the output about 5× more than quantizing the third (measured as KL divergence from the full-precision output), the Fisher-weighted k-means codebooks are then fine-tuned end-to-end to minimize that KL divergence through the loop, which roughly halves the KL again in about 2–6 minutes on one GPU.
- On `Ouro-1.4B` at 0.5 bit, the average over `GSM8K`, `MATH500`, `HumanEval` and `MBPP` rises from 32.3 (`CQ`) and 43.6 (`TaSQ`) to **68.3 for `LoopVQ`** and **73.6 for `TaSQ+LoopVQ`**, against 75.7 for BF16, with similar gains on `Ouro-2.6B` and `Huginn-3.5B`.
- On long chain-of-thought reasoning with `Ouro-2.6B-Thinking` at 0.5 bit, `TaSQ+LoopVQ` scores **63.8 vs. 64.9 for BF16**, while the baselines collapse to 16–28 and often run out the 32K-token budget; `LoopVQ` also leads on `RULER` needle-in-a-haystack retrieval up to 64K context.
- An `SGLang` kernel roughly **halves decode latency at 32K context** and raises peak throughput **4.3× and 6.1×** on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models, but prefill is slightly slower, serving speed is compared only against BF16, and there is no accuracy comparison with the scalar looped-model KV quantizers `FlashLoop` and `ResidualQuant`.

papers.title: $\Phi$asmaNet: A Staged Spectral Token-Refinement Architecture for Fast Gravitational-Wave Signal-to-Noise Ratio Prediction
papers.abstract: Quantifying selection effects in gravitational-wave population studies requires millions of costly signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) calculations. We present $\Phi$asmaNet, a compact neural architecture for structured tabular regression, with staged spectral refinement as an explicit architectural prior. Learned input tokens are refined through ordered attention-based $\Phi$-Stages, each augmented by a $\Phi$-Refractor subspace-mixing module, then revisited through gated top-down $\Phi$-Feedback. Applied to the 11-dimensional parameters of precessing, higher-mode binary black hole signals (IMRPhenomXPHM), it predicts phase-averaged optimal SNR for a single detector at fixed Advanced LIGO design sensitivity. With approximately 732k parameters, it outperforms MLP, 1D-ResNet and Transformer-encoder baselines under matched training across $10^5$--$10^6$ samples. At $10^6$ samples, it achieves $100-\mathrm{MAPE}=98.73\%$ on the held-out test set, $99.29\%$ after rank-preserving monotonic (PCHIP) calibration, and $99.39\%$ ($R^2=0.9998$) in the detection-relevant regime $\rho>8$, with stable accuracy across independent dataset realizations.
