On a single GPU, it sustains approximately $1.2\times10^5$ SNR evaluations per second and processes a $10^6$-injection catalogue end-to-end in approximately 8.3 s, about two orders of magnitude faster than conventional waveform-and-inner-product calculations on a 16-core CPU. Exact distance rescaling through $\rho\propto1/d_L$ supports repeated catalogue-wide detectability evaluations. The fully documented pipeline is intended as a reproducible benchmark, while results on public tabular datasets indicate competitiveness beyond gravitational-wave applications. Although demonstrated for a fixed single-detector configuration, the construction supports extensions to detector networks and epoch-specific sensitivities. (Abridged)
papers.summary: Quantifying selection effects in gravitational-wave population studies demands millions of expensive signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) calculations. `ΦasmaNet` is a roughly 732k-parameter network for structured tabular regression that refines learned input tokens through ordered attention-based stages, each with a subspace-mixing module, and then revisits them through gated top-down feedback; it maps the 11 parameters of precessing, higher-mode binary black hole signals to phase-averaged optimal SNR for a single detector at Advanced LIGO design sensitivity. It outperforms MLP, 1D-ResNet, and transformer-encoder baselines under matched training, reaching 98.73% accuracy by one-minus-MAPE on held-out data, and on one GPU sustains about 120,000 evaluations per second, **processing a million-injection catalogue end to end in roughly 8.3 seconds, about two orders of magnitude faster than conventional waveform-and-inner-product computation on a 16-core CPU**.

papers.title: CATF: A Manager-Worker Framework for Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: We study context-aware time-series forecasting, in which a single target variable is predicted from its own history and a set of contextual variables, such as weather and calendar information. As the context becomes more diverse, a single model struggles to capture all of its regimes, while ensemble learning and Mixture-of-Experts approaches rely on manual data partitioning or soft routing, which increases the inference cost and hinders interpretability. We propose CATF, a Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting framework built on a Manager-Worker architecture: a Transformer-based Manager routes each input to a single Worker based on the context, using hard routing during both training and inference. The Workers thus specialize without manual data partitioning, and any single-model forecaster can serve as a Worker. On five context-rich datasets, four horizons, and two normalization schemes, CATF improves over its standalone counterpart in 162 of 200 comparisons, the best CATF-enhanced model outperforms the best standalone baseline in 19 of 20 settings, and it outperforms the zero-shot Time-MoE foundation model in 15 of 20 settings. A case study on bike-sharing data shows that the Manager routes inputs by the calendar and that each Worker specializes in a different weekly pattern.
papers.summary: In context-aware time-series forecasting a single target is predicted from its own history plus contextual variables like weather and calendar, and as context diversifies one model struggles to cover every regime while ensembles and Mixture-of-Experts need manual partitioning or costly soft routing. `CATF` adopts a manager-worker design in which a transformer-based manager hard-routes each input to exactly one worker based on its context, during both training and inference, so workers specialize without hand-built partitions and any single-model forecaster can serve as a worker. Across five context-rich datasets, four horizons, and two normalization schemes it **beats its standalone counterpart in 162 of 200 comparisons**, with the best enhanced model topping the best standalone baseline in 19 of 20 settings and the zero-shot `Time-MoE` foundation model in 15 of 20; a bike-sharing case study shows the manager routing by calendar and each worker learning a distinct weekly pattern.

papers.title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry
papers.abstract: Efficient preconditioning plays an important role in large-scale first-order optimization. In this paper, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging ($\text{A}^2$ODA) method for unconstrained convex optimization that adopts low-cost preconditioning based on $p$-norm geometry for $p\in[2,\infty]$. The method is line-search-free and employs a new stepsize selection technique based on an aggregated affine lower model. Its update structure is simple and unified across $p\in[2,\infty]$, with the case $p>2$ requiring no more elaborate updates than the Euclidean case $p=2$. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, we derive a convergence bound that separates the effects of constant and gap-dependent curvature, with the latter potentially yielding faster-decaying terms. In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate.
papers.summary: Cheap preconditioning matters for large-scale first-order optimization, and this work proposes an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex problems that preconditions using p-norm geometry for p between 2 and infinity. The method avoids line search, selects stepsizes from a new aggregated affine lower model, and keeps one update structure across all p, so the case of p greater than 2 is no more involved than the Euclidean case. Under a generalized local smoothness condition the convergence bound separates constant from gap-dependent curvature, the latter potentially contributing faster-decaying terms, and **in the plain locally smooth case the bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate**.

papers.title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.
papers.summary: In-context learning with arbitrary labels forces a model to acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so whatever learning happens must happen inside one forward pass; prior work identified candidate components but not how they compose. Studying few-shot sentence classification in three transformers of 3-4B parameters, the authors describe the full mechanism as a key-value memory over label-token positions: middle-layer attention heads write the class of the preceding demonstration into each label token as a key, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching label, an early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates that readout, and a separate head group suppresses the most recently seen label. Every step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals, and **the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour**. The same circuit appears from 0.6B to 8B within one family, survives instruction tuning, transfers to semantic concepts and meaningful labels, and regrows in a transformer trained from scratch.

papers.title: Agnostic Learning by Imitating
papers.abstract: Given a class of machine learning models and sample access to a data distribution with binary labels, which computational task is harder: training a discriminative model that distinguishes positive and negative labels as well as the best member of the class, or training a generative model whose outputs are indistinguishable from real data by all members of the class? We prove that these two fundamental tasks in computational learning theory are not just closely related, but actually equivalent to each other in complexity. One direction of this equivalence was previously known. Indeed, the powerful regularity lemma in complexity theory gives an efficient oracle reduction from the indistinguishability task (a.k.a. multiaccuracy) to the distinguishing task (a.k.a. agnostic learning) in the style of boosting algorithms. Our main contribution is an efficient oracle reduction in the other direction. Taking this idea further, we show that a multiaccuracy oracle is a remarkably powerful primitive, achieving not just agnostic learning but also a wide range of seemingly more demanding learning objectives via similarly efficient and direct constructions. Our results crucially use the power of making adaptive queries to the oracle, and stand in stark contrast to prior work, which showed that post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor is insufficient for even weak forms of learning. On a technical level, we draw a connection between our (offline) problem and a version of no-regret learning in the online setting, which allows us to use follow-the-leader type algorithms to modify the label distribution and aggregate the predictions of the multiaccuracy oracle.
papers.summary: Which is computationally harder: training a discriminative model that separates binary labels as well as the best member of a model class, known as agnostic learning, or training a generative model whose outputs no member of that class can distinguish from real data, known as multiaccuracy? The two tasks turn out to be **equivalent in complexity**, with the previously missing direction supplied here as an efficient oracle reduction from agnostic learning to a multiaccuracy oracle, built by connecting the offline problem to no-regret online learning and using follow-the-leader style algorithms to modify the label distribution and aggregate oracle predictions. Pushing further, a multiaccuracy oracle is shown to reach a range of seemingly more demanding learning objectives by similarly direct constructions; the results hinge on adaptive queries, in contrast to earlier work showing that post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor cannot yield even weak learning.

papers.title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
papers.abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every step is a Born measurement - attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^4$ normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-11}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference, with about 98k parameters outside the embedding, the model reaches $76.98 \pm 0.17$% test accuracy, level with a softmax transformer of the same size ($76.62 \pm 0.36$%). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 45% of test pairs, out of the 53% any single deletion can change, against 32% for the softmax model explained the same way and 40% by its attention x gradient. Attention can look as much like the words annotators highlighted as the evidence does, yet accounts for the answer less well: deleting the word it ranks first changes the Born Transformer's answer in 32% of pairs. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics and to qubits, and a coherent attention layer becomes one circuit equal to the model (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps by Hadamard tests, the device gave the model's answers, also when a word was deleted. With calibration circuits as deep as the overlaps, each word's evidence with the device's attention row sums followed the exact evidence (correlations 0.997 and 0.932 on two pairs chosen in advance); where a pair's evidence is a small total of large opposite terms the earlier runs say it does not, and we say why.
papers.summary: Attributions for a language model's answer are normally approximations, so this work builds a transformer in which every operation is a Born measurement: attention as the normalized fourth power of query-key overlap, a measured product replacing the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout. Holding the attention denominators at their input values makes each class probability a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so integrated-gradient evidence is computed by exact finite quadrature and **per-word contributions sum to the class probability to within 1e-11**. On `e-SNLI` natural language inference with about 98k non-embedding parameters the model matches a same-size softmax transformer (76.98% versus 76.62% accuracy), and deleting its top-ranked word flips the answer in 45% of test pairs against 32% for the softmax model explained the same way. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronics and to qubits, and a coherent attention layer run as an 852-CNOT, 23-qubit circuit on IBM's `ibm_kingston` reproduced the model's answers, with device-measured evidence tracking the exact values except where a pair's total is a small residue of large opposing terms.

papers.title: Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors in Language Models, Durably
papers.abstract: Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms--language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment--that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods--SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning--along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories. Across both organism settings and two model families (Qwen3-4B, GPT-OSS-20B), PEARL achieves strong immediate suppression while preserving task accuracy, and remains durable under further fine-tuning on either the organism's data or unrelated data. It obtains the greatest benefit when the undesirable behavior is broad and cannot be addressed through targeted SFT. Together, our framework and method offer a step toward more durable post-hoc removal of undesired behaviors.
papers.summary: To study how well an undesired behavior can be removed after it appears, the authors build two deliberately misaligned model organisms: a narrow-trigger one that cheats on multiple-choice questions only when a planted hint points to a wrong answer, and a broad-trigger one that answers harmfully across open-ended prompts after fine-tuning on insecure code. They formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and score methods on immediate suppression, durability under further training, and capability preservation, comparing supervised fine-tuning, `GRPO`, and gradient-ascent unlearning. Their method `PEARL` (Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning) is a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached misbehaving trajectories, on the hypothesis that durability requires recovering from a wider range of misaligned states. On `Qwen3-4B` and `GPT-OSS-20B` it **suppresses the behavior while preserving task accuracy and staying durable under further fine-tuning on both the organism's own data and unrelated data**, gaining most where misbehavior is broad and targeted fine-tuning cannot reach it.

papers.title: GUILD: Guided Iterative Data Collection for Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies in robotics are trained on datasets collected through costly real-world teleoperation. Often, the data-collection process is unguided, relying on the teleoperator's intuition, resulting in data that contributes little to overall policy performance. Recent work has shown that curating such unguided datasets can substantially improve policy performance, but these approaches operate by filtering existing datasets after collection and therefore do not prevent the acquisition of uninformative data. In this work, we propose GUILD, a novel Guided Data Collection (GDC) method that actively reasons about which data should be collected to maximize downstream policy performance. We introduce an iterative framework that alternates between 1) task proposal and data collection and 2) data evaluation to close the loop. For task proposal, we leverage semantic priors from vision-language models to identify relevant environments, object configurations, and goals for data collection. However, since semantic relevance does not imply policy improvement, we perform data evaluation. By leveraging predictive data attribution we approximate how the collected trajectories influence policy performance on a target deployment setting. This signal is then used as feedback to guide subsequent data collection, closing the data collection loop. We evaluate our approach in simulation and real robot settings, demonstrating that guided data collection substantially improves sample efficiency and deployment performance compared to passive data collection strategies, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists. More information at https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/guild2026/
papers.summary: Robot imitation learning depends on expensive real-world teleoperation that is usually unguided, so operators collect trajectories that contribute little to final policy performance, and existing curation methods only filter data after the fact. `GUILD` closes the loop during collection by alternating between proposal and evaluation: vision-language models supply semantic priors about which environments, object configurations, and goals to collect next, and predictive data attribution then estimates how the newly collected trajectories actually affect policy performance on the target deployment setting, feeding that signal back into the next round. In simulation and on real robots, guided collection **improves sample efficiency and deployment performance over passive collection, several baselines, and experienced roboticists**.

papers.title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2{\deg} on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.
papers.summary: Inverse kinematics turns end-effector pose commands into joint motion and underpins many vision-language-action policies, but redundancy, singularities, and hand-tuned controllers make precise solutions laborious. `PolicyIK` is a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy that updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can hold the offset a position controller needs at rest, with two-scale pose errors and an error-dependent action gain to resolve millimeter residuals, plus progress and dwell rewards to both reach and stay inside tolerance. A single attempt by the trained `PPO` policy keeps mean final-second error within 1 mm and 0.2 degrees on 93.5% of held-out simulated tasks, rising to 98.9% with a deployment protocol; trained directly on a physical arm with off-policy reinforcement learning it beats all four classical inverse-kinematics controllers under matched time budgets, and **it executes the end-effector commands of the π0.5 vision-language-action policy with 95.7% success in simulated pick-and-place**.

papers.title: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization
papers.abstract: Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher's gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1, with GPT-4o or a larger open-weight model of the same family as the annotator. On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o as judge, three iterations raise the length-controlled (LC) win rate against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral, and the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win rate. With same-family open-weight annotators, the runs retain 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains.
papers.summary: Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game, and its practical variant iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of samples against a teacher's gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection, and a `DPO`-style contrastive update. An independent re-implementation on `Llama 3.1 8B Instruct` and `Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1` lifts the length-controlled win rate against `GPT-4o` on `AlpacaEval 2.0` from 31.7% to 45.3% and from 6.8% to 18.4% over three iterations, with the tuned 8B model scoring above `Llama 3.1 70B Instruct` on every reported win rate. **Replacing the proprietary annotator with a same-family open-weight model retains 62% and 82% of the gain**, so the rating step does not require a closed model; ablations show removing gold responses, the data look-back, or non-teacher-preferred pairs costs 6 to 10 points, while sample count and margin settings move results by at most about 2 points. The authors report pipeline cost, where the practical algorithm departs from the theory, and caution that all runs are single and GPT-4o serves as both teacher and judge.

papers.title: Discourse Analysis of Legislative Bill Discussions
papers.abstract: Legislative hearings are distinct communication events with their own human recognizable structure and logic, yet they have been analyzed as distinct phenomena beyond their transcripts. Understanding legislative hearings at a deeper level is a major step in analyzing the work and power relationships within democratic bodies. In this work, we present a novel end-to-end pipeline for parsing rhetorical structures from legislative committee hearings with the goal of improving legislative discourse analysis and democratic accountability. We also propose a rhetorical structure grammar and find that 55.21% of California state bill discussions in our dataset can be parsed with this grammar. We evaluate our pipeline with two utterance section classifiers on a random subset of over 2,000 annotated utterances corresponding to 100 hearings. We find that a logistic regression-based classifier with grammar-based output masking and utterance tag smoothing outperforms more complex models, achieving an F1 score of 52.8% against our ground truth discourse section labels.
papers.summary: Legislative committee hearings follow a recognizable rhetorical structure that transcript-level analysis does not capture, limiting what can be said about how democratic bodies actually work. The authors propose a rhetorical structure grammar for bill discussions plus an end-to-end pipeline for parsing it, and report that **55.21% of the California state bill discussions in their dataset parse under the grammar**. Evaluating two utterance-section classifiers on a random subset of over 2,000 annotated utterances from 100 hearings, a logistic regression model with grammar-based output masking and utterance tag smoothing beats more complex models, reaching an F1 of 52.8%.

papers.title: DS@GT ARC at CheckThat! 2026: A Verdict-Anchored Pipeline for Generating Fact-Checking Articles
papers.abstract: Misinformation spreads faster than professional fact-checkers can manually verify it and write articles explaining their verdicts. This creates a need to automate the production of fact-checking articles. This paper details work done by the DS@GT ARC team for CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Lab Task 3 Fact-Checking Article Generation. We seek to generate a full fact-checking article from a claim, its original verdict, and a set of scraped source documents. Our team built a four-stage pipeline that cleans noisy evidence, retrieves and clusters relevant sources, generates the article by conditioning \texttt{Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct} on the original fact-checker verdict, and recovers inline citations through deterministic post-processing. We achieved a mean score of 0.428 and ranked 3rd out of 9 teams for the CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Lab Task 3, compared to a baseline mean score of 0.272. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/dsgt-arc/checkthat-2026-task3.
papers.summary: Misinformation outpaces professional fact-checkers' ability to verify claims and write up their verdicts, motivating automated generation of fact-checking articles from a claim, its original verdict, and scraped source documents. The submission to `CheckThat!` 2026 Task 3 uses a four-stage pipeline that cleans noisy evidence, retrieves and clusters relevant sources, conditions `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` on the original fact-checker verdict to draft the article, and recovers inline citations through deterministic post-processing. It scored a mean of 0.428 against a 0.272 baseline, **placing 3rd of 9 teams**.

papers.title: CCDWIKI: Decoupling Case Formulation from Response Generation in Longitudinal CBT Dialogue
papers.abstract: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) demands more than empathic validation, requiring instead a structured formulation of the interplay among situations, automatic thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Therapists formalize this interplay through a Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram, where maintaining longitudinal coherence necessitates continuous evidential adjudication to separate tentative hypotheses from established findings. Current dialogue systems track conversational history via retrieval or static profiles but lack the representational capacity to encode epistemic status. Consequently, provisional interpretations are often prematurely reified as established facts, inadvertently biasing downstream interventions. Addressing this limitation, CCDWiki is introduced as a plug-and-play advisor conceptualizing longitudinal therapy as evidence-grounded hypothesis adjudication. The approach encodes each clinical hypothesis as a mutable entry bound to corroborating and contradicting evidence. Across sessions, accumulating data strengthens supported entries, preserves provisional ones, and retracts contradicted assumptions. The resulting formulation distills into concise guidance for unmodified therapeutic language models. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in both conceptualization and intervention quality without requiring backbone retraining.
papers.summary: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) needs more than empathic validation: therapists maintain a Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram linking situations, automatic thoughts, emotions, and behaviors, and keeping it coherent across sessions means continually judging which hypotheses are still tentative and which are established. Dialogue systems that track history through retrieval or static profiles cannot represent that epistemic status, so provisional interpretations get treated as facts and skew later interventions. `CCDWiki` is a plug-and-play advisor that stores each clinical hypothesis as a mutable entry bound to corroborating and contradicting evidence, strengthening supported entries, preserving provisional ones, and retracting contradicted ones as sessions accumulate, then distilling the formulation into concise guidance for an unmodified therapy language model. Experiments report **improved conceptualization and intervention quality with no retraining of the backbone model**.

papers.title: Human-like cross-language generalisation in deep neural speaker embeddings and its acoustic foundations
papers.abstract: Generalisability is a central question for deep neural networks, including the cross-language generalisation of speaker embeddings. This study examined whether deep neural speaker embeddings generalise across languages and how such generalisation relates to human perception and acoustic structure. Using Cantonese--English bilingual speech presented in within- and cross-language conditions, we derived similarity from 18 state-of-the-art models and compared it with human ratings and acoustic features using linear mixed models and representational similarity analysis. Embeddings exhibited cross-language generalisation that broadly paralleled human behaviour, reflecting accurate identity discrimination and sensitivity to language switching. This generalisation relied on largely shared acoustic cues with language-sensitive weighting, mirroring human patterns. Together, these findings provide converging evidence for human--machine alignment in cross-language voice similarity processing.
papers.summary: The study asks whether deep neural speaker embeddings recognize the same voice across languages, and whether they do so the way humans do. The authors used Cantonese–English bilingual speech in same-language and cross-language conditions. They compared similarity scores from 18 state-of-the-art speaker models with human ratings and acoustic features, using linear mixed models and representational similarity analysis. The embeddings **generalised across languages in a way that broadly paralleled human behaviour**: they told speakers apart accurately and were sensitive to language switching. They also relied on largely shared acoustic cues, weighted differently by language, much as human listeners do.

papers.title: Same Origin, Different Verdicts: Text Production Conditions Confound Machine-Generated Text Detection in Russian
papers.abstract: Automated detection of machine-generated text is applied where the verdict carries a cost for the author, yet origin is a property of the production process, not an observable property of the text. The conditions under which a text is produced push it in the same direction in which a generative model is presumed to push it. This study measures the contribution of these conditions while origin is held fixed. The Russian-language corpus of 1882 documents comprises a machine part, generated by four generation channels (each backed by its own model family) across 45 tasks in three task modes, and an archival human part annotated for source regimentation level before the texts were read. The primary contrast is computed within the machine corpus: both halves of a pair are generated by the same model for the same task and differ only in task wording. Machine-likeness is measured by four operationalisations: an interpretable index with weights fixed before data collection, a trained classifier, a zero-shot metric on an open model, a judge model. The main result is disagreement between procedures: changing the task mode shifted the scores of all four, but three gave a negative shift, the judge a positive one, and none of the four intervals covers zero. The comparison plan and the specifications of procedures 2-4 were fixed after the result of procedure 1, before procedures 2-4 ran; the disagreement survived correction of a corpus defect and of the nested validation. A baseline on the source identifier alone reaches a median AUROC of 1.0000 on the thirteen group splits where it is defined, and removing emphasis markers flipped a confident machine verdict to human without changing the full text by a single character. The scores are properties of a specific measurement system and corpus: they reflect data collection, repetition, formatting, and preprocessing decisions as well as linguistic style.
papers.summary: Detectors of machine-generated text treat origin as something visible in the text. This study tests how much the conditions under which a text was written move detector scores when origin is held fixed. On a Russian corpus of 1,882 documents, the authors compared pairs written by the same model for the same task that differ only in how the task was worded. They scored machine-likeness with four procedures: an interpretable index, a trained classifier, a zero-shot metric, and a judge model. Changing the task mode shifted all four scores, but **three procedures shifted negatively while the judge model shifted positively**, and no confidence interval covered zero. A baseline using only the source identifier reached a median `AUROC` of 1.0, and removing emphasis markers alone flipped a confident machine verdict to human. The authors conclude that detector scores reflect corpus and preprocessing choices as much as authorship.

papers.title: SRRM: A Retrieval-Reconstruction Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Context Memory in Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on consumer-grade hardware, yet their ability to preserve information across progressively longer contexts remains insufficiently understood. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate retrieval-oriented tasks, providing limited insight into whether successful retrieval reflects comprehensive long-context memory preservation. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Simple Retrieval-Reconstruction Memory (SRRM), a lightweight and fully reproducible benchmark that jointly evaluates Targeted Retrieval and Global Information Reconstruction. This study also proposes the Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR), a benchmark-level metric that quantifies the relationship between retrieval and reconstruction performance. SRRM was evaluated using a synthetic dataset on three Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters) across context loads ranging from 10 to 100 factual statements. Experimental results show that reconstruction performance deteriorated substantially faster than retrieval accuracy as contextual information increased, indicating that retrieval alone is insufficient to characterize long-context memory preservation. Among the evaluated models, Qwen2.5-1.5B achieved the highest retrieval accuracy (86.7%), reconstruction performance (45.7%), and MPR (0.53), outperforming the larger Qwen2.5-3B model (72.2%, 18.5%, and 0.26, respectively). These findings demonstrate that increasing parameter count does not necessarily improve long-context memory preservation. Overall, SRRM provides a reproducible and extensible benchmark for systematically evaluating long-context memory while revealing complementary memory behaviors that remain hidden under retrieval-only evaluation frameworks.
papers.summary: Small language models (SLMs) run on consumer hardware are mostly tested on retrieval, which may hide how well they keep the full content of long contexts. The authors introduce `SRRM` (Simple Retrieval-Reconstruction Memory), a lightweight benchmark that scores both targeted retrieval and reconstruction of all the given information. They also propose the Memory Preservation Ratio (`MPR`) to relate the two scores. Testing `Qwen2.5` at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters on 10 to 100 factual statements, they found that reconstruction degraded much faster than retrieval as context grew. Notably, **`Qwen2.5-1.5B` outperformed `Qwen2.5-3B` on every measure (MPR 0.53 vs. 0.26)**, suggesting that more parameters do not guarantee better long-context memory.

papers.title: AI-Driven SaaS Platform Integration: AI Express for Unified Generative AI Services with Pay-As-You-Go Credit Systems and Scalable Microservice Architecture
papers.abstract: Generative AI is currently fragmented, with separate subscriptions required for text generation, image synthesis, and code assistance, leading to high costs and workflow disruptions. AI Express is a SaaS platform that consolidates these capabilities into a unified pay-as-you-go service. The platform provides a range of AI tools, including a Core Code Reviewer that evaluates GitHub repositories, a Text-to-Website generator that converts text into fully functional websites, script generation, grammar checking, data analysis, and watermark removal, all accessible through a single interface without requiring technical expertise.
papers.summary: Generative AI tools for text, images, and code usually require separate subscriptions, which adds cost and fragments workflows. The paper describes `AI Express`, a software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform that bundles these tools behind one **pay-as-you-go credit system** built on a scalable microservice architecture. Its tools include a GitHub repository code reviewer, a text-to-website generator, script generation, grammar checking, data analysis, and watermark removal, all usable without technical expertise.

papers.title: Who May Overrule the Agent? Evidence-Gated Authority in LLM Review Institutions
papers.abstract: Multi-agent language-model systems often add a reviewer to improve an upstream agent's decision. Yet a reviewer can both repair errors and replace decisions that were already correct. We study this as a problem of institutional jurisdiction: conditional on the same proposal, task information, model, and review output, when is the reviewer authorized to make its recommendation binding? We compare broad override authority with an evidence gate that permits replacement only after the reviewer produces a mechanically valid record of a binding-constraint violation and a compliant repair. Across two locally run open-weight models, 96 spatial-policy tasks, and a 96-task portfolio-transfer benchmark, the gate sharply reduces corruption of correct proposals while retaining most repairs of violations. The directions of this tradeoff are partly implied by the rule; its magnitude depends on reviewer transitions and upstream proposal states. A prospective validation then gives the reviewer an explicit choice to retain, replace, or escalate. This eliminates correct-proposal corruption for Qwen, but Mistral still replaces all 48 correct proposals; Qwen also declines every welfare-only repair that Mistral frequently attempts. Thus interface design changes reviewer behavior but is not a model-independent safeguard. The result is not that restricted review is universally better. It is that reviewer competence, action interface, and binding jurisdiction jointly determine both the correction domain and the corruption surface.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems often add a reviewer to check an upstream agent, but a reviewer can overwrite correct decisions as well as fix wrong ones. The authors frame this as a question of when a reviewer should have binding authority. They compare unrestricted override with an evidence gate that allows replacement only after the reviewer produces a mechanically valid record of a constraint violation and a compliant repair. Across two locally run open-weight models, 96 spatial-policy tasks, and a 96-task portfolio benchmark, the **gate sharply reduced corruption of correct proposals while keeping most legitimate repairs**. In a follow-up where the reviewer could retain, replace, or escalate, `Qwen` stopped corrupting correct proposals entirely, but `Mistral` still replaced all 48. Interface design therefore changes reviewer behaviour but does not protect against it independently of the model.

papers.title: Agent Harness Awareness: Turning Verified Telemetry into Operational Control for Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Tool descriptions tell an agent what an action can do, but they do not necessarily reveal whether that action is healthy or suitable at the moment of use. Execution harnesses often possess this information through monitors, traces, and recent failures while the model choosing the next action does not. We call this gap operational blindness. We introduce Agent Harness Awareness, a trust-separated design in which the host supplies a small, fresh, verified state snapshot before a consequential action while retaining measurement, enforcement, evaluation, and final dispatch authority. We test its tools-and-network instance with ToolRoute, a controlled isolation benchmark that holds the task and candidate semantics constant and varies the operational information available to the model. In a 216-decision ablation across GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.7 Flash, verified tool-health state reduced mean observable policy regret by 96.9% against a same-shape neutral control (4,252 ms to 131 ms) and raised single-dispatch completion from 69.4% to 95.8%. In a separate 27-decision end-to-end replication with live local TCP/HTTP execution, OpenTelemetry client spans, and Toxiproxy-injected faults, verified state reduced mean regret from 8,956 ms to 0 ms (zero excess observable operational cost) and completed the live action in 9/9 model-by-fault cases versus 5/9 for the neutral control. These studies establish the tools-and-network instance of Agent Harness Awareness: selected host telemetry materially improves pre-dispatch operational choice. Runtime state, hardware pressure, economics, retry-aware recovery, and heterogeneous selection remain open empirical extensions of the same architecture.
papers.summary: Tool-using agents choose actions from tool descriptions, while the execution harness running them often knows from monitors and recent failures which tools are currently unhealthy. The authors call this gap operational blindness. Their design, `Agent Harness Awareness`, has the host give the model a small, fresh, verified state snapshot before a consequential action, while the host keeps enforcement and final dispatch authority. On the `ToolRoute` isolation benchmark with `GPT-5.6 Sol`, `Claude Sonnet 5`, and `Gemini 3.7 Flash`, verified tool-health state **cut mean policy regret by 96.9% and raised single-dispatch completion from 69.4% to 95.8%**. In a live end-to-end replication with `OpenTelemetry` traces and `Toxiproxy`-injected faults, it completed all 9 model-and-fault cases, against 5 of 9 for the control.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Resource Orchestration for Agentic AI Systems
papers.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems powered by large language models (LLMs) execute as autonomous multi-step pipelines that dynamically invoke tools, integrate observations into memory, and iterate until a task is resolved or a resource budget is exhausted. Unlike classical workflows with fixed graphs, the aggregate compute, bandwidth, and end-to-end latency demands of such pipelines are unknown at dispatch time: they emerge at runtime from intermediate observations and stochastic token sampling, yielding heavy-tailed, multi-modal random variables. This unpredictability forces infrastructure orchestrators into a dilemma: under-provisioning risks mid-execution throttling and deadline violations, while over-provisioning wastes scarce edge or cloud capacity. Existing schedulers require a fully known pipeline graph, while edge resource-management methods rely on parametric or stationary demand models, and neither fits the unknown, non-stationary profiles of agentic pipelines. We formalize this setting as the uncertainty-aware agentic orchestration problem, where the goal is to reserve, at dispatch time, compute and bandwidth allocations that cover actual pipeline demands, and to verify that the pipeline can meet its deadline, each with a prescribed probability. We then propose Conformal Reservation for Orchestration (CRO), an online algorithm that translates a sliding window of past execution traces into dispatch-time resource allocations with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees via conformal prediction. Simulations over heterogeneous task mixes with multi-modal and heavy-tailed profiles show that CRO is the only evaluated method that simultaneously satisfies target probabilistic coverage across all risk levels while, among coverage-feasible methods, attaining the lowest over-reservation, roughly halving the resource waste of the Chebyshev-bound baseline.
papers.summary: The compute, bandwidth, and latency an LLM agent pipeline will need only become known as it runs, which leaves infrastructure orchestrators choosing between under- and over-provisioning. The authors formalize this as the problem of reserving resources at dispatch time so that they cover actual demand and meet the deadline with a prescribed probability. They propose `CRO` (Conformal Reservation for Orchestration), an online algorithm that uses conformal prediction over a sliding window of past execution traces to give distribution-free coverage guarantees. In simulations with multi-modal, heavy-tailed workloads, `CRO` was the only method that met target coverage at every risk level. It also **roughly halved resource waste compared with a Chebyshev-bound baseline**.

papers.title: Challenge-Aware Knowledge Recruitment with Meta-Agent Supervision for Medical Multi-Agent Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models perform strongly on standard medical QA but degrade on harder reasoning tasks, where multi-agent debate often fails to beat strong single-model prompting. We argue that a key limitation is that existing systems select experts and retrieve knowledge from the question alone, rather than from gaps that emerge during reasoning. We propose challenge-aware adaptive recruitment: an external CHALLENGER inspects the evolving reasoning trace and identifies specific factual or expertise gaps. These signals trigger targeted knowledge retrieval or mid-discussion specialist recruitment. On the MEDAGENTSBENCH hard subset (862 questions across nine biomedical datasets), upfront retrieval provides little benefit, while challenge-aware in-between retrieval performs better; on a multi-specialist backbone it improves accuracy on 8 of 9 datasets and adds 6 percentage points over Challenger Only. Ablations indicate benefits from both retrieval timing and gap-specific query signals, and a live web-search experiment shows that the timing advantage persists across retrieval backends. For specialist recruitment, self-triggered adaptation is unreliable, whereas Challenger-triggered recruitment raises GPT-4.1-mini MedQA accuracy from 46% to 54%, with positive direction on all tested generalization datasets. Naively combining retrieval and specialist recruitment degrades performance, highlighting the need to coordinate adaptive intervention channels. These results show that when and why external resources are recruited is a key design choice in multi-agent medical reasoning.
papers.summary: Multi-agent debate on hard medical questions often fails to beat strong single-model prompting. The authors argue this is because experts and knowledge are chosen from the question alone rather than from gaps that appear during reasoning. They add an external `Challenger` agent that inspects the evolving reasoning trace and flags specific factual or expertise gaps, which then trigger targeted retrieval or recruitment of a specialist mid-discussion. On the hard subset of `MedAgentsBench`, retrieval during the discussion beat retrieval up front, and Challenger-triggered recruitment **raised `GPT-4.1-mini` accuracy on `MedQA` from 46% to 54%**. Naively combining retrieval and recruitment hurt performance, which shows the two intervention channels need coordinating.

papers.title: A Feasibility Condition for Confidence-Gated Tiered LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Tiered inference distributes large language model computation across a hierarchy of devices, from on-device and edge hardware to the datacenter, and is increasingly offered as the route to cheaper, lower-latency, and more private serving. Most such systems orchestrate frozen model checkpoints, and most decide what to resolve locally and what to escalate using a confidence signal produced by a forward-deployed model. We give a closed-form condition for when no threshold on that signal makes a tiered cascade worthwhile relative to sending every query to the backstop. Modeling the routing decision as a binary test and separating local from escalation cost through an architecture cost ratio $\kappa$, we derive a feasibility condition bracketed by a signal-free floor, below which a cascade is feasible at any signal quality, and a perfect-signal ceiling, above which none is. Read along the $\kappa$ axis the condition inverts: where local compute is billed, cost binds, matching a recent empirical finding; where it is sunk, on decentralized hardware, feasibility becomes unconditional and signal quality instead sets what the cascade achieves. We turn the condition into three design requirements that existing trained-in primitives satisfy only in isolation, and we propose, as future work, a co-designed architecture and a protocol to test it. The condition and the inversion hold independently of that architecture; they are the paper's contribution.
papers.summary: Tiered LLM inference answers easy queries on local or edge devices and escalates hard ones to a datacenter model, using a confidence signal to decide. The paper treats this routing decision as a binary test and derives a closed-form condition for when no confidence threshold makes such a cascade worth more than sending every query to the backstop. The condition depends on an architecture cost ratio `κ` between local and escalation cost. **When local compute is billed, cost is the binding constraint; when it is already paid for, as on decentralized hardware, a cascade is always feasible** and signal quality only sets how much it gains. The authors turn the condition into three design requirements and propose a co-designed architecture as future work.

papers.title: A Training-Free Socket for DNA in Frozen Language Models
papers.abstract:
Connecting a DNA foundation model to a large language model (LLM) usually requires training a connector, and often the LLM too. We show that a closed-form map is enough for gene-level questions. Our method, the socket, fits one ridge regression (the plug) from frozen Evo 2 features to the host LLM's own representation of the gene's symbol, name, and description at an early layer. The plug's output replaces the hidden state at placeholder positions, and no gradient passes through the host.
  We test it on GeneHop, a five-way multiple-choice benchmark split by homology. In a single run on the held-out test set, under a frozen analysis plan, real DNA beats shuffled DNA on all four hosts: by +22.2 points [19.8, 25.0] on Qwen3.5-4B, +26.1 [24.3, 27.9] on Qwen3.6-27B, +16.7 [14.2, 19.7] on Mistral-7B, and +18.4 [16.2, 21.0] on OLMo-2-7B. All four survive Holm correction, every null control stays within two points of the sham level, and the development results agree within 2.3 points.
  A layer rule that uses no task items was selected on three hosts; it predicted the working layer of the fourth before any DNA-plug scoring on it. A text-only linear map lets one plug feed any other host, at a cost of at most 0.9 points on test. The socket conveys gene identity: nearest-neighbour retrieval recovers 72-84% of the effect, but the plug beats it on every host by 3.0-5.2 points and keeps most of its effect without training homologs.
papers.summary: Connecting a DNA foundation model to an LLM usually means training a connector, and often the LLM as well. The authors show that a single closed-form ridge regression, which they call a plug, can map frozen `Evo 2` features into the host LLM's own early-layer representation of a gene's symbol, name, and description, with no gradients through the host. On `GeneHop`, a five-way multiple-choice benchmark split by homology, **real DNA beat shuffled DNA by 16.7 to 26.1 points on all four hosts**, including `Qwen3.6-27B` and `OLMo-2-7B`. A layer-selection rule chosen on three hosts predicted the working layer of the fourth, and a text-only linear map lets one plug serve other hosts at a cost of at most 0.9 points.

papers.title: VenusGenome: Genome-Aware Masked Autoencoding for Microbial Genome Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Genomic-context models have shown that contextualizing protein embeddings can improve predictions of microbial function. We observe that a gene's protein embedding is partially predictable from the embeddings of neighboring genes in the genome, motivating high-ratio masking that requires reconstruction from sparser genomic context. Genomic modeling must also distinguish biological relationships from assembly conventions, since the ordering of separate contigs does not imply adjacency and strand labels depend on the reference orientation. We therefore introduce VenusGenome, a gene-resolution masked autoencoder that combines visible-only encoding with genome-aware attention incorporating contig boundaries, relative strand orientations, and gene positions. We pretrain this model on a curated corpus of over 1.7 million microbial genome assemblies from isolate and metagenomic sources, using frozen protein embeddings as gene-level inputs. Across genome-level phenotype prediction and gene-level tasks, the resulting frozen representations achieve the highest mean performance among the evaluated models on nine of eleven primary metrics. An exploratory gene-input perturbation analysis further links representation sensitivity to experimentally measured fitness defects. Ablations support the contribution of genome-aware attention and show the benefits of masked autoencoding over BERT-style masked modeling, with further gains from higher masking ratios.
papers.summary: A gene's protein embedding can be partly predicted from the embeddings of its neighbours in the genome. Building on this, `VenusGenome` is a gene-level masked autoencoder trained with high masking ratios. Its genome-aware attention accounts for contig boundaries, relative strand orientation, and gene positions, so that assembly conventions are not mistaken for biological adjacency. Pretrained on over 1.7 million microbial genome assemblies using frozen protein embeddings as inputs, its frozen representations **achieved the best mean performance on nine of eleven primary metrics** across genome-level phenotype and gene-level tasks. Ablations favour masked autoencoding over BERT-style masked modelling and support higher masking ratios.

papers.title: When Does Sharing Work? Scaling a Shared SigLIP2 Across Image, Video, Audio, and Audio-Visual Representations
papers.abstract: Contrastive pretraining has advanced image-text understanding, yet image, video, and audio encoders are still trained independently, with cross-modal alignment realized mainly through post-hoc binding to a frozen anchor space. We present Omni-Encoder, a general multimodal encoder that processes image, video, audio, and audio-visual inputs within a single SigLIP-2 Vision Transformer with fully shared parameters. Unlike anchor-centric binding or per-modality adapters, all modalities are optimized jointly end-to-end, and the framework is organized from input to training. A modality-native input stage first maps each signal into the shared embedding space, including a 1D-convolutional audio tokenizer that converts mel-spectrograms into tokens aligned with visual patches. A multimodal rotary position embedding parameterized by absolute timestamps then places visual frames and audio segments in a unified spatiotemporal coordinate system. Finally, alternating-modality training interleaves image, video, audio, and temporally aligned audio-visual batches and accumulates their gradients into one update, which we find central to stable joint optimization. Omni-Encoder achieves competitive results on 16 benchmarks across all four modalities with one shared parameter set, and joint training improves each modality over its separately trained counterpart. Code and models will be publicly released.
papers.summary: Image, video, and audio encoders are usually trained separately and aligned only afterwards to a frozen anchor space. `Omni-Encoder` instead processes all four input types (image, video, audio, and audio-visual) in a single `SigLIP-2` Vision Transformer with fully shared parameters. A 1D-convolutional tokenizer turns mel-spectrograms into patch-like audio tokens, and a timestamp-based multimodal rotary position embedding places frames and audio segments in one spatiotemporal coordinate system. Training alternates batches from each modality and accumulates their gradients into a single update, which the authors found central to stable optimization. The model is competitive on 16 benchmarks with one parameter set, and **joint training improved every modality over its separately trained counterpart**.

papers.title: PEEK: One-Step-Look-Ahead Exposure Bias Correction for Diffusion Sampling
papers.abstract: Diffusion image generators are successful due to accurate denoising networks and strong numerical samplers. Yet the two components are not fully matched. During sampling, the denoiser predicts for the next step based on flawed input that differ much from the real data. This train-test gap, or exposure bias, caps image generation quality (i.e., blurry, lacking in details or awkward in shape). To mitigate the problem, we propose PEEK, a novel training-free deterministic sampler plugin. At each eligible denoising step, PEEK first performs a provisional one-step update, evaluates the denoiser once at the look-ahead state, and interpolates it with the one-step-later prediction to form the next noisy state. By taking the additional step, we obtain a generally more-image-like prediction from the higher-signal noisy state, mitigating the exposure bias. To optimize the interpolation positions, PEEK searches for an interpolation schedule search made efficient by the prefix and baseline noise-schedule-rebasing caches. On 8 pixel-space and latent-space diffusion models with unconditional, label-guided, and text-guided settings across various output resolutions, PEEK consistently improves over NFE-matched baselines, with FID improvements up to 49.3\% at minimal extra computation cost (e.g., the one-time-per-model calibration takes at most 2.2 minutes across our experiments.). Project website is at https://dachengruoque.github.io/PEEK-Video/.
papers.summary: Diffusion models suffer from exposure bias: at sampling time the denoiser receives inputs that differ from the data it was trained on, which can produce blurry or misshapen images. `PEEK` is a training-free, deterministic sampler plugin that takes a provisional one-step update and evaluates the denoiser at that look-ahead state. It then interpolates this cleaner prediction with the next-step prediction to form the next noisy state. An efficient cached search picks the interpolation schedule, with one-time calibration taking at most 2.2 minutes per model. Across 8 pixel-space and latent-space models in unconditional, class-guided, and text-guided settings, `PEEK` beat baselines with the same number of function evaluations, with **`FID` improvements of up to 49.3%**.

papers.title: Unlocking Turing Tensor Cores: A Measured Throughput Account of From-Scratch Pre-training on a Single 22G RTX 2080 Ti
papers.abstract: The RTX 2080 Ti (TU102) ships full second-generation Tensor Cores in hardware, yet the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication at the driver level, leaving usable tensor throughput well below the hardware peak. turing-unlock lifts this restriction with a kernel module that, before the nvidia driver binds the device, writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex; published measurements report cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rising from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x). On the same 22G 2080 Ti and under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as the companion memory ledger (five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42), we obtain a before/after throughput account: the small tier (75.7M parameters, 512-wide, 8+8 layers, activation checkpointing on) improves in steady-state throughput from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h (9.0% saved); the tiny tier goes from 15,150 to 15,866 tok/s (+4.7%) with wall time savings of 3.8%; the three smaller tiers (pico-micro) gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical, and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. We conclude that the unlock gain is a function of matrix size, rising monotonically with tier -- imperceptible for pico-micro, visible from tiny upward, and cashed out as a double-digit percentage at small -- and that it is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched.
papers.summary: The RTX 2080 Ti has full Tensor Cores, but the driver throttles FP16 matrix multiplication. A kernel module called `turing-unlock` removes this limit, and published measurements report cuBLAS FP16 throughput rising from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS. The authors measure what this means for real from-scratch pre-training on a single 22 GB card, across five sizes of Chinese encoder-decoder models. **The gain grows with matrix size: +11.8% throughput (9% less wall time) for the 75.7M-parameter tier**, +4.7% for the next size down, and at most +0.3% for the three smallest. Peak memory was bit-identical across all tiers, and final quality metrics were bit-identical or matched within 10^-3, so the unlock speeds up training without changing its dynamics.

papers.title: CAST-Bench: Tracing Every Sound to Its Source in Multi-Shot Audio-Video Generation
papers.abstract: Existing benchmarks for joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation evaluate perceptual quality and audiovisual alignment, but balanced sound-source sam?pling and separate reporting by shot structure remain limited. This makes it dif?ficult to determine whether a specific sound is missing, attributed to the wrong source, or lost across shot transitions. To address this, we introduce CAST?BENCH, a benchmark designed to trace every generated sound back to its in?tended source in multi-shot audio-video generation. The core idea is to formu?late T2AV correctness as an audiovisual contract in which each requested sound must be emitted by the right source, synchronized with the corresponding visual action, and carry the right semantic content. Concretely, the benchmark orga?nizes 900 prompts into 9 sound-source categories, with 100 prompts per cate?gory, spanning speech, animals, instruments, ambient sounds, and other emitter types. The prompts include 439 single-shot and 461 multi-shot narratives, each derived from a structured specification that links every audio event to its emit?ter, subject, and temporal slot. The benchmark provides an 18-metric evaluation suite covering three dimensions: Visual Performance, Content Consistency, and Audio & Semantic Alignment. We further benchmark 12 representative gen?erators and find that visual quality is nearly saturated across leading systems, yet audio semantic scores still differ markedly. Across the nine shared mod?els, multi-shot prompts receive lower aggregate scores under the subset-specific scoring rules and yield different model rankings. Multi-person speech, con?sistent speaker identity across shots, and cross-shot event retention remain the main unresolved challenges. All prompts and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/yucong-liu/CAST-Bench-public.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation measure perceptual quality and sync, but cannot easily tell whether a sound is missing, comes from the wrong source, or gets lost across shot transitions. `CAST-Bench` treats correctness as an audiovisual contract: each requested sound must come from the right source, line up with the matching visual action, and carry the right content. The benchmark has 900 prompts across 9 sound-source categories, split into single-shot and multi-shot narratives, and an 18-metric evaluation suite. Evaluating 12 generators showed that **visual quality is nearly saturated while audio-semantic scores still vary widely**. Multi-shot prompts scored lower and reordered the model rankings, with multi-person speech and consistent speaker identity across shots remaining the hardest cases.

papers.title: LLM-based NPCs in Video Games: A Systematic Mapping Study
papers.abstract: For decades, non-player characters (NPCs) have been driven by rule-based systems whose personalities and interactions are scripted before release. Large language models (LLMs) promise NPCs that converse openly, adapt to new situations, and behave in ways developers did not fully author, prompting a wave of research and commercial experimentation. Yet the field lacks a unified picture of what has been built, how well it works, and at what cost. We address this gap with a systematic mapping study of 377 papers from the academic literature, yielding 42 papers analysed against a main research question and ten sub-questions across four thematic axes. We provide the first quantitative characterisation of component adoption, latency, safety coverage, and reproducibility: short-term memory and world-state grounding are near-universal (60% and 69%), whereas long-term memory (31%), reflection (38%), and retrieval-augmented generation (14%) remain rare, and response times span 2.6 to 15 seconds. Finally, we identify six structural barriers to commercial adoption and offer evidence-based recommendations for developers and researchers.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) promise non-player characters (NPCs) that converse openly and adapt beyond scripted behaviour, but no one has mapped what has actually been built and how well it works. This systematic mapping study screened 377 papers and analysed 42 against ten sub-questions covering architecture, performance, safety, and reproducibility. Short-term memory (60%) and world-state grounding (69%) are common, while **long-term memory (31%), reflection (38%), and retrieval-augmented generation (14%) remain rare**. Reported response times range from 2.6 to 15 seconds. The authors identify six structural barriers to commercial adoption and give evidence-based recommendations for developers and researchers.

papers.title: Constraint-Preserving Flow Matching for Spectral Graph Generation
papers.abstract: Spectral graph generation models graphs through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of their Laplacians, providing a compact and continuous alternative to direct graph construction. However, these eigensystems must retain the structural properties of graph Laplacians. Existing approaches preserve eigenvector orthonormality but do not enforce the Laplacian nullspace constraint, potentially producing eigensystems inconsistent with Laplacian structure. To address this, we introduce Laplacian-Constrained Stiefel Flow Matching (LaSFM), which preserves the nullspace condition alongside eigenvector orthonormality and positive eigenvalues during generation. We characterize the underlying constrained Stiefel manifold and formulate flow matching on it. We further extend LaSFM to property-guided generation, steering samples toward desired graph properties while maintaining these constraints. Experiments demonstrate improved performance on both spectral and graph-level metrics, along with better alignment with target properties.
papers.summary: Spectral graph generation represents a graph by the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of its Laplacian. Existing methods keep eigenvectors orthonormal but ignore the Laplacian's nullspace constraint, so they can produce eigensystems that no real graph has. `LaSFM` (Laplacian-Constrained Stiefel Flow Matching) characterizes the constrained Stiefel manifold and performs flow matching on it. This **preserves the nullspace condition, orthonormality, and positive eigenvalues throughout generation**. It also supports property-guided generation that steers samples toward target graph properties while keeping these constraints, and it improves both spectral and graph-level metrics.

papers.title: SurgTransfer: Multi-Step Latent Action Modeling for Action Transfer in Surgical World Model
papers.abstract: Surgical world models have the potential to provide intra-operative guidance, accelerate risk-free training and facilitate transfer of expert surgical maneuvers. However, the use of world models for transferring surgical expertise has been largely unexplored. Moreover, recent approaches in this domain have mainly relied on ground truth kinematics actions or expert annotations for specific tasks, limiting their applicability beyond the narrow range of tasks with ground-truth annotations. In contrast, existing works in the natural domain have shown promising results in learning latent actions solely from unlabeled videos and transferring the learned actions across contexts. We observe that this paradigm is short-sighted for the surgical domain, failing to capture the hierarchical and goal-directed structure of surgical procedures. Thus, we propose a novel multi-step action learning framework to learn context-invariant latent actions that are easily transferable across various surgical contexts. We perform extensive experiments on the publicly available datasets, SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023, verifying our approach with both quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation by surgical experts. We have published our code and the implementation details at https://github.com/bhattarailab/Surgical-Vision-World-Model.
papers.summary: Surgical world models could transfer expert maneuvers across contexts, but existing approaches depend on ground-truth kinematics or task-specific annotations. Latent action models from general-domain video avoid labels, but the authors argue they miss the hierarchical, goal-directed structure of surgical procedures. `SurgTransfer` instead learns **multi-step latent actions from unlabeled video that stay the same across contexts** and transfer between different surgical scenes. The authors evaluated it on `SurgToolLoc-2022` and `PitVis-2023` with quantitative metrics and qualitative assessment by surgical experts.

papers.title: LIBRA: Programmatic Induction of Executable Tool Libraries
papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly retrieve tools from large catalogs, yet most retrievers rank each tool independently by request similarity. For multi tool tasks, this recovers the goal matching tool while omitting prerequisite tools required by the workflow.We introduce LIBRA, a framework for Library Induction by Runtime Assembly that turns a flat tool catalog into an executable tool library. An LLM proposes per tool contracts of candidate invocations, reusable outputs and state changes, and success conditions; LIBRA then tests these compositions in a sandbox and retains the relations supported at runtime. Constructed before user queries, the library requires no dependency annotations, tool use trajectories, or task specific training, and supports both one-shot and agentic retrieval. On AppWorld, BFCL, and SciToolEval, LIBRA improves one-shot Recall and NDCG over the same dense retriever by 7.9 and 3.7 percentage points on average. Within ToolReAGt, it yields corresponding gains of 4.5 and 2.9 points after ten retrieval iterations.
papers.summary: Tool retrievers for LLM agents usually rank each tool independently by its similarity to the request. On multi-tool tasks this finds the tool that matches the goal but misses the prerequisite tools the workflow needs. `LIBRA` turns a flat tool catalog into an executable library before any queries arrive. An LLM proposes a contract for each tool (its invocations, reusable outputs, state changes, and success conditions), and compositions are tested in a sandbox so that only dependencies that hold at runtime are kept. It needs no dependency annotations, trajectories, or task-specific training, and on `AppWorld`, `BFCL`, and `SciToolEval` it **improved one-shot Recall by 7.9 points and NDCG by 3.7 points** over the same dense retriever, with further gains inside the agentic retriever `ToolReAGt`.

papers.title: Jev with Foresight: Safe Language-Guided Autonomous Driving via a Language World Model
papers.abstract: Large language models understand passengers' driving commands, but as driving agents they reason in generated text for seconds and must infer each action's consequences implicitly from the scene. We present Jev-AD, which pairs Jev, a typed decision model that answers predefined questions with probabilities, not generated text, with a language world model that predicts for every candidate action how nearby vehicles move over the next two seconds. Code turns these predictions into foreseen consequences, which Jev compares instead of inferring them from coordinates. In simulated highway merging (500 car-episodes), this foresight lowers the same decision model's collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision, and Jev-AD achieves the passenger's intent in 93% of free-form command trials. In 500 replayed real-world NGSIM episodes, foresight lowers the collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%, and the world model, learned from this traffic, foresees 93% of dangerous actions. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/jev-ad-website.
papers.summary: LLM driving agents can follow passengers' commands, but they spend seconds generating text and must infer what each action will lead to from coordinates alone. `Jev-AD` pairs `Jev`, a typed decision model that answers predefined questions with probabilities instead of generated text, with a language world model that predicts how nearby vehicles will move over the next two seconds under each candidate action. Code converts these predictions into explicit consequences that `Jev` compares. In simulated highway merging, this foresight **cut the collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision** while fulfilling the passenger's intent in 93% of free-form command trials. On replayed real-world `NGSIM` traffic, collisions fell from 48.2% to 2.8%.

papers.title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments
papers.abstract: As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream.
