Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.
papers.summary: Long-lived agents have to learn how unfamiliar environments work, reuse that knowledge across successive tasks, and keep it current as the environment changes. `ReScopeBench` tests this across 18 interactive environments. It separates structural experience (how an environment is organized and accessed) from rule experience (reusable principles and constraints). It builds task streams around shared experience and inserts silent environmental changes, then tracks both task performance and how each agent's saved experience changes over time. Across 20 models, retained experience improves performance, but **agents struggle to keep that experience up to date when the environment changes**, and they sometimes fail tasks even when the needed knowledge is correctly recorded.

papers.title: Hybrid LLM-Deterministic Pipelines for Enterprise-Scale Code Migration at Bloomberg
papers.abstract: Large organizations carry a long tail of infrastructure migrations that are worth doing but rarely urgent enough to compete with feature work, because each one costs significant engineering time per repository. This paper reports on our industrial experience from Automated Uplift, a multi-month initiative applying LLM-assisted migration pipelines across thousands of Bloomberg repositories. We examine two distinct production campaigns: a heterogeneous Python packaging migration (approx. 1,900 candidate repositories) and a uniform C++ build system migration (approx. 6,700 candidate repositories). Together, these campaigns generated 2,333 pull requests, resulting in 729 successful migrations. We detail our hybrid architectural solution which maximizes deterministic processing, confines the LLM to bounded file transformations within a pre-computed context, and incorporates runtime production telemetry (such as execution logs and usage traces). Our findings show that generating migrations turned out to be the easier part; the bottleneck was the cost, for owning teams, of reviewing, testing, and deploying them. These costs were lowered when changes could be verified directly in the pipeline before opening a PR (as with C++ compilation and test validation), and when the population was uniform enough for fixes to carry over from one repository to the next. We conclude by distilling our experience and findings into actionable, transferable patterns for architecting hybrid LLM-deterministic pipelines and scaling code migrations across the enterprise
papers.summary: Bloomberg's Automated Uplift initiative applied LLM-assisted migration pipelines to thousands of internal repositories in two campaigns: a varied Python packaging migration (about 1,900 candidate repositories) and a uniform C++ build-system migration (about 6,700). The architecture does as much as possible deterministically, limits the LLM to bounded file transformations within a pre-computed context, and feeds in runtime production telemetry such as execution logs and usage traces. The campaigns produced 2,333 pull requests and **729 successful migrations**. Generating the changes turned out to be the easy part. The bottleneck was the cost to owning teams of reviewing, testing, and deploying them, and that cost fell when changes could be verified inside the pipeline (for example, by compiling and testing C++) and when repositories were similar enough for fixes to carry over from one to the next.

papers.title: Can Large Language Models Review the Scientific Literature? A Test Against a 102-Article Benchmark
papers.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support scientific literature reviews, yet evaluations often examine individual tasks rather than the review process as a whole. We assess six AI tools across four stages: finding relevant articles, interpreting them, synthesizing across them, and proposing future research. The benchmark is a published review of the Spanish plume weather pattern and its 102-article corpus.
  In the initial searches, five tools collectively identified 57 articles, with the best individual tool finding 42. Institutional library access increased discovery from 42 to 82 articles for Codex and from 15 to 79 for Claude Code. Given the complete corpus of 102 PDFs, three tools correctly identified all 18 articles discussing the Spanish plume substantially, but incorrectly classified 40% to 79% of the 84 passing mentions as substantial. The same three tools produced syntheses evaluated blindly by two domain experts. Although largely accurate, the syntheses provided limited insight and sometimes contained unsupported claims, quotation errors, and exaggerated statements of consensus. Finally, all three tools proposed research directions broader than the Spanish plume literature, although two approached questions identified in the benchmark review.
  No single tool performed best across all tasks. We provide eight recommendations for researchers using AI tools in literature reviews. Our findings suggest that LLMs can assist with discovering and interpreting scientific literature, particularly when institutional access is available, but cannot replace expert judgment in evaluating evidence or synthesizing research.
papers.summary: Six AI tools, including `Codex` and `Claude Code`, were tested on a full literature-review workflow, using a published review of the Spanish plume weather pattern and its 102-article corpus as ground truth. The best tool found 42 articles on its own, and institutional library access raised discovery to 82 for `Codex` and 79 for `Claude Code`. Given all 102 PDFs, three tools correctly identified all 18 articles that discuss the topic substantially, but they misclassified 40% to 79% of passing mentions as substantial. Two domain experts, grading blind, found the tools' syntheses largely accurate but limited in insight, with some unsupported claims, quotation errors, and overstated consensus. **No single tool was best across all stages**, and the authors give eight recommendations for researchers.

papers.title: Objective-Conditioned Active Preference Learning for Multi-Objective Alignment
papers.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with several objectives, such as helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty, typically relies on preference judgment for each objective, growing the annotation cost linearly with the number of objectives. Active preference learning can reduce this cost by selecting the comparisons whose labels are expected to change the policy most. Existing remedies either lack an objective-aware query selection mechanism for the multi-objective setting or regard conflicting preferences as harmful, therefore excluding them from the training data. We introduce OGC-DPO (Objective-conditioned Gradient Coverage DPO), an active learning framework that treats each (response pair, objective) combination as a separate query and measures its informativeness through the policy's own implicit gradient, without relying on an external reward model. OGC-DPO then selects the queries that most expand each objective's gradient coverage. Empirical experiments across varying numbers of objectives demonstrate the effectiveness of OGC-DPO over existing active preference learning methods under the same annotation cost. Further analysis demonstrates that informative conflicts, rather than being uniformly harmful, provide a useful policy training signal.
papers.summary: Aligning large language models with several objectives at once, such as helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty, normally needs preference labels for each objective, so annotation cost grows with the number of objectives. `OGC-DPO` (Objective-conditioned Gradient Coverage DPO) is an active learning method that treats each pairing of a response pair with an objective as a separate query. It scores how informative each query is using the policy's own implicit gradient, with no external reward model, and picks the queries that most expand each objective's gradient coverage. At the same annotation budget it outperforms existing active preference learning methods, and the analysis shows that **informative conflicting preferences are a useful training signal** rather than noise to filter out.

papers.title: SlackBench: Benchmarking Agents on Collaborative Projects Grounded in Real Code Repositories
papers.abstract:
AI Agents are becoming digital coworkers that can browse the web, write code, run experiments, and assist humans over extended horizons. Yet existing benchmarks fall short of real knowledge work: many rely on synthetic data or isolated tasks, missing the complex, multi-party dynamics of collaborative projects, where critical information is scattered across conversations, code, and evolving decisions. Even simple workplace questions may require locating relevant channels and direct messages, recovering context from long discussions, inspecting repository state, reconciling stale or conflicting evidence, and synthesizing across sources.
  We introduce SlackBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on realistic research and engineering workflows that require joint reasoning over workplace communication and evolving repository state. Grounded in privacy-preserving reenactments of real academic research projects, SlackBench provides reproducible environments with realistic multi-party dialogue, evolving decisions, and corresponding code changes grounded in GitHub repositories and Google Docs. It contains 140 queries spanning heterogeneous-source agentic search, abstention on unanswerable or false-premise questions, goal-directed summarization, and circumstance inference over long conversations. These tasks are not reducible to static corpus question answering: agents must determine which conversations matter, traverse threads, inspect repository state, and synthesize evidence across communication and code artifacts. Across 33 frontier models and agent harnesses, the best system scores around 80% and most agents score below 66%, highlighting substantial headroom for improvement. SlackBench thus provides an extensible framework for evaluating agents in collaborative work environments. The SlackBench dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuanzhiMao/SlackBench .
papers.summary: `SlackBench` evaluates agents on realistic collaborative research and engineering work, where answering a question means reasoning over workplace chat together with a code repository whose state changes over time. It is built from privacy-preserving reenactments of real academic projects, with multi-party dialogue, decisions that evolve, and matching changes in GitHub repositories and Google Docs. Its 140 queries cover search across mixed sources, abstaining on unanswerable or false-premise questions, goal-directed summarization, and inferring circumstances from long conversations. Across 33 frontier models and agent harnesses, the best system scores **around 80%** and most score below 66%.

papers.title: TSFM Meets LLM: Context as Covariates
papers.abstract: Textual information is ubiquitous in real-world time series datasets, appearing as news, reports, and annotations that hold key predictive signals not deducible from numerical history alone. Large Language Models (LLMs) interpret text but lack numerical precision, while Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) are quantitatively accurate but cannot reason about the effects of text. Moreover, the lack of large-scale paired multimodal datasets limits progress in bridging this gap. In this work, we address this challenge by providing a scalable approach for generating realistic multimodal datasets by annotating real-world time series with LLMs. Building on this, we propose Context as Covariates (CoCo), a forecasting framework in which an LLM distills its textual reasoning into numerically grounded forecast and confidence covariates that guide a TSFM backbone, thereby exploiting the strengths of both LLMs and TSFMs. We align the two models in stages, first fine-tuning the LLM via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a reward tied to covariate-induced improvement in forecasting performance, and then fine-tuning the TSFM on covariates generated by the aligned LLM. Our experiments show that models trained on our synthetic multimodal corpus generalize to real benchmarks spanning finance, economics, weather, traffic, and security. Notably, CoCo with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the LLM and Chronos2 as the TSFM achieves up to 12% MAE improvement over state-of-the-art TSFMs and LLM forecasters, such as GPT-4o. Code, checkpoints, and the evaluation datasets are publicly available.
papers.summary: LLMs can interpret news and reports that affect a time series but are imprecise with numbers, while time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast accurately but cannot reason about text. `CoCo` (Context as Covariates) has an LLM turn its reading of the text into numeric forecast and confidence covariates, which then guide a TSFM. Training data comes from a scalable pipeline that uses LLMs to annotate real-world series. The LLM is first fine-tuned with Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`), rewarded by how much its covariates improve the forecast, and the TSFM is then fine-tuned on those covariates. Pairing `Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507` with `Chronos2`, CoCo achieves **up to 12% lower mean absolute error (MAE)** than state-of-the-art TSFMs and LLM forecasters such as `GPT-4o`, on benchmarks spanning finance, economics, weather, traffic, and security.

papers.title: When to Ask, When to Answer: Strategic Clarification for Ambiguous Reference Resolution in Dialogue
papers.abstract: For humans, referential disambiguation is a collaborative process involving clarification questions asked when they will meaningfully change the outcome. However, large language models (LLMs) have been shown to be biased toward premature answering, preferring definite single-turn responses over more clarification exchanges. In this paper, we study the problem of "strategic clarification" -- asking clarification questions in a reference game when their answers will narrow the set of candidate referents. We construct a controlled test environment from the SIMMC 2.1 dataset that records how many questions each ambiguous reference needs to be successfully resolved, and examine how baseline LLM behavior and common post-training methods ask clarifying questions vs. attempt to answer the referent. We also propose BACE (Belief-Aware Critic with Epistemic tracking), a lightweight action chooser method on top of a frozen LM backbone, and show that BACE more consistently chooses the optimal number of clarifying questions than methods such as GRPO and ArCHer.
papers.summary: LLMs tend to answer ambiguous references right away rather than ask clarifying questions, even when a question would narrow down the candidates. Using a controlled reference game built from the `SIMMC 2.1` dataset, which records how many questions each ambiguous reference needs before it can be resolved, the study compares base LLM behavior with common post-training methods. It proposes `BACE` (Belief-Aware Critic with Epistemic tracking), a lightweight module on top of a frozen language model that decides whether to ask or answer. **`BACE` chooses the optimal number of clarifying questions more consistently** than `GRPO` and `ArCHer`.

papers.title: MA-SafeDiffuser: Safe Multi-Agent Planning with Diffusion Probabilistic Models
papers.abstract: We propose MA-SafeDiffuser, a multi-agent extension of SafeDiffuser that equips diffusion-based trajectory planners with finite-time diffusion invariance guarantees for joint-agent safety specifications. Building on the single-agent construction that embeds control barrier function (CBF) constraints into reverse-diffusion updates, we: (i) formalize joint safe sets as intersections of per-agent and pairwise barrier sets; (ii) derive centralized and decentralized (communication-aware) constrained denoising procedures with provable invariance under mild assumptions; (iii) address local-trap and deadlock phenomena via time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs; and (iv) develop a lightweight benchmarking suite including a multi-agent Maze2D domain. Empirically, MA-SafeDiffuser reduces violation counts relative to unconstrained diffusion baselines, while retaining planning quality. We provide algorithms, proofs, and reference implementations.
papers.summary: `MA-SafeDiffuser` extends `SafeDiffuser` from one agent to many, adding finite-time safety guarantees to diffusion-based trajectory planners for joint-agent safety specifications. It embeds control barrier function (CBF) constraints into the reverse-diffusion updates and defines the joint safe set as the intersection of per-agent and pairwise barrier sets. It derives centralized and decentralized, communication-aware constrained denoising procedures that provably keep trajectories in the safe set under mild assumptions, and it handles local traps and deadlocks with time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs. On a new benchmarking suite that includes a multi-agent `Maze2D` domain, it **reduces safety violations** compared with unconstrained diffusion baselines while keeping planning quality.

papers.title: Rewrite, Then Veto: Rewriter-Agnostic Edit Gating for LLM-Based Post-OCR Correction
papers.abstract: LLMs can repair noisy OCR transcripts of historical documents, but they also change text that was already correct. We propose EditVeto, a veto gate placed after a full-context LLM rewrite. The rewrite is character-aligned to the OCR input, its differences are split into blocks, and a 0.6B-parameter gate keeps or reverts each block. An oracle analysis motivates the design: given the true error locations, per-span generation is worse than no correction, whereas vetoing a full rewrite's edits helps. Trained on rewrites by two Qwen3 models and evaluated, frozen, on the eight HIPE-OCRepair-2026 test sets, the gate improves all five rewriters tested, two of them unseen in training: weighted cMER falls by 0.0026-0.0044 and the preference score rises by 0.15-0.25 (paired bootstrap, p ~ 0.0002 each). On published competition outputs it lowers cMER for three of four teams but raises it for the winning run (0.0050 to 0.0065). In a second, disclosed test look, a retrained gate still improves LoRA-tuned rewriters (cMER -0.0011 to -0.0021), and an ensemble of their gated edits reaches a cMER of 0.0069 and a preference score of 0.928, mostly through fine-tuning and pooling rather than gating. Built only on public models and data, it is behind the winner (0.0050) and tied with the second-ranked run (0.0071), both from the only team using domain pre-training, and ahead of all other published runs. A third, secondary look shows the unchanged gate improving zero-shot Qwen3.8-27B (cMER 0.0114 to 0.0108) but only the preference score of its LoRA-tuned version.
papers.summary: LLMs can fix noisy optical character recognition (OCR) transcripts of historical documents, but they also change text that was already correct. `EditVeto` aligns a full-context LLM rewrite with the OCR input character by character, splits the differences into blocks, and uses a 0.6B-parameter gate to keep or revert each block. Trained on rewrites from two `Qwen3` models and evaluated frozen on the eight `HIPE-OCRepair-2026` test sets, the gate **improved all five rewriters tested**, including two not seen in training. It lowered weighted character error rate (cMER) by 0.0026 to 0.0044. On published competition outputs, it lowered cMER for three of four teams but raised it for the winning run.

papers.title: Towards Efficient Whole Page Ranking with One-Pass Inference
papers.abstract:
Whole-page ranking jointly optimizes advertisements and organic content to balance business outcomes and user engagement under complex layout and business constraints. Existing non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches enable efficient page generation but typically score candidate items independently of previously selected items, limiting their ability to capture order-dependent interactions. Autoregressive (AR) methods address this limitation through sequential conditioning, but incur substantial inference overhead that challenges large-scale deployment. Bridging this quality-efficiency gap remains a challenge in industrial whole-page ranking.
  We propose Multi-Item Scoring (MIS), a prefix-aware NAR-style framework that incorporates sequential context into efficient multi-item scoring. MIS integrates global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring within a shared representation architecture. By computing reusable representations once per request and performing lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search, MIS captures important sequential dependencies without repeated full-model inference.
  Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS demonstrate that MIS approaches the generation quality of an autoregressive CGA baseline while achieving 4.07x and 3.54x faster CPU decoding, respectively. In a randomized evaluation on a large-scale social-video platform, MIS improves the realization metric by 0.104% and watch time by 0.058%, while reducing ranking-service CPU consumption by 9.73%. These results demonstrate that prefix-aware multi-item scoring can narrow the quality gap between NAR and AR generation while retaining the efficiency required for industrial scalability.
papers.summary: Whole-page ranking places ads and organic content together on a page. Non-autoregressive (NAR) methods are fast but score each item without regard to the items already placed, while autoregressive (AR) methods capture those order effects at much higher inference cost. `MIS` (Multi-Item Scoring) computes shared representations once per request, then runs lightweight scoring conditioned on the items already placed during a constrained beam search. On `KuaiRand-1K` and `RL4RS` it nearly matches the generation quality of an autoregressive `CGA` baseline while decoding **4.07x and 3.54x faster** on CPU. In a randomized test on a large social-video platform, it improved watch time and cut ranking-service CPU use by 9.73%.

papers.title: Iterated creation, grading, and revision of data science projects by language models
papers.abstract: We evaluate the extent to which agentic AI models can complete an end-to-end data science project, and how this improves with feedback. A 'writer' model with specific tools creates a complete data science project including downloading, cleaning, and analyzing a dataset, and writing a short paper about it. The project is executed and a 'grader' model evaluates it. The writer can then revise its submission, and this repeats for a total of three rounds. We consider seven models from five developers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, and Z.AI. Each model is both a writer and a grader, so there are 49 writer-grader pairs and we run each pair three times. Of the 147 initial submissions, 107 run and render, and the average score increases from 59 per cent to 76 per cent after the final round of feedback. By writer the extent of the increase ranges from 3 percentage points for Anthropic's Opus 5.5 to 46 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5, and by grader it ranges from 13 percentage points for Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash to 32 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5. When a model grades its own writing the score tends to be about 9 percentage points higher than the average of what the other models give it. About half of the difference that we see from round to round is within the grader's own noise. Feedback generally results in the highest marks, but even just having the chance to revise, or having the additional budget, in terms of time or tool calls, without any feedback, results in considerable increases for some of the models but not for others. We find that how much such a loop helps depends on which model plays which role, but weaker models generally do not improve stronger models.
papers.summary: Seven models from five developers each act as a writer and as a grader. The writer builds an end-to-end data science project (download a dataset, clean it, analyze it, and write a short paper), and the grader scores the result over three rounds of revision. Of 147 initial submissions, 107 ran and rendered, and **average scores rose from 59% to 76% after feedback**. Gains ranged by writer from 3 percentage points for `Opus 5.5` to 46 for `Haiku 4.5`. Models scored their own work about 9 points higher than other graders did, and about half of the round-to-round change fell within the grader's own noise. How much the loop helps depends on which model plays which role, and weaker graders generally did not improve stronger writers.

papers.title: Whose Transparency is it Anyway? Understanding Generative AI Transparency Needs and Gaps Across Stakeholders
papers.abstract: Transparency has become a central principle in AI governance, yet there is little agreement about what transparency means, for whom, and in what contexts. Drawing on interpretive flexibility within the Social Construction of Technology, this paper examines how different stakeholders understand and experience transparency in generative AI. This study draws from a global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders, and policymakers, complemented by a structured focus group with end-users, grounding the quantitative findings in qualitative insights from the group most underserved by current transparency practice. We present three key findings. First, all three groups share similar understandings of what transparency means and what it should afford, centered on ensuring accuracy and privacy. Second, gaps between the importance of transparency features and their perceived availability are substantially larger for end-users than builders, revealing how power shapes what gets built and who it serves. Only 28% of end-users report that current transparency practices reflect their needs very well, compared to 53% of builders and 49% of policymakers. Third, transparency is situationally constructed, priorities shift with context and task structure, with role-specific frames activating when context demands them and receding when it does not. We argue that meaningful AI transparency requires moving beyond a one-size-fits-all solution, including current emphases on AI disclosure and static documentation, toward pluralistic transparency infrastructures that reflect the needs of diverse users and stakeholders.
papers.summary: What transparency in generative AI should mean is studied through a global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders, and policymakers, plus a focus group with end-users, using the Social Construction of Technology framework. All three groups broadly agree that transparency should support accuracy and privacy. However, end-users see much larger gaps between the transparency features they consider important and what is actually available: **only 28% of end-users say current practices meet their needs very well**, compared with 53% of builders and 49% of policymakers. The authors also find that transparency priorities shift with context and task, and they argue for pluralistic transparency infrastructures rather than one-size-fits-all disclosure and static documentation.

papers.title: VirtualTrialHarness: Coordinating Agentic Operationalization of Virtual Trial Protocols Across Complex Clinical Schemas
papers.abstract: Virtual trials use routinely collected clinical data to evaluate treatment strategies, but translating a study protocol into an executable analysis requires determining how clinical concepts and study requirements should be represented in the available data and applied consistently across the workflow. These decisions depend on local data representations and operational conventions and can involve source selection, patient and encounter identity, linkage, and temporal interpretation. Here we introduce VirtualTrialHarness (VTHarness), an agent framework that coordinates virtual-trial operationalization by selecting reusable procedural skills for each workflow stage and uses explicit contracts to maintain consistent study decisions across stages. We also introduce VTBenchmark for evaluating source selection and cohort construction. Across three complex synthetic environments, VTHarness successfully produced all required cohort outputs matching the references in 95.1% of workflows after requirement clarification, compared with 60.4% using retrieval from the same procedural corpus. Procedural skills improved source recovery across three language models and increased source overlap with analyst code in 13 Mayo Clinic cases. Site-specific adaptation enabled reference-matched cohort execution across eight MIMIC-IV tasks. Within the Mayo Clinic Virtual Trials Program, the framework supported investigator review of cohort construction and endpoint analysis. These findings support coordinating procedural guidance with workflow decisions to improve virtual-trial implementation across complex clinical schemas.
papers.summary: Virtual trials evaluate treatments using routinely collected clinical data, but turning a study protocol into an executable analysis requires many site-specific decisions, such as which data sources to use, how to identify patients and encounters, how to link records, and how to interpret timing. `VirtualTrialHarness` is an agent framework that picks reusable procedural skills for each workflow stage and uses explicit contracts to keep study decisions consistent across stages. It is evaluated with a new benchmark, `VTBenchmark`. In three complex synthetic environments, it produced all required cohort outputs matching the references in **95.1% of workflows**, compared with 60.4% for retrieval from the same procedural corpus. It also adapted to eight `MIMIC-IV` tasks and supported real studies in the Mayo Clinic Virtual Trials Program.

papers.title: Decision Models as Scalable Economic Surrogates that Capture Human Variation
papers.abstract: Decision Models (DMs), a new class of AI models, give fast responses and return a probability distribution over a fixed set of options. These properties make them candidate human surrogates in economic simulations and surveys, a role increasingly filled by Large Language Models (LLMs), which are costly at scale and under-represent the variation in human behaviour. We present a first evaluation of DMs as human surrogates in economics, comparing 10 DMs with 8 LLMs in three economic settings: a household spending survey on consumption, several classic economic games and a labour-market field experiment. Frontier DMs, those that score highest on general decision-making benchmarks, reproduce the variation in human responses more closely than LLMs in all three settings. They capture the modal human response as well as LLMs in the spending survey, but less well in the economic games. Frontier DMs are also roughly ten times faster than the fastest LLM and can be over a hundred times cheaper. Together, these results suggest that DMs capture the heterogeneity of human behaviour better than LLMs and make large-scale economic simulations more feasible.
papers.summary: Decision Models (DMs) are a newer class of AI model that respond quickly and return a probability distribution over a fixed set of options, which makes them candidate stand-ins for human participants in economic simulations and surveys. Ten DMs and eight LLMs were compared on a household spending survey, several classic economic games, and a labour-market field experiment. **Frontier DMs reproduced the variation in human responses more closely than LLMs in all three settings.** They matched LLMs at predicting the most common human answer on the survey but did worse on the games. They were also roughly ten times faster than the fastest LLM and up to over a hundred times cheaper.

papers.title: AGORA: Reliability-Aware Aggregation of LLM Judges via Item-Response Theory
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge is a common substitute for costly human evaluation, and aggregating several judges is the standard remedy for any single judge's bias. Judge pools mix judges of very different reliability, while the human-labeled sets that validate them hold a few hundred items or fewer. In this regime the per-item mean weights weak judges as heavily as strong ones, and confusion-table models such as Dawid-Skene must estimate a per-judge error table from too few items. We propose AGORA (Aggregation Of Reliability-weighted Assessments), an item-response-theory aggregator that places every item on one latent quality scale and describes each judge by a sensitivity parameter and ordered rating thresholds, so judge reliability is learned from all items jointly and without human labels. Across three benchmarks, AGORA matches or exceeds Dawid-Skene on large evaluation sets, and its advantage widens as the set shrinks toward a few hundred items. It remains accurate as pools grow more uneven, a label-free dispersion statistic indicates in advance when trust weighting helps, and its learned trust weights track per-judge human validity.
papers.summary: Combining several LLM judges is the usual way to offset any single judge's bias, but simple averaging weights weak judges as heavily as strong ones, and confusion-matrix models such as `Dawid-Skene` need more labeled items than most validation sets contain. `AGORA` (Aggregation Of Reliability-weighted Assessments) uses item response theory: it places every item on one shared latent quality scale and gives each judge a sensitivity parameter and ordered rating thresholds. This lets it learn judge reliability from all items jointly, without human labels. Across three benchmarks it matches or beats `Dawid-Skene`, and **its advantage grows as the evaluation set shrinks to a few hundred items**. A label-free statistic also predicts when reliability weighting will help.

papers.title: How Finely Can Vision-Language Models See Biology? Bio-VQA: A Benchmark for Taxonomic, Morphological, Spatial and Individual Reasoning
papers.abstract: In biodiversity monitoring, a single image raises several questions: which taxon, how many, which trait, and whether the individual has been seen before. Vision-language models (VLMs) could answer all of these from the image, but their ability is largely untested in biology, as existing benchmarks focus mostly on species identification within a few taxonomic groups. We present Bio-VQA, the largest biological visual question answering (VQA) benchmark and the only one to span four aspects of biological visual understanding: hierarchical taxonomic reasoning, fine-grained attribute grounding, quantitative spatial reasoning, and individual re-identification. Bio-VQA contains 1.86M questions over 217K images from 11 public datasets, and extends right-or-wrong scoring to graded scoring, so a near-miss counts for more than a distant one. Evaluating 18 open-weight models from 3.75B to 38.4B parameters, we find that general visual capabilities do not transfer to biological organisms: the best model counts animals exactly on 41.7% of images with 2 to 10 individuals, less than half its accuracy on everyday objects at the same counts. Taxonomic accuracy falls to one sixth, from 0.72 at phylum to 0.12 at scientific name, and scaling helps mostly at coarse ranks. The gap to a domain specialist widens accordingly, from 0.731 against BioCLIP-2's 0.874 at class (1.2x) to 0.269 against 0.544 at scientific name (2x). On trait size measurement, 15 of the 18 models do no better than an image-blind baseline that predicts one fixed number for every specimen, and on re-identification, 17 of the 18 models fall below chance under adversarial conditions. These failures persist across a tenfold range of model size. We hope Bio-VQA becomes a standard test of how well VLM capabilities transfer to the biological domain.
papers.summary: `Bio-VQA` is a biological visual question answering (VQA) benchmark of 1.86M questions over 217K images from 11 public datasets. It tests vision-language models (VLMs) on taxonomic reasoning, fine-grained traits, counting and spatial reasoning, and recognizing individual animals, with graded scoring so that near-misses earn partial credit. Across 18 open-weight models from 3.75B to 38.4B parameters, general visual skills transfer poorly to biology. The best model counts animals exactly on only 41.7% of images, and **taxonomic accuracy falls from 0.72 at phylum to 0.12 at scientific name**. Most models do no better than an image-blind baseline at measuring trait sizes, and these failures persist across a tenfold range of model size.

papers.title: Discarded or Unreachable? Diagnosing and Repairing Spatial Relation Failure in Vision--Language Similarity
papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models score left/right relations near chance, but the symptom has two causes that call for opposite repairs: the relation may survive in the pooled embedding yet be unreachable by native image-text similarity, or pooling may discard it while the dense features retain it. On clean two object photographs, across ten encoders, the lateral polarity is linearly decodable from the flip odd component of the pooled vector at 0.77-0.99, yet a search over a million captions leaves nine of the ten at chance under native scoring: an access failure. On controlled C4 orbits, where the relation is the only thing that varies, pooling keeps the arrangement axis at 0.998-1.000 and loses its polarity, which the patch grid retains: a pooling failure. Both sit downstream of the dense features, so one readout covers both. Our zero parameter, query conditioned spatial moment recomputes the geometry from the patch grid and stores it as a vector beside the native embedding. On a 118,287 image index it raises left/right pairwise accuracy against reversed geometry negatives from 0.51-0.53 to 0.81-0.96 and conditional R@1 among 21 category matched candidates from 0.05 to 0.37-0.75, at under a millisecond per batched query, while reproducing the native ranking exactly for queries that name no relation.
papers.summary: Contrastive vision-language models perform near chance on left/right relations, and the analysis traces this to two different failures that need different fixes. In some cases the relation survives in the pooled embedding but cannot be reached through ordinary image-text similarity, which the authors call an access failure. In others, pooling throws away the relation's direction while the patch-level features keep it, which they call a pooling failure. A parameter-free, query-conditioned spatial moment recomputes the geometry from the patch grid and stores it alongside the native embedding. This **raises left/right pairwise accuracy from about 0.52 to 0.81–0.96** on a 118,287-image index, at under a millisecond per batched query, without changing rankings for queries that mention no spatial relation.

papers.title: MESA: An Evaluation Framework for Compositional, Semantic, and Spatial Generalization in Robotics
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in foundation models for robotic manipulation, systematic evaluation of their capabilities remains elusive. Existing benchmarks are either narrow and saturated, offering little signal on SOTA methods, broadly scoped, providing diversity at the cost of controlled experimentation, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets. We introduce MESA, an evaluation framework designed for precise, reproducible measurement of language-conditioned policy generalization. MESA provides five evaluation suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four distinct axes of generalization: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition, enabling researchers to diagnose where and why policies fail, not just whether they fail. To populate these suites at scale, we develop MESA-Gen, a pipeline for task and demonstration generation built by improving MimicGen. We instantiate the framework on two platforms and release both: the single-arm MESA suite, and BiMESA, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization. We evaluate seven baseline methods spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs, finding that the strongest model achieves only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, providing meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress. MESA rankings are broadly consistent with RoboArena scores, suggesting that MESA captures method-level differences relevant beyond simulation. Project website: https://pairlab.github.io/MESA.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for robot manipulation policies tend to be either saturated, too loosely controlled, or dependent on training with messy open-source data. `MESA` is an evaluation framework with five suites that separate in-distribution performance from generalization along four axes: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition. Its tasks and demonstrations are generated with `MESA-Gen`, an improved version of `MimicGen`. It ships a single-arm suite and `BiMESA`, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization. Among seven baselines spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained vision-language-action models, **the best reaches only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA**, and MESA's rankings broadly agree with `RoboArena` scores.

papers.title: Just the Facts: How Dialogues with AI Reduce Conspiracy Beliefs
papers.abstract: Personalized dialogues with AI substantially reduce conspiracy beliefs. To identify why, we conducted two experiments with U.S. adults recruited online (total N = 2,193) that removed possible causes one at a time. The debunking effect was robust to disclosing the AI's persuasive goal, framing the exchange as a debate, instructing the AI to inform rather than persuade, halving its response length, altering how beliefs were measured, and replacing the dialogue with a single tailored message. Only instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments substantially reduced the debunking effect. Content analyses of the AI's output and participants' own accounts linked larger reductions in conspiracy beliefs to factual argumentation rather than rapport, storytelling, or appeals to empathy. AI dialogues appear to reduce conspiracy beliefs primarily by supplying relevant, well-reasoned counterevidence. Our results suggest that humans might be similarly effective if they could supply comparable evidence.
papers.summary: Two experiments with 2,193 U.S. adults removed possible causes one at a time to find out why personalized dialogues with AI reduce conspiracy beliefs. The effect held when the AI disclosed its persuasive goal, when the exchange was framed as a debate, when responses were halved in length, and when the dialogue was replaced by a single tailored message. **Only instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments substantially weakened the effect.** Content analyses linked larger belief reductions to factual counterevidence rather than rapport, storytelling, or empathy, which suggests that humans could be similarly effective if they could supply comparable evidence.

papers.title: Readable Is Not Steerable: Pre-Registered Tests of Physical Structure in Learned Fluid Representations
papers.abstract: Self-supervised world models are often said to organize their latents around physical quantities. We test this on 2D decaying Navier-Stokes flow in three pre-registered studies, each tested once on held-out data. In Study 1, a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) trained to predict the flow fails the pre-registered criteria for organizing its latent around fluid quantities better than an untrained network of the same architecture (not supported); a JEPA trained on non-physical linear dynamics and a static invariance model that never sees time do as well or better. In Study 2, plain autoencoders that render the field make enstrophy prominent in their slowest unsupervised latent directions (best r 0.80-0.86 vs 0.38 untrained; fresh seeds, sealed data). Adding VICReg lowers this prominence in every comparison, though not by the pre-registered margin for vorticity, while raising the autoencoders' linear decodability (partially supported). In Study 3, we build steerable directions ("dials") by routing: the decoder gets overall scale only through a small conditioning code, while its other pathway carries a degraded copy of spectral shape. Label-free rules find a loudness dial in all 8 trained models and a shape dial in 3 of 5 fresh seeds on sealed data, against a pre-registered bar of 4; neither control shows a shape dial (partially supported). Across the studies, what a latent contains and what can be controlled through it come apart. In exploration, a supervised direction reading spectral shape almost perfectly moved nothing when steered. During the build, the loudness dial had to be found by its effect on the output (closest to a pure rescaling), not by data variance; for shape, a variance rule and an effect-constrained rule each worked in 3 of 5 seeds. The program used about 70 logged hours on one consumer GPU; all pre-registrations, deviations, code and outputs are public.
papers.summary: Three pre-registered studies on 2D decaying Navier-Stokes flow, each evaluated once on held-out data, test whether self-supervised world models organize their latent spaces around physical quantities. A joint-embedding predictive architecture (`JEPA`) failed to organize its latents around fluid quantities any better than an untrained network of the same architecture. Plain autoencoders did make enstrophy prominent in their slowest latent directions, and adding `VICReg` reduced that prominence. Steerable directions ("dials") could be built by routing information through the decoder, but **what a latent encodes and what can be controlled through it came apart**: a supervised direction that read spectral shape almost perfectly changed nothing when steered. The whole program ran in about 70 logged hours on one consumer GPU.

papers.title: Multimodal Fusion Methods for Whole-Slide Images and Clinical Data in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.abstract: Multimodal AI fusion of histology and clinical data is an active research area in computational pathology, but fusion methods are rarely compared under identical conditions and across different clinical endpoints. We present a modular framework in which slide-level embeddings, obtained by training an attention-based aggregator over patch embeddings from a frozen foundation model, and per-visit clinical embeddings are fed into 15 interchangeable fusion methods with a shared output dimension and prediction head (except decision-level methods). Using a prospective cohort of newly diagnosed inflammatory bowel disease patients, we predicted STRIDE-II-aligned remission outcomes from baseline or follow-up visits. The best fusion method reached macro-F1 of 0.57-0.75, outperforming both single-modality models in four of six scenarios, and differed by outcome and input. Image reliance, the drop in balanced accuracy when the slide embedding is removed, tended to follow the remission type - highest for histological and lowest for endoscopic remission; methods with similar accuracy relied on the slide to very different degrees.
authors: Mark van der Giezen (University of Stavanger
Emiel A. M. Janssen (University of Stavanger
papers.summary: Methods for combining histology slides with clinical data in computational pathology are rarely compared under the same conditions. The authors build a modular framework that feeds slide-level embeddings from a frozen foundation model, plus per-visit clinical embeddings, into 15 interchangeable fusion methods. They use it to predict `STRIDE-II`-aligned remission in a prospective cohort of newly diagnosed inflammatory bowel disease patients. The best fusion method reached a macro-F1 of 0.57–0.75 and **beat both single-modality models in four of six scenarios**, though which method won depended on the outcome and input. Reliance on the slide image was highest for histological remission and lowest for endoscopic remission, and methods with similar accuracy depended on the slide to very different degrees.

papers.title: BrainBind: Bridging Synchronized EEG and fMRI through Long-Form Naturalistic Video Representations
papers.abstract: Real-world vision is dynamic and scene-rich, while EEG and fMRI resolve it at complementary temporal and spatial scales. Most neural decoding systems, however, align one modality in isolation and mostly against static images or short clips. We study the synchronized case: EEG and fMRI are recorded during the same long-form naturalistic viewing, giving a shared stimulus but also recurring narrative context and many semantically similar candidates. We present BrainBind, a framework that maps synchronized EEG and fMRI into frozen long-form video embedding spaces and treats those spaces as common visual-semantic references, not literal neural codes. On CineBrain, a five-seed Recall@K 2 x 4 matrix across two video anchors and four system configurations shows distinct retrieval profiles. With Omni, fMRI organizes the full candidate list most strongly (MRR = 23.82, nDCG@10 = 25.31), while Joint-Dual gives the highest mean label-aware R@1 (13.52%) with a distinct rank-wide profile. The complementary episode-disjoint evaluation quantifies the contribution of repeated stimulus identity and narrative context to the random split. Across these experiments, proxy choice and system configuration produce distinct top-rank and rank-wide retrieval profiles within the present synchronized dataset. The code is available at https://github.com/Forainest789/Brainbind.
papers.summary: Most neural decoding systems align a single brain-recording modality with static images or short clips. `BrainBind` instead maps electroencephalography (EEG) and functional MRI (fMRI) recorded at the same time, during long-form naturalistic video viewing, into frozen long-form video embedding spaces. It treats those spaces as shared visual-semantic references rather than literal neural codes. On `CineBrain`, retrieval profiles vary with the video anchor and system configuration: fMRI with the `Omni` anchor ranks the full candidate list best (**MRR = 23.82**), while the `Joint-Dual` configuration gives the highest mean label-aware R@1 (13.52%). An episode-disjoint evaluation measures how much repeated stimuli and narrative context inflate results on a random split.

papers.title: Anduin: A sybil-resistant agentic marketplace reputation system
papers.abstract:
As autonomous AI agents enter permissionless onchain markets, selecting new service providers remains a core challenge. Existing reputation systems depend on scarce resources like human curation, identity credentials, or voluntary reviews, while naive volume rankings are vulnerable to Sybil attacks.
  We evaluate whether existing onchain payment histories can yield provider ratings that are resilient against Sybil attacks. Using a 157-day dataset comprising 66M agentic transactions worth $6.1M across 16 blockchains, we model payment flows as a bipartite graph between buyers and providers. A provider's rating is derived from graph paths linked to a buyer's existing trusted network. We propose three Sybil-resistant rating algorithms: a max-flow rating and two relaxed algorithms optimized for stronger rating performance.
  Evaluating these algorithms against simulated adversaries across 813 buyers, we show that rating manipulation costs 20% of those buyers' total spend and is around 23x harder to manipulate than the standard similarity rule (collaborative filtering).
papers.summary: Autonomous AI agents buying services in permissionless onchain markets need a way to pick providers, but naive volume rankings are easy to game with Sybil attacks (one actor running many fake identities). Using 157 days of data covering 66M agentic transactions worth $6.1M across 16 blockchains, the authors model payments as a buyer–provider bipartite graph and rate each provider by graph paths that connect it to a buyer's existing trusted network. They propose a max-flow rating and two relaxed variants that rate providers more accurately. Against simulated adversaries across 813 buyers, manipulating a rating costs 20% of those buyers' total spend, making it **about 23x harder to manipulate than collaborative filtering**.

papers.title: Verified but Vacuous: Three Failure Surfaces of LLM-Driven Verified Code Generation
papers.abstract: What should ``verified'' mean when evaluating LLM-generated code? Many existing pipelines report a single verification number. We argue this collapses three distinct properties measured in a conditional audit sequence: verifier acceptance (Surface A), \emph{syntactic specification binding (Surface B: does the proof obligation bind to the spec?), and \emph{semantic specification fidelity} (Surface C: does the spec capture the informal requirement?). Two empirical demonstrations show the surfaces separate. \textbf{First ($A \neq B$), via Li@Opus (a same-model reproduction of \citet{li2025dafny}'s Dafny-as-intermediate-representation (IR) pipeline under Claude Opus 4.7) on three Python benchmarks}: it reaches \textbf{99.1\% verifier acceptance} on HumanEval while only \textbf{1.9\%} carry a certificate binding to a spec-defined predicate or function. \textbf{Second ($B \neq C$), via VCG on two Rust benchmarks}: we use VCG (which is our own in-house Dafny-as-intermediate pipeline) on Rust because the Rust target lets us enforce fully-verifiable output (every component ships as a Dafny certificate, ensures-binding gate passing by construction). Even inside that construction, \textbf{11.48\% (MBPP-Rust) and 14.82\% (VeriContest LC slice) of structurally-verified samples still fail hidden tests}. On the LC slice of VeriContest, \textbf{VCG's reported End2End rate is 7.79\% (535/6870).} The cited external rates are 5.51\% (GPT-5.5) and 1.88\% (single-shot Opus 4.7). These give descriptive differences of 2.3 percentage points and 4.14$\times$, respectively; task-budget, repair and harness differences prevent a matched-performance claim.
papers.summary: LLM-generated verified code is usually scored with a single verification number. The authors argue that this number hides three separate properties: whether the verifier accepts the code, whether the proof obligation actually binds to the specification, and whether the specification captures the informal requirement. Reproducing a `Dafny`-as-intermediate-representation pipeline with `Claude Opus 4.7` on `HumanEval`, they find **99.1% verifier acceptance but only 1.9% of certificates binding to a spec-defined predicate or function**. With their own `VCG` pipeline on Rust, where spec binding holds by construction, 11.48% (`MBPP-Rust`) and 14.82% (`VeriContest` LC slice) of structurally verified samples still fail hidden tests.

papers.title: RAGCompass: Generalizable Retriever Routing via Reranking
papers.abstract: Different retrievers exist for retrieval-augmented generation, yet none performs best for all queries. Therefore, the key question is: given a query and retrieved passages from different retrievers, which one is most suited for that query? Existing routers usually make predictions from query-specific features and a fixed pool of retrievers; such routers have no output for an unseen retriever and are incapable by design on a new corpus. To fill these gaps, RAGCompass reads the retrieved passage sets themselves: passages from an unfamiliar retriever or corpus stay directly comparable to other passages, so routing stays well designed where a query-only map would fail. We contrastively fine-tune a reranker against the answer each evidence set produces, which accounts for most of the gain; a small comparison head adds a moderate improvement, and neither component has retriever-specific parameters. RAGCompass improves answer F1 by 28% relative to the best fixed retriever, and outperforms fusion baselines, three query-only routers, and a prompted 8B language model. Generalization experiments show that RAGCompass keeps most of its gain under an unseen corpus, retriever, or reader, while query-only baselines fall to the best fixed retriever or below.
papers.summary: No single retriever performs best for every query in retrieval-augmented generation, and existing routers predict from query features alone, so they cannot handle a retriever or corpus they were not trained on. `RAGCompass` routes by reading the passage sets each retriever returns. It uses a reranker contrastively fine-tuned on the answers each evidence set produces, plus a small comparison head, and neither part has retriever-specific parameters. It **improves answer F1 by 28% relative to the best fixed retriever** and beats fusion baselines, three query-only routers, and a prompted 8B model. Most of the gain holds with an unseen corpus, retriever, or reader, while query-only routers drop to the best fixed retriever or below.

papers.title: Hybrid Spark: Adaptive Speculative Decoding That Lets the Content Choose the Drafter
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up large language model (LLM) serving, but its gain depends on the workload's \emph{shape}, such as batch size and context length, and on its \emph{content}. A model-based drafter proposes a short block on any content, while a model-free drafter such as n-gram lookup proposes long copies at almost no cost when the output repeats its input, as in code editing. Adaptive verification spends a batch-wide verification budget on the draft tokens most likely to be accepted, but it supports only one model-based drafter. Model-free drafters provide no per-token confidence, so they cannot take part in budget allocation, and deployments must either fix one drafter or split their GPUs between drafters. We present \sys, a framework that runs a model-based and a model-free drafter on every step and gives each request the better of their chains, within adaptive verification and entirely on the GPU, which keeps asynchronous scheduling intact. The key idea is a price per verified draft token: the goodput that slot would earn elsewhere in the batch. Once the model-free drafter's tokens carry calibrated acceptance estimates, fit once on general text, this price puts both drafters' chains on one scale. Instantiated with \dspark and an n-gram drafter in vLLM, \sys achieves 1.10--1.62\x the output throughput of \dspark on code editing at batch size~4 and 1.04--1.27\x at batch size~128, while staying at 0.97--1.01\x of it on chat at temperature~0. A single deployment can therefore serve both workloads.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving. Model-based drafters work on any content, while model-free drafters such as n-gram lookup excel at repetitive outputs like code editing, but adaptive verification has so far supported only one model-based drafter. The proposed framework runs both drafter types on every step and gives each request the better chain, entirely on the GPU. It does this by pricing each verified draft token at the throughput that slot would earn elsewhere in the batch, using acceptance estimates for the n-gram drafter that are calibrated once on general text. Implemented in `vLLM` with `DSpark` and an n-gram drafter, it reaches **1.10–1.62x the output throughput of `DSpark` on code editing at batch size 4** while staying at 0.97–1.01x on chat, so one deployment can serve both workloads.

papers.title: Whiel: A Neurosymbolic Platform for Certified Relational Program Verification
papers.abstract: We present the Whiel (a contraction of Whi(le-R)el) system for Lean-certified reasoning about imperative relational programs. The system can encode containment and equivalence problems for Datalog, its extensions with negation, and the core fragment of graph query languages. It can also represent optimized or incremental evaluation algorithms that are not expressible in the original query language, as well as first-order specifications of integrity constraints, schema mappings, and views arising in data integration, exchange, and sharing. Whiel's program states are database instances, and its imperative structure enables compositional Hoare-style reasoning with first-order relational specifications, using prophecy variables and leveled invariants to support inductive arguments. Whiel supports neurosymbolic discovery of loop invariants whose verification conditions can be checked using the Vampire first-order theorem prover. Counterexamples are fed back into the neurosymbolic pipeline, while proposed solutions are translated into Lean proof certificates. To validate the Whiel system, we evaluate its performance on a curated benchmark suite. In summary, we envision the Whiel system as a tool for tackling mathematically demanding, typically undecidable problems involving complex query and constraint languages, with a high degree of trust in its output.
papers.summary: `Whiel` is a system for reasoning about imperative programs whose states are database instances, with every proof certified in `Lean`. It can encode containment and equivalence problems for `Datalog` and its extensions, the core of graph query languages, optimized or incremental evaluation algorithms, and first-order constraints from data integration and exchange. Proofs use Hoare-style reasoning with prophecy variables and leveled invariants. A neurosymbolic pipeline proposes loop invariants, the `Vampire` theorem prover checks them, counterexamples are fed back, and accepted solutions are **translated into Lean proof certificates**. The authors evaluate the system on a curated benchmark suite and aim it at hard, typically undecidable query and constraint problems.

papers.title: ViBench 2.0: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Software Building
papers.abstract: On Replit, our agentic engineering platform, users now build entire products without writing code, through successive feature requests to an agent. Yet existing coding benchmarks evaluate single, fully specified tasks, and many are near saturation. We introduce ViBench 2.0, a benchmark for long-horizon software building that we use to select our platform's models. Its 17 full-stack web products, modeled on widely used software, grow over 241 feature requests and are judged only when finished, as a user would judge them: a browser agent runs 544 test plans, and a build passes only if every plan does, under a grading protocol validated to keep this strict score reliable. Evaluating nine models, we find a reliability gap: the three strongest pass up to 98% of test plans yet deliver a fully working product in at most 65% of builds, and no open-weight model delivers one. The gap is closing fast: across three releases of one model family, pass@1 on the public products rises from 3% to 53% while the cost per build falls by more than half. We release eight products with the harness and grader, hold out nine, and report lessons from production use.
papers.summary: Existing coding benchmarks test single, fully specified tasks and many are nearly saturated, while users of Replit's agent platform now build whole products through a series of feature requests. `ViBench 2.0` contains 17 full-stack web products, modeled on widely used software, that grow over 241 feature requests and are judged only when finished: a browser agent runs 544 test plans, and a build passes only if every plan does. Across nine models, the three strongest pass up to 98% of test plans but **deliver a fully working product in at most 65% of builds**, and no open-weight model delivers one. Across three releases of one model family, pass@1 on the public products rose from 3% to 53% while cost per build fell by more than half. Eight products are released with the harness and grader, and nine are held out.

papers.title: Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization for Autonomous AI Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous software agents can act through tools, delegate work, and change their models or execution environments while earlier authorizations remain in flight. We present Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization (ACCA), an approach designed to be harness-independent, for maintaining operational authority according to currently justified assurance. It distinguishes evidence validity from contextual applicability, derives assurance claims from eligible evidence, and resolves a multidimensional effective-authority envelope within a principal-declared ceiling and applicable policy. A typed dependency graph supports selective re-evaluation of authorization-relevant changes. An authority epoch changes when effective authority changes; a distinct optional authorization-basis version supports revalidation of action-specific authorization conditions. Protected effect-time enforcement can reject stale actions before a consequential resource change, subject to the available commit mechanism. A compositional Domain Governance Profile expresses domain-specific semantics without granting authority. Controlled scenario tests implemented as a regression suite using a trading profile exercise default-deny rules, evidence-conditioned contraction and recovery, policy divergence, selective non-response, and stale-action rejection at a local gateway before the simulated-broker boundary. The study establishes implementation-level evidence in one domain, not a cross-domain guarantee of harmful-behavior prevention.
papers.summary: Autonomous agents can call tools, delegate work, and change their models or environments while earlier authorizations are still in effect. Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization (`ACCA`) keeps an agent's authority in line with the assurance its current evidence supports. It derives assurance claims from evidence that is both valid and applicable, resolves an effective-authority envelope within a ceiling declared by the principal, and uses a typed dependency graph to re-evaluate only what changed. When authority changes, a new authority epoch lets the system **reject stale actions at execution time, before they change a resource**. Regression-suite scenarios with a trading profile exercise default-deny rules, contraction and recovery of authority, and stale-action rejection, providing implementation-level evidence in one domain only.

papers.title: Spatio-Temporal Multi-Order Interaction for Video Recognition
papers.abstract: Many temporal approaches for video recognition rely on explicit cross-channel aggregation projections, which have quadratic complexity in the number of channels, introducing significant computational overhead. In addition, the spatio-temporal representation used for video recognition is biased either toward local order interactions (for CNNs) or toward global order interactions (for transformers). Starting from the multi-order spatial representation of MogaNet, our method introduces two complementary contributions to tackle these problems. First, for the temporal modelling, we introduce parallel multi-order processing with depthwise-only convolutions and implicit gating-based aggregation, which is linear in the number of channels, inducing a considerable computational reduction. Second, we propose a dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions, which allows a better spatio-temporal representation without increasing the computational cost. By combining these two contributions, our proposed VideoMogaNet achieves performance on par with or better than state-of-the-art action recognition approaches across multiple video benchmarks (UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, Diving48), while considerably reducing the cost of the temporal branch.
papers.summary: Temporal modules for video recognition often use cross-channel projections whose cost grows quadratically with channel count, and their spatio-temporal features lean toward either local interactions (CNNs) or global ones (transformers). Building on `MogaNet`'s multi-order spatial representation, `VideoMogaNet` adds parallel multi-order temporal processing that uses only depthwise convolutions and gating-based aggregation, so its cost grows linearly with channel count. It also adds a dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions at no extra compute. The model **matches or beats state-of-the-art action recognition** on `UCF101`, `HMDB51`, `Kinetics-400`, and `Diving48` while considerably reducing the cost of the temporal branch.

papers.title: Route to Remember: Adaptive Memory Selection for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: The memory of production agents is increasingly becoming a bottleneck and is built almost exclusively from text: key points are extracted from out-of-limit context and retrieved into context at query time. Therefore, every new query incurs an additional cost that grows with the accumulated history. Weight memory is a complementary alternative that internalizes knowledge into model parameters and answers with no context at all, and has recently proven effective in self-evolving agents for internalizing skills and behaviors. However, its application in episodic and semantic memory, such as user-specific facts, remains comparatively unexplored, and a gap remains between earlier attempts at weight memory and text-based systems regarding recall performance. We study how to make weight memory competitive as a long-term factual store by applying on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). It trains a context-free student from a teacher, which is the same model conditioned on the user's memory, together with a verify-then-regenerate router that lets weight and text memory each cover the queries they handle best. On the HaluMem benchmark, OPSD matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines, including full-context prompting and retrieval systems, while reading fewer tokens per query. We further conduct an extensive study that characterizes the behavior of weight memory and analyzes how different training recipes affect its performance. As agent harnesses move toward persistent, multi-session deployments, these results position weight memory as a practical, low-cost component of agent memory and provide insights into feasible training and evaluation protocols for combining it with retrieval.
papers.summary: Agent memory is usually text that is retrieved into context, so the cost of every query grows with the accumulated history. The authors ask whether weight memory, which stores knowledge in model parameters, can serve as a long-term store for facts such as user-specific details. They apply on-policy self-distillation (`OPSD`): a context-free student is trained against the same model conditioned on the user's memory. A verify-then-regenerate router then sends each query to weight memory or text memory, whichever handles it better. On `HaluMem`, **`OPSD` matches or surpasses full-context prompting and retrieval baselines while reading fewer tokens per query**, and the authors study how training recipes affect performance.

papers.title: Contextual Pictograms for Repairing Multilingual ASR Errors
papers.abstract: Speech transcription errors can be difficult to recognize when competing word hypotheses are unfamiliar or visually similar. We describe an interface that combines alternative transcripts, replay and contextually checked pictograms for selected uncertain concepts. The system will initially support French and Spanish functional utterances. A counterbalanced study will assess whether pictorial feedback helps listeners recover the speaker's intended action beyond text alternatives alone. We will also quantify semantic mismatch and additional interaction time, since an inappropriate image can reinforce the wrong interpretation rather than repair it.
papers.summary: Speech transcription errors are hard to spot when competing word hypotheses are unfamiliar or look alike. The proposed interface pairs alternative transcripts and replay with contextually checked pictograms for selected uncertain concepts, starting with French and Spanish functional utterances. A planned counterbalanced study will test **whether pictures help listeners recover the speaker's intended action beyond text alternatives alone**. It will also measure semantic mismatch and extra interaction time, since an inappropriate image could reinforce the wrong reading.

papers.title: VIPBench: A Human-Aligned Benchmark for Voice Identity Perception in the Age of Voice Cloning
papers.abstract: Speaker-recognition benchmarks test how accurately a model recovers the speaker label of a recording, treating voice identity as a property of the person who produced it. However, these benchmarks do not evaluate how humans perceive voice identity. Whether a listener hears two voices as the same person has consequences for intellectual property rights, cybersecurity, and everyday life. We introduce the Voice Identity Perception benchmark (VIPBench), which contains 124,876 same-or-different judgments from 1,290 listeners on 9,800 recording pairs from 100 public figures. The pairs include real recordings, voice clones generated by a text-to-speech system, and morphs between two speakers' voices. We also define four tasks that evaluate the alignment between speaker-representation models and human identity perception. The first two tasks measure how well a model's similarity score predicts the proportion of listeners who respond "same" and the majority response. The other two measure whether a model and listeners find the same speaker pairs similar, and whether a model's relationship to listener judgments holds equally for real and synthetic recordings. We evaluate eleven publicly available speech models. Listener judgments diverge from speaker labels most often for voice clones: in 41% of responses, listeners judged a clone and a real recording of the same speaker to be different people. No model reaches the noise ceiling; the best model explains 61% of the explainable variance. Models trained with speaker labels align with listeners better than self-supervised models do, yet a model with a 12% error rate on speaker labels aligns with listeners as well as models with error rates below 2%. VIPBench enables the evaluation of speaker models against human perception on real, cloned, and morphed speech, and our results motivate training speaker models directly on listener judgments.
papers.summary: Speaker-recognition benchmarks test whether a model recovers who produced a recording, not whether humans hear two voices as the same person. The Voice Identity Perception benchmark (`VIPBench`) collects 124,876 same-or-different judgments from 1,290 listeners on 9,800 recording pairs from 100 public figures, covering real recordings, text-to-speech voice clones, and morphs between two speakers. It defines four tasks that measure how well speaker models align with these judgments. **In 41% of responses, listeners judged a clone and a real recording of the same speaker to be different people**, and no tested model reaches the noise ceiling; the best of eleven explains 61% of the explainable variance. Models trained with speaker labels align better than self-supervised ones, but one model with a 12% speaker-label error rate aligns as well as models with error rates below 2%.

papers.title: Attributing Agent Failures to Their History Needs an Executed Counterfactual: Toward a Reporting Standard
papers.abstract: Published explanations of why long-horizon agents fail are commonly taxonomies labeled over completed trajectories: a judge reads a transcript and names the failure. We argue that a claim attributing an agent's behavior to its history should carry intervention-verified evidence, per instance or via a validated estimator: freeze an executable mid-trajectory state, alter only the history the agent sees, and continue - executed rather than inferred from the transcript, at a state whose restoration has been measured, with a replay certificate matched to the estimand. Each of the four manipulation classes we name has a precedent, and several methods already execute interventions from checkpoints, re-executed prefixes or recorded conversation states (for example DoVer, REFLECT, Min et al., Who&When Pro, Causal Agent Replay), but none reports a measured replay certificate. Two cautionary measurements, neither applying the standard, follow: a carrier taxonomy whose "concentration" could not be separated from benchmark construction (adjusted odds ratio 1.15, interval crossing 1), and hash-identical snapshots that, restored into identically seeded processes, agreed with one another in 24 of 24 states while differing from the live continuation in 9 and 20 of 24. Restoring the captured position of a random stream made all 24 agree with the live run.
papers.summary: Explanations of why long-horizon agents fail usually come from a judge labeling completed transcripts. The authors argue that any claim attributing behavior to an agent's history should instead come from an executed intervention: freeze a mid-trajectory state, alter only the history the agent sees, and continue. The restored state should also carry a measured replay certificate. They note that methods such as `DoVer`, `REFLECT`, and `Causal Agent Replay` already execute interventions but report no such certificate. In a cautionary measurement, hash-identical snapshots restored into identically seeded processes agreed with each other but **diverged from the live run in 9 and 20 of 24 states**, until the position of the random stream was also restored.

papers.title: Quantifying Trait-State Hierarchy in EEG Foundation Model and Signal Processing Embeddings
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) measures brain activity through recording electrical potentials of the scalp. EEG recordings capture two distinct sets of characteristics in the signal: (1) \emph{Traits} -- information that remains relatively constant over the course of a recording session, such as subject identity, age, and sex; (2) \emph{States} -- signatures that encode responses to external stimuli, including visual, auditory, and motor information. There is limited understanding of how different EEG modeling features (signal processing and foundation models) encode state and trait characteristics. In this work, we quantify state- and trait-level features captured by EEG embeddings using a hierarchy metric and kNN purity on Brain-Computer Interface dataset trials, and find that a majority of EEG features form a macro-trait hierarchy (embeddings form trait-level clusters with micro-states within). Our linear probe results indicate that this hierarchy structure leads to suboptimal state distinguishability, negatively impacting BCI performance of EEG foundation models. To mitigate this, we explore normalization techniques that reduce trait-specific information in embeddings and provide a $\sim$ 10\% improvement in balanced accuracy for state classification. Additionally, we observe that when fine-tuning models for downstream state decoding, embedding spaces transform from macro-trait to macro-state hierarchies, which in turn lead to better state decoding.
