papers.summary: User preferences change over time, but usually only along some dimensions, while existing non-stationary bandit methods forget everything at the same rate. `PEARL` (Prediction Error-Adaptive Regularized Learning) partly undoes the confidence buildup in a neural contextual bandit, but only along feature directions where predictions turned out unexpectedly wrong. The authors prove that non-adaptive policies suffer linear regret after a shift and that `PEARL`'s regret grows with the number of users whose preferences shifted rather than the whole population. On `PRISM`, a personalized benchmark for choosing LLM responses (1,500 users, 21 LLMs), it **beats the best neural bandit baseline by 2.5 points** and sliding-window or discounted methods by 3 to 10 points, using a roughly 100K-parameter MLP that runs on CPU in milliseconds and leaves LLM weights frozen.

papers.title: Risk Control Certifies Rates, Not Magnitudes: An Audit of Selective Fetal Biometry
papers.abstract: Prenatal ultrasound biometry must return a head circumference (HC) and refuse when the image cannot support one. Selective prediction trades coverage against error, but its finite-sample guarantees bound the rate of gross errors, not their magnitude. We audit a tool-grounded biometry pipeline on two separately pre-registered four-way splits of the 999 labelled HC18 images, retraining the segmenter three times on each. Calibrating the contour-completeness threshold by exact Clopper-Pearson risk control returns a certificate indistinguishable from a hand-set floor, yet the pipeline still emits a 271.3 mm error: a small, geometrically complete ring fitted to an image whose true HC is 324.6 mm. The accepted candidate scores 0.94 completeness, so the score cannot see the failure, and one outlier among $\approx 150$ answers leaves the certified risk bound ($\alpha = 0.10$) intact. A second, untouched split reproduces the mechanism on a different image (233.3 mm). Constraining the admissibility region---the anatomical range in which the measurand is defined---removes the family instead: raising the lower bound from 50 to 55 mm costs 0.4 coverage points and cuts the worst-case error on both splits to 11.4 and 11.1 mm, whereas suppressing it through the completeness threshold costs 19.0 and 12.1 points. At an anatomically defined 70 mm the frozen tests give 1.91 and 1.81 mm MAE.
papers.summary: The authors audit a pipeline that measures fetal head circumference (HC) from prenatal ultrasound and refuses to answer when an image is unsuitable, using two pre-registered splits of the `HC18` dataset. Calibrating the refusal threshold with exact Clopper-Pearson risk control gives a valid certificate, yet the pipeline still outputs a **271.3 mm error**, because a single gross outlier fits within a bound on error rates and the completeness score cannot detect it. Tightening the allowed anatomical range removes this failure mode at little cost: raising the lower bound from 50 to 55 mm costs 0.4 coverage points and caps worst-case error near 11 mm. The general lesson is that risk-control guarantees bound how often gross errors occur, not how large they are.

papers.title: Generative AI for urban planning: synthesizing land-use maps with satellite imagery via DualControlNet
papers.abstract: Various land-use models characterize land-use patterns and facilitate scenario planning. However, existing models are largely predictive, forecasting transitions based on numeric data without synthesizing new land-use maps from simple text prompts. Meanwhile, generative AI in urban systems remains unimodal, weakly controllable, and evaluated mostly by generic image quality rather than domain-specific metrics. To address these gaps, we introduce DualControlNet, a generative land-use model that jointly synthesizes high-resolution land-use maps and satellite imagery, addressing multimodality, controllability, and verification challenges. Trained on over 40,000 paired tiles from Orlando and Chicago, DualControlNet is evaluated using land-use, spatial consistency, and image quality metrics. Relative to unimodal baselines, DualControlNet improves land-use diversity consistency by 62.8% and building coverage ratio consistency by 16.3%, more than doubles cross-modal spatial consistency, and triples visual quality. Scenario-based experiments demonstrate that DualControlNet supports sustainable development through multidimensional controls, increasing density and diversity, and responding to text prompts like "high-density development." Overall, this work advances land-use modeling via a multimodal, controllable, and verifiable generative framework, lowering technical barriers and enabling intuitive exploration of urban futures.
papers.summary: Existing land-use models forecast change from numeric data but cannot generate new land-use maps from text prompts, and generative AI for cities is usually single-modality and judged on generic image quality. `DualControlNet` generates high-resolution land-use maps and matching satellite imagery together, trained on over 40,000 paired tiles from Orlando and Chicago. Compared with single-modality baselines, it improves land-use diversity consistency by 62.8% and building coverage consistency by 16.3%, and **more than doubles cross-modal spatial consistency**. Scenario experiments show it responds to controls for density and diversity and to text prompts such as requests for high-density development.

papers.title: CARTBench: Rubric-Based Evaluation of Shopping Advice for Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products in multi-turn conversations. However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. These principles also guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting, our structured recommendation strategy. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. In the first full-suite evaluation under the frozen rubrics, 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice. To examine these limitations, we diagnose shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Da1yuqin/CARTBench.
papers.summary: `CARTBench` evaluates LLM shopping assistants on complex and ambiguous requests that unfold over time, using real commercial shopping cases from 17 retail domains with timestamped dialogue and 1,603 product records. Scoring uses case-specific rubrics, totaling 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety, derived from principles distilled from strong replies in completed orders. Among 10 commercial and open-weight models, including `GPT-6.1-Sol` and `Claude-Opus-5`, 3 exceed 90% on Core but **none exceeds 45% on Excellence**. The authors trace this gap to shared failures in using product evidence and in handling changing requirements and decisive unknowns.

papers.title: Auditable Unlearning for LLMs
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove a user's data from a trained model after a deletion request. Existing methods are majorly evaluated on three axes - how well they forget, how much capability they retain, and how robust they are to membership inference attacks, but not on whether the provider can offer the user any evidence that the deletion occurred. To fill this gap, we introduce auditability as a fourth axis, defined as the separation between requested (forget set) and retained (retain set) data under a statistic the provider computes. We show that across eleven unlearning methods on TOFU, MUSE and RWKU no method satisfies all four axes, with different methods falling short on different axes. To address this, we propose a two stage method that can be used on top of any unlearning method, in the the first stage we propose ${GapWiden}$ which uses a hinge loss to increase the difference between audit statistics of forget set and retain set. In the second stage we propose ${GapVeil}$, an inference time rejection-sampler which uses the base model as the drafter and re-samples based on the audit statistics of the drafted response. We observe that using our method, auditability and leakage reach oracle parity for every unlearning method, and forget performance converges to the oracle; retain performance improves for nine of eleven methods but remains short of parity. Our results show that evidence of deletion or auditability can be constructed by design, and that treating it as an explicit requirement changes the viability of existing unlearning methods.
papers.summary: Machine unlearning methods are judged on forgetting, retained capability, and resistance to membership inference attacks, but not on whether the provider can show the user evidence that their data was deleted. The authors add auditability as a fourth criterion, defined as how well a provider-computed statistic separates forgotten data from retained data, and find that **none of eleven unlearning methods meets all four criteria** on `TOFU`, `MUSE`, and `RWKU`. They propose a two-stage add-on for any method: `GapWiden`, a hinge loss that widens the audit-statistic gap, and `GapVeil`, an inference-time rejection sampler that uses the base model as drafter. With it, auditability and leakage match the oracle for every method and forgetting approaches the oracle, while retained performance improves for nine of eleven methods but stays short of parity.

papers.title: AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust
papers.abstract: When does an AI assistant improve human decision-making, and when does it hurt? We argue that the answer depends not just on AI accuracy but also on how much its evidence overlaps with the human's and how the human combines the two. A worker makes a binary decision by observing her own signal and receiving a recommendation from an AI. We develop a human behavioral model with two primitives: her awareness of the overlap and her trust in the AI. Our analysis gives a closed-form phase diagram over AI capability and overlap, with regions of complementarity, impairment, and automation. A worker who neglects the overlap (correlation neglect) can be made less accurate by a more capable AI, double-counting the shared evidence. Trust reshapes the regions - undertrust may compensate for correlation neglect, so that the trust level maximizing accuracy depends on the deployment parameters. Empirically, we identify the two model parameters by pairing the same workers with different AIs, and break the accuracy loss into a correlation-neglect cost and an undertrust cost, one tied to reducing overlap on the AI side, the other to calibrating trust on the human side. On ChatBench, AI assistance raises accuracy by 21 points, yet workers apply only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight to AI information; GPT-4o falls in the automation region and Llama-3.1-8b stays at the complementarity boundary; and calibrating trust recovers about 2.6 points for GPT-4o but almost nothing for Llama-3.1-8b.
papers.summary: Whether an AI assistant helps or hurts a human's decision depends on its accuracy, on how much its evidence overlaps with the human's, and on how the human combines the two. The authors model a worker making a binary decision with two parameters, awareness of that overlap and trust in the AI, and derive a closed-form map of regions where the pair complements each other, where the AI impairs the human, and where full automation is better. A worker who ignores the overlap double-counts shared evidence and can be **made less accurate by a more capable AI**, and some undertrust can partly offset this. On `ChatBench`, AI help raises accuracy by 21 points, yet workers give AI information only about a quarter of the weight a fully rational Bayesian would, and calibrating trust recovers about 2.6 points with `GPT-4o` but almost nothing with `Llama-3.1-8b`.

papers.title: When Does Better Confidence Improve a Knowledge-Graph Audit?
papers.abstract: Confidence estimates guide human review in LLM-built knowledge graphs, but better error prediction can yield little improvement in an audit. We study this gap through repairability, selection headroom and label validity. Modelling non-adaptive auditing as budgeted covering, we characterise the minimal decision-relevant error statistics and bound the regret of scalar-preserving first-order planning by a structural mass $\Delta^{\mathrm{cl}}$. We simulate ideal repair against benchmark-aligned labels for five extraction configurations and two cross-document graphs on Re-DocRED, followed by frozen confirmation on test and replication on 500 hash-selected training documents. On the held-out cross-document graphs, an error-rate $\times$ fan-out queue leaves 3.98-4.74 percentage points more errors than a joint model with the same actions. By comparison, opening shared actions for that joint planner reduces residual errors by 0.89-1.43 points relative to its own fact-only plans, in point estimates. Equivalence between joint and independent-block models remains inconclusive. Generic LLM verification improves three of four model-budget configurations on each held-out set. LLM adjudication identifies possible benchmark omissions.
papers.summary: Confidence scores are used to decide which facts in LLM-built knowledge graphs a human should review, but better error prediction does not always lead to a better audit. The authors model the audit as a budgeted covering problem, identify which error statistics actually matter for the decision, and bound the regret of simpler scalar-based planning. In simulated repair on `Re-DocRED`, ranking items by error rate times fan-out leaves **3.98 to 4.74 percentage points more errors** on held-out cross-document graphs than a joint model with the same actions. Generic LLM verification helps in three of four model-budget settings, and LLM adjudication flags likely omissions in the benchmark itself.

papers.title: CellCanon: An Agentic Cellular World Model for Prediction, Explanation, and Observation-Driven Updating
papers.abstract: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.
papers.summary: `CellCanon` is an agentic world model of the cell that predicts single-cell gene expression under new conditions, explains its predictions with cited evidence, and updates as new measurements arrive, all through one shared world state. On 339 held-out `SciPlex3` conditions across three cell lines, it improves differential-expression AUPRC by **63.3% over the best baseline** and Macro-F1 by 17.3%, while using over 98% fewer language-model tokens than gene-by-gene reasoning. Its explanation module answers every answerable question with supporting proofs and flags all cases with insufficient evidence. With one measured source context per drug, the update module surpasses the best fine-tuned baselines without changing model weights.

papers.title: RECAP: Context-Aware Prediction Recycling with Request-Local and Persistent Memories for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Recycling a target model's own predictions offers a training-free source of proposals for speculative decoding. In vision-language models, however, existing recycling indexes predictions by the last token alone, conflating predictions computed under different images and prefixes; we find that such reuse fails most often at image-sensitive decoding states. Longer keys reduce this aliasing but match fewer states. We introduce \method, which stores target predictions under one-, two-, and three-token keys: contextual memories live only for the current request and are thus implicitly conditioned on its image, while token-level memory persists across requests to retain coverage. At each lookup, entropy-confidence weighting fuses the retrieved predictions according to their key specificity and concentration. Best-first search composes the fused transitions into a candidate tree, supplemented by suffix-matched continuations, and one target pass verifies the tree under greedy decoding. Without training or an auxiliary draft model, \method\ achieves mean speedups over autoregressive decoding of $1.66\speed$ and $1.56\speed$ across seven single-turn benchmarks on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.6-7B, exceeding the strongest training-free baseline, Token Recycling ($1.51\speed$ and $1.37\speed$). Our implementation is available in https://github.com/Senmo996/RECAP-official-code.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding can be made training-free by reusing a model's own past predictions as drafts, but in vision-language models, indexing those predictions by the last token alone mixes up predictions made under different images and contexts. `RECAP` stores predictions under one-, two-, and three-token keys: memories tied to the current request implicitly account for its image, while token-level memory persists across requests for coverage. Retrieved predictions are weighted by key specificity and confidence, assembled into a candidate tree by best-first search, and checked in a single target-model pass. Without training or a separate draft model, it reaches **mean speedups of 1.66x on `Qwen2.5-VL-7B`** and 1.56x on `LLaVA-1.6-7B`, ahead of `Token Recycling` at 1.51x and 1.37x.

papers.title: Information-Matched Auditing of Conversational Emotion-Shift Forecasting: A Leakage-Safe Evaluation Protocol
papers.abstract: Comparisons in conversational emotion-shift forecasting are easily distorted when a learned model receives rich features but its transition baseline is given a noisy or unavailable current-emotion label, when hyperparameter budgets differ, or when target-turn information enters the representation. We present an information-matched, leakage-safe auditing protocol that closes these gaps with an explicit commitment point, executable causality tests, equal four-configuration validation searches, and seed-dialogue-aware inference. Applying it to six causal model families on four text corpora and two feature-source sensitivity configurations shows that a deployable train-only current-emotion classifier feeding the transition baseline yields a different verdict than an oracle diagnostic where both sides receive gold current emotion. Under the deployable condition, learned models improve over the predicted-label baseline on all four primary corpora; DailyDialog gains are large and survive a 72-comparison Holm correction (best ROC-AUC gain = +0.167, adjusted p=.0144). Under matched gold information, the baseline remains competitive on IEMOCAP and stronger on MELD, while every model retains a large DailyDialog advantage. We additionally report precision-recall AUC, calibration, a strictly utterance-local feature control, same-person self-shift forecasting, and a future-access dose-response test. An eight-item leakage checklist accompanies the protocol. Code, raw seed predictions, and reporting artifacts are available from the corresponding author upon request.
papers.summary: Comparisons in forecasting emotion shifts in conversation can be skewed when learned models get richer information than the baselines, when tuning budgets differ, or when information from the target turn leaks into the input. The authors propose an auditing protocol with an explicit commitment point, executable causality tests, equal validation searches, and an eight-item leakage checklist, and apply it to six model families on four text corpora. When the baseline gets realistic predicted emotion labels, learned models win on all four corpora, with **gains on `DailyDialog` surviving strict multiple-comparison correction** (best ROC-AUC gain +0.167). When both sides get gold labels, the simple transition baseline stays competitive on `IEMOCAP` and wins on `MELD`, so the conclusion depends on which information condition is used.

papers.title: Selective, Risk-Controlled Emotion Forecasting in Conversation: From a Persistence Barrier to Departure Detection with Conformal Guarantees
papers.abstract: Forecasting emotion in conversation is increasingly framed as predicting the next emotional state's value. We show this targets a hard quantity in a state-observed testbed and propose a learnable, deployable reformulation instead. On valence-arousal-dominance trajectories from a dyadic corpus, repeating a speaker's own previous state sets a persistence baseline that no frozen-encoder correction meaningfully improves upon and a state-space filter exceeds; the floor requires the historical state to be observed, since an estimated anchor collapses persistence below a direct forecaster. What survives is the timing of a departure from persistence, learnable on three of four corpora and near chance on the highest-base-rate corpus, a negative result we report. We recast the task as selective departure forecasting: a lead-time-weighted metric with a leakage protocol, and commitment policies whose best choice switches with the departure rate. A dialogue-level conformal risk control bounds the expected loss of committed predictions, meeting the target in all twelve configurations tested, though the guarantee is bought through abstention, with coverage and alarm recall falling sharply on the hardest corpus. One tested language model's confidence fails as a ranking signal where another succeeds, a model-dependent failure not yet attributable to family versus scale. Code and result logs are available from the corresponding author upon request.
papers.summary: Emotion forecasting in conversation is usually framed as predicting the value of the next emotional state, but on valence-arousal-dominance trajectories from a two-speaker corpus, simply repeating a speaker's previous state sets a persistence baseline that frozen-encoder corrections barely improve on. The authors instead recast the task as selective departure forecasting, which predicts when a speaker will move away from persistence. It uses a lead-time-weighted metric, a leakage protocol, and commitment policies. A dialogue-level conformal risk control method bounds the expected loss of committed predictions and **meets its target in all twelve tested configurations**. That guarantee comes through abstention, and coverage drops sharply on the hardest corpus, where departure timing is near chance.

papers.title: EchoKV: Self-Corrective KV Cache Eviction via Iterative Query Feedback
papers.abstract: KV cache eviction is not merely a token-ranking problem: the workspace retained for generating eviction queries also determines the quality of those queries. Consequently, an early workspace error can distort later query observations and reinforce an incorrect final eviction decision, particularly when evidence is dispersed across a long context. We present EchoKV, which discovers and addresses this failure mode with iterative correction. It initializes a feedback-compatible bootstrap workspace using proposals at future decode positions, then uses early decode-generated queries to recover the workspace before the remaining lookahead steps. It uses the same number of workspace forward passes as LAQ while adding a tensor re-scoring operation for workspace repair. On LongBench (16 tasks, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), EchoKV shows notable improvements over LAQ on several tasks requiring dispersed evidence, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long single-document comprehension. Across budgets and backbones, EchoKV selectively improves evidence-intensive tasks while maintaining comparable performance on the remaining LongBench subsets. These results identify query--workspace coupling as a practical failure mode of query-driven KV eviction.
papers.summary: Query-driven KV cache eviction methods such as `LAQ` build a temporary workspace to generate lookahead queries, so an early error in that workspace can distort later queries and reinforce bad eviction decisions. `EchoKV` starts from a bootstrap workspace built from proposals at future decode positions, then uses early decode-generated queries to repair the workspace before the remaining lookahead steps. It uses the same number of workspace forward passes as `LAQ`, plus one tensor re-scoring operation. On `LongBench` with `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2` and `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, it **improves notably on tasks that need dispersed evidence**, such as multi-hop cross-document QA, while staying comparable on the other subsets.

papers.title: CHARM+: Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism
papers.abstract: As sequence lengths continue to grow, distributed attention based on sequence parallel (e.g., Ring-Attention) has become a mainstream solution for large language models (LLMs). Nevertheless, inherent communication dependencies limit computation-communication overlap, reducing GPU utilization. Moreover, in cross-hardware (NUMA or node) architectures, due to imbalanced communication bandwidth, frequent communication synchronization will limit overall performance. Based on these insights, we propose CHARM+, Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism. We reorganize sequential communications into several levels and achieve intra-level parallelism and computation overlap. Furthermore, we decouple cross-hardware communication from intra-hardware communication, eliminating synchronization overhead caused by bandwidth imbalance. Forward and backward algorithms were evaluated on multiple hardware architectures and consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods. Compared to Ring-Attention, our forward and backward algorithms achieve average speedups of 1.3x and 1.7x on a dual-NUMA PCIe architecture, and 2.8x and 2.9x on a dual-node NVLink architecture, respectively.
papers.summary: Sequence-parallel distributed attention such as `Ring-Attention` suffers from communication dependencies that limit overlap with computation, and from synchronization stalls when bandwidth is unbalanced across NUMA domains or nodes. `CHARM+` reorganizes sequential communications into levels that run in parallel and overlap with compute, and it decouples cross-hardware communication from intra-hardware communication. Compared with `Ring-Attention`, forward and backward passes are 1.3x and 1.7x faster on a dual-NUMA PCIe system and **2.8x and 2.9x faster on a dual-node NVLink system**.

papers.title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials
papers.abstract: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.
papers.summary: Patient world models are pitched as clinical trial simulators, but whether they actually understand what an intervention does has not been measured. The authors build a benchmark of 9,996 within-trial contrasts from 7,207 registered trials and define interventional skill as the error a model removes compared with an intervention-blind copy of itself trained without any intervention-identifying fields. A registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator beats a trivial baseline but has **negative interventional skill (-0.12)**: it does better when the intervention is hidden. A frontier language model reading only the trial protocol reaches 0.20 and reverses its prediction when the arms are swapped in 86% of contrasts, while smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection.

papers.title: Do Saliency Maps Fail Dense Breasts? A Chance-Normalized, Confounder-Aware Audit of Explanation Fairness in Mammography
papers.abstract: Saliency maps, offered as evidence that mammography classifiers use the cancer, are untested in dense breasts, which can hide cancers. We tested whether they locate cancers worse there, and why. On 1,345 malignant CBIS-DDSM views, we scored three CNNs' Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients and occlusion maps by whether their peak hits the lesion and a chance-normalized lesion-to-background saliency ratio (bits; +1 doubles it). Unadjusted gaps were large: Grad-CAM peaks hit 44% of dense vs. 58% of non-dense lesions. Case mix, chiefly more calcifications in dense breasts, explained about half or more of each gap. Occlusion kept a significant average of -0.56 bit gap. Controls also implicate the classifiers: unadjusted gaps exceeded an image-only conspicuity map's, and models relied less on dense-breast lesions. We recommend reporting density gaps before and after case-mix adjustment, per classifier, with conspicuity and lesion-reliance controls.
papers.summary: This audit asks whether saliency maps from mammography classifiers locate cancers less reliably in dense breast tissue, where cancers are harder to see. Across 1,345 malignant `CBIS-DDSM` views, three CNNs are scored with `Grad-CAM`, `Integrated Gradients`, and occlusion maps, using peak-hit rate and a chance-normalized lesion-to-background saliency ratio. `Grad-CAM` peaks hit 44% of dense-breast lesions versus 58% of non-dense ones, but **case mix, mainly more calcifications in dense breasts, explains about half or more of each gap**. Occlusion keeps a significant residual gap, and controls suggest the classifiers themselves rely less on dense-breast lesions.

papers.title: Autonomous agents for electricity-system planning
papers.abstract: Planning electricity systems requires repeated decisions that connect regional resources, investment, operation and network constraints. Here we present an autonomous planning framework that carries prepared regional scenarios through proposal, numerical evaluation, feedback interpretation, redesign and final plan selection. Agents propose investment bounds, storage operating conditions and feeder interventions, interpret numerical feedback, and decide how to revise designs and when to stop. The framework automatically executes annual investment-and-dispatch optimization and representative-feeder verification, applies fixed acceptance criteria and retains the lowest-cost accepted candidate. We evaluate forty carbon-constrained trajectories across ten system-year scenarios in five electricity systems and four countries, using two model deployments and single- and multi-agent architectures. All forty retain candidates satisfying the implemented physical and fixed annual operational carbon-budget checks. Twenty-eight of forty matched reference designs exceed the new scenario ceilings. A separate archive of ninety-six trajectories under a common 1,000 Mt annual ceiling provides matched references and broader regional coverage. The results demonstrate autonomous planning under explicit emissions constraints using public regional data and published institutional demand outlooks.
papers.summary: An autonomous LLM-agent framework handles electricity-system planning end to end. Agents propose investment bounds, storage operating conditions, and feeder interventions, read numerical feedback from automatically executed investment-and-dispatch optimization and feeder verification, revise their designs, and decide when to stop. Across forty carbon-constrained trajectories covering ten scenarios in five electricity systems and four countries, using single- and multi-agent setups, **all forty kept candidates that passed the physical and carbon-budget checks**. In 28 of the 40 cases, the matched reference designs exceeded the new emission ceilings.

papers.title: Autonomous ETL Pipelines for Salesforce M&A Consolidation: A Reference Framework, Jitterbit Mapping, and Reproducible Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Merging companies that each run Salesforce must consolidate their customer data into a single organization while both source systems remain in use. This requires reconciling different schemas and picklists, resolving duplicate customers across and within organizations, preserving relationships between records, and keeping the target current until cutover. This article proposes a reference framework for an autonomous extract-transform-load pipeline for this task. It combines partitioned bulk extraction, declarative mapping templates, rule-based and statistical quality gates, master data management with deterministic and blocked fuzzy matching, constrained loading with per-record error capture, and change data capture guarded by a data-health circuit breaker. Each stage is mapped to Jitterbit Integration Studio constructs. The framework was implemented as an open reference prototype and evaluated on synthetic two-organization scenarios with known ground truth at three scales, from 32,040 to 383,973 source records, over five random seeds. At a preset threshold, hybrid matching reached pairwise F1 scores of 0.918 for accounts and 0.885 for contacts; calibrating the threshold per object would raise these to 0.938 and 0.963. The quality gates prevented all load failures and all silent loss of unmapped picklist values without wrongly flagging any clean record, whereas removing them produced about 1,000 load failures per run. Over five simulated days of hourly incremental synchronization, replayed events were ignored, an injected upstream fault was contained in the batch in which it occurred, and the target agreed with a full rebuild on more than 99.3 percent of field values. Validation on a production deployment remains future work.
papers.summary: When two merging companies each run Salesforce, their customer data has to be consolidated into one organization while both systems stay live. The authors propose a reference extract-transform-load pipeline with declarative mappings, quality gates, deterministic and fuzzy duplicate matching, constrained loading, and change data capture behind a data-health circuit breaker, and they map each stage to `Jitterbit Integration Studio`. On synthetic two-organization scenarios of up to about 384k records, hybrid matching reaches pairwise F1 of 0.918 for accounts and 0.885 for contacts, and **the quality gates prevented all load failures**, compared with about 1,000 per run without them. Validation on a production deployment is left for future work.

papers.title: Routes of Reasoning: Reading and Reshaping Test-Time Compute in MoE Models
papers.abstract: Reasoning models allocate test-time compute across distinct behaviors such as planning, deriving, and verifying. However, models frequently "overthink," continuing to verify and re-derive long after finding a correct answer. This wastes expensive compute and can even degrade performance. Existing interventions, such as token budgets or steering, primarily regulate reasoning duration rather than targeting specific behaviors. In this work, we demonstrate that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers provide a natural, training-free interface for behavioral control. We first split reasoning traces into sentence-level segments and label each with one of six reasoning behaviors (planning, execution, restatement, fact, reflection, and conclusion), so that every token carries the behavior of its segment. Linear probes on router logits predict this label nearly as well as probes on the residual stream, the model's full hidden state and the standard target for probing, while using about half as many features. These signals generalize: experts associated with a reasoning behavior on one dataset predict the same behavior on the others, across six datasets spanning five domains (math, code, science, knowledge, and commonsense). Building on this, we selectively edit expert router scores during inference to curb overthinking. Across four models and four benchmarks, this intervention reduces the number of generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (and up to 63.3%). Crucially, it encourages the model to stop once the problem is solved, rather than skipping essential reasoning steps. Accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 percentage points, and frequently improves. Ultimately, MoE routing offers both an interpretable lens into reasoning states and a lightweight mechanism for optimizing test-time compute.
papers.summary: Reasoning models often overthink, verifying and re-deriving long after they have reached a correct answer. The authors show that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router logits encode reasoning behaviors such as planning, reflection, and conclusion nearly as well as the full residual stream, and that these signals generalize across six datasets in five domains. Editing router scores at inference time, with no training, **cuts generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (up to 63.3%)** across four models and four benchmarks. Accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 percentage points and often improves, because the model learns to stop once the problem is solved rather than skipping steps.

papers.title: Split-KV: Efficient Context Parallelism for Training Diffusion Drafters
papers.abstract: Diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by denoising multiple draft tokens in parallel. Their training uses anchor sampling to construct compact draft queries and performs cross-attention with a block-sparse mask over a much longer context. We empirically show that acceptance length remains stable as context scales with a fixed query budget, while increasing the query budget yields diminishing quality gains, jointly establishing a practical regime with queries far shorter than the context. No existing context parallelism (CP) method jointly exploits this query--context asymmetry and meets the nonlinear, sample-dependent load-balancing requirement created by anchor sampling. We present Split-KV, an exact CP method that keeps key/value shards local and limits per-layer attention communication to query-sized tensors, making this communication independent of context length. Its global query view further enables a cost-aware longest-processing-time-first (LPT) strategy that balances context key/value chunks by their realized attention cost. At a CP size of 64, Split-KV retains 85--91\% weak-scaling efficiency and achieves up to $3.67\times$ speedup over the fastest available CP baseline. LPT achieves $<$1\% imbalance and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best load-balancing baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/zxgx/verl.
papers.summary: Diffusion drafters speed up speculative decoding by denoising several draft tokens in parallel, and their training uses short query sets that attend over much longer contexts. The authors show that acceptance length stays stable as context grows with a fixed query budget. They then present `Split-KV`, an exact context-parallelism method that keeps key/value shards local and communicates only query-sized tensors, so communication does not depend on context length. A cost-aware longest-processing-time-first scheduler balances the uneven attention load. At a parallel size of 64, `Split-KV` keeps 85–91% weak-scaling efficiency and is **up to 3.67x faster than the fastest existing baseline**.

papers.title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output ($\Delta H$), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/nota-github/MAEP.
papers.summary: In Mixture-of-Experts multimodal LLMs, expert weights make up over 90% of model size, and existing pruning methods score expert importance the same way for every token, ignoring that experts may serve vision and language differently. `MAEP` (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning) is a training-free method that separates expert importance by modality in one forward pass. It uses a redistribution-aware output-change metric, treats low-attention vision tokens as a pruning signal, and treats text-side importance as a signal for which experts to keep. On three MoE multimodal LLMs, including `InternVL3.5-30B-A3B` and `Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B`, it beats modality-agnostic baselines on most multimodal benchmarks and **shrinks a roughly 58 GB model enough to fit on a single 40 GB GPU**.

papers.title: Deep Meets Classical: A CPU-Efficient Decision-Fusion Model for Automatic Modulation Classification
papers.abstract: Automatic modulation classification (AMC) underpins spectrum sensing and non-cooperative signal identification in cognitive radio, yet the two standard CPU-feasible approaches to it, a compact convolutional neural network (CNN) on raw in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) samples and a classical higher-order-cumulant feature classifier, are rarely compared against each other conditioned on signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). We show that they are, in fact, complementary: the CNN is markedly more robust at low SNR, where hand-crafted statistics collapse toward chance, while the cumulant classifier is more accurate at high SNR, where higher-order statistics cleanly separate dense constellations. We exploit this complementarity with FuseAMC, a lightweight decision-fusion model that trains a logistic-regression meta-combiner over the concatenated class-posteriors of an approximately 198k-parameter residual CNN and a gradient-boosted-tree cumulant classifier, on a validation split disjoint from test. On RadioML 2016.10a (5 seeds, 44k-frame held-out test set), FuseAMC reaches 55.8% overall accuracy, improving on the best cumulant-feature baseline by 5.1 points and on the CNN alone by 3.2 points (paired-bootstrap 95% confidence-interval lower bounds of 5.0 and 3.1 points, both positive), while matching the best classical baseline in its own strong high-SNR regime and the CNN in its strong low-SNR regime. With about 0.2 million parameters, a model footprint of a few megabytes, and roughly 3 MFLOPs per frame, the whole pipeline trains and runs on one CPU core, targeting general-purpose and embedded processors without hardware acceleration.
papers.summary: For automatic modulation classification (AMC) in cognitive radio, a compact CNN on raw in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) samples turns out to complement a classical higher-order-cumulant classifier: the CNN is stronger at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and the cumulant model is stronger at high SNR. `FuseAMC` combines the two with a logistic-regression meta-classifier over their class probabilities. On `RadioML 2016.10a` it reaches 55.8% accuracy, **5.1 points above the best cumulant baseline and 3.2 points above the CNN**. With about 0.2M parameters and roughly 3 MFLOPs per frame, the whole pipeline trains and runs on a single CPU core.

papers.title: BAM: Bivariate Additive Models for Interpretable Tabular Prediction
papers.abstract: Generalized Additive Models with pairwise interactions (GA$^2$Ms) are regarded as glass-box models, since each pairwise shape function can be visualized as a contour plot. In practice, the shape functions learned by methods such as EBM or NODE-GAM are so complex (irregular contours and sharp local fluctuations) that a practitioner cannot meaningfully interpret them or check them against domain knowledge. Auditability in this stronger sense requires substantially simpler shape functions. We argue that such simplification can match the accuracy of standard GAMs if the right feature pairs are captured. We propose Bivariate Additive Models (BAMs), a class of GA$^2$Ms in which every pairwise shape function is constrained to a simple parametric form, instantiated as an asymmetric bivariate Gaussian. Each component is visualizable as a unimodal contour map, and its feature pair is selected automatically during training. Experiments on six tabular benchmarks show that BAM attains predictive accuracy comparable to standard GAMs and approaches that of GA$^2$Ms. We also show the trade-off between accuracy and the number of components to inspect.
papers.summary: Generalized additive models with pairwise interactions are considered interpretable, but in practice methods such as `EBM` and `NODE-GAM` learn shape functions too irregular for a practitioner to check against domain knowledge. Bivariate Additive Models (`BAM`) restrict every pairwise component to a simple asymmetric bivariate Gaussian, which gives a unimodal contour map, and select the feature pairs automatically during training. On six tabular benchmarks, **`BAM` matches standard additive models in accuracy and comes close to pairwise-interaction models**, and the authors chart the trade-off between accuracy and the number of components a person has to inspect.

papers.title: Graph-Mediated Large Language Model Systems in the Agentic Era: Reasoning, Knowledge, Retrieval, Execution, and Coordination
papers.abstract: Graphs play an increasingly important role in large language model (LLM) systems, supporting structural reasoning, knowledge grounding, retrieval, and memory. As these systems evolve toward the agentic era, graphs also organize execution dependencies and multi-agent communication, linking intermediate observations and retained information to subsequent decisions. However, understanding their contribution requires distinguishing the function of each graph operation, the component responsible for its computation, and the subsequent use of its output. This survey introduces an operation-level role--locus taxonomy for reasoning, knowledge and evidence, retrieval and memory, execution, and coordination. We compare how graph observations and external computations guide decisions, how memory representations and updates support later tasks, and how dependencies constrain execution and information delivery. These comparisons distinguish improvements in local metrics from downstream task performance while retaining the conditions under which results were reported. We then organize benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics, and system costs into an evaluation framework. Finally, we identify open challenges in adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery. The survey provides a basis for assessing when graph mechanisms are useful and for evaluating their effects across components and stages.
papers.summary: This survey covers how graphs are used in LLM systems for structured reasoning, knowledge grounding, retrieval, memory, execution dependencies, and multi-agent coordination. It introduces an operation-level taxonomy that separates what each graph operation does, which component computes it, and how its output is used later. The survey compares approaches on whether gains in local metrics actually carry over to downstream task performance. It also organizes benchmarks, process diagnostics, and system costs into an evaluation framework, and **identifies open problems in adaptive stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery**.

papers.title: Robots in the City: Persona-Based Perceptions of Urban Robots
papers.abstract: Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street remains unclear. We examine how robot presence and type affect perceived safety across urban contexts. We generate 18 images of Seoul streets that vary in time of day, road class, and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid). Two multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, choose the safer image in each pair, and 25 human respondents complete the same task. Both models prefer streets without robots and favor the delivery robot over the humanoid. Robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, whereas road class has smaller effects. In the model rationales, the delivery robot appears as a physical obstacle, whereas the humanoid appears as either a threat or a source of protection. Like humans, both models chose robots more often at night, but chose the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often, and Gemma showed a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans. These results show that the effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and that persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.
papers.summary: To study how robots change the perceived safety of city streets, the authors generated 18 images of Seoul streets that vary by time of day, road type, and robot presence (none, a delivery robot, or a humanoid). They asked two multimodal LLMs, `Qwen3.8-27B` and `Gemma4-26B`, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, and 25 human respondents to pick the safer image in each pair. Both models prefer streets without robots, favor the delivery robot over the humanoid, and choose robots more often at night, as humans also do. However, the models **chose the humanoid far less often than humans did**, which suggests persona-conditioned models capture only part of human judgment.

papers.title: Ray-Tracing-Based Dynamic Channel Sounding With Autoregressive Wi-Fi CSI Prediction
papers.abstract: Channel sounding in Wi-Fi multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems must balance channel state information (CSI) accuracy against CSI acquisition overhead. Device mobility causes channel aging, while autoregressive CSI prediction introduces errors that accumulate over sounding intervals. However, standardized statistical channel models cannot fully capture the environment-specific channel dynamics encountered in physical artificial intelligence (AI) applications, motivating the use of Sionna-based ray tracing to evaluate CSI prediction under device mobility and evolving propagation geometry. This paper develops a dynamic sounding framework that integrates autoregressive CSI prediction with signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR)-constrained interval selection. A Transformer with rotary position embedding that converts device positions into CSI sequences predicts CSI across multiple subcarriers for beamforming updates between sounding exchanges. We formulate sounding-interval selection as a predicted average-throughput maximization problem under per-stream SINR lower-bound constraints, including CSI acquisition and processing overhead. A prediction-error perturbation analysis provides the SINR bounds, and cumulative-sum enumeration globally solves the finite single-variable problem. Actual SINR feasibility holds whenever the prediction errors satisfy the bounds. Ray-tracing experiments assess channel prediction, trajectory transfer, and autoregressive prediction errors. In single-STA Wi-Fi 7 link-level simulations, predicted-CSI beamforming improves mean goodput by 67.3%, 112.7%, and 119.1% over stale CSI for linear, circular, and cosine trajectories, respectively.
papers.summary: Wi-Fi multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems must trade channel state information (CSI) accuracy against the overhead of measuring it, especially when devices move. The authors combine a Transformer with rotary position embeddings, which predicts CSI from device positions, with a method that picks the sounding interval to maximize predicted throughput under per-stream signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) constraints. The SINR bounds come from a prediction-error analysis, and the interval is chosen by exact enumeration. In `Sionna` ray-traced Wi-Fi 7 link-level simulations, beamforming with predicted CSI **improves mean goodput by 67–119% over stale CSI** across three movement trajectories.

papers.title: On the Design of Hyper-Connections: Simplification, Stability, and Scalability
papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.
papers.summary: Hyper-Connections, an alternative to standard residual connections used in some frontier language models, add training overhead, and it has been unclear which of their components matter. The authors find that learned read/write gating without mixing, or unconstrained mixing with fixed gates, each performs about as well as `mHC`, and that repeated access to the expanded residual state is the main source of overhead. The resulting `SimpleHC` removes residual mixing and shares memory access across layers. It adds **only 2.4% training time over a plain residual baseline**, matches `mHC` on MoE models from 15B to 30B, and shows smoother gradients and stable training under stress.

papers.title: Clips2Story: Training-Free Video Storyboarding and Editing Using Multimodal Retrieval-Embedded Generation
papers.abstract: Video editors often work with large collections of fragmented footage and must select and organize relevant clips into a coherent story. However, many existing video editing and summarization methods assume a temporally ordered source video and aim to preserve its original narrative and temporal structure. In this paper, we introduce Clips2Story, a training-free, LLM-based pipeline that enables users to create keyword-specified short videos from a pool of video clips. Given a pool of clips and a user-specified keyword, we first extract text-based multimodal descriptors for each clip and retrieve the clips most relevant to the keyword. We then provide the textual descriptors of these candidate clips to an LLM, which selects and arranges them into an editable storyboard with connective narrations. Finally, we assemble the selected clips and retrieve accompanying visuals for the narrations to compose the output video. To evaluate the proposed pipeline, we construct a synthetic evaluation dataset from 100 long-form videos across five genres by segmenting each video into short clips using a scene-change detection model and shuffling the resulting clips to remove their temporal order. Through objective evaluation and qualitative examples, we demonstrate that Clips2Story can effectively retrieve keyword-relevant clips and compose coherent storyboards based on user-specified keywords. Human evaluation further shows that Clips2Story outperforms a strong baseline in terms of narrative coherence, keyword alignment, and overall realism.
papers.summary: `Clips2Story` is a training-free LLM pipeline that builds a short, keyword-focused video from an unordered pool of clips. It extracts text descriptors for each clip, retrieves the ones relevant to the keyword, has an LLM arrange them into an editable storyboard with connecting narration, and then retrieves visuals for the narration to assemble the final video. For evaluation, the authors split 100 long-form videos across five genres into shuffled clips. In human evaluation, **`Clips2Story` beats a strong baseline on narrative coherence, keyword alignment, and realism**.

papers.title: From Waste to Discovery: Recycling High-Scored Unexposed Candidates in Taobao Feed Recommendation
papers.abstract: Helping users discover new interests is vital to the long-term health of industrial recommender systems, yet the usual remedy, boosting exposure of under-explored (discovery) content, often backfires in production. We report URED (Unexposed Recycling for Efficient Discovery), a training-free recall-stage system serving Taobao feed recommendation at Alibaba for over six months to tens of millions of daily active users. It rests on a production-validated insight: naive boosting fails because it injects cold, information-poor candidates that rankers systematically over-estimate, buying no discovery gain while risking engagement. Items scored highly but never exposed (signals industrial pipelines routinely discard) form a pool that is both relevant and reliably predictable. Over a 30-day horizon URED aggregates them and re-injects at recall time through a lightweight pipeline spanning offline storage, distributed aggregation, and low-latency online serving, adding under 1% latency via a single O(1) lookup per request with no model retraining. Online A/B tests show +3.47% discovered categories and +8.47% content richness with engagement preserved: completion video views rise significantly (+2.62%) and total views move positive (+0.36%, not significant). Ablations confirm both design pillars are necessary: a one-day window collapses the discovery gain to +0.55% (not significant), and random injection without score filtering yields no gain while trending negative on engagement (-0.17%). Across production recall channels, URED reaches 13.9x the platform-average discovery rate (6.3x the strongest nearline baseline) at engagement quality on par with the platform average. We share deployment details and lessons for practitioners facing the exploration-exploitation dilemma under tight resource constraints.
papers.summary: Pushing under-explored content in industrial recommenders often backfires, because rankers overestimate cold, information-poor candidates. `URED` (Unexposed Recycling for Efficient Discovery) instead collects items that scored highly but were never shown over a 30-day window and re-injects them at the recall stage. It needs one O(1) lookup per request, adds under 1% latency, and requires no retraining. It has served Taobao's feed for over six months. Online A/B tests show **+3.47% discovered categories and +8.47% content richness with engagement preserved**, and ablations show that both the long window and the score filtering are necessary.

papers.title: Intra-Architecture Source Attribution for Stable Diffusion: A New Task with Benchmark Dataset and Baseline
papers.abstract: Designing systems that attribute a generated image to its source model has lately become a major area of AI research. Most existing datasets and systems related to image source attribution are targeted towards the detection of architectural signatures of the source models. Distinct from this, focusing on stable diffusion, we introduce a novel task, IntrAA-SD, Intra-Architecture source Attribution for Stable Diffusion, where the source models to be differentiated share the same architectural backbone and differ only due to fine-tuning. The proposed task aligns with the emergence of fine-tuned generators having the same architecture, like Juggernaut XL and RealVis XL, which are fine-tuned versions of Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL). We provide a first-of-its-kind $140$K-image benchmark dataset containing images generated from different fine-tunes of SDXL, along with in-domain and out-of-distribution prompts. We also provide a baseline framework for IntrAA-SD, which leverages a style-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts network. It uses a frozen CLIP backbone to capture the image style and gate the MoE, which processes fine-tuned trace features from a high-resolution LoRA-adapted DINOv2 network. The fine-tuned models used, the prompting strategies considered, and the formation details employed in the novel dataset are elaborated. Our baseline intra-architecture source attribution method is evaluated in terms of attribution accuracy on our dataset, and ablation studies are also performed. Code and dataset is available at https://github.com/mallikagarg/IntrAA-SD.
papers.summary: The authors introduce `IntrAA-SD`, a task of attributing a generated image to a specific fine-tune of the same Stable Diffusion architecture, such as `Juggernaut XL` versus `RealVis XL`, both derived from `SDXL`, rather than telling different architectures apart. They release a **140K-image benchmark** from multiple `SDXL` fine-tunes, with both in-domain and out-of-distribution prompts. The baseline is a style-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts model in which a frozen `CLIP` backbone captures image style and routes inputs to experts that process features from a LoRA-adapted, high-resolution `DINOv2` network.

papers.title: How Far Can You Steer? Behavior-Capability Frontiers in Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.abstract: Activation steering can modify language-model behavior without parameter updates, but behavioral efficacy alone does not determine whether an intervention is usable. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steers targeted behaviors using activation directions derived from contrasting examples, potentially degrading unrelated model capabilities in the process. We therefore study CAA through a behavior-capability frontier, selecting interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to an explicit bound on capability degradation. We evaluate this framework across four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3%, and 5% (absolute percentage points). Validation-selected behavioral effects generalize strongly to held-out data ($\rho = 0.945$), while joint behavior-capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited additional improvement at 5%. Control experiments indicate that these effects depend on learned behavior directions rather than generic activation perturbations. Representational geometry is significantly but only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer. Finally, secondary capability, out-of-distribution, and open-ended evaluations show that interventions satisfying protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation. These results characterize activation steering as a constrained intervention whose usable range depends on model, behavior, direction, layer, and evaluation budget, rather than a universal control knob.
papers.summary: Contrastive Activation Addition (`CAA`) steers language-model behavior by adding activation directions derived from contrasting examples, but it can degrade unrelated capabilities. The authors evaluate it as a behavior-capability frontier, choosing the steering setting that maximizes behavioral gain under an explicit capability-loss budget, across four instruction-tuned models and seven behaviors. Behavioral effects generalize well to held-out data, and **joint behavior-capability survival rises from 37.5% at a 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%**, with little further gain at 5%. Interventions that pass protected benchmarks can still harm untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation.

papers.title: How Unbalanced Must a Latin Rectangle Be?
papers.abstract: We view a $k\times n$ Latin rectangle as $n$ points in the grid $[n]^k$. Each symbol gives one point, whose coordinates are the columns it occupies. The rectangle is balanced when these points are pairwise equidistant in the $\ell_1$ metric. Its imbalance measures the distance from this ideal. We study the minimum imbalance from three sides. Constructively, we use a simulated annealing that moves symbols within rows and only penalises column clashes. Against the reference table of Voboril et al. (2025), it improves 33 of the 51 non-square values for $8\le n\le 13$, by up to 39.4%, and matches the rest. A cheap invariant, the row group, certifies that none of the 33 new rectangles is isotopic to rows of a group table, so the earlier column-swapping local search cannot reach any of them. Exactly, a computer-assisted branch and bound proves that the minimum imbalance of a $3\times 9$ rectangle is $56$. D\'iaz et al. found this value, but its optimality was open. A sharper pruning bound, derived from the identity $I=2\sum(d-t)^+$, reduces the search tree by a factor of $2.4$ to $3.3$ on the instances with $k\ge3$ that we solve. Asymptotically, the minimum imbalance is $\Theta(n^3)$ for every fixed $k$. A pigeonhole argument gives a lower constant of order $k\,4^{-k}$, and random rectangles give an upper constant of order $\sqrt k$. For $k=2$, the limit of $\min I/n^3$ exists, a permuton attains it, and it lies between $4/375$ and $0.1196$. Perfect balance is an $\ell_1$-equilateral problem, so it forces $k=\Omega(n/\log n)$ rows. For $2\times n$ rectangles, single two-minute annealing runs improve five of the seven six-hour MIP upper bounds for $14\le n\le 20$. Finally, the Lean 4 kernel checks every rectangle reported in this paper against a 74-line specification that imports only Lean's core library. We also prove the pigeonhole lower bound in Lean with Mathlib.
papers.summary: A k-by-n Latin rectangle can be viewed as n points in a grid, one per symbol, and it is balanced when those points are pairwise equidistant in the L1 metric. The authors study how small the imbalance can be using three methods. A simulated annealing search improves 33 of 51 known non-square values for 8 ≤ n ≤ 13 by up to 39.4%. A computer-assisted branch and bound proves that the minimum imbalance of a 3×9 rectangle is 56. Asymptotic analysis shows the minimum is **Θ(n³) for every fixed k**. Every reported rectangle is checked by the `Lean 4` kernel, and the pigeonhole lower bound is formally proved with `Mathlib`.

papers.title: Familiar letters, not related languages, let unseen languages into a shared space of meaning
papers.abstract: Hundreds of languages have written text but almost no translations, and whether a model learning one from untranslated text builds on a related language or familiar letters is unclear: they usually coincide. Here we show that familiar letters, not a related language, let an unseen language into a shared space of meaning. GlyphMind, a tokenizer-free vision transformer that reads text as pixels and lets any sentence be shown in any script, was pretrained to align translations across 27 writing systems. Adapted on untranslated Lao, a language and script it had never seen, it retrieved English translations seven times as often as the strongest simple baseline. Rewritten in unfamiliar letters, Lao did not enter although its close relative Thai was in pretraining; Santali, which had none, entered in Devanagari, familiar from Hindi, but not in its own script. Transliteration into familiar scripts may thus open multilingual models to languages without translations.
papers.summary: Hundreds of languages have written text but almost no translations, and the paper asks whether a model learning such a language from untranslated text benefits from a related language or from a familiar script. `GlyphMind` is a tokenizer-free vision transformer that reads text as pixels; it was pretrained to align translations across 27 writing systems. Adapted on untranslated Lao, it retrieved English translations seven times as often as the strongest simple baseline. Controlled script swaps show that **familiar letters, not linguistic relatedness, determine whether an unseen language enters the shared meaning space**, which suggests transliteration into familiar scripts as a route for low-resource languages.

papers.title: Holistic Parallel Supervision for Expressive Speech to Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Expressiveness is central to speech-to-speech translation (S2ST), yet existing datasets rarely align source and target speech jointly in content, prosody, timing, and speaker identity. Consequently, current systems often rely on indirect conditioning or transfer mechanisms. To obtain this supervision, we introduce a training-data construction strategy that combines professional dubbing, which provides human-performed correspondence in content, prosody, and timing, with multilingual voice conversion to reduce speaker mismatch. We evaluate this supervision using existing expressive S2ST systems and DirectS2ST, an end-to-end method developed in this work that predicts the complete target-speech representation directly from source speech. Experiments on English-German and English-Spanish show that holistic parallel supervision improves expressive realization across all evaluated systems. DirectS2ST exhibits the largest gains in content, prosody, timing, speaker similarity, and human-rated expressiveness. To our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic investigation of holistic parallel supervision for expressive S2ST.
papers.summary: Expressive speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) lacks training data in which source and target speech are aligned in content, prosody, timing, and speaker identity together. The authors build such data by pairing professional dubbing with multilingual voice conversion to reduce speaker mismatch. They also propose `DirectS2ST`, an end-to-end model that predicts the full target-speech representation directly from source speech. On English-German and English-Spanish, this holistic parallel supervision improves expressiveness for every system tested, and **`DirectS2ST` shows the largest gains** in content, prosody, timing, speaker similarity, and human-rated expressiveness.

papers.title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
papers.abstract: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given: a fixed archive, drawn from a fixed distribution. We argue that the supply is the problem, and that cultural evolution has the theory of it. We read model collapse as Rogers' paradox: a population that comes to rely on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied, because copies go stale unless someone keeps learning for themselves. We test the identification in three steps. First, Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge language models, from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer, retain under other mixtures of fresh data. Second, when the world itself changes, a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data to keep up the faster the world changes, as Rogers' model says it must and as analyses that assume a fixed target cannot; a lineage that restarts every generation from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated, because those weights are knowledge that is never copied. Third, we close the loop: when the people who write a model's training data can ask the model instead of finding things out, the supply of fresh data becomes endogenous. At equilibrium, the model is exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to find out for themselves, the population is no better off than without the model, and every increase in the share of model-written text must be paid for by more people learning for themselves. Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox. Filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse; only checks that carry new information act as critical learning.
papers.summary: The authors argue that model collapse, the loss of rare knowledge when generative models train on earlier models' outputs, is an instance of Rogers' paradox from cultural evolution: a population that relies on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied. Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge models from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer retain under other mixes of fresh data. It also predicts that a lineage copying its own past needs more fresh data the faster the world changes. When people can ask the model instead of finding things out themselves, the equilibrium model is **only as reliable as independent learning is costly**, which leaves the population no better off than without it. Users who verify answers break the paradox, while filters that select plausible text accelerate collapse.

papers.title: When Every Choice Is Correct: A Causal Study of Numerical Preference in Language Models
papers.abstract: When a language model chooses a number between 1 and 30, every integer in the range is valid, yet the model can favor particular answers. We use numerical choice to study how preference is processed across layers and tokens. Perturbation probing and gradient attribution nominate neurons for activation interventions. In a selected Qwen3-4B case, a pre-answer edit changes 17 to 15 while both runs first emit 1. After the edit ends, selective cache and attention-output replacements trace part of its continuing influence on the second digit. Replacing one attention head's output or the other heads' outputs jointly produces similar immediate readout contributions; both interventions restore 17 but have different final log-odds effects on 7 versus 5. Holding later multilayer perceptron (MLP) outputs at their values from the edited run without either replacement reduces this effect gap from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat. Later computation therefore changes how similar local contributions affect the continuation. Retrospective estimates across eighteen contexts capture much of the probability movement but miss the selected answer switch. Prompt tests also separate influence from answer changes: one held-out prompt retains influence without switching, and only one of twelve fresh wordings qualifies for the reader/MLP test; there, joint MLP clamping again reduces the gap between the two reader effects while the answer remains 17. These results use numerical choice as a controlled case for studying persistent state and conditional downstream processing; they do not establish the origin or a complete circuit of natural numerical preference.
