papers.summary: When a language model picks a number between 1 and 30, every answer is valid, yet models still favor particular ones; the authors use this setting to study how preference is processed across layers and tokens. Perturbation probing and gradient attribution nominate neurons for intervention, and in one `Qwen3-4B` case a pre-answer edit changes the output from 17 to 15. Cache and attention-output replacements trace how that edit continues to influence the second digit. Clamping later multilayer perceptron (MLP) outputs **shrinks the gap between two interventions' effects from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat**, showing that later computation conditions how similar local contributions affect the continuation. The authors state that the results do not establish a complete circuit for natural numerical preference.

papers.title: Practical Estimation of the Bayes Optimal Fairness-Accuracy Tradeoff with Soft Labels
papers.abstract: There is a fundamental limit to the best prediction error of any model for a given data distribution. In classification, the Bayes error quantifies this limit and serves as both a benchmark for trained models and a criterion to detect overfitting. The state-of-the-art Bayes error estimation techniques for binary classification use only soft labels (positive class probabilities) and require no input features or auxiliary training. We extend such notions to constrained classification problems, such as fairness. Fair classification is an important case of constrained or multi-objective classification. It requires a model not only to be accurate but also to yield fair outcomes (equal or near-equal true positive rates) across different demographic groups (e.g., race and gender). This leads to an inherent fairness-accuracy tradeoff or a Pareto frontier that is used to compare fair classifiers against each other. The focus of our work is to estimate the fundamental limit for this fairness-accuracy tradeoff. We derive an explicit expression for the fair Bayes error rate (i.e., best achievable error rate subject to given fairness constraints), and construct consistent, instance-free estimators for it using only soft labels and group information. We provably bound the bias and the sample complexity of our estimators. Empirically, our method produces a robust, low-variance estimate of the optimal fairness-accuracy tradeoff curve, even when the soft labels are noisy and derived from a classification model on hard labels.
papers.summary: The Bayes error is the lowest error any classifier can reach on a given distribution, and recent estimators compute it using only soft labels, meaning positive-class probabilities. The authors extend this idea to fairness-constrained classification. They derive an explicit expression for the fair Bayes error rate and build consistent, instance-free estimators that need only soft labels and group membership. They prove bounds on bias and sample complexity. Experiments show **robust, low-variance estimates of the optimal fairness-accuracy Pareto frontier**, even when the soft labels are noisy or come from a model trained on hard labels.

papers.title: Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription
papers.abstract: Streaming speech recognition is increasingly consumed by machines, such as translators and voice agents, that act on each token as it appears. A token that is later revised costs wasted work or a wrong action. In this work, we present Confucius4-R2T2 (short for Real Real-Time Transcription), a stable-prefix streaming ASR model that never modifies its earlier output while maintaining high accuracy and low latency. R2T2 is obtained by post-training Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio while freezing its pre-trained audio encoder and projector. The adaptation is based on the concept of Longest Stable Prefix (LSP), a new notion that we introduce in this work. We prove that LSP is monotone under the prefix order, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal among labels that equal a whole earlier output. Learning from LSP labels converts a full-context model into a stable-prefix streaming one without any architectural change. Extensive evaluations show that R2T2 brings streaming recognition close to the base model's full-context quality while delivering stable text with low emission lag. Its gains extend beyond the post-training languages, demonstrating a practical path from full-context ASR to stable streaming. We open-source the model weights and code at https://huggingface.co/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2 and https://github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2.
papers.summary: Streaming speech recognition (ASR) output increasingly feeds machines such as translators and voice agents, so any token that is later revised wastes work or triggers a wrong action. `Confucius4-R2T2` post-trains `Qwen3-ASR-1.7B` on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio, with the audio encoder frozen, using labels derived from a new notion called Longest Stable Prefix (LSP). The authors prove that LSP is monotone, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal. Training on LSP labels turns a full-context model into one that **never modifies its earlier output**, with no architectural change, while staying close to the base model's full-context accuracy at low emission lag. The weights and code are open-source.

papers.title: SVGFaith: A Two-Layer Meta-Evaluation of Faithfulness Metrics for Text-to-SVG Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-SVG systems are commonly evaluated by applying raster-image metrics to rasterised outputs, yet whether these scores capture fine-grained prompt faithfulness remains unclear. We introduce SVGFaith, a two-layer meta-evaluation framework in which the more faithful candidate of each pair is determined by construction or by human judgment. SVGFaith-Diagnostic contains 1,842 controlled contrastive pairs across eight capability axes, split evenly between two directions: two renderings compared against one prompt, and two descriptions compared against one rendering. SVGFaith-Arena contains 1,327 human-annotated comparisons of real generator outputs. On SVGFaith-Diagnostic, CLIP and three other image--text embedding metrics reach at least 0.789 pairwise accuracy on object identity but at most 0.672 on spatial relations and attribute binding, where chance is 0.5. We further introduce SVGFaith-Score, an interpretable pointwise metric. A domain-tuned decomposer turns each prompt into a dependency graph of atomic visual requirements, a visual question answering model scores whether each requirement is satisfied, and a requirement's score is discounted when its prerequisites score low. In addition to the overall score, the per-requirement scores show which requirements are judged unsatisfied and which inherit discounts from their prerequisites. SVGFaith-Score significantly outperforms all nine baselines, including a Qwen3.5-122B-A10B judge, on Arena and in both Diagnostic directions. Code and data: https://github.com/Yukinonooo/SVGFaith.
papers.summary: Text-to-SVG generators are usually scored with raster-image metrics, and it is unclear whether those metrics capture fine-grained faithfulness to the prompt. `SVGFaith` is a meta-evaluation framework built from 1,842 controlled contrastive pairs across eight capability axes plus 1,327 human-annotated comparisons of real outputs. `CLIP` and similar embedding metrics handle object identity well but score **at most 0.672 pairwise accuracy on spatial relations and attribute binding**, where chance is 0.5. The proposed `SVGFaith-Score` breaks each prompt into a dependency graph of atomic visual requirements and checks each one with a visual question answering model. It outperforms all nine baselines, including a `Qwen3.5-122B-A10B` judge.

papers.title: Reglos: A Self-Evolving Personal Memory Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.
papers.summary: Personal memory agents increasingly let coding agents rewrite the harness that turns stored memory into model context, but a patch tested only on the failures it targets can overfit. `Reglos` is a training-free memory agent with an append-only per-user record and a recursive self-improvement loop. In that loop, a coding agent proposes harness patches from failure traces, and a critic from a different model family screens each patch for benchmark gaming. Once the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. Using the same backbone for every system, `Reglos` outperforms `Mem0`, `MemOS`, and `EverOS`, reaching **84.0% on `LongMemEval-S` with `Qwen3.8-27B`** and 87.2% with `GPT-5.6 Luna`.

papers.title: Touch\'{e}World tech report : Towards Online Unified Camera--Hand Exploration in Generative Worlds
papers.abstract: Recent video world models allow users to explore generated environments through camera navigation. Continuous hand motion provides a fine-grained action channel for interacting with the people and objects encountered during exploration. We present Touch\'{e}World, a framework that integrates gesture-driven interaction into a camera-controlled video world model. Given an initial image and a scene-description prompt, the model generates video conditioned on temporally aligned camera and hand controls. We construct joint camera--hand training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos through annotation completion, consistency-based filtering, and temporal alignment. Building on a pretrained camera-controlled world model, we combine spatial hand-skeleton conditioning with numerical hand-motion features through parameter-efficient adaptation. Causal adaptation and few-step distillation support chunk-level online generation, allowing users to update their controls based on generated visual feedback. We further introduce Touch\'{e}Bench to evaluate hand-motion following, camera--hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Together, these components establish a framework for studying continuous exploration and hand-driven interaction within generative worlds.
papers.summary: Video world models let users explore generated scenes by moving the camera, and `ToucheWorld` adds continuous hand gestures as a second control channel for interacting with people and objects. The authors assemble joint camera-and-hand training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos through annotation completion, consistency filtering, and temporal alignment. They then adapt a pretrained camera-controlled world model with hand-skeleton and hand-motion conditioning using parameter-efficient adaptation. Causal adaptation and few-step distillation enable **chunk-level online generation**, so users can adjust their controls in response to what is generated. A new benchmark, `ToucheBench`, evaluates hand-motion following, camera-hand coordination, online interaction, and object response.

papers.title: Adapting Qwen3 to Tajik from 0.6B to 8B: Lower Text Loss Did Not Mean Better Understanding
papers.abstract: Small LoRA adapters trained on Tajik news and books lowered Qwen3's Tajik text loss at every size we tried, from 0.6B to 8B, by 0.60 to 1.45 nats per token, but none of them improved Tajik reading comprehension where it can be measured. On Belebele the 1.7B and 8B adapters left accuracy unchanged and the 4B adapter lowered it by 3.7 points; at 0.6B the score rose by 4.2 points but sits near chance and coincides with a change in which answer letter the model prefers, so we do not read it as understanding. At 8B, continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text was followed by a Belebele gain of 9.9 points. After a further supervised fine-tuning stage, our main model, e3, is 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B on Belebele; its English MMLU changed by -1.2 points, and a loss larger than 3.3 points is excluded. The same heavy recipe applied to Qwen3-0.6B-Base brought its text loss close to that of the 8B model after books-only pretraining, while its multiple-choice answers stayed near chance and its English MMLU fell by 7.6 points. We report 15 trained models and their 5 starting models from June to October 2025, scored in 2026 on one harness with paired intervals, and we report what went wrong: lost training records, a thinking-mode dataset with almost no reasoning in it, later branches whose training data was never documented, and a 4-bit release that contains no transformer layers.
papers.summary: The authors adapt `Qwen3` models from 0.6B to 8B parameters to Tajik and find that small LoRA adapters lower Tajik text loss at every size **without improving reading comprehension** on `Belebele`. At 8B, continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text, followed by supervised fine-tuning, yields a model 11.4 points above `Qwen3-8B` on `Belebele` with English `MMLU` down only 1.2 points. The same heavy recipe applied to the 0.6B base model brought its text loss close to the 8B model's while its multiple-choice answers stayed near chance. The report covers 15 trained models and documents what went wrong, including lost training records and a 4-bit release that contains no transformer layers.

papers.title: ProcessPrefBench: Evaluating Cross-Task Transfer of Individual Process Preferences from Naturalistic Human-AI Interaction
papers.abstract: In natural human-AI dialogue, users' corrections, requests, and self-descriptions carry reusable signals about how they want work to be done. These signals reveal individual process preferences, user-specific standards for evidence, depth, analytical focus, procedure, and delivery. We ask whether a preference revealed in one dialogue can shape an assistant's later answer when the task does not restate it. ProcessPrefBench uses three months of natural dialogues from two knowledge workers to build 66 source-target cases separately judged for source evidence and target applicability. Sources are preselected, so the benchmark tests application rather than retrieval. We test three models with target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts. Target-specific 0-2 rubrics score preference realization, and a task gate flags severe failures. Compared with target-only prompting, full-history and imperative distilled-preference prompting raise preference realization by 0.204 and 0.244 points on the 0-2 scale, respectively, with no reliable advantage from distillation. Fabricated-evidence failures rise from 5.8% under target-only prompting to 10.1% under full-history and 10.4% under imperative prompting. ProcessPrefBench highlights a tension in learning from dialogue, where drawing on prior interactions can improve preference realization yet also invite fabricated evidence. We hope it helps build assistants that honor a user's process preferences without sacrificing factual reliability.
papers.summary: Users reveal individual process preferences, such as standards for evidence, depth, and delivery, through corrections and requests in conversation. `ProcessPrefBench` tests whether a preference revealed in one dialogue carries over to a later task that does not restate it. The benchmark has 66 source-target cases drawn from three months of real dialogues by two knowledge workers. Compared with target-only prompting, full-history and distilled-preference prompts raise preference realization by about 0.2 points on a 0-2 scale, with no reliable benefit from distillation. They also **nearly double fabricated-evidence failures, from 5.8% to over 10%**, which exposes a tension between personalization and factual reliability.

papers.title: Which One Is Sounding? Binaural Sounding Instance Disambiguation for Audio-Visual Segmentation
papers.abstract: Existing audio-visual segmentation methods mainly predict sound-related regions or category masks and often fail to identify the sounding instance when multiple same-class candidates coexist. Recent audio-visual instance segmentation methods address instance-level prediction but rely largely on motion and cross-frame association, which may become unreliable under sparse observations or inconspicuous motion. To this end, we introduce binaural audio, whose interaural differences encode source-direction information, to provide spatial constraints for distinguishing the sounding instance among same-class visual candidates. We propose Binaural Sounding Instance Disambiguation for Audio-Visual Segmentation (BiSID-AVS), which progressively refines category-level candidate responses into a mask of the true sounding instance. BiSID-AVS first grounds category-consistent candidate regions through audio prompting, then projects binaural cues into an image-plane spatial response map, and finally refines the true sounding instance through dual-level spatial conditioning at the feature and decoder levels. Experiments on the binaurally extended AVS-Synthetic benchmark and Habitat-AVS dataset for robotic indoor perception show that BiSID-AVS achieves the best performance on the multi-candidate subsets, improving instance-level mIoU by 35.19 and 41.21 percentage points, respectively, while substantially reducing false activation on non-sounding same-class regions.
papers.summary: Audio-visual segmentation methods often cannot tell which of several same-class objects is producing a sound, and instance-level methods that rely on motion fail when motion is sparse or subtle. `BiSID-AVS` uses binaural audio, whose interaural differences encode source direction, to pick out the sounding instance. It first grounds category-level candidate regions through audio prompting, then projects binaural cues into an image-plane spatial map, and finally refines the mask with spatial conditioning at both the feature and decoder levels. On multi-candidate subsets of a binaural `AVS-Synthetic` benchmark and the `Habitat-AVS` robotics dataset, it **improves instance-level mIoU by 35.19 and 41.21 percentage points**.

papers.title: UniCompress: From Multi-LoRA Experts to One Compact Model for Edge Intelligence
papers.abstract: Embodied and edge systems increasingly rely on vision-language models (VLMs) to support heterogeneous skills, yet deploying a separate task adapter for each skill while retaining a high-precision backbone creates substantial memory and management costs. We present UniCompress, a deployment-oriented framework that converts multi-task expertise into one compact, adapter-free model. Starting from a consolidated BF16 Qwen3-VL-4B teacher, UniCompress constructs an asymmetric INT2 student using GPTQ initialization and teacher-guided quantization recovery. The approach jointly quantizes and recovers the projection weights in the vision encoder and language backbone, enabling aggressive compression of the complete vision-language model while preserving its multi-task behavior. We evaluate UniCompress on four heterogeneous embodied tasks: posture recognition, household-safety understanding, multimodal dialogue routing, and mobile-GUI action prediction. UniCompress reduces the approximate weight storage from 8.9 GB in BF16 to 2.1 GB in INT2, corresponding to a reduction of approximately 76%. It improves the INT2 macro task score by 34.3 percentage points over GPTQ-INT2 while remaining within 0.9 points of the consolidated BF16 teacher. These results demonstrate the potential of teacher-guided joint vision-language INT2 recovery for deploying a single multi-skill VLM on resource-constrained embodied platforms.
papers.summary: Edge and embodied systems often run a separate adapter for each skill on top of a high-precision vision-language model (VLM), which is costly in memory and management. `UniCompress` merges multi-task expertise into a single adapter-free model, starting from a BF16 `Qwen3-VL-4B` teacher and producing an INT2 student through `GPTQ` initialization and teacher-guided quantization recovery. It quantizes both the vision encoder and the language backbone. Weight storage falls from 8.9 GB to 2.1 GB, and the INT2 macro task score is **34.3 points above plain `GPTQ`-INT2 and within 0.9 points of the BF16 teacher** across four embodied tasks, including mobile-GUI action prediction.

papers.title: SysPilot: Cross-Library Performance Autotuning via Library Performance Contracts
papers.abstract:
Modern scientific and machine-learning applications compose many independently developed libraries. When these libraries run together, their independently managed runtimes can oversubscribe shared resources: using the same CPU cores, fighting over GPUs, or contending for memory bandwidth. Avoiding such contention requires careful configuration across library boundaries. Existing autotuners do not directly investigate what resources are shared between libraries, which runtime signals correlate with interference. As a result, they are inefficient for finding optimal configurations to mitigate contention.
  This paper presents SysPilot, a cross-library performance autotuning system based on Library Performance Contract (LPC). A Library Performance Contract captures a library's resource demands, assumptions, controls, and observability signals in LPCL, a specification language for describing library resource requirements. SysPilot synthesizes contracts from documentation and code artifacts, composes contracts from the libraries used by an application, derives resource-conflict hypotheses, profiles the application to validate those hypotheses, and selects candidate configurations. This design makes the Library Performance Contract a reusable unit of performance knowledge: a contract for a library can be reused across many applications that depend on that library. We evaluate SysPilot on a benchmark suite of cross-library contention scenarios. The results show that SysPilot matches the performance of autotuners that rely on application-specific manual information while retaining cross-application reuse. Compared with general-purpose autotuners such as OpenTuner and SMAC3, SysPilot improves benchmark performance metrics by up to an additional 38% over the best configuration found by these autotuners, while using 3x fewer runs.
papers.summary: Applications that combine independently developed libraries often suffer resource contention, such as oversubscribed CPU cores, competition for GPUs, or memory-bandwidth conflicts, and generic autotuners do not reason about what the libraries share. `SysPilot` describes each library with a Library Performance Contract, written in a specification language called `LPCL`, that records the library's resource demands, controls, and observable signals. Contracts are synthesized from documentation and code and can be reused across applications. The system composes contracts to form conflict hypotheses, validates them by profiling, and selects configurations. Against `OpenTuner` and `SMAC3`, it achieves **up to 38% better performance with 3x fewer runs**, and it matches autotuners that rely on manual application-specific knowledge.

papers.title: Overview of the NTCIR-19 SciClaimEval Task: Cross-modal Claim Verification in Scientific Papers
papers.abstract: This paper presents an overview of \emph{SciClaimEval}, a pilot task at NTCIR-19 on verifying scientific claims against the tables and figures of the papers in which they appear. Our dataset pairs authentic claims from 180 papers in machine learning, natural language processing, and medicine with contrastive versions of their tables and figures, one supporting the claim and one minimally modified so that it does not. The task comprises two subtasks: deciding whether a piece of evidence supports a claim, and selecting which of two evidence versions does. Twenty-two teams registered, the highest number among NTCIR-19 tasks, and 14 submitted 177 runs. Most systems built on multimodal large language models, relying on prompting and multi-stage inference rather than task-specific fine-tuning. On the first subtask, the best systems reached 98.1\% pair accuracy, but all six top-ranked systems relied on the contrastive pairs; the best system that judged each claim-evidence pair on its own scored 24.3 points lower. Open-weight models, embedded in carefully designed pipelines, matched proprietary ones. Yet verifying a single claim against its evidence, the setting that matters in practice, remains an open problem.
papers.summary: SciClaimEval, a pilot task at NTCIR-19, asks systems to verify claims from 180 papers in machine learning, NLP, and medicine against those papers' tables and figures. Each piece of evidence comes in a supporting version and a minimally modified non-supporting version. Fourteen teams submitted 177 runs, mostly multimodal large language model pipelines built on prompting rather than fine-tuning, and open-weight models matched proprietary ones. The best systems reached 98.1% pair accuracy, but all six top systems relied on the contrastive pairs, and **the best system that judged each claim on its own scored 24.3 points lower**. Verifying a single claim against its evidence therefore remains an open problem.

papers.title: Drift-adaptive Representation Preservation for Domain-Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Pretrained vision models provide strong general-purpose representations, but in Domain-Incremental Learning (DIL), where the input distribution changes sequentially, adapting to new domains often degrades performance on previously learned ones. We observe that forgetting is not uniform across domains and classes and is not explained by training order alone. This motivates us to track each past domain-class concept individually. We use representation drift, defined as the deviation of a past concept's current representation from a fixed anchor, as a measurable surrogate for forgetting risk. The measured drift then serves two complementary roles. A consolidation loss assigns stronger preservation to high-drift pairs, while prototype construction down-weights highly drifted domains to reduce their influence on the class reference. Preservation is thus allocated by measured drift rather than assumed importance. To obtain this signal during training without storing past raw data, we repurpose a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA). For each domain-class pair, we store only a compact context summary in the backbone feature space and rerun it through the learned context-to-target relation to measure its drift from the fixed anchor. Across DomainNet, Office-Home, CORe50, and CDDB-Hard, our method sustains a strong accuracy-forgetting balance on every benchmark, using substantially less training memory than accuracy-competitive methods and the smallest storage among compared methods.
papers.summary: In domain-incremental learning (DIL), pretrained vision models forget earlier domains as the input distribution shifts, and the authors observe that this forgetting varies by domain and class in ways training order does not explain. They track each past domain-class pair through its representation drift from a fixed anchor and use that drift as a proxy for forgetting risk. Drift sets how strongly a consolidation loss preserves each pair and down-weights highly drifted domains when class prototypes are built. To measure drift without storing raw data, they repurpose a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (`JEPA`) that keeps only a compact context summary per pair. Across `DomainNet`, `Office-Home`, `CORe50`, and `CDDB-Hard`, the method keeps a strong accuracy-forgetting balance **with the smallest storage among compared methods**.

papers.title: Reasoning-Trace Overflow in Code Generation: An Empirical Study of Explicit Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning can help language models generate code, but it also introduces a practical risk: the model may spend so much of its output budget reasoning that it never produces usable code. We study this behaviour in relatively small open-weight reasoning models, framing it as reasoning-trace overflow. Across seven models and six code benchmark settings, we measure how much of a fixed 32k-token output budget is spent on reasoning, whether that reasoning improves pass@1, and whether lightweight inference-time controls can mitigate overflow. Our results show that the value of reasoning is highly conditional. Overflow is rare on simpler function-level tasks, but becomes common on harder code-generation benchmarks and for particular model families: on several model--benchmark pairs, more than half of generations exhaust the full 32k-token budget while still reasoning. Most complete overflow is associated with repetitive reasoning loops, although substantial long reasoning also occurs without looping. Disabling reasoning can therefore be competitive for overflow-prone models, simply because it ensures that an answer is produced. At the same time, reasoning remains valuable for stronger models on harder algorithmic and code-understanding tasks. Finally, prompt steering can substantially reduce overflow for some models but is inconsistent, while budgeted transitions provide more direct control and can improve both performance and token efficiency for overflow-prone models. These findings suggest that explicit reasoning should be treated as a controllable resource for code generation, rather than an always-on capability.
papers.summary: Explicit reasoning can help small open-weight models write code, but a model can also spend its whole output budget reasoning and never emit an answer, which the authors call reasoning-trace overflow. Across seven models and six code benchmark settings with a 32k-token budget, overflow is rare on simple function-level tasks. On harder benchmarks, however, **more than half of generations exhaust the budget while still reasoning** for several model-benchmark pairs, mostly because of repetitive reasoning loops. Disabling reasoning can be competitive for overflow-prone models, while stronger models still benefit from reasoning on hard tasks. Prompt steering reduces overflow inconsistently, and budgeted transitions give more reliable control and better token efficiency.

papers.title: Reconciling Privacy with Provenance for Language Model Watermarks
papers.abstract: Watermarking has great potential for regulating the use of language models (LMs), but its deployment has been marred by controversy, as many users argue that fine-grained tracking of LM usage violates their privacy. This tension reduces the effectiveness of watermarks, as users engage in evasion strategies such as paraphrasing that can remove much of the watermark signal. We show that provenance and privacy can be reconciled if we shift the goal of watermark design from tracking individuals to estimating aggregate usage. We develop locally differentially private watermarks which provably limit the evidence that any individual text can contribute to detection, while still enabling accurate estimation of population frequencies. We introduce the Red-Green Sequence (RGS) watermark, a private and computationally efficient watermark that achieves accurate frequency estimation at high privacy levels across various models, sample sizes and generation entropies in settings that reflect realistic deployment scenarios. On C4 language modeling tasks, we attain $0.0019$ MSE with $0.0038$ mean absolute bias at a low $\varepsilon$ of 1, while in more challenging settings such as an essay writing task with only 100 text samples, we still find errors on the order of $0.0113$ MSE with $0.004$ mean absolute bias at $\varepsilon=2$.
papers.summary: Users resist language model watermarks because fine-grained tracking threatens their privacy, and evasion such as paraphrasing weakens the signal. The authors reframe the goal from tracking individuals to estimating aggregate usage, and they design locally differentially private watermarks that provably limit how much evidence any single text contributes to detection. Their `Red-Green Sequence` (`RGS`) watermark is computationally efficient and estimates population frequencies accurately at strong privacy levels. On `C4` it reaches **0.0019 mean squared error at ε = 1**, and it stays accurate on an essay-writing task with only 100 samples.

papers.title: Beyond Risk Cues: A Mechanism-Level Benchmark and Verifiable Debate for Scam Video Detection on the Web
papers.abstract: Online scam videos pose significant threats to individuals and society. Existing studies primarily focus on binary classification, offering limited insights into how scams work and the reasoning behind detection decisions. Moreover, they often overlook the challenge of distinguishing scam videos from superficially similar non-scam content, such as advertisements, and the robustness of detection models against misleading arguments. These limitations hinder reliable scam video detection. To address these limitations, we introduce MechScam, a benchmark comprising 6,614 videos covering diverse scam mechanisms and non-scam categories. MechScam provides explanations supported by video evidence, annotations of potential scam elements and their context, and misleading arguments constructed from genuine evidence. Recognizing that genuine evidence can still be used to justify misleading conclusions, we further propose ScamCourt, a debate framework in which trained prosecution and defense debaters present opposing arguments, while a trained judge makes decisions based on a transcript with verified citations. Extensive experiments show that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle to distinguish scam videos from similar non-scam content. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reducing false positives and showing stronger resistance to misleading arguments. Together, MechScam and ScamCourt contribute to more reliable and interpretable scam video detection. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/SuperYFan/MechScam.
papers.summary: Scam-video detection research mostly treats the problem as binary classification, which says little about how scams work and is weak at separating scams from look-alike content such as advertisements. `MechScam` is a benchmark of 6,614 videos covering scam mechanisms and non-scam categories, annotated with evidence-backed explanations and misleading arguments built from genuine evidence. The authors also propose `ScamCourt`, in which trained prosecution and defense debaters argue opposing cases and a trained judge decides from a transcript with verified citations. State-of-the-art multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle to tell scams from similar legitimate videos, while **`ScamCourt` outperforms larger MLLMs and fine-tuned baselines**, with fewer false positives and greater resistance to misleading arguments.

papers.title: The Harness Is the Model: Agent Scaffolding Changes a Fixed LLM's Compliance with Banking Conduct Rules, Unevenly Across Models
papers.abstract: Banks validate language models, but they deploy systems: a model inside a harness that decides what it sees, which tools it can call and who checks its actions. We test whether that harness changes compliance with banking conduct rules when the model is held fixed. Four open-weight models each ran five harnesses (a pipeline that makes one structured decision, a ReAct-style tool loop, a loop in which the policy is reachable only through search, a loop with a long benign customer memory, and a loop with a same-model compliance reviewer) on 156 pre-registered cases in a simulated retail bank whose 11 rule families paraphrase EU consumer-credit, payments, investor-protection, data-protection and anti-money-laundering provisions. Every one of the 3120 two-turn episodes was scored deterministically from the executed tool trace, with violations and over-refusals counted separately. Pooled across models the harness moved the correct-case rate only between 87.3% and 92.1%, but within a model it mattered a great deal: for one model the spread between its best and worst harness was 11.5 percentage points, enough to move it from first to last place among the four models, while for another the harness made no detectable difference; the model x harness interaction itself was suggestive rather than conclusive. The same-model reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals, contrary to our pre-registered prediction. Rules that require date arithmetic failed in every harness. In an exploratory analysis with two LLM judges and a blind human check, 26% of violations were accompanied by a customer message that denied the action the agent had just executed, which a transcript-only review would record as a correct refusal. For model-risk management the unit of validation should be the model-harness pair, and conduct testing should read the action log, not the conversation.
papers.summary: Banks validate language models on their own, but they deploy them inside harnesses: the surrounding code that controls what the model sees, which tools it can call, and who checks its actions. The authors held each of four open-weight models fixed and ran it in five harnesses on 156 pre-registered cases in a simulated retail bank whose rules paraphrase EU conduct regulations, scoring all 3,120 episodes deterministically from the executed tool trace. Pooled across models, the harness barely moved the correct-case rate (87.3% to 92.1%). Within a single model it could matter a great deal: one model's **11.5-point spread between its best and worst harness moved it from first to last place**, while another model showed no detectable effect. A same-model compliance reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals, rules that need date arithmetic failed in every harness, and 26% of violations came with a customer message denying the action the agent had just executed.

papers.title: Ab Initio Accuracy Beyond the Cutoff: Distributed Message-Passing Equivariant Attention at Tens-of-Millions-of-Atom Scale
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics predicts molecular motion from atomic forces and trajectory integration. Density functional theory (DFT) provides first-principles forces, but its $O(N^3)$ cost limits simulations to thousands of atoms; empirical force fields scale to millions but miss bond breaking and charge transfer. Equivariant message-passing Transformers learn the ab initio potential at linear cost. Stacked layers propagate information beyond a single cutoff, giving four layers a receptive field up to 23{\AA}. At this frontier, scale is limited by communication: layers exchange boundary features across devices, force backpropagation repeats the exchange, and moving atoms change neighbor graphs and tensor shapes. We present Tessera, a distributed runtime that fixes workload shapes between rebuilds. It sorts atoms along a space-filling curve into equal-count shards, ensuring identical atom counts and tensor shapes per rank. Peer sets scale as $K^{0.5}$, not $K$. A conservative neighbor skin preserves topology across updates, enabling each rebuild interval to replay as one CUDA Graph. Fused kernels, three-level neighbor search, and overlapped All-to-All complete it. On 512 GPUs, Tessera sustains 30.7M atoms at 89.7% weak-scaling efficiency (77--90% across three per-GPU loads); per-step time rises 1.11--1.29x as machine and problem grow 16x. Graph reuse cuts full-step time $1.87\times$. Across an $8\times$ device increase, neighbor-search cost grows $1.7\times$, versus $3.0\times$ for Morton order. In a live $10.24$M-atom salt solution, NVE energy drift is $0.42\,\mu$eV/atom/ps over $10$ ps, and structure matches a serial reference. A 10.06M-atom Norovirus capsid sustains 100 ps of NVT at $\approx 8$ ps/day on 256 A100 GPUs. Over 200,000 steps, it has no broken bonds or anomalously close pairs and uses three compiled variants, with no graph breaks or eager fallbacks.
papers.summary: Equivariant message-passing Transformers can learn first-principles (density functional theory) atomic forces at linear cost, but at large scale they are limited by communication between devices and by neighbor graphs that keep changing as atoms move. `Tessera` is a distributed runtime that sorts atoms along a space-filling curve into equal-sized shards, keeps the neighbor topology fixed between rebuilds so each interval replays as a single CUDA Graph, and adds fused kernels and overlapped All-to-All communication. On 512 GPUs it sustains **30.7M atoms at 89.7% weak-scaling efficiency**, and graph reuse alone cuts full-step time 1.87x. A 10.06M-atom Norovirus capsid ran 100 ps of stable simulation on 256 A100 GPUs, at about 8 ps per day.

papers.title: From Handcrafted to Generative: RLVR-Optimized Icon Generation for Alexa+
papers.abstract: Alexa+ devices with screens display animated icons during conversations to visually reinforce what is being said. The original set of these icons was hand-drawn by designers one at a time, a process that produces polished results but is time-consuming and cannot scale to the range of topics encountered in open-ended conversation. We describe an automated pipeline, deployed in production, that generates these vectorised animated icons from a text description alone and surfaces relevant animations to customers based on their ongoing conversation. The pipeline decomposes icon creation into a sequence of stages (image generation, semantic decomposition, vectorisation, styling, and animation). Its quality is determined at the very first of these, image generation, on which every downstream stage depends. We therefore focus on improving this first and most critical stage. Because the icons are rendered on small display canvases under strict design guidelines, generations are often unsuitable for production. Supervised fine-tuning is not viable, as no dataset of line-art icons exists under these constraints. Instead, we design objective verifiers that automatically flag generations violating the design guidelines, and use them to fine-tune a flow matching image generation model via reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). The fine-tuned model raises the pass rate from 15.7% to 58.7% (3.7x) under a VLM judge that is independent of the reward model. Both the trained model and the verifier are deployed in the production pipeline, where the verifier also serves as the automated quality gate before final design review.
papers.summary: Alexa+ devices show animated line-art icons during conversations, and designers originally drew these by hand, which cannot keep up with open-ended conversation topics. The authors describe a production pipeline that generates vectorised animated icons from text in several stages, and they focus on the first stage, image generation, because every later stage depends on it. With no suitable dataset available for supervised fine-tuning, they wrote objective verifiers that flag violations of the design guidelines and used them to fine-tune a flow-matching image model through reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (`RLVR`). Judged by an independent vision-language model, the pass rate rose **from 15.7% to 58.7% (3.7x)**, and the verifier now also serves as the automated quality gate in production.

papers.title: ModalSearcher: Weaving Visual Evidence into Autonomous Cross-Modal Deep Search
papers.abstract: Static and incomplete parametric knowledge limits the performance of multimodal large language models on novel-knowledge and knowledge-intensive tasks, especially those requiring multi-hop evidence acquisition. Existing multimodal agentic search methods often fix visual evidence at the input or a predefined trajectory position, making it difficult for agents to select search modalities as their information needs evolve and to handle complex real-world queries. We define this capability as autonomous cross-modal search: an agent chooses among direct reasoning, text-to-text search, text-to-image search, and reverse-image search, actively introduces visual evidence when appropriate, and switches between and integrates modalities across multiple hops. We propose ModalSearch-Pipeline, a scalable procedure for constructing an interleaved multimodal knowledge graph. It samples paths with diverse depths and modality compositions and uses backward question construction to obscure entity names and image targets that would expose reasoning shortcuts while retaining necessary disambiguating clues, yielding text-only, image-initialized, and arbitrarily interleaved multi-hop problems. We train the ModalSearcher Agent with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment, and construct ModalSearch-Bench. Experiments show that ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B under the same agentic workflow across five multimodal knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks, with consistent gains on independently constructed active visual-search benchmarks.
papers.summary: Multimodal search agents usually fix where visual evidence enters a trajectory, so they cannot decide for themselves when to search with text, with images, or by reverse-image lookup as their information needs change. The authors build `ModalSearch-Pipeline`, which samples paths from an interleaved multimodal knowledge graph and writes questions backward, hiding entity names and image targets so the agent cannot take shortcuts. They use the resulting data to train `ModalSearcher` with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live web environment, and they release `ModalSearch-Bench`. Under the same agentic workflow, `ModalSearcher-8B` **improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over `Qwen3-VL-8B`** across five knowledge-intensive multimodal QA benchmarks, with consistent gains on separately built active visual-search benchmarks.

papers.title: Growing One's AI Tools: A Paradigm of Practice-Grown Tools
papers.abstract: Professionals have long used software built for them by others. This article reports the growth of a professional computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tool built by its own user, a conference interpreter without programming training. Drawing on an eight-week version-controlled record with telemetry from 133 logged sessions and over 20,000 recognized utterances, the article traces how real conference work drove the tool through 62 commits and six versions. The record shows capabilities deployed on the day their need appeared and one strategy change that cut median end-to-end delay by over a third within one afternoon. The article then proposes the paradigm of practice-grown tools, defined by the shift from using to growing, the co-evolution of tool and practice through breakdown and repair, bounded local computation, and an assessment corollary, and it formulates three propositions toward tool-inclusive assessment of practitioners, from tool-making literacy to a compute-standardized format for certifying what they and their tools achieve together.
papers.summary: A conference interpreter with no programming training built their own computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tool, and this article traces how it grew. The evidence is an eight-week version-controlled record with telemetry from 133 sessions and more than 20,000 recognized utterances, covering 62 commits and six versions driven by real conference work. Capabilities were deployed on the day the need for them appeared, and **one strategy change cut median end-to-end delay by over a third in a single afternoon**. From this case the author proposes a paradigm of practice-grown tools, in which tool and practice evolve together, and three propositions for assessing practitioners together with the tools they build.

papers.title: Accelerating Long-Context Decoding in Large-Scale Hybrid LLMs Without Retraining
papers.abstract: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.
papers.summary: Hybrid language models replace most full-attention layers with linear attention, but the few full-attention layers that remain still dominate decoding cost at long context lengths. Without any retraining or weight changes, the authors replace those layers with combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of the most relevant tokens, with window size and budget chosen per layer by a multi-objective search. Across six hybrid models from 4B to 397B parameters, the chosen configurations keep baseline accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding at 256k tokens becomes **up to 2.22x faster on `Qwen3.5-4B`**, 2.23x faster on `Qwen3.5-122B-A10B`, and 2.06x faster on `Ornith-1.0-397B`.

papers.title: SafeStart: Mitigating the Overlooked Safety Cost of Active Expert Reduction in MoE LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models send each token through a few of many expert subnetworks. Serving methods make these models faster by running even fewer experts per token, and they are validated on accuracy benchmarks. We show that these methods can weaken the model's refusal of harmful requests, and we introduce SafeStart, which largely restores refusal while keeping most of the speedup. In vLLM on one RTX A6000, keeping about two thirds of the selected experts speeds up offline decoding by 15 to 28% at batch size 8. We find that, at this setting, under a jailbreak that tells the model not to refuse, the share of harmful requests that the model answers rises by 18.4 percentage points on Qwen1.5-MoE, 9.5 on OLMoE, and 6.6 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, the three of nine models where it rises significantly, while MMLU accuracy drops by less than two points. We discover that most of this increase arises while the model processes the prompt and generates its first few tokens. SafeStart therefore runs all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens, and the reduced set of experts afterwards, through a fused kernel in vLLM. With experts removed, SafeStart keeps at least 85% of the offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8 and 32 and brings the change under this jailbreak to between -2.1 and +1.3 points for three expert-reduction methods on these three models. On 889 held-out requests, in an analysis fixed before generation, truncation raises harmful compliance by 5.8 to 21.4 points, and SafeStart leaves a rise of 0.6 to 2.6 points, non-inferior to the original model on two of the three models. Our results show that faster MoE serving need not cost safety: a serving system can keep most of the gain from running fewer experts by running all of them at the start of each response, and it should test refusal, not only accuracy, before it enables such a method.
papers.summary: To serve Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models faster, some methods route each token through fewer experts, and these methods are usually validated only on accuracy benchmarks. In `vLLM` on a single RTX A6000, keeping about two thirds of the selected experts sped up decoding by 15 to 28% and cost less than two points of `MMLU` accuracy. Under a jailbreak that tells the model not to refuse, however, harmful compliance rose by up to 18.4 points on `Qwen1.5-MoE`, and most of that increase arose during prompt processing and the first few generated tokens. `SafeStart` therefore runs all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens, then switches to the reduced set through a fused kernel. It **keeps at least 85% of the decode speedup while bringing the jailbreak-induced change to between -2.1 and +1.3 points**.

papers.title: Grounding in the Dark: Text-Only Training for Zero-Shot Video Temporal Localization
papers.abstract: Video-LLMs are typically trained on paired video-text data for temporal tasks, yet collecting precise temporal annotations and training on large-scale video datasets are both costly. We investigate whether a text-only LLM, with no vision-language pretraining, can be trained on textual video descriptions alone to perform temporal grounding and receive video only at inference time. This setting removes paired video data from training altogether and is a step toward training multimodal models without paired annotations. We generate a 134K-example corpus of textual sequences with up to 100 time steps, adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, and evaluate on Charades-STA and QV-Highlights without training on videos from either benchmark. LLM2CLIP, whose text encoder supports longer inputs, represents detailed descriptions better than CLIP (61.54 versus 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid) and transfers them better to video. Still, replacing text with frame embeddings at inference yields only 4.99 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 11.12 on QV-Highlights, revealing a large modality gap. To bridge it, we propose Nearest Entity Replacement (NER), a training-free mapping that represents each video frame by the normalized mean of its nearest text-entity embeddings, so that the model receives the kind of input it was trained on. NER reaches 14.45 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights, outperforming the strongest of four families of modality-gap baselines by 5.00 and 1.71 points. NER thus enables partial transfer from text to video, while more reliable grounding will likely require encoders with better-aligned text and visual representations.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether a text-only language model, trained purely on textual descriptions of videos, can perform video temporal grounding when it sees real video only at inference time. They generate a 134K-example corpus of timed textual sequences and adapt `Qwen3-8B` with LoRA on `CLIP` or `LLM2CLIP` text embeddings, then evaluate zero-shot on `Charades-STA` and `QV-Highlights`. Simply swapping in frame embeddings at inference exposes a large modality gap (4.99 mtIoU on `Charades-STA`). Their training-free Nearest Entity Replacement (`NER`) represents each frame by the mean of its nearest text-entity embeddings, which **raises scores to 14.45 and 20.72 mtIoU** and beats the strongest baselines for closing the modality gap, although reliable grounding remains out of reach.

papers.title: CARM: Conformal Adaptive Risk Masking for Reliable Scientific Super-Resolution
papers.abstract: Deep learning-based super-resolution (SR) can reconstruct fine-scale Earth-observation fields from coarse observations, but reconstruction accuracy alone does not provide a calibrated rule for identifying reliable spatial regions. Conformal Mask Calibration (CMC), built on conformal risk control, converts a spatial uncertainty score into a trust mask and controls the expected worst-case local distortion under exchangeability. However, its fixed threshold can become miscalibrated in Earth-observation streams affected by seasonality and episodic events. We propose $\textit{CARM}$ (Conformal Adaptive Risk Masking), a statistical framework for adaptive spatial risk control under temporal distribution shift. CARM maintains experts with heterogeneous update rates and aggregates their threshold proposals online using an asymmetric surrogate loss, balancing rapid adaptation to distribution changes against stability during relatively stationary periods. All updates are causal and use only mature feedback available after a fixed delay, allowing CARM to operate with any SR model that provides a spatial uncertainty score. We prove that the time-averaged mask-conditioned risk converges to at most $\alpha$ at an $O(1/T)$ rate, without distributional assumptions and for any choice of aggregation weights across experts. On a daily South China Sea chlorophyll-$\textit{a}$ SR stream, CARM reduces the empirical violation rate from $43.49\%$ to $9.38\%$ and the moving-average exceedance frequency from $47.29\%$ to $1.22\%$ at $\alpha=0.10$, while retaining a non-trivial trusted region. Experiments on ERA5 wind and OSTIA sea-surface temperature further show consistent relative improvements across multiple SR backbones.
papers.summary: Deep-learning super-resolution can reconstruct fine-scale Earth-observation fields, but it needs a calibrated way to mark which regions of the output can be trusted. An existing method, Conformal Mask Calibration, turns an uncertainty score into a trust mask with a fixed threshold, and that threshold drifts out of calibration under seasonal and episodic distribution shift. `CARM` (Conformal Adaptive Risk Masking) runs several threshold experts that update at different rates, combines their proposals online with an asymmetric loss, and uses only feedback that is available after a fixed delay. The authors prove that time-averaged risk converges to at most the target level with no distributional assumptions. On a South China Sea chlorophyll-a stream, **CARM cuts the empirical violation rate from 43.49% to 9.38%**, with consistent gains on `ERA5` wind and `OSTIA` sea-surface temperature data.

papers.title: Reasoning-Aware Cross-Modal Association Unlearning in Multimodal Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) integrate visual inputs with textual and parametric knowledge, allowing sensitive information to be accessed through cross-modal associations during reasoning. This raises privacy concerns when a visual input should no longer provide access to such information. Machine unlearning can remove this influence without retraining the model from scratch. However, multimodal unlearning methods mainly target samples, concepts, or knowledge content, without separating the knowledge from the cross-modal association through which it is accessed. In reasoning models, target information may disappear from the final answer while remaining in intermediate reasoning, or be replaced by incorrect substitute knowledge. We therefore study cross-modal association unlearning, where the forget target is a designated visual-to-knowledge association: the model should suppress target-bearing behavior under the designated visual context while preserving access to the same knowledge in permitted contexts. We propose Visual-Keyed Counterfactual Rebinding (VKCR), a parameter-efficient framework for cross-modal association editing. VKCR first localizes the edit to a compact association-conditioned parameter subspace. It then reduces support for the designated target at task outputs and counterfactually rebinds the affected reasoning behavior by discouraging target-bearing or unsupported continuations while favoring valid non-sensitive alternatives. We further introduce CLEAR-R and MLLMU-R to evaluate target leakage, hallucinated reassociation, reasoning preservation, and modality-specific utility. Experiments show that VKCR substantially reduces image-conditioned target leakage and hallucinated reassociation, including across heterogeneous task formulations, while preserving non-sensitive visual reasoning and permitted text-only knowledge.
papers.summary: Multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) can reach sensitive information through associations between an image and stored knowledge, and that information can persist in intermediate reasoning even after it disappears from the final answer. The authors define cross-modal association unlearning, which suppresses a designated link from a visual context to a piece of knowledge while keeping that knowledge available in permitted contexts. Their parameter-efficient method, Visual-Keyed Counterfactual Rebinding (`VKCR`), confines the edit to a compact parameter subspace and steers reasoning toward valid non-sensitive alternatives. On the new benchmarks `CLEAR-R` and `MLLMU-R`, **`VKCR` substantially reduces image-conditioned target leakage and hallucinated reassociation** while preserving non-sensitive visual reasoning and permitted text-only knowledge.

papers.title: AssameseLM-E2B: An Open-Weight Assamese Language Model for Efficient Consumer-Grade Deployment
papers.abstract:
While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in high-resource languages, their performance often degrades in low-resource languages due to tokenization inefficiencies, generative instability, and linguistic interference. This paper presents AssameseLM-E2B and its instruction-tuned variant, AssameseLM-E2B-it, a 2-billion-parameter model adapted specifically for low resource Assamese language. Built upon the Gemma-4 architecture, the model incorporates an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary to reduce tokenization overhead by nearly 500% compared with multilingual 2B--3B baselines. We employ a parameter-efficient Continual Pre-Training (CPT) pipeline with Hybrid LoRA, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a balanced, multi-domain dataset to enhance instruction-following and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities.
  Evaluation demonstrates a Bits-per-Byte (BPB) score of 0.7488 on FLORES-200, alongside an overall RAG score of 96.7% and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. Comparative analysis reveals significant limitations in general-purpose baselines, including receptive-productive decoupling, generative degradation on Romanized Assamese, and unintended Bengali script assimilation. These results demonstrate the potential of parameter-efficient adaptation for developing capable, locally deployable language models for low-resource languages under constrained computational resources.
papers.summary: Large language models degrade on low-resource languages such as Assamese because of inefficient tokenization, unstable generation, and interference from related languages. `AssameseLM-E2B` is a 2-billion-parameter model built on `Gemma-4` with an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary, adapted through parameter-efficient continual pre-training with hybrid LoRA and then supervised fine-tuning for instruction following and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It reaches 0.7488 bits per byte on `FLORES-200`, **an overall RAG score of 96.7%**, and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. General-purpose baselines, by contrast, degrade on Romanized Assamese and drift into Bengali script, and the model is sized for deployment on consumer hardware.

papers.title: Editing Large Language Models with Geometry-Aware Regularization
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has become a key technique for updating knowledge in large language models. However, existing methods neglect the geometric structure of the knowledge representation space, leading to two key limitations: they cannot distinguish which pre-trained knowledge should be preferentially preserved (core vs. non-core) nor which new edits are inherently difficult (hard vs. easy). To address this, we propose GEdit, a geometry-aware framework built on a Low-Rank Plus Diagonal (LR+D) factor model that captures the intrinsic low-rank structure of Transformer FFN hidden representations. GEdit features two complementary mechanisms. First, the low-rank regularization applies targeted protection on a low-rank core knowledge subspace. Second, the adaptive regularization dynamically adjusts the regularization strength based on each edit request's editability: relaxing constraints for hard edits to ensure success, and tightening them for easy edits to better preserve pretrained knowledge. Extensive experiments on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3-8B under large-scale editing scenarios, including both mini-batch and fully sequential editing settings with up to 10,000 continuous updates, show that GEdit consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both editing success and knowledge preservation.
papers.summary: Knowledge-editing methods for large language models ignore the geometry of the representation space, so they cannot tell which pre-trained knowledge most needs protecting or which new edits are inherently hard. `GEdit` models Transformer feed-forward hidden representations with a low-rank-plus-diagonal factor model. It applies targeted regularization to protect a low-rank core-knowledge subspace and adjusts regularization strength per edit, relaxing it for hard edits and tightening it for easy ones. On `GPT2-XL`, `GPT-J`, and `LLaMA-3-8B`, in both mini-batch and fully sequential settings with **up to 10,000 consecutive edits**, `GEdit` consistently outperforms prior methods on both edit success and knowledge preservation.

papers.title: CoSafe: Cooperative Runtime Safety Assurance for Mixed-Traffic Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract:
With the rapid development of autonomous driving systems (ADSes), real-world roads are evolving into mixed-traffic environments where autonomous vehicles (AVs) and other traffic participants (e.g., human-driven vehicles (HDVs), cyclists, and pedestrians) coexist and interact with each other. However, current ADSes still incur various safety violations in mixed traffic scenarios, raising a strong demand for runtime safety assurance frameworks that can continuously monitor hazards and prevent potential violations. Existing ego-centric assurance approaches are insufficient for mixed traffic, where violations often arise from locally reasonable yet jointly incompatible decisions among multiple vehicles and cannot be reliably resolved through independent takeover.
  To bridge this gap, we propose CoSafe, a modular and ADS-agnostic cooperative runtime safety assurance framework for mixed-traffic autonomous driving to extend runtime safety assurance from ego-centric takeover to scene-level cooperative intervention. CoSafe leverages vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication to enable roadside units (RSUs) to monitor scene-level hazards and jointly mitigate hazards involving multiple vehicles. We integrate CoSafe with seven state-of-the-art ADSes, and our evaluation on the InterDrive benchmark demonstrates that CoSafe improves the driving score of AVs by 70.03% on average, reduces safety violations by 87.80%, and accurately identifies unsafe AVs with an F3 score of 0.930, while satisfying real-time constraints.
papers.summary: In mixed traffic, safety violations by autonomous vehicles often come from decisions that each look reasonable locally but clash with one another, which a single vehicle taking over on its own cannot reliably fix. `CoSafe` is a cooperative runtime safety framework that works with any autonomous driving system: roadside units use vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication to monitor hazards across the whole scene and coordinate interventions that involve multiple vehicles. Integrated with seven state-of-the-art driving systems and evaluated on the `InterDrive` benchmark, it **reduces safety violations by 87.80%**, improves driving scores by 70.03% on average, and identifies unsafe vehicles with an F3 score of 0.930 while meeting real-time constraints.

papers.title: Loop Before You Leap: What Recurrent Depth Can and Cannot Buy in Data-Limited Pretraining
papers.abstract: Multimodal models have often scored below text-only baselines in the BabyLM Challenge (Klerings et al., 2024; Takmaz et al., 2025). We test whether additional recurrent computation helps close this gap. Recurrence increases computation by reusing layers without adding parameters or training data. Using a single implementation, we compare standard and looped Transformers under a 100M-word budget, with three seeds per main condition. Each image is represented by one feature vector from a frozen DINOv2 encoder, used as a prefix token. Caption words count toward the budget, so multimodal training also changes the language data. In a pre-registered text-only comparison, a 12-layer stack repeated four times exceeds a standard 48-layer Transformer by 5.4 BLiMP percentage points at matched inference compute. However, multimodal training lowers BLiMP accuracy by about 3.8 points in both architectures, with no clear mitigation from recurrence. An exploratory loop-side no-image control, trained with the multimodal language data and batching schedule, scores 5.7 points below the text-only baseline. Adding the visual prefix raises accuracy by 1.85 points on average, but this contrast is uncertain with three seeds. These results suggest that changes in language data and its presentation are a major source of the drop. Diagnostic tests show that the models use visual information; its contribution to grammatical generalization remains uncertain under this single-vector interface.
papers.summary: Multimodal models have often scored below text-only baselines in the `BabyLM` challenge, and the authors test whether looped (recurrent-depth) Transformers, which reuse layers to add computation without adding parameters, can close that gap under a 100M-word budget. In a pre-registered text-only comparison at matched inference compute, **a 12-layer stack looped four times beats a standard 48-layer Transformer by 5.4 `BLiMP` points**. Adding images through a single frozen `DINOv2` prefix vector lowers `BLiMP` by about 3.8 points in both architectures, and recurrence does not clearly help. Control runs suggest the drop comes mainly from changes in the language data and how it is presented, rather than from the visual input itself.
papers.highlight_summary:
Multimodal models in the BabyLM Challenge (pretraining on a 100M-word budget) often score below text-only baselines on grammar benchmarks. The authors test whether looping (reusing a Transformer's layers for extra computation without adding parameters) closes that gap. They also run controls showing that much of the gap comes from changes to the language data, not from the images.

- A 12-layer LLaMA-style stack (`97M` parameters) is applied **four times** with the text embeddings re-added after each pass, and is compared against standard 12-, 24- and 48-layer Transformers; in the multimodal runs, each image enters as a single frozen `DINOv2` feature vector placed before the caption, and caption words count toward the 100M-word budget.
- In a pre-registered comparison at matched inference compute, the looped model beats the 48-layer standard model on `BLiMP` by **5.4 points in text-only training** (76.16 vs 70.80) and **3.7 points with multimodal training**, but its gain over the parameter-matched 12-layer model is only about 1 point (p≈0.12).
- Deeper standard models reach lower training loss but score progressively worse on `BLiMP` (75.21, then 73.84, then 70.80 as depth goes from 12 to 24 to 48 layers), which suggests that sharing weights across loops limits overfitting at this data scale.
- Multimodal training costs about **3.8 `BLiMP` points in both architectures**, so looping gives no measurable mitigation (the gap between the two architectures' drops is −0.01 points, 95% CI [−1.44, 1.41]); a looped no-image control trained on the multimodal language data scores **5.71 points below** the text-only model, and adding the image vector recovers only 1.85 points (95% CI [−1.67, 5.37]).
- Limitations: the models do use the images (shuffling image features raises caption loss by about 1.5 nats per token), but runs use only three seeds, each image is reduced to one global vector, the effect of looping is not separated from the effect of re-adding text embeddings, and the batch-matched no-image control was run only for the looped model.

papers.title: A Definition of Catastrophic Performance
papers.abstract: A central challenge in AI is specifying objectives that align with human preferences. While existing theoretical results elucidate how misspecification impacts performance, they typically do not distinguish between merely suboptimal and catastrophic outcomes. To enable rigorous analysis of catastrophic risk from AI misalignment, we introduce a formal definition of catastrophic performance. Our definition is based on two reference values. The first, baseline value, captures the value attained if no agent is deployed. The second, orthogonal value, captures the value of a trajectory that is unrelated to human preferences, in a sense we describe. Orthogonal value is typically far worse than baseline value. We interpret these reference values through examples in which past human activity has altered the state of the environment to human benefit. Starting at the resulting state, an AI agent is deployed with the goal of accelerating further progress. Catastrophic performance represents this agent's undoing of benefits afforded by human activity.
papers.summary: Theoretical results on objective misspecification usually do not separate merely suboptimal outcomes from catastrophic ones. The authors propose a formal definition of catastrophic performance built on two reference values: a baseline value, which is what is attained if no agent is deployed, and an orthogonal value, which is the value of a trajectory unrelated to human preferences and is typically far worse than baseline. They illustrate the definition with settings in which past human activity has improved the environment and an AI agent is deployed to accelerate further progress. **Catastrophic performance is the agent undoing the benefits that human activity had secured.**

papers.title: Zuse: A Decision Model for European Languages
papers.abstract: Decision models read a document and return a probability for each of a fixed set of options instead of generating text. Several appeared in 2026, but none has published results outside English. We describe Zuse, three decision models (4B, 9B and 27B) that train a low-rank adapter and a pointer head on frozen open-weight bases, targeting 27 European languages, and use them to study how this design behaves across languages and tasks. On a broad European suite of 11 sources excluded from training, covering 9 task groups and 27 languages, a development set that also guided model selection, the 27B model reaches 87.5% accuracy with a pooled expected calibration error of 0.016, and 0.035 when weighted per source. Post-hoc analyses of these single-seed results give three findings. First, miscalibration is structured by task rather than language: on parallel reading and topic items in 26 languages the confidence gap varies about as much as sampling noise, while across sources it spans -0.07 to +0.09, with knowledge tasks overconfident and acceptability judgements underconfident at all three sizes, so one fitted temperature cannot correct both. Second, the share of decisions that can be automated at a 5% error budget follows chance-corrected skill (Spearman 0.97 over 33 source and model pairs) more closely than raw accuracy (0.91). Third, reach beyond the training languages is set by the base model: across 210 languages, changing the training run moved scores by at most about 2 points within a size, while languages outside the base's documented list trail by 23 to 28 points at every size. On English public suites Zuse is behind Jev and Kev, including Kev models on the same bases. We also report two pitfalls in building multi-source training data: label-word collision between topic schemes, and an injection augmentation that taught a shortcut. Zuse can be tried at https://bineric.com/zuse.
papers.summary: Decision models read a document and return a probability for each of a fixed set of options instead of generating text, and none had previously published results outside English. `Zuse` trains a low-rank adapter and a pointer head on frozen open-weight bases at 4B, 9B, and 27B parameters, targeting 27 European languages. On a held-out European suite the 27B model reaches **87.5% accuracy with a pooled expected calibration error of 0.016**. Post-hoc analyses show that miscalibration varies by task rather than by language, that the share of decisions that can be safely automated tracks chance-corrected skill, and that reach beyond the training languages is set by the base model. On English public suites, `Zuse` trails the `Jev` and `Kev` decision models.

papers.title: Rubric Curriculum RL: Exploiting the Generation-Verification Gap in Non-Verifiable Domains
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has led to significant gains in math and code generation. Extending these gains to open-ended domains remains challenging: ground-truth verification is unavailable, human annotation is expensive, and learned reward models are prone to reward hacking. The generation-verification gap, where judging good outputs is easier than producing them, offers a potential path to improvement. However, rubric-based judges are often imprecise and stationary, so policies can overfit or reward hack them. We introduce Rubric Curriculum RL (RcRL), which exploits this gap without new data, human annotations, or stronger teacher models. We combine pairwise preferences over rollouts with a curriculum over rubric criteria, yielding a more discriminative signal than absolute scoring and a non-stationary objective. Whereas baselines plateau within a few hundred steps, RcRL preserves output entropy and keeps improving past 1000 steps. On creative writing, RcRL achieves a 70.5% human win rate against the base model, with gains across benchmarks and judges. On HealthBench, RcRL improves over the base model by 14.6% (full set) and 25.4% (consensus subset), outperforming all training baselines, including instance-specific rubrics.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards works well for math and code, but open-ended domains have no ground-truth checker, and rubric-based judges are imprecise and fixed, so policies overfit or reward-hack them. Rubric Curriculum RL (`RcRL`) exploits the fact that judging outputs is easier than producing them: it combines pairwise preferences over rollouts with a curriculum over rubric criteria, giving a sharper and non-stationary training signal without new data, human labels, or a stronger teacher model. Where baselines plateau within a few hundred steps, `RcRL` preserves output entropy and keeps improving past 1,000 steps.
