As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.
papers.summary: Borrowing from closed-loop neurostimulation, the authors treat LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the model's internal state determines how it is perturbed, rather than applying a fixed intervention. To account for the gap between tractable linear dynamical models and the actual nonlinear transformer, they design an `H-infinity` robust controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization errors. Across steering benchmarks the controller beats existing baselines, with **especially large gains under out-of-distribution conditions** and varying sequence lengths. They also introduce robust steerability, a pre-deployment measure of how much dynamics mismatch steering can tolerate, which shows task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale.

papers.title: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Target-conditioned diffusion drafters predict candidate tokens in parallel, yet each new block must wait for updated target-model hidden states. This forces drafting and verification to run sequentially, limiting speedup even though each block is generated in one pass. We introduce D3D, a standalone diffusion drafter that removes this inter-round dependency. D3D combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to achieve long accepted prefixes without target hidden states. This independence lets D3D draft successor blocks during verification in one packed pass, enabling asynchronous speculative decoding. We progressively prune layers according to their effect on acceptance length to reduce the cost of packed drafting. Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99\% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the target. Across seven benchmarks, D3D averages 5.00$\times$ and 5.71$\times$ decoding speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, compared with 4.03$\times$ and 3.67$\times$ for DFlash. On GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, speedup reaches 7.48$\times$. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/fudan-generative-vision/D3D.
papers.summary: Diffusion drafters for speculative decoding propose a whole block of tokens in one pass, but each new block waits for the target model's updated hidden states, so drafting and verification cannot overlap. `D3D` is a standalone diffusion drafter that combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision, achieving long accepted prefixes without needing target hidden states. This lets it draft the next blocks during verification in one packed pass, enabling asynchronous speculative decoding, and layer pruning cuts drafting cost while keeping over 99% of acceptance length. Across seven benchmarks it averages **5.00x and 5.71x decoding speedups with `Qwen3-8B` and `Qwen3-32B` targets**, against 4.03x and 3.67x for `DFlash`, and reaches 7.48x on `GSM8K`.

papers.title: EviSeek: An Evidence-Centric Agentic Framework for Embodied Active Information Seeking
papers.abstract: Active embodied question answering requires agents to acquire evidence through viewpoint changes and physical interaction. The central challenge is to avoid undirected interaction: taking plausible actions without specifying what evidence they should reveal for answering the question. Action plans and accumulated histories alone can leave the informational purpose of an interaction implicit. We introduce EviSeek, a training-free framework that makes question-derived evidence demands explicit acquisition objectives, linking observation-conditioned actions and selectively retained evidence to the information the agent seeks. On 3,436 ESI-Bench questions, EviSeek improves accuracy over the Single-model agent by 7.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL-32B and 3.7 points with Gemini 3.1 Pro, while improving visual-support-weighted accuracy and reducing mean token usage. These findings support making the informational purpose of interaction explicit, with action selection and evidence retention organized around what the agent needs to learn to answer the question.
papers.summary: In active embodied question answering, an agent gathers evidence by changing viewpoint and physically interacting with its environment, but agents often act without specifying what each action is meant to reveal. `EviSeek` is a training-free framework that turns the question into explicit evidence demands and uses them to guide action choice and decide which evidence to keep. On 3,436 `ESI-Bench` questions it **improves accuracy over a single-model agent by 7.1 points with `Qwen3-VL-32B`** and 3.7 points with `Gemini 3.1 Pro`. It also improves visually supported accuracy and reduces average token usage.

papers.title: EvoGuard: Mitigating Degradation in Online Skill Evolution
papers.abstract: Skills let language agents reuse experience across tasks as natural-language documents. Recent work evolves skills from interaction, but existing methods have limitations when skills evolve online. Prior methods update a skill offline from a batch of trajectories collected over many tasks. Some then adopt the new skill without any check, which can degrade the skill over time. Others keep it only if it improves performance on a held-out validation set, which is too slow and costly to run after every update. We introduce EvoGuard, a pairwise skill selector that mitigates skill degradation at low latency and cost. We first run the agent iteratively to build pools of skills and score each skill on a private test set to obtain utility labels. We pair the skills and use rejection sampling to keep only pairs with a clear utility gap. The selector is trained on the logits of two label tokens to pick the better skill. At deployment it decides in a single forward pass, which is significantly faster than evaluation on the private test set. Compared with adopting every new skill, EvoGuard improves success by 11.0% on ALFWorld, 5.9% on ScienceWorld, and 2.7% on LiveCodeBench.
papers.summary: Language agents can store reusable skills as natural-language documents, but when skills evolve online, adopting every update can degrade them over time, and validating each update on a held-out set is too slow and costly. `EvoGuard` trains a pairwise selector on skill pools labeled by their utility on a private test set, using rejection sampling to keep only pairs with a clear utility gap. The selector reads the logits of two label tokens to pick the better skill in a single forward pass. Compared with adopting every new skill, it **improves success by 11.0% on `ALFWorld`**, 5.9% on `ScienceWorld`, and 2.7% on `LiveCodeBench`.

papers.title: SUMONE: A Simple and Efficient Summarizer for Plug-and-Play Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Long-horizon language-model agents accumulate increasingly large interaction histories, making context compaction essential for efficient execution. Existing learned compaction methods often rely on downstream task outcomes or solver behavior, coupling training to specific tasks or agents. We introduce SumOne, a standalone summarizer trained to preserve information in agent histories through masked reconstruction. Given a summary of the expired history, a frozen reconstructor recovers randomly masked portions of the original trajectory; reconstruction quality, combined with a length penalty, provides a task-agnostic reward for optimizing the summarizer with GRPO. This yields self-supervision directly from raw trajectories, without reference summaries or downstream task execution. At inference time, only the lightweight summarizer is retained, enabling plug-and-play context compression for otherwise unchanged agents. We conduct a systematic evaluation of SumOne in long-horizon search and software-engineering tasks. SumOne reduces estimated inference cost by approximately 78\% on DeepSearchQA and 75\% on SWE-bench Verified relative to operating with full context, with absolute decreases of 0.04. The same checkpoint also transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents accumulate large interaction histories, and existing learned compaction methods tie their training to specific tasks or agents. `SumOne` trains a standalone summarizer with `GRPO`, using a task-agnostic reward: a frozen reconstructor must recover randomly masked parts of the original trajectory from the summary, with a penalty for summary length. This needs no reference summaries and no downstream task runs, and at inference only the lightweight summarizer is kept as a plug-in context compressor. It **cuts estimated inference cost by about 78% on `DeepSearchQA` and 75% on `SWE-bench Verified`** compared with keeping the full context, with reported absolute decreases of 0.04, and the same checkpoint transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without further fine-tuning.

papers.title: AmbiHTMLBench: A Benchmark for HTML-based Visually Rich Document parsing
papers.abstract: Traditional document parsing systems use Markdown as their output representation, which is effective for linear text but does not fully preserve fine-grained spatial structure, table geometry, visual hierarchy, or rendering semantics. We show that HTML is advantageous for heterogeneous and layout-sensitive documents whose representations must remain editable, inspectable, and reusable, and introduce AmbiHTMLBench to systematically study this setting. In this benchmark, given a real-world document, a model must recover executable HTML that preserves its content, organization, and visual appearance. The benchmark contains 1,115 diverse pages with structured annotations and evaluates predictions in two different ways: The objective protocol aligns ground-truth and predicted rendered blocks and measures table fidelity, page-level text error, and a two-dimensional layout consistency; a complementary reference-anchored protocol measures perceived fidelity by aligning LLM judges with human preferences. Across ten primary multimodal systems, the best objective score is 0.8092, while the subjective winner is different, demonstrating that automatic decomposition and human-perceived fidelity capture complementary properties. We further fine-tune a small-parameter expert model and find that task-specific adaptation yields good performance on document-to-HTML reconstruction task. These results position AmbiHTMLBench as a diagnostic testbed for building smarter and more logical document parsing systems.
papers.summary: Document parsers usually output Markdown, which loses spatial structure, table geometry, and visual hierarchy. The authors argue that HTML preserves these better for layout-heavy documents and introduce `AmbiHTMLBench`, in which a model must reconstruct executable HTML from 1,115 real-world pages. Predictions are scored two ways: an objective protocol that aligns rendered blocks to measure table fidelity, text error, and two-dimensional layout consistency, and a reference-anchored protocol that uses LLM judges aligned with human preferences. Across ten multimodal systems, the best objective score is 0.8092, but **the objective and human-perceived winners differ**, and a small fine-tuned expert model performs well on the task.

papers.title: Within-Family EfficientNet Scaling under Fixed-Resolution Transfer Learning for Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography Retinal Disease Classification
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: CNNs perform well in retinal disease classification from spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT), but whether EfficientNet's natural-image scaling hierarchy transfers to medical-image transfer learning at fixed resolution remains unclear. This study evaluates EfficientNet-B0-B7 for four-class SD-OCT classification and accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Methods: Eight ImageNet-pretrained variants (4.05-64.10M instantiated backbone parameters) were evaluated at 224x224 on the Kermany dataset. Grayscale images were replicated to RGB and processed using model-embedded preprocessing and augmentation. Training comprised frozen-backbone head training followed by partial fine-tuning. Metrics covered classification, discrimination, efficiency, and visual analyses. Results: Test accuracy varied non-monotonically from 95.93% (B0) to 96.95% (B1); B7 achieved 96.73%. B1 had the highest accuracy and Drusen F1 (0.8780), while B7 had Drusen F1 of 0.8720 and the highest Drusen recall (0.9177). Drusen had the lowest F1 across all variants and contributed 82.2% of the summed squared deviation in class-specific F1; class ranking remained Normal > CNV > DME > Drusen. The OCT accuracy ranking differed from the reported ImageNet hierarchy, where B7 ranked first. The accuracy-to-parameter ratio fell from 19.82 to 1.48 percentage points per million total parameters. The final train-test gap had a weak, non-significant association with test accuracy (r = 0.26, p = 0.53). Conclusions: Larger EfficientNet variants did not consistently improve SD-OCT classification. B1 achieved the highest accuracy and Drusen F1, whereas B7 showed a secondary accuracy recovery at greater model size and CPU latency, indicating task and protocol dependent scaling effects. As cross-partition duplicates have not been independently audited, results are conditional on the supplied split.
papers.summary: This study tests whether `EfficientNet`'s scaling hierarchy from natural images carries over to classifying retinal disease in spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) scans at a fixed 224x224 resolution. Variants `B0` through `B7`, pretrained on `ImageNet`, were fine-tuned for four-class classification on the `Kermany` dataset. Accuracy varied non-monotonically, and **`B1` scored highest at 96.95%** against 96.73% for `B7`, so larger models did not reliably help. Drusen was the hardest class for every variant, and accuracy per parameter fell sharply with model size.

papers.title: Microdroplet Generator Surrogate Enhancement and Inverse Design Through an Uncertainty-Guided Framework
papers.abstract: Microfluidic droplet generation is critical for many applications, yet efficient device design in high-dimensional parameter spaces remains computationally prohibitive due to complex multiphase flow dynamics. This work presents a unified methodology that couples adaptive surrogate enhancement with simulation-driven inverse design. High-fidelity Volume-of-Fluid simulations provide ground-truth data, while neural network ensembles predict flow regimes and droplet diameters. Ensemble-based uncertainty quantification identifies epistemic uncertainty using consensus levels for regime classification and the coefficient of variation for diameter prediction, revealing that uncertainty concentrates near regime transition boundaries where physics is highly sensitive to parameter perturbations. A physics-informed enrichment strategy targets these critical zones and addresses class imbalances by deploying additional targeted simulations and retraining the surrogates forming the ensembles. A framework that integrates Particle Swarm Optimization for constrained inverse design, balancing accuracy with predictive confidence and physical consistency is therefore proposed. Validation on independent test datasets demonstrates that the enriched ensembles achieve higher accuracy, with the fraction of predictions within the 0-3% error range on droplet diameter nearly doubling, and high-error cases (above 10%) dropping substantially. The inverse design procedure reliably identifies physically realizable configurations meeting target droplet sizes. This approach significantly reduces computational costs while ensuring reliable predictions, offering a framework with potential applicability to the optimization of a broad range of microfluidic systems.
papers.summary: Designing microfluidic droplet generators requires searching high-dimensional parameter spaces, where simulating multiphase flow is expensive. Neural network ensembles trained on Volume-of-Fluid simulations predict flow regimes and droplet diameters, and disagreement within each ensemble shows that uncertainty concentrates near the boundaries between flow regimes. Targeted extra simulations in those zones retrain the surrogates, and `Particle Swarm Optimization` then performs constrained inverse design that weighs accuracy against predictive confidence. After enrichment, **the share of diameter predictions within 3% error nearly doubles**, and the inverse design reliably finds physically realizable configurations for target droplet sizes.

papers.title: ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) answers questions by retrieving over a knowledge graph built from a corpus. Yet retrieval strategies are designed around the structure their own construction pipeline produces, and whether they survive a change of construction is rarely tested. We study this cross-construction portability: whether one retrieval procedure, with no construction-specific schema, relation names, or retuning, stays effective when the graph is built differently. We introduce ArcRAG, which induces a query-local graph interface at inference time (the node labels, relation descriptors, and property keys reachable from the entities a question names), plans multi-hop traversals against it, and executes and repairs them as Cypher. We build each of the MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and TriviaQA corpora as a schema-guided graph (typed nodes, a closed relation set, source provenance) and as an open-information-extraction graph (untyped nodes, free-text relations), with the retriever's configuration fixed across them. We compare against a construction-agnostic Direct-Cypher agent, ablate each stage across retry and pass budgets on both graph families, and compare with results reported for prior GraphRAG systems, most of which design retrieval together with their own graph construction. Across the two constructions, we find that retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph: query-time interface induction keeps a construction-agnostic retriever effective when the construction changes, although construction still shapes absolute accuracy.
papers.summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) systems usually design retrieval around the knowledge graph their own pipeline builds, and rarely test whether retrieval still works when the graph is built differently. `ArcRAG` infers a query-local graph interface at inference time (the node labels, relation descriptors, and property keys reachable from the entities a question names), then plans multi-hop traversals and executes and repairs them as `Cypher` queries. With its configuration fixed, it is evaluated on `MuSiQue`, `HotpotQA`, and `TriviaQA`, each built both as a schema-guided graph and as an open information extraction graph. The results show that **retrieval need not be co-designed with graph construction**, although the construction still affects absolute accuracy.

papers.title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
papers.abstract: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth $K$ and interaction depth $T$ via $Pass@(K,T)$, we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings. Project Page: https://rethinking-agentic-rl.github.io/
papers.summary: Multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) looks strong on long-horizon tasks, but the authors ask where those gains actually come from and how much they depend on interaction limits. Using a `Pass@(K,T)` metric that varies both the number of samples K and the number of turns T, they find that **trajectory-level RL gains depend on generous turn budgets and shrink sharply when budgets tighten**. Agentic RL does not uniformly improve single-step decisions; its benefit lies mainly in recovering from errors and staying on track over long horizons. They briefly examine process supervision signals and propose `BudgetMix RL`, which varies interaction budgets during training and performs robustly across execution settings.
papers.highlight_summary:
Multi-turn agentic RL lifts LLM agents' success rates on long-horizon tasks, but those gains depend on having enough interaction turns. The authors evaluate along two axes, sampling breadth K and turn budget T, using `Pass@(K,T)`. They find RL mainly improves error recovery and long-horizon execution rather than individual decisions, and they propose `BudgetMix RL` to make the gains hold up under tight budgets.

- Across `DeepCoder-MT`, `BFCL`, `InterCode-SQL` and `FrozenLake`, `GRPO`-trained `Qwen3` agents beat their base models' `Pass@K` boundary as K grows, but **the advantage shrinks and can even reverse when the turn budget T is small**, even on tasks where plenty of headroom remains.
- When base and RL policies are compared from the same states, RL picks the better next action on **only 46.8% of `DeepCoder-MT` states and 42.8% of `FrozenLake` states**, yet after an injected error it wins **65.7–67.3%** of the time and finishes more often from those states (**51.3% vs. 38.6%** on `FrozenLake`, **38.5% vs. 22.9%** on `DeepCoder-MT`).
- A likelihood analysis on `Terminal-Bench` suggests RL learns to chain plausible steps into complete trajectories rather than produce new kinds of actions: RL actions stay locally plausible under the base policy, but successful RL trajectories reach a cumulative log-likelihood ratio of **~228 vs. 26** for successful base-model trajectories. During training, trajectory reward rises **+0.331** while per-step reward falls **0.097**.
- `BudgetMix RL` leaves the reward unchanged and instead samples each task's turn budget uniformly from 10%–100% of the maximum, stating the budget in the prompt. Across `GRPO`, `GiGPO` and `PPO` it gains an average of **+7.5, +5.3 and +4.0 points** over full-budget RL at 25%, 50% and 75% budgets, and roughly matches it at the full budget.
- Accurate process supervision (oracle Q-values, `GiGPO`) also reduces budget dependence on `FrozenLake`, but it brings no improvement on `BFCL`, where no exact step-level oracle exists. The authors therefore present their mitigation discussion as preliminary, with experiments limited to 4B and 8B `Qwen3` models.

papers.title: Model Merging Does Not Require Uniform LoRA Ranks
papers.abstract: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned experts into a single model without retraining. Standard practice trains every expert at the same LoRA rank, which couples the rank choice across experts even though each domain has its own best rank. We show this coupling is a property of the merge method, not of merging. We train 36 experts on three domains (mathematics, instruction following, multilingual) at four ranks and three model scales, then merge with six methods at uniform ranks and at each domain's own best rank. Giving experts different ranks costs averaging and utility-based selection nothing, and gains them up to 1.8 pp of multi-domain accuracy, while the conflict-resolution methods are inconsistent and can lose up to 4 pp. The split has a simple cause. Merging keeps only a fixed share of the pooled spectral components, and methods that choose them by size discard many that would have reduced loss. They also tend to discard the same expert: the instruction adapter has the smallest singular values, so it is dropped almost entirely and IFEval falls by 16 to 25 pp. Choosing components by their effect on loss instead keeps all three experts, and leaves accuracy nearly flat across an 8$\times$ rank range (0.7 pp, against 6.7 pp for TIES at 4B scale). Rank can therefore be chosen per expert whenever the merge operator does not select by magnitude.
papers.summary: When merging separately fine-tuned experts, the usual practice is to train every `LoRA` adapter at the same rank, even though each domain has its own best rank. Across 36 experts in math, instruction following, and multilingual tasks at three model scales, merged with six methods, giving each expert its own rank costs averaging and utility-based selection nothing and gains up to 1.8 percentage points, while conflict-resolution methods such as `TIES` are inconsistent and can lose up to 4 points. The cause is that magnitude-based component selection discards the instruction adapter, which has the smallest singular values, so **`IFEval` drops by 16 to 25 points**. Selecting components by their effect on loss keeps all experts and leaves accuracy nearly flat across an 8x range of ranks.

papers.title: FPTR: Feasibility-Preserving Transactional Refinement for Deadline-Constrained Joint Beam and Resource Allocation
papers.abstract: Short-interval wireless schedulers must return a complete, feasible beam-and-resource allocation before each execution deadline, and a late or invalid output gives no utility in the current control cycle. Searching longer can increase transmitted traffic, but it may also miss the deadline or leave only an infeasible intermediate solution. We propose Feasibility-Preserving Transactional Refinement (FPTR), which always keeps a validated feasible allocation, the incumbent. Each refinement stage builds a separate candidate and leaves the incumbent unchanged. A candidate replaces the incumbent only if it is complete, passes the feasibility validator before its stage cutoff, and strictly improves the objective; otherwise it is discarded. Four refinement stages use this rule: buffer-aware resource selection, compatibility-group (CG) user sharing, beam-mask rebuilding from remaining demand, and joint reassignment of two resources. On 150 fixed synthetic instances, the full pipeline (Full) raises traffic by 3.83% on average over a lightweight beam-first reference and by 1.79% over its Base constructor. In a separate suite with matched inputs, Full exceeds six independent search baselines (ALNS, tabu search, GA, simulated annealing, iterated local search, and GRASP) by 6.68-8.35%, where outputs later than 100 ms receive zero utility. All 750 Full runs in the internal suite returned feasible allocations, and none exceeded 100 ms. Separating mandatory output construction from optional refinement lets spare computation time improve the allocation without endangering the incumbent. The open-source implementation supports independent reproduction.
papers.summary: Short-interval wireless schedulers must produce a complete, feasible beam-and-resource allocation before a hard deadline, and a late or invalid result is worth nothing. `Feasibility-Preserving Transactional Refinement` (`FPTR`) always holds a validated feasible allocation and runs four refinement stages that build separate candidates, replacing the current allocation only when a candidate is complete, validated before its stage cutoff, and strictly better. On synthetic instances with a 100 ms deadline, the full pipeline beats six search baselines, including `ALNS`, tabu search, and genetic algorithms, by **6.68-8.35% in transmitted traffic**, and all 750 runs returned feasible allocations on time.

papers.title: LibriSpeech-Real-QA: A Benchmark for Streaming Question Answering
papers.abstract: Most speech large language models (SLMs) still process speech in an offline manner. They only start responding after they receive the complete speech segment. However, many real-world applications require streaming speech interaction, for which the audio continuously flows in and the machine is required to answer questions based on the so far received audio chunks. For example, a user may ask the system to continuously count how many times a person's name has been mentioned while they are speaking. We observe a lack of benchmarks and evaluation protocols for real-time speech interaction. Motivated by this, we propose LibriSpeech-Real-QA, a dataset and a benchmark for real-time speech interaction. We construct different types of real-time question-answer pairs from LibriSpeech to evaluate whether speech LLMs can identify target words in streaming audio. We evaluate several popular real-time commercial models and find that they still tend to respond only after the speech turn has finished. We demonstrate that we can enable a pretrained SLM to perform this task, where we explore several modeling designs and establish a solid baseline for future research.
papers.summary: Most speech large language models (SLMs) wait for the whole utterance before responding, but many applications need answers while audio is still arriving, such as counting how often a name has been mentioned so far. `LibriSpeech-Real-QA` is a dataset and benchmark, built from `LibriSpeech`, of real-time question-answer pairs that test whether models can spot target words in streaming audio. **Popular real-time commercial models still tend to answer only after the speaker finishes**, and the authors show that a pretrained SLM can be adapted to the task, comparing several designs to set a baseline.

papers.title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
papers.abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and dilute the agent's attention to task-relevant information. Existing token pruning and summarization methods remain constrained by discrete text representations, limiting the achievable compression ratios.
  In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that agents must consume tool observations as explicit text tokens. To this end, we propose Coca-Cola, a continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents. Coca-Cola compresses tool observations into latent tokens and embeds them into the input embedding space of the agent. We further introduce Action-Preserving Training, which aligns the agent's next-action distributions under full and compressed observations. This trains the compression model to learn action-sufficient latent tokens that retain decision-critical information. Experiments with web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families show that Coca-Cola reduces the agent's token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97%, while consistently improving task performance. These results suggest that Coca-Cola offers a promising approach for context compression in agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/Coca-cola.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents usually append raw tool outputs to their context, which inflates token usage and spreads the model's attention across noisy observations. `Coca-Cola` instead compresses tool observations into continuous latent tokens injected directly into the agent's input embedding space, and is trained with `Action-Preserving Training` so that the agent's next-action distribution under compressed observations matches its distribution under the full text. On web-search agents across four QA benchmarks and two model families, it **reduces token consumption by 70-89% and end-to-end runtime by 24-56%** while also improving task performance.

papers.title: CRESiST: Self-Enhancing Explorative Policy Learning for Simultaneous Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Simultaneous Speech Translation (SimulST) requires balancing translation quality and latency. While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in offline translation, current LLM-based SimulST systems predominantly rely on prefix-incremental generation. This paradigm suffers from redundant Key-Value cache recomputation and necessitates external Voice Activity Detection to process unbounded streams. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose an end-to-end interleaved read-write framework built upon an omni-modal LLM. By interleaving speech chunks and text tokens, our architecture achieves full KV cache reuse, natively supporting segmentation-free, infinite-length inference. Furthermore, to learn optimal streaming policies without rigid offline alignments, we introduce a novel Actor-Critic self-enhancement pipeline. An RNN-T Actor dynamically samples read-write trajectories, while an LLM-based Critic evaluates these paths via intrinsic semantic and latency rewards, distilling the optimal policy back to the Actor. Extensive experiments on sentence-level (FLEURS, CoVoST2) and document-level (MuST-C, ACL 60/60) benchmarks demonstrate that our model establishes new state-of-the-art quality-latency Pareto frontiers, substantially outperforming existing cascaded and static-alignment baselines.
papers.summary: LLM-based Simultaneous Speech Translation (SimulST) systems typically regenerate output as the input prefix grows, which wastes Key-Value (KV) cache computation and requires external Voice Activity Detection to segment unbounded audio streams. `CRESiST` builds an end-to-end interleaved read-write framework on an omni-modal LLM, fully reusing the KV cache and supporting segmentation-free inference on streams of any length. An RNN-T Actor samples read-write trajectories, an LLM-based Critic scores them with semantic and latency rewards, and the best policy is distilled back into the Actor. The system reports **new state-of-the-art quality-latency trade-offs** on `FLEURS`, `CoVoST2`, `MuST-C`, and `ACL 60/60`.

papers.title: NaijaFacts: A Framework for Disentangling Language from Knowledge in Facts about Nigeria
papers.abstract: Multilingual benchmarks for African languages mostly translate generic questions into local languages, measuring linguistic competence but not whether models know facts about Africa. We introduce \naija, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, authored by native speakers and grounded in authoritative official statistics, with every question available in English, Nigerian Pidgin, \yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa. Answering similar questions for the UK and US yields a country by language matrix that disentangles a language effect (the model knows the fact but degrades in a low-resource language) from a knowledge effect (the fact is absent in every language). Across eight frontier and Nigeria-adapted models, the knowledge effect dominates: English-query accuracy is 49--50\% for the US/UK but 20\% for Nigeria. The language effect is smaller and tracks web representation, degrading from English to \yoruba{} (9 points on Nigeria, up to 24 on US/UK questions). We find scale does not help: the strongest models reach 66--79\% on the UK and the US but none exceed 31\% on Nigerian statistics. Extending to all 54 African countries with our best performing frontier model shows the same profile continent-wide, 96\% on culture and 98\% on politics against 26\% on statistics, so the gap is not specific to Nigeria.
papers.summary: Multilingual benchmarks for African languages usually translate generic questions, which tests language ability rather than whether models know facts about Africa. `NaijaFacts` poses factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, grounded in official statistics, in English, Nigerian Pidgin, Yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa, and pairs them with similar UK and US questions to separate a language effect from a knowledge effect. Across eight models, the knowledge gap dominates: **English-query accuracy is about 50% for US/UK questions but 20% for Nigeria**, and no model exceeds 31% on Nigerian statistics. Extending the evaluation to all 54 African countries shows the same pattern, with high accuracy on culture and politics but only 26% on statistics.

papers.title: ElecLoad: Adaptive Electricity Load Forecasting Guided by Multiple Events
papers.abstract: Accurate electricity load forecasting provides critical decision support for energy procurement, generation scheduling, and supply-demand balancing, contributing to the economic efficiency and operational reliability of power systems. However, future electricity demand can be affected by the complex interplay of multiple events described in Web notices, weather alerts, and event schedules. Their effects vary over time and can reinforce or offset one another, making electricity load difficult to forecast accurately. While existing methods can incorporate context as additional input, how to use the effects of multiple events and their interactions to guide the load forecasting process itself remains to be explored. To address this gap, we propose ElecLoad, a context-aware agent for multi-event electricity load forecasting that adaptively organizes the forecasting process. Specifically, we train ElecLoad to combine historical load with context to analyze each event's relevance to the target load, the timing of its effects, and potential interactions among events. Guided by this analysis, ElecLoad adaptively chooses to forecast the entire forecast horizon directly or to partition it into segments according to changes in event effects. When the horizon is partitioned, sub-agents independently generate initial forecasts for each segment. The main agent then reviews these forecasts, and the sub-agents perform selective refinement guided by its feedback. Experiments on multiple electricity load datasets show that ElecLoad achieves state-of-the-art performance in most evaluation scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/zhjai/ElecLoad.
papers.summary: Electricity demand is shaped by multiple interacting events, such as public notices, weather alerts, and scheduled events, whose effects change over time and can reinforce or cancel each other. `ElecLoad` is a context-aware agent trained to analyze each event's relevance, the timing of its effect, and how events interact, then decide whether to forecast the whole horizon at once or split it into segments. When it splits the horizon, sub-agents forecast each segment and refine their forecasts based on feedback from a main agent. The method achieves **state-of-the-art performance in most evaluation scenarios** across several load datasets.

papers.title: Dialect Matters: A Dialect-Aware Baseline for Igala-English Machine Translation
papers.abstract: The massive permeability of intelligent systems in every sphere of human activities have greatly enhanced clarity, ease of work, and increased general global understanding which has significantly awaken the use of intelligent systems by all users. Intelligent systems greatly rely on precise dataset/corpus for the correctness of their output. Despite efforts by researchers to address Low-resource language in the Natural Language Processing (NLP), Igala still has zero parallel corpora despite efforts by researchers. We present a dialect-aware baseline for Igala-English machine translation, among first open systems and first with dialectal variation analysis. Our dataset of 1137 sentences (899 training) is first with dialect tags: Idah 459 (40.4%), Ankpa 297 (26.1%), Ibaji 160 (14.1%), Other 187 (16.4%), Ogugu 32 (2.8%). Same English yields 20-60 Igala forms. Mixed-dialect training achieves balanced BLEU 11.66 versus Idah-only model which drops 4.7 BLEU on Ibaji (13.2 on Idah, 8.5 on Ibaji), proving dialect fairness requires mixing. Fine-tuned from Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-mul (78M), epoch ablation shows convergence at 8 epochs and overfitting at 15. BLEU 11.66, chrF 46.69. Analysis shows 899 sentences on log-linear trend consistent with African low-resource literature. This work provides first dialectal impact analysis for Igala and establishes baseline for future work.
papers.summary: Igala, a Nigerian language, has had essentially no parallel corpora for machine translation. The authors release 1,137 Igala-English sentence pairs tagged by dialect and fine-tune `Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-mul` (78M parameters) on them. **Training on mixed dialects gives a balanced BLEU of 11.66**, while a model trained only on the Idah dialect drops 4.7 BLEU on Ibaji, which shows that dialect coverage matters for fair translation quality.

papers.title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL
papers.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) works well when correctness can be checked, but emotional expression in generated video has no single correct target, and fixed rewards invite reward hacking. `EmoReward` plans grounding cues from the emotional prompt, scores videos with several signal primitives, and fuses them through instance-level gates. A `RewardMemory` component then estimates each primitive's reliability from the finished training run and fixes bounded weight multipliers for the next run, without updating the reward models themselves. Experiments on `HunyuanVideo 1.5` show **gains across multiple RL algorithms**, with transfer results on `SD 3.5` and `FLUX`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Fixed reward fusions handle emotional video generation poorly: facial, motion and color cues are each reliable only in some scenes, and a fixed mix makes reward hacking easier. `EmoReward` calibrates which reward providers to trust at two levels: inside each video through rule-based gates, and across training runs through a frozen reliability table learned from the previous run's reward traces. No reward model is retrained.

- A planner turns each prompt into an `EmoScript` (valence and arousal targets, facial action-unit intensities, body cues, an expression window), and seven frozen providers score the video, including a VLM judge, facial action units, `CLIP-AUTT`, `R1-Omni` and motion naturalness. `Reflective Reward Gating` then masks or down-weights providers using phase, face-confidence, conflict and subtlety gates, and renormalizes the weights over the providers that remain active.
- `RewardMemory` correlates each provider's scores with the reference outcome inside each emotional regime of a completed run, then turns these correlations into bounded multipliers (temperature 0.5, log-cap 1) that stay fixed for the next run; memory can boost a provider but cannot revive evidence the gates have marked invalid.
- On `HunyuanVideo 1.5`, `VideoAlign` Overall improves over every optimizer baseline: **+0.32** for `DanceGRPO` (gating only), **+0.23** for `FlowGRPO`, and **+0.56** for `SAGE-GRPO` (−0.83 to −0.26). `PickScore` and `CLIPScore` changes are small and mixed.
- In a seven-policy controlled comparison under `SAGE-GRPO`, the full system has the best reliability selectivity (**0.428**) and composite scores (**0.922** core, **0.884** emo). In an 18-person study (540 judgments per cell), it raises Good ratings for emotion fidelity to **60.0%** versus 53.0% for `SAGE-GRPO` and cuts Bad ratings to **15.4%** versus 31.5%.
- Caveats: `VideoAlign` serves as both the training reward and the memory's outcome signal, so the gains partly measure agreement with the objective rather than independent emotional fidelity; only one reference-to-calibrated run transition is tested, there is no matched global-memory control, and transfer to `SD 3.5` and `FLUX` gives mixed results that depend on the objective.

papers.title: IDSISA: Influence-Distilled Sharded Training for Efficient Machine Unlearning
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training examples to comply with privacy regulations. Full retraining gives strong guarantees but is computationally prohibitive at scale; approximate methods are efficient but lack formal guarantees. SISA (Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, and Aggregated training) achieves certified deletion through data sharding and independent retraining, but random partitioning scatters forget requests across most shards, and isolated retraining degrades utility. We introduce IDSISA (Influence-Distilled SISA), which uses influence functions to concentrate forget-prone samples into few shards and distillation from unaffected shards to recover utility lost to isolation. The deletion guarantee inherited from SISA's retraining step remains exact and requires no probabilistic qualification; the distillation-based utility recovery is a separately quantified, empirically bounded approximation ($\epsilon_{\text{cert}} \leq 0.015$ in expectation). We further formalize certification under sequences of repeated deletion requests, where cross-shard distillation can create dependencies between shards; we prove that a closure-based cascading retraining procedure restores the deletion guarantee to the full aggregated model under any deletion sequence. Experiments on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10, ResNet-18/CIFAR-100, BiLSTM/IMDB, TCN/IMDB, and a fully connected network on Fashion-MNIST show $14-91\%$ better selective forgetting, up to $50\%$ better utility retention in relative terms (with consistent percentage-point gains on the other architectures, where a relative baseline is undefined), and unlearning-time changes ranging from $-6.7\%$ to $+6.4\%$ depending on architecture, relative to SISA.
papers.summary: `SISA` (Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, and Aggregated training) enables exact machine unlearning by retraining only affected shards, but random partitioning spreads deletion requests across most shards and isolated training hurts accuracy. `IDSISA` uses influence functions to concentrate samples likely to be deleted into a few shards and distills knowledge from unaffected shards to recover utility. The deletion guarantee remains exact, and a cascading retraining procedure is proven to preserve it under repeated deletion requests. Across image and text tasks, it reports **14-91% better selective forgetting** than `SISA`, with unlearning time roughly unchanged.

papers.title: From Admission to Retention: Predicting Durable Offspring in Quality-Diversity Search
papers.abstract: Automated failure discovery can be framed as a diversity problem: the objective is to expose distinct ways a system fails rather than a single critical adversarial case. Yet uniform parent sampling provides no way to allocate search effort toward individuals likely to produce durable archive contributions. We study this credit assignment problem in an unstructured Quality-Diversity (QD) archive, testing whether signals available before an individual has reproduced distinguish offspring that merely enter the archive from those still retained generations later. Across a planar-arm benchmark and two robotic-locomotion tasks, the same signals are often associated with entry and persistence in opposite directions. In particular, lineage depth is the clearest such signal, and its persistence discrimination grows with population capacity, which is associated with lower turnover. Biasing parent selection toward the signals with the strongest measured association to survival nevertheless does not improve search: moderate bias matches uniform sampling, and strong bias reduces QD-score.
papers.summary: Quality-Diversity (QD) search can be used to find many distinct ways a system fails, but uniform parent sampling cannot steer effort toward individuals whose offspring will last in the archive. The authors test whether signals available before reproduction predict offspring that both enter the archive and are still retained generations later, using a planar-arm benchmark and two robot locomotion tasks. The same signals often predict entry and persistence in opposite directions, with lineage depth the clearest persistence signal. However, **biasing parent selection toward these signals does not improve search**: moderate bias matches uniform sampling and strong bias lowers the QD-score.

papers.title: Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment
papers.abstract: Agent trajectories often contain both successful decisions and failed attempts, yet optimization with sparse trajectory-level rewards struggles to identify which critical decisions should be reinforced or suppressed. We observe that meaningful distinctions among on-policy trajectories can be distilled into natural-language process rubrics and used as process supervision signals. Based on this insight, we propose Online Rubric Self-Distillation (ORSD), which leverages self-derived process rubrics for dense token-level supervision, thereby augmenting outcome-centric reinforcement learning. Specifically, the current policy independently generates multiple rubric bundles at each step according to the same group of trajectories, extracting candidate process rubrics from cross-trajectory behavioral differences. A frozen verifier then evaluates all rubric items against each trajectory in the group, and selects one candidate bundle based on bundle-level alignment between rubric satisfaction and task success. ORSD treats the selected rubric bundle as privileged information during training, then compares the log-likelihoods of the original tokens with and without the rubric. The resulting likelihood gap provides token-specific process credit, which is added to the original trajectory-level GRPO advantage through additive advantage shaping. ORSD thus bridges trajectory-level outcome supervision and fine-grained process supervision, enabling token-level credit assignment using process signals. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that ORSD accelerates policy improvement and boosts final task performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B under the same environment-interaction budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/AnnaXChun/ORSD.
papers.summary: Agent trajectories mix good decisions with failed attempts, and sparse trajectory-level rewards cannot tell which steps deserve credit. `Online Rubric Self-Distillation` (`ORSD`) has the policy generate natural-language process rubrics from differences across a group of trajectories, uses a frozen verifier to choose the rubric bundle that best matches task success, and treats that bundle as privileged information. The change in each token's log-likelihood with and without the rubric becomes a token-level credit signal added to the `GRPO` advantage. On `ALFWorld` and `WebShop` with `Qwen3-1.7B` and `Qwen3-4B`, ORSD **speeds up policy improvement and raises final performance** under the same interaction budget.

papers.title: When Do Summaries Become Instructions? Unsupported Policy in LLM Agents' Self-Written Handoff Summaries
papers.abstract: Long-running LLM agents compact their context, replacing most history with a summary. We ask whether handoff summaries state permissions or requirements the record does not support, whether such sentences change what the next instance (the successor) does, and where they come from. Synthetic tool-use tasks carry a ground-truth permission ledger; same-snapshot replay reruns the successor with those whole sentences replaced by neutral filler. Two AI readers, reading only rule-flagged held-out summaries, confirmed unsupported restrictions in 1.2% and 2.4% of all readable summaries from two open-weight models, and unsupported authorizations in 0.1% and 1.3%. For restrictions, a pre-specified replay test was not significant (p = 0.58); a follow-up, planned after it, found a fragile effect (p = 0.027). Neutralizing false approvals cut unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 held-out runs (post hoc; later set: 17 to 11 of 48). Most development restrictions followed the agent's earlier reasoning that an action needs approval (post hoc). In pre-specified tests, replacing the system prompt's "Some actions need approval." with one saying where requirements come from cut unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8% of development summaries and, on held-out templates, from 1.8% to 0.3% (both p < 10^-9), while requests for approvals the ledger requires barely changed. Code and data: https://github.com/Chuw1/handoff-audit
papers.summary: Long-running LLM agents compact their context into handoff summaries, and the authors check whether those summaries invent permissions or restrictions that the record does not support, and whether this changes what the next agent instance does. Using synthetic tool-use tasks with a ground-truth permission ledger and replays that swap suspect sentences for neutral filler, they find unsupported restrictions in 1.2-2.4% of summaries and unsupported authorizations in 0.1-1.3%. Neutralizing false approvals reduced unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 runs, although that analysis was post hoc. In pre-registered tests, **rewording the system prompt's "Some actions need approval" to explain where requirements come from cut unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8%**, without suppressing legitimate approval requests.

papers.title: Addition by Subtraction: Toward Mitigating Fragile Safety Alignment in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) undergo safety alignment to prevent harmful generations, yet they remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Recent work reveals a deeper structural weakness: safety alignment can be highly sparse, such that pruning a small number of safety-critical neurons or ablating a single refusal direction can substantially undermine aligned behavior. In this work, we take the first steps toward strengthening safety alignment such that it is less dependent on sparse model components. We propose Addition by Subtraction, which gradually removes identified safety-critical neurons during finetuning and uses preference optimization to re-establish safety-aligned behavior through other parts of the model. Our results show that the resulting models are substantially more robust to pruning-based attacks. Remarkably, these benefits generalize beyond the white-box attacks motivating our design: Addition by Subtraction improves robustness against other sparsity-based interventions, including refusal-direction ablation, as well as a broad range of black-box jailbreak attacks. The finetuned models also exhibit improved truthfulness while largely preserving general capabilities. Comprehensive experiments across four models from three vendors demonstrate consistent improvements in safety robustness, reducing attack success rates by up to 90% for some attacks.
papers.summary: LLM safety alignment can be sparse: pruning a few safety-critical neurons or removing a single refusal direction can undo it. `Addition by Subtraction` gradually removes the identified safety-critical neurons during fine-tuning while preference optimization rebuilds safe behavior in other parts of the model. The resulting models resist pruning attacks and also hold up better against refusal-direction ablation and many black-box jailbreaks, **reducing attack success rates by up to 90%** across four models from three vendors, while improving truthfulness and largely preserving general capabilities.

papers.title: RAGAM-AI: A Hybrid Reinforcement Learning based Agentic approach powered by Generative AI for Edge Resource Management
papers.abstract: Resource management for distributed edge networks hosting different services has been handled efficiently using Reinforcement learning (RL). Reward generalization in complex workflows is still an open issue within the RL realm. Therefore, this work proposes RAGAM-AI, a hybrid framework that combines the capabilities of RL algorithms and Generative-AI (Gen-AI) for powering an Agentic AI workflow that optimizes resource allocation at the Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) units. This framework further resolves the reward generalization issue by utilizing Large Language Model (LLM) for feedback. A Multi- Agent Soft-Actor Critic (MASAC) using Math{\Sigma}tral as a reward oracle is implemented for managing resource allocations at the MEC. RAGAM-AI interprets system state information and evaluates multi-objective trade-offs guiding the resource orchestration loop over distributed edge server agents. The complexity of the framework is further brought down by incorporating surrogate reward model. The overall performance is evaluated against the single agent SAC, REINFORCE and random policies for benchmarking. On using RAGAM-AI, lower allocation deviations for CPU, memory and bandwidth resources are reported while minimizing the latency and data rate costs. A scalable AI as a feedback (AIAF) solution optimizing network resources with significant performance improvement is thus presented.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used to allocate resources at Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) servers, but rewards that generalize across complex workflows remain difficult to design. `RAGAM-AI` combines a Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic (`MASAC`) with an LLM, `MathΣtral`, that acts as a reward oracle evaluating multi-objective trade-offs, plus a surrogate reward model to reduce cost. Compared with single-agent `SAC`, `REINFORCE`, and random policies, it reports **lower CPU, memory, and bandwidth allocation deviations** together with lower latency and data-rate costs.

papers.title: One Scale, Four Texts: Gaps, Overlaps and Silent Repairs in Published Grading Schemes
papers.abstract: Category systems often reach their users as text, and readers apply them with tacit repairs. We ask what such a text determines once the repairs are removed, using diabetic retinopathy grading, where one international scale circulates in several documents. We transcribe four texts (the English screening definitions of 2025, the international scale as tabulated in 2017 and as published in 2003, and an Italian guideline of 2015) into one rule language over 24 finding variables, and make every point a text leaves open a named precisification. Exhaustive enumeration of 1,425,807,360 finding profiles, re-derived by an SMT solver and spot-checked by an OWL reasoner, shows that every text that assigns actions leaves some eyes without a category under every reading; that the 2017 tabulation has a proliferative class that is empty when read literally and a macular gap that the 2003 text lacks, so that no function maps the 2003 grades onto the 2017 grades; and that on image findings alone the English and Italian texts order some pairs of eyes in opposite ways. On 927 annotated photographs from three public datasets, with retinal thickening assumed absent, the English text and the 2017 tabulation disagree on referral for 26.8% of the eyes of one dataset (DDR) on which both decide, and in a pre-registered experiment classifiers trained on each text's labels side with their own text. Thickening cannot be seen on a colour photograph; left free, every disagreement involving England becomes undecidable, so it rests on what the camera cannot show. In a second pre-registered study, language models that answered without deliberating repaired most gap and overlap items even when told to read literally, while Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 reported the defects far more often; within two models, deliberation reduced silent repair without removing it.
papers.summary: Readers of written classification schemes quietly fill gaps and resolve contradictions. The authors measure what four published diabetic retinopathy grading texts actually determine by encoding them in a single rule language and exhaustively enumerating about 1.4 billion finding profiles, cross-checked with an SMT solver and an OWL reasoner. Every text that assigns actions leaves some eyes without a category, and the 2003 and 2017 versions of the international scale cannot be mapped onto each other. On real photographs, **the English screening text and the 2017 tabulation disagree on referral for 26.8% of decided eyes in one dataset**, and classifiers trained on each text's labels side with their own text. In a pre-registered study, language models answering without deliberation silently repaired most defects even when told to read literally, while `Claude Sonnet 5.5` and `Claude Opus 5.5` reported the defects far more often.

papers.title: Signed, Sealed, Leaked: Trust Beyond Signature for MCP Toolchains
papers.abstract: AI agents rely on third-party tools, such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, whose publishers can be authenticated and whose execution can be restricted by runtime security policies. Yet authenticity does not guarantee benign behaviour: a legitimately signed tool may perform its advertised function while concealing malicious code that leaks confidential information. We demonstrate this trust failure with a signed MCP tool that embeds sensitive data in requests to a policy-allowed destination. Meta's MCPGuard-Dynamic, a state-of-the-art runtime defence, blocks a direct exfiltration attempt in the same run, yet fails to prevent this attack in every trial. We introduce germline execution, which limits information disclosure without inspecting or trusting tool implementations. Each tool invocation runs in ephemeral copies forked from a data-free germline process, each receiving only information authorised for its destination. Even if malicious code executes, what it can disclose is bounded by the data available to its copy. Under explicit assumptions on copy confinement and a data-free germline, we prove sink noninterference for every signed release and, for releases deterministic within our replay model, show that a verified witness establishes a flow violation. Across 153 attack runs, no unauthorised disclosure was detected under germline execution, compared with 5.9-74.5% of runs under baseline defences and an ablation. Invocations served by a single copy completed in 10-49 ms, 2-28x faster than restarting the tool for every invocation, the conventional way to clear state. These results show that data-isolated execution protects agent toolchains against malicious code concealed within authenticated software.
authors: Jing Jie Tan (National University of Singapore)
papers.summary: Signing Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools proves who published them but not that they are benign. The authors build a signed MCP tool that leaks confidential data inside requests to an allowed destination, and Meta's `MCPGuard-Dynamic` fails to stop it in every trial. Their proposed `germline execution` runs each tool invocation in a short-lived copy forked from a data-free process and gives each copy only the data authorized for its destination, so concealed malicious code can disclose no more than that. Under stated assumptions they prove a noninterference property, and across 153 attack runs **no unauthorized disclosure occurred, versus 5.9-74.5% of runs under baseline defenses**, with invocations taking 10-49 ms.

papers.title: Time-Division Multiplexing: The Operational Rhythm and Temporal Organization Layer of Digital Life
papers.abstract: Continual agents must handle urgent interaction while retaining alternatives, replaying errors, and committing safe long-term changes. A previous digital-life framework distinguishes online (busy) and offline (idle) channels, but leaves open whether these are separate programs or phases of a common process and how their operations should be ordered. Motivated by recent observations of rapidly alternating perceptual representations in primate cortex, we develop a temporal organization layer with phase-tagged micro-epochs, an observable duty cycle, independent content and resource controls, and three nested clocks separating candidate exploration from durable commitment. We give a projected duty-cycle update, state its deterministic descent guarantee and the additional noise term required for a stochastic guarantee, and specify coupled busy/idle execution contracts. Five synthetic experiments (64 seeds each) examine descent and noise, objective misalignment, gain asymmetry, resource coupling, and dropped replay logs. In the gain/noise model the best tested gain ratio is 1.55; decoupled scheduling yields 26.6% versus 11.1% success on a constructed urgent/high-load subset. A frozen-backbone Qwen3-8B prototype further checks orchestration, but its proxy outcomes are not task-benchmark evidence. The results establish a testable scheduling design and identify its conditions of validity, not machine consciousness or general-purpose agent superiority.
papers.summary: Continual agents must handle urgent interaction while still exploring alternatives, replaying errors, and committing safe long-term changes. Building on an earlier "digital life" framework with busy and idle channels, and drawing on observations from primate cortex, the authors propose a temporal organization layer with phase-tagged micro-epochs, an adjustable duty cycle, and three nested clocks that separate exploration from durable commitment. They state a descent guarantee for the duty-cycle update and run five synthetic experiments, in which **decoupled scheduling reaches 26.6% versus 11.1% success** on a constructed urgent, high-load subset. A frozen `Qwen3-8B` prototype checks the orchestration, though the authors note that these results are not task-benchmark evidence.

papers.title: From Reconstruction to Imputation: Test-Time Optimization for Missing Time-Series Channels
papers.abstract: Complete sensor-channel failures create a difficult form of time-series missingness: local interpolation is unavailable, and deploying a separately trained imputer for every failure pattern may be impractical. We ask whether a sequence reconstructor trained without artificial mask augmentation and then frozen can be converted into an imputer at inference time. Our method treats the missing entries of each test window as optimization variables, clamps all observations, and backpropagates through the frozen model to minimize reconstruction error only on observed coordinates. The resulting observed-self-consistency objective requires neither artificial mask augmentation nor full-channel dropout during reconstructor training. We characterize when this refinement is informative through the cross-Jacobian from missing inputs to observed residuals, and use an optional temporal-smoothness prior when that coupling is weak. Across five real-world datasets with exactly one channel synthetically masked per test window and four reconstruction architectures, no-prior test-time refinement reduces MAE relative to one-pass reconstruction in 19 of 20 dataset-backbone combinations. Compared with mask-aware imputers trained under either standard structured masks or matched full-channel dropout, the best refined reconstructor achieves the lowest MAE on two datasets and trails the strongest baseline on three. These gains require substantially more inference time and are sensitive to cross-channel coupling. Our results establish test-time self-consistency as a conditional inference-time adapter for frozen reconstruction models that complements mask-aware imputation without retraining the reconstructor.
papers.summary: When an entire sensor channel fails, interpolation is impossible, and training a separate imputer for every failure pattern is impractical. The proposed method turns a frozen sequence reconstructor into an imputer at test time by treating the missing values as optimization variables, holding observed values fixed, and backpropagating to minimize reconstruction error on the observed coordinates. The approach works best when missing and observed channels are strongly coupled, with an optional smoothness prior when they are not. Across five datasets and four architectures, **test-time refinement lowers MAE versus one-pass reconstruction in 19 of 20 combinations** and is competitive with mask-aware imputers, at the cost of much more inference time.

papers.title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI
papers.abstract: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. The project website is available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos-simulation.
papers.summary: NVIDIA adapts its `Cosmos` world foundation models into a shared framework for real-time interactive world simulation, where visual observations stream back in response to actions and scene controls. The framework can either predict the visual consequences of actions directly or render observations from physical state kept by an external simulator. Demonstrations cover camera navigation, robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation, and **code and model checkpoints are publicly released** as a base for building virtual environments to train and evaluate embodied agents.
papers.highlight_summary:
Physical AI agents need virtual environments they can act in and get visual feedback from in real time. The framework adapts `Cosmos` world foundation models into streaming, interactive world simulators that produce new visual observations in response to actions and scene controls.

- The framework supports two modes: it either **predicts the visual consequences of actions directly**, or **renders observations from physical state held by an external simulator**, so the generative model can serve as a visual layer on top of a conventional physics engine.
- It is demonstrated on **camera navigation and robot manipulation**, **controllable video transfer**, and **multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation**, all built on one shared foundation.
- Users and embodied agents can both interact with the environment as it evolves, which positions the framework as infrastructure for **training and evaluating Physical AI policies** rather than only for offline video generation.
- **Code and model checkpoints are publicly released** through NVIDIA's `Cosmos` GitHub repository and a Hugging Face collection.
- The abstract gives no quantitative results such as latency, frame rate, visual fidelity, or physical-consistency metrics, so how well the system performs in real time and how accurately it simulates physics cannot be judged from this material.

papers.title: From Certified Pairs to a Certified Hub: Reasoner-Checked Crosswalks for the Information Exchange Standard
papers.abstract: A national digital twin was conceived as an ecosystem of twins connected through mappings to a common foundation, but the roadmap that promises to confirm those mappings are valid never says what valid means. We give the test a precise form, coherence and conservativity of the merged ontology, borrowed from logic-based alignment repair, and apply it to the Information Exchange Standard (IES), first pair by pair and then to whole hubs. Crosswalks from IES into thirteen ontologies across seven sector groups, anchored on the building ontologies BOT, Brick, and SAREF4BLDG, pass through separate stages of matching, human review, certification of each SKOS correspondence against the two class hierarchies, and reasoning with HermiT. Pair by pair, the stages catch different failures: certification alone removed all 526 conservativity violations of the raw crosswalks, review alone left 73, and together they made eleven of twelve overlapping pairs coherent and conservative. Pairwise certification does not compose. Merging the three certified building crosswalks into one hub made five Brick classes unsatisfiable, through a homonym between the IES and Brick notions of a floor that only BOT's disjointness axioms expose; rejecting that one row gave a coherent and conservative hub that entails 290 cross-ontology links nobody wrote down. The core hub is inconsistent before any crosswalk is added, because two published standards, the Open Energy Ontology and BFO 2020, contradict each other; with either one left out it is coherent and conservative. A hub, not a pair, is the unit an ecosystem of twins has to certify.
papers.summary: National digital-twin roadmaps promise validated mappings between ontologies but never define what 'valid' means. The authors define it as coherence and conservativity of the merged ontology, then test crosswalks from the `Information Exchange Standard` (`IES`) into thirteen ontologies using matching, human review, per-correspondence certification, and reasoning with `HermiT`. Certification removed all 526 conservativity violations in the raw crosswalks, but **pairwise certification does not compose**: merging three certified building crosswalks made five `Brick` classes unsatisfiable because of a homonym for 'floor', and the core hub was already inconsistent because `Open Energy Ontology` and `BFO 2020` contradict each other.

papers.title: Does Frontier AI Strengthen Cyber Defense? Evidence from Project Glasswing
papers.abstract: Defenders and attackers race to find the same software flaws. I use the launch of Project Glasswing, which gave a small group of large US tech firms early access to Claude Mythos Preview, a model for finding software vulnerabilities, to study how access to frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers, and attackers. Using the universe of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, I find that firms with access more than doubled their disclosures relative to Chinese and Russian tech firms without access, disclosed about 150 percent more high-impact vulnerabilities, and fixed reported flaws as quickly as before. As treated firms found more flaws themselves, external researchers, who sell their findings through bug bounties, reported about half as many vulnerabilities in treated firms' code and more in other firms' code, without leaving the market. There is no evidence that attackers exploited the additional vulnerabilities: the share exploited within a month of disclosure fell by about two thirds, mainly because a smaller share was already exploited when disclosed, while the number exploited did not change. Frontier AI helped defenders find and fix more flaws before attackers exploited them, but its restricted release creates an asymmetry in software security between firms in different countries.
papers.summary: Using Project Glasswing, which gave a small group of large US tech firms early access to the vulnerability-finding model `Claude Mythos Preview`, as a natural experiment, this economic study measures how frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers, and attackers across all publicly disclosed vulnerabilities. Firms with access **more than doubled their vulnerability disclosures** relative to Chinese and Russian firms without access, disclosed about 150% more high-impact flaws, and patched as quickly as before. Bug-bounty researchers shifted roughly half their reports to other firms' code, and the share of flaws exploited within a month of disclosure fell by about two thirds. The author concludes that restricted release creates a security asymmetry between firms in different countries.

papers.title: Noise-regularized training of quantum circuit Born machines under a finite shot budget
papers.abstract: Quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) can learn distributions that are hard to sample from classically, but their value depends on generalizing from finite training data. Here, we study how hardware noise affects this generalization. We show that, for any noise process, the generalization gap of a QCBM trained with the maximum mean discrepancy is bounded by the complexity of the distributions the noisy model can reach. Scrambled local Pauli noise contracts this complexity but biases the model towards the uniform distribution, so residual noise acts as a regularizer whose optimal strength can be intermediate. We propose GENIE, a framework that realizes a chosen noise level with capped error mitigation and selects it during training from held-out data within a fixed execution budget, with provably bounded regret. In simulations on synthetic and census data, GENIE stays close to the best of four noise-control strategies, whereas every fixed noise level falls short in many settings.
