papers.summary: Quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) are generative models whose usefulness depends on generalizing from finite data, and this work asks how hardware noise affects that. The authors prove that for any noise process, the generalization gap under maximum mean discrepancy training is bounded by the complexity of distributions the noisy model can reach, and show that **scrambled local Pauli noise acts as a regularizer whose best strength can be intermediate**. They propose `GENIE`, which sets a chosen noise level via capped error mitigation and tunes it on held-out data within a fixed shot budget with bounded regret, and it stays close to the best of four noise-control strategies on synthetic and census data.

papers.title: Trick-or-Treat: Adversarial Evaluation of Multimodal Medical Reasoning with Synthetic Images
papers.abstract: We used medical image synthesis to create a challenging multimodal evaluation framework that exposes hallucination behaviors in frontier models. Evaluating multimodal reasoning has historically been difficult because existing medical datasets rarely pair different image modalities, such as radiographs and external clinical photographs. To address this gap, we introduce Trick-or-Treat, an adversarial multimodal medical benchmark that pairs real chest radiographs with synthetic clinical photographs to challenge models' cross-modal reasoning. For each of a wide range of conditions, we created two pairs of images, where the pairs share a single chest radiograph but contain different external photographs. In matched pairs, the chest radiograph and photograph both contain findings suggesting the same disease (e.g., varicella pneumonia suggested by lung opacities and crusted skin lesions seen in chickenpox). In mismatched pairs, the photograph depicts an alternative clinical finding that would not lead to the same unifying diagnosis (e.g. replacing crusted skin lesions with ordinary acne). Synthetic photograph generation allows clinical findings to be varied while the person's features and photographic setting stay consistent, reducing confounding. In an investigation of three frontier models, we found that models hallucinated clinically significant photograph findings in 45-57.5% of mismatched pairs, up from 25-37.5% for the same photographs shown alone. When faced with mismatched pairs, models tended to ignore mismatches and instead hallucinated findings that better matched the radiograph (e.g. misreading acne as crusted skin lesions to justify diagnosing chickenpox). Trick-or-Treat both demonstrates concerning error pattern in frontier models' medical reasoning and provides a proof of concept for the use of synthetic images in adversarial multimodal evaluation.
papers.summary: Medical datasets rarely pair different image types, which makes cross-modal clinical reasoning hard to test. `Trick-or-Treat` pairs real chest radiographs with synthetic clinical photographs that either support the same diagnosis or show an unrelated finding, while holding the person and photo setting constant to reduce confounding. Across three frontier models, **hallucinated photograph findings rose to 45-57.5% in mismatched pairs, versus 25-37.5% for the same photos shown alone**, with models typically misreading the photo to fit the radiograph's diagnosis.

papers.title: Human Motion Prediction via Continual Prior Compensation
papers.abstract: Human Motion Prediction (HMP) aims to predict future human poses at different moments according to observed past motion sequences. Previous approaches mainly treated the prediction of different temporal moments as a single prediction task and learned the predictions of varied moments simultaneously, which would encounter a main limitation: the learning of short-term predictions (referring to ``near-future'' prediction) could be hindered by the predictions of long-term (referring to ``far-future'' prediction) motions. In this paper, we develop a novel temporal continual learning framework called Continual Prior Compensation (CPC) to progressively train HMP models, in which we divide the prediction task of motions corresponding to varied temporal moments into several subtasks and train the model in a multi-stage manner. To mitigate the prior information forgetting in the progressive training, we further introduce a learnable random variable Prior Compensation Factor (PCF) to explicitly measure the prior knowledge loss. We theoretically show that the PCF can be efficiently learned together with the model parameters by minimizing a reasonable upper bound of the objective function. The proposed CPC is further enhanced to estimate the prior information loss for each subtask and a new framework called Continual Prior Compensation++ (CPC++) with Fine-Grained Prior Compensation Factor (FGPCF) is finally developed. Our CPC and CPC++ frameworks are quite flexible and can be easily integrated with different HMP backbone models and adapted to various datasets and applications. Extensive experiments on three HMP benchmark datasets using multiple SOTA HMP backbones (PGBIG, siMLPe, MotionMixer, and LTD) demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of our frameworks.
papers.summary: Human Motion Prediction (HMP) models usually learn short- and long-term pose forecasts jointly, which can let far-future predictions hurt near-future accuracy. `Continual Prior Compensation` (`CPC`) splits the task into time-horizon subtasks trained in stages, and adds a learnable Prior Compensation Factor that measures and offsets knowledge forgotten between stages, learned by minimizing an upper bound on the objective. An extension, `CPC++`, estimates this loss per subtask, and both **plug into existing backbones such as `siMLPe`, `PGBIG`, `MotionMixer`, and `LTD` with consistent gains** on three HMP benchmarks.

papers.title: Replicability, Reproducibility, and Robustness in Political and Social Science Research with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This chapter addresses the central reproducibility problem of research with large language models. LLM output is probabilistic and varies across models and versions, which can have significant effects on downstream statistical results. The chapter distinguishes between replicability, reproducibility, and robustness, and proposes a probabilistic standard based on the distribution of results, not identical outputs. It introduces a standardized prompt script, tests within-model variation for encoders and decoders, and develops error-structure analysis to diagnose where models err and whether their errors align. Using three datasets, the chapter shows that measurement choice can reverse the sign of downstream regression coefficients. Existing design-based corrections with gold-labeled subsamples restore validity, but come at the cost of estimate precision. The main contribution of the chapter is a stacked ensemble of open-weight models that improves precision in the correction step while retaining estimate validity.
papers.summary: LLM outputs vary across runs, models, and versions, which undermines reproducibility when they are used as measurement tools in political and social science. The chapter separates replicability, reproducibility, and robustness, proposes judging results by their distribution rather than identical outputs, and introduces a standardized prompt script plus an error-structure analysis of where models fail and whether their errors align. Across three datasets, **the choice of measurement model can flip the sign of downstream regression coefficients**; design-based corrections with gold-labeled subsamples restore validity at the cost of precision, which a stacked ensemble of open-weight models partly recovers.

papers.title: Beyond accuracy: what AI assurance needs to establish in public services
papers.abstract: Public bodies increasingly rely on AI-produced evidence, including classifications, summaries and assessments. These outputs can inform policy decisions and service delivery, making their reliability a matter of public accountability. Establishing whether this evidence can be relied upon requires testing its outputs and examining how organisations decide whether those tests are sufficient. We combine technical evaluation with analysis of AI governance requirements, informed by measurement theory and management-based regulation. We compare eight GPT-4o configurations classifying 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 policy topics, against human-coded labels and across unchanged repeats. Accuracy ranges from 68.2% to 70.3%, yet 24.3% of questions receive different labels, with changes in topic shares and rankings. Configurations agree more with one another than with human coding: agreement does not guarantee correctness. Under the implemented score-extraction procedure, the proportion flagged for human review ranges from 0.9% to 41.0%. We analyse 37 UK and EU policy documents. Both sets expect testing and oversight, but reporting expectations do not consistently cover changing answers, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions or review routing. Some UK guidance explicitly addresses stability. The UK sample emphasises public bodies checking their own use; the EU places substantial testing duties on providers while leaving them important choices about measures and acceptance thresholds. Without appropriate checks, evidence could misrepresent policy issues, redirect attention or resources, and leave errors undetected. Public policy should require organisations to justify reliance through checks beyond aggregate accuracy, clear responsibility, access to expertise and scrutiny of results.
papers.summary: Combining a technical evaluation with a review of 37 UK and EU policy documents, the authors ask what public bodies must check before relying on AI-produced evidence. Eight `GPT-4o` configurations classifying 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 topics all reached 68-70% accuracy, yet **24.3% of questions received different labels across configurations and repeats**, shifting topic shares and rankings. Configurations agreed more with each other than with human coders, and the share flagged for human review ranged from 0.9% to 41%. The policy documents mostly do not require reporting on unstable answers, shared errors, or selective evaluation.

papers.title: Where Search Agents Go Off the Rails: Graph-Grounded Step-Level Verification
papers.abstract: Search-augmented reasoning systems can reach correct answers while making errors in intermediate steps. Reliable auditing must check whether evidence $D$ covers the question $Q$, reasoning $T$ addresses $Q$, and $T$ is grounded in $D$. We introduce GraphRail, which represents requirements, evidence, and reasoning as structured claims and compares them without a generative judge or gold answer. Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three reasoning frameworks, GraphRail improves error recall over generative verifiers while remaining stable under stochastic extraction. Its diagnoses can also guide online reasoning, providing a traceable way to detect and correct intermediate errors.
papers.summary: Search-augmented reasoning systems can reach correct answers despite faulty intermediate steps, so auditing them requires checking that evidence covers the question, reasoning addresses it, and reasoning is grounded in the evidence. `GraphRail` turns requirements, evidence, and reasoning into structured claims and compares them as a graph, without a generative judge or gold answer. Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three reasoning frameworks, it **finds more intermediate errors than generative verifiers** while staying stable under stochastic extraction, and its diagnoses can guide online correction during reasoning.

papers.title: AgentTrustCI: Build-Time Policy, Grounding, and Trajectory Tests for Java LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Infrastructure security does not establish whether an LLM agent selected an allowed tool, grounded its answer in tool output, or followed a required workflow. AgentTrustCI is a Java/JUnit 5 framework that expresses these application-layer expectations as policy, grounding, and trajectory checks over recorded traces. A deterministic replay implementation supports repeatable build-time tests; a judge interface provides an extension point for optional semantic evaluation. On 55 synthetic cases spanning seven enterprise domains, the full pipeline correctly classifies all 30 injected faults and 25 passing controls, including ten non-trivial controls, and misses none of 12 designated critical cases. Each single-layer configuration correctly classifies 35 cases because the corpus deliberately isolates ten faults per layer. A grounded answer obtained through a disallowed sequence illustrates the additional coverage of trajectory checks. Repeated measurements quantify validator execution separately from process startup and reporting. These results establish coverage of the authored regression suite, not production accuracy. We describe a production-trace validation protocol, optional LLM-judge integration, and maintenance of expectations as workflows evolve. The contribution is a practical pattern for expressing behavioral contracts within an existing Java release pipeline.
papers.summary: Infrastructure security does not show whether an LLM agent chose an allowed tool, grounded its answer in tool output, or followed a required workflow. `AgentTrustCI` is a Java/`JUnit 5` framework that expresses these expectations as policy, grounding, and trajectory checks over recorded traces, using deterministic replay for repeatable build-time tests and an optional LLM-judge interface. On 55 synthetic cases across seven enterprise domains, **the full pipeline correctly classified all 30 injected faults and 25 passing controls**, though the authors stress that this shows coverage of their authored suite, not production accuracy.

papers.title: LifeVal: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Personalized Agentic Consumer Tasks
papers.abstract: We introduce LifeVal, a benchmark evaluating AI model performance on personalized agentic consumer tasks. LifeVal covers the most valuable life tasks that a personalized digital superassistant could automate, representing over 1.7 trillion US dollars in annual willingness-to-pay across 148 consumer task categories (e.g., managing finances, moving apartments, searching for a job, finding childcare). To construct our activity distribution, we conducted a new survey of willingness-to-pay for a digital superassistant across a demographically representative sample of over 3,800 consumers, cross-referencing our results against the American Time Use Survey (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) and the Multinational Time Use Study (Fisher et al., 2025). For the most valuable consumer activities, we recruited task creators to create AI evaluation tasks personalized using real ChatGPT conversations and memories, reference files, and personal context. Task creators had to pass our expertise threshold (including personally completing the task multiple times and seeing the results through in their real lives for over a year) and also write a rubric, ensuring that our evaluation measured the best personalized completion for that task. All tasks had to pass at least three rounds of human quality-control before acceptance into our final evaluation sets.
papers.summary: `LifeVal` is a benchmark of personalized agentic consumer tasks, such as managing finances, moving apartments, or finding childcare, weighted by what people would pay a digital assistant to do them. Task categories come from a willingness-to-pay survey of over 3,800 demographically representative consumers, cross-checked against US and multinational time-use studies, and together cover **148 categories representing over $1.7 trillion in annual willingness-to-pay**. Each task is personalized with real `ChatGPT` conversations, memories, and files, written with a rubric by creators who have done the task themselves, and passed at least three rounds of human quality control.

papers.title: Don't Replace, Complement: A Detector-Agnostic Subspace Signal for Near-OOD Detection
papers.abstract: Post-hoc out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is mature on far-OOD yet remains weak on near-OOD. These two settings differ in their use of class-characteristic feature directions: far-OOD inputs largely fail to activate those of their predicted class, whereas near-OOD inputs activate them much as in-distribution samples do. Because the axis separating far-OOD leaves near-OOD almost indistinguishable from ID, a score optimized for one setting is misaligned with the other; where a detector already saturates far-OOD, added near-OOD sensitivity is bought partly against it. This divergence motivates a targeted near-OOD signal designed to complement existing scores. We propose PLUS (Per-class Low-dimensional sUbspace Signal). For each class, PLUS selects the $m$ most class-active neurons from a sparse autoencoder, orthonormalizes the corresponding decoder directions to form a low-dimensional subspace, and scores an input by its per-class whitened squared Mahalanobis distance $z$ within the subspace of its predicted class. Designed as a dedicated complement rather than a standalone detector, the signal $z$ is fused additively with any calibrated base score at a single, fixed weight. This weight is a single global constant: no value is adjusted per backbone, per OOD dataset, or per deployment, and all calibration statistics are estimated from ID validation data alone. When applied to 18 existing detectors spanning diverse method families, $z$ consistently improves near-OOD AUROC in all 126 detector--backbone combinations. Far-OOD performance is broadly maintained or improved, with only marginal declines where the base score is near-optimal, making $z$ a robust, detector-agnostic complement across backbones.
papers.summary: Post-hoc out-of-distribution (OOD) detectors work well on far-OOD inputs but poorly on near-OOD ones, which activate the same class-specific feature directions as in-distribution data. `PLUS` (Per-class Low-dimensional sUbspace Signal) picks each class's most active sparse-autoencoder neurons, builds a low-dimensional subspace from their decoder directions, and scores inputs by whitened Mahalanobis distance within the predicted class's subspace. Added to existing detectors with a single fixed weight calibrated only on in-distribution data, it **improved near-OOD AUROC in all 126 detector-backbone combinations** tested across 18 detectors, while largely keeping far-OOD performance.

papers.title: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus
papers.abstract: Tech-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV) is a pervasive online harm affecting women and gender minority groups through its many direct and covert forms. Current models and annotated datasets for gendered harm detection are dominated by data from, and models trained in, Global North languages. In collaboration with civil society organizations (CSOs) from Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, we developed a community-led approach to crowdsource culturally and linguistically relevant instances of TFGBV in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. We annotated the crowdsourced data using active learning to develop a small but performant dataset (N=3022) called ALTO to improve TFGBV detection in the three languages. Through benchmarking and fine-tuning experiments, we show that existing harmful content detection models show poor TFGBV recall within ALTO and improve with fine-tuning. We found that models often miss covert harms across all languages, while error rates are markedly higher in Swahili. We report the experimental results and release the annotation taxonomy, dataset, and trained models.
papers.summary: Datasets and models for detecting tech-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV) mostly cover Global North languages. Working with civil society organizations in Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, the authors crowdsourced and annotated, with active learning, `ALTO`, a 3,022-example dataset in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. Existing harmful-content detectors showed **poor recall on TFGBV, especially for covert harms and in Swahili**, and improved with fine-tuning; the taxonomy, dataset, and models are released.

papers.title: Beyond the principle-practice gap: Responsible AI as situated epistemic and ethical practice
papers.abstract: Responsible AI scholarship has found that ethical principles are frequently not reflected in AI design and development. Conceptualised as a `gap' between principle and practice, this is framed as a problem of implementation, awareness or compliance, and by implication, a deficit of systems or individual behaviour. This paper sets out an alternative explanation. Drawing on fourteen semi-structured interviews with actors designing and governing AI-enabled anti-trafficking systems across law enforcement, commercial, research, and survivor-support contexts, it argues that such apparent gaps emerge from the varied and complex institutional and professional conditions through which actors come to recognise some issues, but not others, as ethical problems requiring action. We show that epistemic choices are intertwined with ethical judgements, and trace four interconnected moments---perception, judgement, situated action and socio-technical materialisation---through which concerns become intelligible, are weighed and acted upon, and are embedded in technical artefacts and governance arrangements. Actors often hold genuine ethical commitments, but these commitments are shaped by institutional logics and professional moral economies: some concerns are materialised, while others are narrowed, deferred or left unrealised. We show that ethical agency is exercised within and between competing constraints of profession, role, prior experience, and institutional settings. The paper argues that responsible AI governance requires purposeful and well-developed epistemic infrastructures that can cut across these constraints to establish institutional conditions through which the knowledge of affected communities and potential harms becomes receivable and actionable in design.
papers.summary: Responsible AI research often describes a 'gap' between ethical principles and practice as a failure of implementation or compliance. Based on fourteen interviews with people building and governing AI-enabled anti-trafficking systems, the authors argue that **such gaps arise from institutional and professional conditions that shape which issues people recognize as ethical problems at all**. They trace four moments (perception, judgement, situated action, and socio-technical materialisation) and call for epistemic infrastructures that make affected communities' knowledge actionable in design.

papers.title: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes models reason over relations given in context rather than relying on memorized associations, and `Rel-Bloom` tests this directly with 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 `Wikidata` relations, posed at five Bloom-taxonomy levels and under factual, counterfactual, and anonymized conditions. Across 43 models, six languages, and 226,800 predictions, open-weight models dropped sharply from Apply to Analyze questions, and **even `Gemini 3.1 Pro`, at 99.5% on other levels, scored only 60.7% on Evaluate items**. Difficulty rankings held across languages, and counterfactual contexts were generally harder than factual ones.

papers.title: Dexterous Robotic Hands in the Foundation-Model Era: A Full-Stack Survey of Hardware, Data, Cross-Embodiment Transfer, Learning, and Evaluation
papers.abstract: Dexterous robotic hands are increasingly coupled to large-scale human data and foundation models, yet progress in hardware, representation learning and evaluation is often assessed separately. This survey reviews work from January 2024 to early November 2026, with earlier studies included to establish technical lineages. We organize the literature into five interdependent layers: hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; and evaluation and applications. Human hand-object understanding and tactile sensing provide two cross-cutting perspectives. A system-level architecture, comparative tables and five case analyses connect design choices across these layers. We distinguish within-study experimental comparisons from heterogeneous corpus statistics, vendor specifications and company-reported results. Three conclusions emerge. First, the value of human data depends on kinematic, visual and contact alignment, not recording volume alone. Second, shared action representations and foundation policies do not remove embodiment-specific constraints on force, latency and contact. Third, task completion is insufficient to establish physical correctness or deployment readiness. Evidence remains limited for zero-shot transfer of contact-rich skills between morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization. We identify eleven open problems and propose reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons that can make full-stack progress more measurable. The review is a structured narrative synthesis rather than a pooled performance ranking or an exhaustive systematic review.
papers.summary: This survey covers dexterous robotic hand research from January 2024 to November 2026, organized into five layers: hardware, data collection, cross-embodiment transfer, learning and foundation models, and evaluation, with tactile sensing and human hand-object understanding as cross-cutting themes. It concludes that **the value of human data depends on kinematic, visual, and contact alignment rather than volume**, that shared action representations do not remove embodiment-specific limits on force and latency, and that task completion alone does not establish physical correctness. It lists eleven open problems and proposes reporting standards for more measurable progress.

papers.title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.
papers.summary: In streaming video understanding, models repeatedly decide whether to respond or keep watching, and existing Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) methods give every turn the same trajectory-level credit, which can reward redundant replies and penalize useful follow-ups. `TurnWise` assigns credit per turn by scoring each decision's remaining return through silence-completed prefixes, and averages token losses within each turn before averaging across turns so short and long decisions count equally. **Without a learned critic or extra rollouts**, it outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.
papers.highlight_summary:
Streaming video assistants trained with `GRPO` give every respond-or-wait decision in a trajectory the same advantage, so a redundant reply can inherit credit from an earlier success, and a useful follow-up can be penalized for earlier failures. `TurnWise` gives each decision its own credit based on the reward still to be earned from that turn onward, and weights every turn equally in the loss.

- **How credit is assigned:** each trajectory prefix is re-scored with all later turns set to silence (`NO REPLY`), and subtracting that score from the full reward gives each turn's remaining return. The turn's advantage is that remaining return compared against the other rollouts in its group, computed from cached judge scores with no learned critic, extra rollouts or extra judge calls.
- **How the loss is weighted:** token losses are averaged within each turn and then across turns, so a long response and a short wait count equally regardless of output length.
- **Main results:** `TurnWise` gets the best aggregate scores on `ProactiveVQA`, `OVO-Timing` and `StreamingBench` with both backbones. On `Qwen2.5-VL-3B` it reaches **43.56 PAUC, 21.59 Timing F1 and 49.43 accuracy**, ahead of the best RL baseline by **+3.96, +3.87 and +0.69** points. On `Qwen3-VL-4B` the margins are **+6.26, +1.92 and +2.38**.
- **Why both parts are needed:** combining the two cuts the repetition rate by **61.5%** compared with credit assignment alone (15.53 to 5.98) and adds 2.96 Timing F1. In training logs, turn-level credit flips **59.83%** of repetitive replies that had a positive trajectory-level advantage to a negative one.
- **Limitations:** the experiments are small (3B–4B models, 3,983 RL instances, 4 rollouts per group) and use a single reward from `MMDuet2`. The `StreamingBench` gain on the 3B model is under one point, the α ablation is non-monotonic, and the method relies on scoring trajectories with silent suffixes, which needs an explicit wait action.

papers.title: Template Gap Reconstruction for Shell Output Simulation with Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.
papers.summary: Small language models can simulate shell output without executing commands, but decoding the full output forces them to reproduce recurring utility formatting along with the parts that actually vary. Template gap reconstruction (`TGR`) selects a reusable output template containing fixed text and placeholders, and the model generates only the gaps, using a template bank built from 18.7 million outputs across varied environments. `TGR` matches or beats full-output decoding on output edit similarity, reaching 0.964 versus 0.812 on shorter gap sequences, and **cuts generated tokens by 26.3-38.3%**.

papers.title: ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. We further analyze the models' internal representations and find clear semantic structure: task representations cluster according to the operations applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even when realized through substantially different rules and scenarios. Together, our results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.
papers.summary: It is unclear whether large reasoning models (LRMs) form abstractions that generalize across conceptually related tasks. `ConceptARC at Scale` is a generator for ARC-style grid tasks targeting specific concepts, used to build `ConceptARC-100`, a dataset of 1,600 manually reviewed tasks, 100 for each of `ConceptARC`'s 16 concepts. Evaluating recent LRMs and models trained from scratch shows which concepts they solve reliably, and analysis of internal representations finds that **task representations cluster by the operation applied to objects**, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even across very different rules and scenarios.

papers.title: Smartphone-Aided VR Exergames for HIIT: Gamifying Fitness with Real-Time Pose Estimation
papers.abstract:
This paper introduces an innovative virtual reality (VR) exergame system designed to gamify High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) workouts through 11 predefined combo moves, including squat-punch combinations, bilateral arm strikes, and diagonal stretch combos. Unlike conventional tracking methods that often rely on wearable motion capture suits or limited headset-based sensors, our system uses a standard smartphone camera placed on a tripod to capture full-body movement. This approach offers a cost-effective and scalable alternative, particularly well-suited to the fast, dynamic motions typical of HIIT routines.
  The smartphone footage is processed in real time using a pose estimation algorithm, with extracted biomechanical data analyzed by a backend server built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI models to structured data sources and tools, and a GPT-4o large language model. The system generates personalized assessments of form accuracy, movement efficiency, exercise intensity, and potential injury risks, tailored specifically to high-impact, time-sensitive exercises.
  A within-subject study involving 20 participants (ages 18-25) compared experiences in VR and Non-VR HIIT sessions. Results indicated significantly higher enjoyment (Mean = 3.5 vs 2.8, p = 0.02), improved immersion/focus (Mean = 3.2 vs 2.8, p = 0.03), and increased likelihood to recommend (Mean = 3.2 vs 2.7, p = 0.04) under the VR condition. Confidence to continue did not differ significantly between conditions (p = 0.15), while perceived intensity remained comparable. The MCP system showed strong agreement with expert evaluation (87.5%, N = 10 sessions, one certified trainer), supporting its reliability as a feedback tool.
papers.summary: A virtual reality (VR) exergame for High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) tracks full-body movement with a tripod-mounted smartphone camera and real-time pose estimation instead of wearable suits. Pose data goes to a backend built on the Model Context Protocol (`MCP`) and `GPT-4o`, which assesses form, efficiency, intensity, and injury risk. In a within-subject study with 20 participants, VR sessions scored significantly higher on enjoyment, immersion, and willingness to recommend, and **the system's feedback agreed with a certified trainer in 87.5% of 10 sessions**.

papers.title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
papers.abstract: Strong single-turn editing performance does not guarantee reliable multi-turn interaction: as edited outputs are repeatedly reused, small unintended changes can accumulate into severe visual drift. This long-term drift is often mitigated through training on multi-turn data or cross-turn rollouts, potentially altering pretrained priors, or through specialized inference-time mechanisms that are difficult to scale to foundation models. We introduce TailSteer, a final-stage training framework that improves multi-turn robustness while retaining the generative and editing capabilities acquired through earlier training. TailSteer follows a simple principle: keep early denoising dynamics close to those of the base model and concentrate preservation corrections near the trajectory tail, where fine-grained deviations can be suppressed. These corrections are learned from the editor's own on-policy denoising rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference without requiring curated ground-truth editing pairs. Experiments across the FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen families show that TailSteer substantially reduces cumulative drift over 15-20 editing turns while largely preserving base-model performance on extensive text-to-image and single-image editing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that long-horizon editing robustness can be unlocked in foundation models after TailSteer, rather than by relearning their existing capabilities.
papers.summary: Image editors that do well on a single edit often drift badly over many rounds, because each output is fed back in and small unintended changes pile up. `TailSteer` is a final-stage training framework that keeps the early denoising steps close to the base model and applies preservation corrections only near the end of the denoising trajectory, where fine-grained deviations can be suppressed. The corrections are learned from the editor's own on-policy rollouts, with the unchanged source content serving as the reference, so no curated ground-truth editing pairs are needed. Across the `FLUX`, `SenseNova`, and `Qwen` model families, it **substantially reduces cumulative drift over 15-20 editing turns** while largely keeping base-model performance on text-to-image and single-edit benchmarks.

papers.title: EvoWorld: Towards Out-of-Sight World Evolution in Generative Video Models
papers.abstract: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.
papers.summary: Generative video models render plausible pixels but have no explicit way to track world state or reason about what an event should cause, so their outputs are often static or causally inconsistent. The authors define a new task, `Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution`, in which a model must render an event, infer its consequences, and show a causally plausible outcome even for parts of the world outside the current view. Their baseline, `EvoWorld`, pairs a vision-language model that acts as a "world brain", observing generated segments and reasoning about state transitions, with a segment-autoregressive video renderer. Together with the new `EvoWorld-Data` and `EvoWorld-Bench`, experiments show **substantially better event-conditioned causal evolution than recent video models** without losing visual quality or consistency.

papers.title: Route First, See Later: Enabling Vision Agents to Reason Scientifically by Separating Routing Policy from Action Spaces
papers.abstract:
Scientific image-analysis workflows require agents to select among diverse capabilities like description, detection, counting, and segmentation. Current multi-tool architectures conflate intent interpretation with visual execution, masking whether a failure arises from flawed reasoning (misrouting) or failed perception (invalid tool execution). This lack of auditability renders agents unreliable for high-stakes scientific automation. We introduce ZETA, an extensible architecture that operationalizes the decoupling of routing policy from action execution. ZETA resolves scientific intent before invoking specialized visual tools, treating measurement as a deterministic operation grounded in explicit geometry rather than generative output. This architecture exposes the "black box" of agent decision-making, allowing routing correctness and downstream execution to be evaluated as independent failure modes.
  To our knowledge, we provide the first controlled study in scientific vision-agent routing that isolates explicit routing-policy specification while holding the legal action interface fixed. Evaluation on a zero-shot benchmark of 51 scientific-intent queries shows that explicit routing semantics can substantially improve routing accuracy, particularly at semantically adjacent action boundaries, although improvements vary across models. For Qwen 3.8, explicit routing-policy specification improves segmentation routing accuracy from 6.2% to 75.0% and detection routing accuracy from 60.0% to 100%. ZETA's execution traces make routing decisions and downstream artifacts separately observable, providing a basis for distinguishing intent-selection errors from visual execution failures. ZETA establishes the necessary infrastructure to isolate execution errors from interpretive ones, a critical requirement for deploying reliable scientific vision agents.
papers.summary: Vision agents for scientific image analysis have to choose between capabilities such as description, detection, counting, and segmentation, but current multi-tool designs mix up interpreting intent with executing visual tools, so it is unclear whether a failure came from misrouting or from bad perception. `ZETA` separates the routing policy from action execution: it resolves the scientific intent first, then calls specialized tools that treat measurement as a deterministic operation grounded in explicit geometry. In a controlled zero-shot study of 51 scientific-intent queries with the action interface held fixed, spelling out the routing policy explicitly raised `Qwen 3.8`'s **segmentation routing accuracy from 6.2% to 75.0%** and its detection routing accuracy from 60.0% to 100%, although the gains varied across models. Its execution traces make routing errors and visual-execution errors separately observable.

papers.title: FedFiOT: Fisher-Weighted Optimal Transport for Model Merging in One-Shot and Few-Round Federated Learning
papers.abstract: One-shot and few-round federated learning (FL) reduce communication burden by constructing a global model within one or a few communication rounds, but often achieve lower performance than conventional multi-round FL. Without frequent synchronization, client models may drift apart, causing neurons that learn similar features to occupy different positions across clients. At the same time, local data heterogeneity can cause corresponding parameters to differ in their importance to each client's predictions. Together, these challenges cause direct averaging to combine mismatched neurons and assign equal weight to parameters despite differences in their importance. We propose FedFiOT, a Fisher-weighted optimal transport framework for one-shot and few-round FL that leverages Fisher information to quantify parameter importance and guide neuron alignment and model aggregation. FedFiOT jointly optimizes neuron correspondences and global model parameters through alternating minimization of a shared Fisher-weighted objective. Theoretically, we show that FedFiOT's optimization procedure monotonically decreases the layer-wise merging objective and establish a stationarity bound that quantifies the effects of client heterogeneity and nonuniform Fisher weighting.Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competing baselines in both one-shot and few-round federated learning settings.
papers.summary: One-shot and few-round federated learning (FL) save communication but usually trail multi-round FL, because client models drift apart: neurons that learn similar features end up at different positions, and parameters matter to different degrees depending on each client's data. `FedFiOT` uses Fisher information to measure how important each parameter is, and uses that both to align neurons across clients through optimal transport and to weight the aggregation, alternately optimizing the neuron correspondences and the global parameters under one shared objective. The authors prove the procedure monotonically decreases the layer-wise merging objective and give a stationarity bound that accounts for client heterogeneity. Experiments show **consistent improvements over baselines in both one-shot and few-round settings**.

papers.title: Ranking Agreement Does Not Reveal Paragraph-Edit Agreement in Two Released Paper Acceptance Predictors
papers.abstract: A fast acceptance classifier could select revisions for a slower evaluator. We ask whether agreement on existing papers supports that use. We compare a classifier of word and document features with two released text-only acceptance predictors fine-tuned from the same language model with three billion parameters. For 198 papers from the International Conference on Learning Representations, we compare model rankings of the original papers and of paragraph rewrites screened automatically for unchanged facts, claim strength, and attribution. The classifier ranks original papers closely with one predictor and moderately with the other, but shows no detectable agreement with either on which rewrites raise scores. The tests specified in advance used reduced numerical precision. Rounding error dominated the small score responses. We therefore rescored the released weights in full 32-bit precision as a post hoc check; edit agreement remained near zero. At this precision, when each predictor chooses among five rewrites per paper, its average raw score is under two points out of 100 higher than with random choice. The evidence covers presentation rewrites and two open predictors from one family; transfer to costly evaluators remains untested. Revision selectors should therefore be checked against the intended evaluator on the revisions they rank.
papers.summary: The question is whether a fast paper-acceptance classifier that agrees with a slower evaluator on existing papers can be trusted to choose which revisions will raise that evaluator's score. On 198 papers from the International Conference on Learning Representations (`ICLR`), a word-and-document-feature classifier was compared with two released text-only acceptance predictors fine-tuned from the same 3-billion-parameter language model, using paragraph rewrites automatically screened to keep facts, claim strength, and attribution unchanged. The classifier ranked the original papers similarly to the predictors, but **showed no detectable agreement with either on which rewrites raise scores**, and this held after a post hoc rescoring in full 32-bit precision, carried out because rounding error had dominated the pre-specified tests. When each predictor picks among five rewrites per paper, its average score is less than 2 points out of 100 above random choice, so the authors conclude that revision selectors should be checked against the intended evaluator on the revisions themselves.

papers.title: Transforming Integer Grids to Spatial Intuition: Perception, Not Planning, Governs ARC-AGI-3
papers.abstract: Sample-efficient fluid intelligence requires agents that rapidly form working models of unfamiliar interactive environments. ARC-AGI-3 tests this across uninstructed visual games scored by Relative Human Action Efficiency, which penalizes exploratory waste quadratically. When frontier models read raw integer grids, serialization destroys spatial topology, and they spend hundreds of actions rediscovering basic boundaries and symmetries. We introduce SARBLOH, an open-weight agent built on the premise that spatial perception, not planning capacity, governs interactive reasoning on ARC-AGI-3. A zero-parameter O(HW) perception engine turns each frame, in 35 ms, into an object inventory with bipartite temporal tracking, a geometric briefing that separates proven invariants from affordance hypotheses, and an annotated canvas. Paired with a code-as-action runtime, the agent writes algorithmic hypotheses instead of low-level moves. Across eight presentations, grounded perception raises the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 points while cutting token use by 89.4%. On 23 held-out games, geometric invariants generalize with 100% accuracy, while single-frame affordance guesses fall to 6-50%, so active verification probes remain necessary. On the public set, Run A (briefing off) solved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours at 59.4% single-pass efficiency; Run B (briefing on) reached 63.5%. Within the nine-hour budget on one Kaggle RTX PRO 6000 GPU, SARBLOH scored 16.53 on the hidden Kaggle evaluation, 13.7x the first Milestone winner.
papers.summary: On `ARC-AGI-3`, which consists of uninstructed visual games scored by Relative Human Action Efficiency, frontier models that read raw integer grids lose spatial structure and waste hundreds of actions rediscovering basic boundaries. `SARBLOH` is an open-weight agent built on the premise that perception, not planning, is the bottleneck. A zero-parameter perception engine turns each frame, in 35 ms, into an object inventory with tracking over time, a geometric briefing that separates proven invariants from guesses about what actions do, and an annotated canvas, and a code-as-action runtime lets the agent write algorithmic hypotheses instead of low-level moves. Grounded perception raised the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 while cutting token use by 89.4%; geometric invariants generalized perfectly to 23 held-out games while single-frame action guesses did not. Running on one Kaggle GPU within the nine-hour budget, the agent **scored 16.53 on the hidden evaluation, 13.7x the first Milestone winner**.

papers.title: Message-passing graph persistence
papers.abstract: Message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs) are limited in expressive power by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman test. Persistent homology (PH) provides topological descriptors that can complement GNN representations, but existing approaches typically compute persistence separately from the representation learning process. In this paper, we introduce Message-Passing Graph Persistence (MGP), a family of topological descriptors that incorporates message passing into graph filtrations. At each filtration step, node embeddings are updated using the current subgraph and associated with persistence events. These embeddings also determine the representatives of connected components during persistence computation. We prove that MGP is invariant under graph isomorphism and that it is strictly more expressive than the PH-based descriptors it extends. We evaluate MGP on an expressivity benchmark and on several graph classification and regression datasets. Experiments show that MGP outperforms other PH-based descriptors on most of these datasets.
papers.summary: Message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs) are limited in expressive power by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman test, and persistent homology (PH) descriptors that could complement them are usually computed separately from representation learning. `Message-Passing Graph Persistence` (`MGP`) builds message passing into the graph filtration: at each step, node embeddings are updated on the current subgraph, attached to persistence events, and used to choose the representatives of connected components. The authors prove `MGP` is invariant under graph isomorphism and **strictly more expressive than the PH descriptors it extends**. It outperforms other PH-based descriptors on most of the expressivity, classification, and regression datasets tested.

papers.title: Task-Efficient Agent Evaluation Using Cached Traces
papers.abstract: Efficient benchmarking estimates a system's full benchmark performance from a small number of task executions. Standard approaches rely solely on the binary correctness of executions from a collection of already-evaluated reference systems. An agentic system, however, produces a rich trace for each execution that can reveal substantially more about its capabilities. Leveraging this information requires useful trace representations. We propose representing a trace by extracting a structured summary of it with an LLM and embedding the summary with a standard text encoder. These representations preserve correctness- and task-related signal while minimizing the presence of system identity-, model family- and harness-related signals that dominate raw trace embeddings. Given this representation for each task execution from all reference systems, we construct low-dimensional representations of the systems and predict a new system's score from its position among the reference systems. On SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0, augmenting an item-response model with this geometry-based prediction reduces mean absolute error from 0.13 to 0.08 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-4}$) and from 0.14 to 0.12 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-3}$), respectively, when provided a single random executed task. Further, given access to the full set of reference systems, our approach dominates baselines for any given number of executed tasks on both benchmarks.
papers.summary: Efficient benchmarking tries to estimate a system's full benchmark score from a few task runs, but standard methods use only pass/fail results and ignore the rich traces that agentic systems produce. The authors have an LLM extract a structured summary of each trace and embed it with a standard text encoder, which keeps signal about correctness and the task while removing much of the system-, model-family-, and harness-identity signal that dominates raw trace embeddings. They then place a new system among the already-evaluated reference systems in a low-dimensional space and predict its score from that position. Added to an item-response model and given just one random executed task, this **cuts mean absolute error from 0.13 to 0.08 on `SWE-bench Verified`** and from 0.14 to 0.12 on `Terminal-Bench 2.0`, and with all reference systems available it beats the baselines at every task budget.

papers.title: Measuring Risk, Not Harm: Detecting Psychological Harm Risk Factors in LLM Conversations
papers.abstract: Psychological harms from interactions with large language models cannot be monitored directly because they may emerge over repeated interactions and depend strongly on subjective individual user context. We propose measuring risk, not harm: detecting observable AI behaviors that constitute risk factors for psychological harm at the AI response level and aggregating these signals to support longitudinal monitoring. We operationalize eight such behaviors and construct a synthetic multi-label corpus of 47,062 AI responses and 373,873 response-factor labels, with targeted human annotations for validation and evaluation. We then compare trained embedding-based classifiers, direct LLM judging, and a classifier--judge cascade. All detectors are model-agnostic and operate only on LLM outputs, requiring no access to internal model states. We apply these detectors to several out-of-distribution human-AI conversation data sets from prior research. On held-out human-labeled data, the best cascade achieves macro precision of 0.86, recall of 0.76, and F1 of 0.79. On WildChat, it reduces LLM-judge calls by 97.1\% relative to direct judging. On DelusionEval, risk-factor detections cluster within conversations. Together, our results show that response-level behavioral risk-factor detection can provide a scalable measurement layer for longitudinal psychological-safety monitoring without conflating observable AI behavior with latent user harm.
papers.summary: Psychological harm from LLM interactions cannot be monitored directly, because it can build up over time and depends on each user's circumstances. The authors instead detect observable AI behaviors that act as risk factors, defining eight such behaviors and building a synthetic multi-label corpus of 47,062 responses with 373,873 labels, plus targeted human annotations. They compare embedding-based classifiers, direct LLM judging, and a classifier-then-judge cascade, all of which work only on model outputs. On held-out human-labeled data the best cascade reaches macro F1 of 0.79, and on `WildChat` it **reduces LLM-judge calls by 97.1%** compared with direct judging; on `DelusionEval`, detections cluster within conversations, which supports aggregating them for longitudinal monitoring.

papers.title: LLMs Don't Know What They Know: Benchmarking Temporal Self-Knowledge for Financial Backtesting
papers.abstract: Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes it is asked to predict. Practitioners guard against this by trusting a vendor's stated knowledge cutoff, by asking the model what it knows, or by instructing it to answer as of a past date. To verify whether any of these safeguards can be trusted, we introduce FinDendro, a benchmark of 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026, covering monthly macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices and Federal Reserve decisions. Each fact yields four prompts: a value question, Recall and Predict questions that pair each candidate value with a claim of knowing or guessing without a declared date, and a Predict question with a historical declared date. Controls for persistence and dominant outcomes keep chance accuracy near 0.27. Results show that for most frontier models, self-reports understate knowledge. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know 38%, and answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Knowledge claims can persist beyond the measured knowledge boundary, by up to seven quarters, and a declared date removes most of the claims of prior knowledge while leaving accuracy unchanged. Backtests inside a model's training window therefore cannot be certified leak-free by self-report, instruction or stated cutoff. These findings motivate behavioral measurement of temporal knowledge boundaries, and FinDendro provides a benchmark and procedure for selecting backtest periods based on demonstrated factual knowledge.
papers.summary: LLM backtests in finance are only valid if the model did not already know the outcomes, and practitioners rely on stated knowledge cutoffs, the model's own self-reports, or instructions to answer as of a past date. `FinDendro` tests these safeguards with 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026 (macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices, and Federal Reserve decisions), each asked in several forms, with controls that keep chance accuracy near 0.27. For most frontier models, self-reports understate what they know: `GPT-5` **answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know only 38%**, and answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Claims of knowledge can extend up to seven quarters past the measured knowledge boundary, and declaring a past date removes most claims of prior knowledge without lowering accuracy, so none of these safeguards can certify a backtest as leak-free.

papers.title: SAUCE: Summary Analysis Using Conversation Entailment
papers.abstract: With the growing need for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) and their applications to speech, challenges persist in summarizing and evaluating conversations that lack a clear end goal. We introduce SAUCE -- a reference-free, fact-based evaluation pipeline for cross-lingual conversational speech summarization. It measures the accuracy and the fact coverage of a summary through the entailment between conversation and text. We compare SAUCE against several popular summarization metrics and demonstrate the effectiveness of capturing information loss due to transcription and translation error and identifying broken summaries. Crucially, unlike black-box LLM evaluators or dense embedding metrics, SAUCE is inherently explainable: it maps summary scores to discrete, verifiable facts, allowing users to pinpoint exact hallucinations or omissions. We illustrate how this interpretability helps developers systematically profile LLM behaviors and gives end-users an actionable tool to verify summary accuracy in noisy, real-world conditions. Preliminary investigations show SAUCE strongly align with human judgment.
papers.summary: Summaries of open-ended conversations are hard to evaluate, especially for cross-lingual speech where transcription and translation errors add noise. `SAUCE` is a reference-free evaluation pipeline that scores a summary's accuracy and fact coverage by checking entailment between the conversation and individual facts in the summary. Compared with popular summarization metrics, it captures information lost to transcription and translation errors and flags broken summaries. Because each score maps to discrete, checkable facts, users can pinpoint specific hallucinations or omissions, and preliminary results show **strong alignment with human judgment**.

papers.title: Rules, Traces and Routing Statistics: Training and Calibration Data for Open Models on ARC-AGI-2
papers.abstract: We study which training and calibration data help three open models solve ARC-AGI-2 tasks when the solver runs offline on four L4 GPUs for at most 12 hours. We compare data offline on public tasks and report 189 runs on the 120 hidden semi-private tasks. For the NVARC Qwen3-4B grid model, we built a corpus of 12,000 executable rules in a typed language and 95,993 tasks; a rule is admitted only if its behaviour on a fixed probe set differs from that of every admitted rule, and a task only if its pairs refute a shortlist of nearest competing rules and defeat 12 shortcut solvers. Continued fine-tuning on 1,920 real task records with revised four-GPU scheduling raised the semi-private score from 28.96 (mean of the released model) to 33.06 (mean of five runs, best 34.86); no checkpoint trained with synthetic tasks, even all 95,993 of them, improved on the real-task model. For the Qwen3.8-27B reasoning model, we fine-tuned on 1,036 of its own reasoning traces with correct final answers and compared sets that add traces of other models and synthetic tasks. With an inference procedure built around the model (a thinking cap enforced in the serving engine, a Python program checked on the demonstrations after each answer, a long first attempt per input), the score rose from 26.81 to 44.03, the level the ARC Prize Foundation measured for the base model without a time limit (42.36); most of the gain came from the inference procedure. For the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next mixture-of-experts model (125B parameters, 6B active), GPU memory limited concurrency. Pruning from 512 to 384 experts per layer by router-weighted activation saliency grew the key-value cache from 0.55M to 1.39M tokens; a 296-expert list adapted with ARC routing statistics, keeping experts for program tokens, plus an FP8 indexer cache, reached 1.96M. With a tool that checks programs, the model scored 56.67, our best result.
papers.summary: The authors study which training and calibration data help three open models solve `ARC-AGI-2` offline on four L4 GPUs within 12 hours, reporting 189 runs on the 120 hidden semi-private tasks. For the `NVARC` `Qwen3-4B` grid model, continued fine-tuning on 1,920 real task records raised the score from 28.96 to 33.06, while no checkpoint trained on synthetic tasks, even all 95,993 generated from 12,000 executable rules, did better. For the `Qwen3.8-27B` reasoning model, fine-tuning on its own correct reasoning traces combined with an inference procedure (an enforced thinking cap, Python programs checked against the demonstrations, and a long first attempt) raised the score from 26.81 to 44.03, with most of the gain coming from the inference procedure. For the `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` mixture-of-experts model, pruning experts using ARC-specific routing statistics and adding an FP8 indexer cache expanded the key-value cache from 0.55M to 1.96M tokens, and with a program-checking tool it reached the **best score of 56.67**.

papers.title: Enabling AWS Cloud FPGA Development Using High-Level Vitis HLS
papers.abstract: We present a toolchain for development of ML models on AWS EC2 F2 cloud FPGA infrastructure from high-level language, implementing a complete Vitis HLS to HDK bridge to AFI workflow that has been absent from the academic literature despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability. We introduce a four-level methodology (FP32 PyTorch, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, physical FPGA) to aid in localizing errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors. Together these tools allow coding agents to effectively implement FPGA designs from user directions, testing and debugging as needed. We document the deployment workflow, timing closure strategies, and practical HLS engineering decisions that proved crucial. We validate using TinyBERT fine-tuned for address Named Entity Recognition, implementing the embedding layer and the first of four encoder layers on the FPGA hardware. Our implementation streams weights from host DRAM, yielding poor performance compared to CPU/GPU implementations; we discuss forward paths.
papers.summary: Despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability, the academic literature has lacked a complete workflow from high-level synthesis to deployed designs on AWS cloud FPGAs. The authors build a toolchain bridging `Vitis HLS` to the AWS hardware development kit and Amazon FPGA Images on EC2 F2 instances, along with a four-level verification method (FP32 `PyTorch`, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, and physical FPGA) for localizing errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors. They report that **these tools let coding agents implement, test, and debug FPGA designs from user directions**, and document timing-closure strategies and practical engineering decisions. As validation, they run the embedding layer and the first encoder layer of a `TinyBERT` address named-entity-recognition model on the FPGA, though streaming weights from host memory makes it slower than CPU or GPU.

papers.title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.
papers.summary: Looped Transformers gain effective depth by re-running shared layers, but their memory grows with the loop count, compute can only change in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. `LooM` (`Loop-invariant Memory`) loops only the decoder layers after the first in a causal encoder-decoder, and these layers read a global memory written once per token and publish a token's key-value (KV) entry only on their first visit, so **the cache does not grow with the loop count**. The layers loop independently, giving any budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and a single model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, `LooM` beats a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy, and long-context perplexity at the same cache size.

papers.title: Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token
papers.abstract: Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model's rollout activations. We train context--answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated.
papers.summary: Under stochastic decoding, one prompt can lead a language model to many different answers, and characterizing that spread normally requires many expensive rollouts. The authors train context-answer metamodels that map the activations produced while reading the context to point or distribution forecasts of the mean-pooled activations of the eventual answers. The metamodels **forecast answer activations with high fidelity** and capture rollout variability; they improve as training grows to 500,000 prompts and generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets. Their forecasts also retain signal that predicts behavior, and context activations from `Qwen2.5` can predict answer activations from `Qwen3.5` and `Gemma 4`.

papers.title: Before You Continue: Evaluating Time-Sensitive Safety Awareness in Conversational Assistants
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly help users with everyday activities that involve time-dependent constraints. However, users may not mention these constraints in later requests, requiring assistants to recognize and adjust their advice accordingly. To evaluate such capability, we introduce TASC (Temporal Action Safety in Conversation), a benchmark that evaluates whether LLMs apply time-dependent constraints when responding to conversational requests. TASC consists of 3,418 inputs derived from 128 templates, along with a separate set of 33 scenarios designed to compare models' ability to calculate elapsed time with their ability to apply that information. Across 13 models, assistants account for time-dependent constraints in only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action violates a rule, while rarely warning users unnecessarily. More importantly, models fail to apply these constraints in 62.1% of cases despite correctly calculating the elapsed time. Explicitly providing the timing resolves only about half of these failures, revealing a gap between temporal reasoning and its application in conversational advice.
papers.summary: Users often mention a time-dependent constraint early in a conversation, such as when they took a medication, and do not repeat it in later requests. `TASC` (`Temporal Action Safety in Conversation`) tests whether assistants apply such constraints, with 3,418 inputs built from 128 templates plus 33 scenarios that separate calculating elapsed time from acting on it. Across 13 models, assistants account for the constraint in **only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action breaks a rule**, while rarely issuing unnecessary warnings. In 62.1% of cases models fail to apply the constraint even though they calculate the elapsed time correctly, and stating the timing explicitly fixes only about half of those failures.

papers.title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.
papers.summary: `ServerBench` asks LLM coding agents to design complete, specialized LLM serving systems, with the agent coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. Agents optimize a single objective, "dollars per dollar" (latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost), measured with stateful replay that preserves session dependencies, and an independent check verifies each submitted system.
